names.name: Eastern North Carolina barbecue
names.said: In the east, 'barbecue' is the meat itself: chopped pork from a whole hog. Nobody says 'pulled pork'.

text.what: The whole pig, split and cooked over coals or on a gas or electric cooker, then chopped — skin, ham, shoulder, loin and belly together, 'every part of the hog except the squeal' — and dressed after cooking with a thin sauce of vinegar, salt, black pepper and crushed red pepper. No tomato. It is served with mayonnaise slaw, cornbread or hushpuppies, and often boiled potatoes, on a tray or a sandwich with the slaw on the meat. The style belongs to the Coastal Plain east of Raleigh; Ayden, Goldsboro, Wilson, Kinston, Rocky Mount and Greenville are its towns.
text.story:
The whole hog is the older way, across the whole South. *Tradition holds —* it grew out of plantation and farm life, where a pig was killed, cooked over a trench of hardwood coals through the night and eaten by the whole community at church homecomings, political rallies and hog killings. The cooks at those pits were, for most of two centuries, Black men, enslaved and then paid; Adrian Miller's *Black Smoke* traces that labor and its erasure from the menus and legends that followed. The vinegar-and-pepper dressing is the sauce of the English colonial kitchen — vinegar was the preservative and the seasoning both — and the absence of tomato is what the east points to when it explains itself against the Piedmont.

The named lineages start in the twentieth century. Bob Melton opened a pit at Rocky Mount in 1924 and was called the 'king of Southern barbecue' by Life magazine. Adam Scott, a Black cook and preacher in Goldsboro, began selling barbecue from his back yard in 1917 and bottled a sauce that still carries his name. The Jones family of Ayden claims a cooking line back to Skilton Dennis, who *tradition holds* sold barbecue from a wagon in 1830; Pete Jones opened the Skylight Inn in 1947, and after a 1979 National Geographic article called his restaurant 'the barbecue capital of the world' he put a copy of the U.S. Capitol dome on the roof.

The east's argument with the west is a set-piece. Two newspaper columnists ran a mock war over it: Jerry Bledsoe, self-styled 'world's leading, foremost barbecue authority', for Lexington, and Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer, 'oracle of the holy grub', for the east — Bledsoe wrote that Rogers 'has ruined any chances of this state being distinguished in its barbecue'. The joke reached the legislature: bills in 2006 to make the Lexington Barbecue Festival the state's official barbecue festival were defeated, and the 2007 compromise named it the official food festival of the Piedmont Triad instead, so that no one style could be called the state's. Readers still take sides, and the two styles are the axis on which every North Carolina barbecue conversation turns.
text.how: A hog of 80 to 180 pounds dressed weight is split down the backbone and laid skin-up over the heat, then turned skin-down to crisp at the end; on a wood pit the coals are shoveled in from a burn barrel every half hour through a night. At many eastern pits the cooker is gas or electric, which the state's health rules made easier than a wood pit. The meat is chopped on a block with cleavers, the crisp skin chopped in for texture, and seasoned on the block with the vinegar sauce and salt. A plate is barbecue, slaw and cornbread; a sandwich is barbecue and slaw on a soft bun; a tray is the same without bread.
text.today: The whole-hog pits of the east are the ones the national press writes about: Skylight Inn and Sam Jones BBQ in Pitt County, B's in Greenville, Grady's in Dudley, Wilber's in Goldsboro (reopened 2021 after a 2019 closure), Parker's in Wilson. Many more eastern places cook shoulders or hams rather than the whole animal and are still called eastern by their sauce.

x_composition.method: Volumes from the Wikibooks Cookbook's Eastern North Carolina Barbecue Sauce, converted to weights at 1 cup = 236.6 mL and standard USDA weights: cider vinegar 239 g a cup, molasses 337 g a cup, honey 339 g a cup, table salt 6 g a teaspoon, ground black pepper 2.3 g a teaspoon, ground red pepper 1.8 g a teaspoon. Twelve cups of vinegar is 2,868 g; one cup of molasses plus two of honey is 1,015 g; salt and the two peppers together are 85 g; the batch is 3,968 g. Percentages are of that total by weight. No water is added, so water_pct is zero even though vinegar is mostly water. No tomato and no mustard appear in the recipe.

names.name: Lexington-style barbecue
names.said: In the Piedmont the sauce is 'dip' and the slaw is 'red slaw' or 'barbecue slaw'. Barbecue is ordered chopped, coarse-chopped or sliced, and 'brown' means the crusty outside of the shoulder.

text.what: Pork shoulders cooked slowly over hardwood coals, usually hickory, then chopped, coarse-chopped or sliced and dressed with a thin red sauce the Piedmont calls dip: vinegar, ketchup or tomato, water, salt, pepper and red pepper, sweeter or hotter by the house. It comes with red slaw — cabbage dressed with the same dip instead of mayonnaise — and hushpuppies, on a tray or a bun. The style belongs to the Piedmont west of Raleigh. Lexington, a Davidson County town of about 20,000 that calls itself the Barbecue Capital of the World and counted more than twenty barbecue restaurants in 2003, is its center; Greensboro, Salisbury, Shelby and High Point are its other towns.
text.story:
Sid Weaver sold barbecue from a tent by the old Davidson County courthouse in 1919, and Jess Swicegood ran a stand a few yards from his within the decade. Warner Stamey, born in 1911, boarded with his sister in Lexington for high school and learned the pits from both men; he sold barbecue in Shelby after graduating, came back in 1938 to buy Swicegood's place and rename it, and in 1953 opened Stamey's on High Point Road in Greensboro. Stamey's own history credits him with putting hushpuppies beside barbecue. Alton Beck, who had worked for Weaver, built the town's first bricks-and-mortar barbecue restaurant on West Center Street in 1938. Wayne Monk, who had worked for Holland Tussey and took Stamey as his model, opened Lexington Barbecue beside U.S. 29/70 in 1962; in 1983 a politically connected local attorney asked whether he would cook for President Reagan, and he served the heads of government at that year's economic summit in Williamsburg, Virginia — Thatcher and Mitterrand among them. In 2003 the James Beard Foundation named the restaurant an America's Classic.

The east–west argument is a newspaper invention that outlived the columns. Jerry Bledsoe of the Greensboro Daily News, self-styled 'world's leading, foremost barbecue authority', and Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer, 'oracle of the holy grub', traded columns for decades over whether ketchup belongs in the sauce. Bledsoe said Rogers 'has ruined any chances of this state being distinguished in its barbecue'; Rogers wrote that people who would put ketchup in sauce fed to innocent children 'are capable of most anything'. The joke reached the General Assembly in the 2005–06 session, when House Bill 21 and Senate Bill 47 would have made the Lexington Barbecue Festival the official barbecue festival of North Carolina; with nearly half the state eating eastern, neither passed. House Bill 433 passed in 2007 with a narrower title — 'Official Food Festival of the Piedmont Triad Region of the State of North Carolina' — which named no style official for the state.
text.how: Shoulders roast for about ten hours over coals from a wood fire beside the pits — at Lexington Barbecue mostly oak, with hickory when it can be had — meat side down over the embers until it browns, then turned. Some Piedmont places cook on gas or electric cookers. The cooked shoulder is chopped, coarse-chopped or sliced to order, and the crusty outside can be asked for as 'brown'. The dip goes on at the block and stands on the table. A tray is barbecue and red slaw; a plate adds hushpuppies; a sandwich is chopped pork and red slaw on a bun.
text.today: Lexington counted more than twenty barbecue restaurants for about 20,000 people in 2003; Lexington Barbecue, Bar-B-Q Center and Cook's are in and around town, Stamey's in Greensboro, Red Bridges Barbecue Lodge in Shelby. The Lexington Barbecue Festival closes Main Street each October — October 24 in 2026 — and has been the Official Food Festival of the Piedmont Triad since 2007.

confusable_with.tell: Red slaw and a reddish dip on chopped or sliced shoulder mean Lexington; pale mayonnaise slaw and a clear vinegar sauce on meat with crisp skin chopped through it mean the east. If the counter understands 'brown', you are in the Piedmont.

South Carolina's light tomato sauce is the same vinegar-and-ketchup idea, and the SC Barbeque Association maps it with the Piedmont. The tell is on the plate: red slaw and hushpuppies are Lexington; hash over rice is South Carolina.

names.name: Heavy tomato barbecue
names.said: Menus call it 'sweet', 'mild' or 'house'; 'heavy tomato' is the map's term.

text.what: Pork shoulders and butts, ribs and chicken cooked over hickory or on cookers and served with a thick, sweet, red sauce of tomato, brown sugar or molasses, vinegar and spices — the sauce the state tourism office says you are most likely to find on a grocery shelf, and the one most of the country means by barbecue sauce. The four-sauce map gives it the western and northwestern corner of South Carolina: Greenville, Spartanburg, Anderson, Greenwood, the Savannah River side. Hash here is often beef, or pork and beef with onions, over rice.
text.story:
The heavy tomato sauce is the newcomer. The South Carolina Barbeque Association's history says it 'evolved only recently, that is, in the last sixty or so years', pushed by commercial brands, and the wider record agrees: Heinz bottled the first major-label barbecue sauce in 1940, General Foods' Open Pit followed, Kraft came in around 1960 and advertised its way to first place, and after the war the sugar and the ingredient count of sauces climbed. The typical commercial sauce is Kansas City's, 'thick, reddish-brown, tomato-based, and made with sugar, vinegar, and spices', and Wikipedia's South Carolina article says the heavy tomato sauce of the west is 'more similar to sauces popular in other states'. *Inference —* a sauce that arrived by bottle would settle where the older sauces were thinnest on the ground, at the state's western edge, farthest from the whole-hog coast and the German Midlands.

Henry's Smokehouse in Greenville cooks pork butts twelve hours and ribs more than eight over hickory logs in open pits and puts two sauces out, a tomato-based mild and a mustard-based spicy. Greenwood's Festival of Discovery, each July, hosts a Kansas City Barbeque Society-sanctioned Carolina barbecue and Black Kettle hash competition and the South Carolina state championship cook-off, with a Blues Cruise through the uptown venues.
text.how: Simmer tomato — ketchup, paste or sauce — with brown sugar or molasses, vinegar, salt, black pepper and spices until it thickens. It is a finishing and table sauce: brushed on ribs and chicken near the end of cooking or served alongside, spooned over chopped pork on the plate, where it sits on the meat rather than soaking in. Hash in the Upstate is beef, or pork and beef, cooked with onions and served over rice.
text.today: Henry's Smokehouse runs rooms in Greenville and Simpsonville and a food truck; the Festival of Discovery brings its cook teams to Greenwood each July (July 8–10 in 2027). National bottles of the same kind share the western shelves with the state's mustard and vinegar sauces.

names.said: Nobody orders 'light tomato'; it is the map's word. At the counter it is the house sauce, mild or hot.

text.what: Pork — whole hog in the Pee Dee, shoulders and hams in the upper Midlands — cooked over coals or on cookers and served with a thin sauce that is the Carolinas' vinegar-and-pepper with ketchup stirred in. On South Carolina's four-sauce map, as the state tourism office and the South Carolina Barbeque Association publish it, it holds the Pee Dee and the upper middle of the state along the North Carolina line. Hash comes with it, of beef as often as pork toward the Upstate. It is the South Carolina twin of Lexington's dip, and the Barbeque Association's history maps the North Carolina Piedmont and the South Carolina Pee Dee as one light-tomato country.
text.story:
The light-tomato sauce is the youngest of the vinegar family. The South Carolina Barbeque Association dates it to about 1900, 'vinegar and pepper with tomato ketchup added', and Wikipedia's account has it born of cheap mass-produced ketchup in the early twentieth century and of North Carolina's influence on the Upstate. The general history of barbecue sauce runs the same way: sugar, ketchup and Worcestershire came into sauces in the 1920s, and everything after the war got sweeter. *Inference —* the Lexington dip and the light-tomato sauce are the same invention made twice, or once and carried; the SCBA's own history treats the North Carolina Piedmont and the South Carolina Pee Dee as one light-tomato country, and the Piedmont's dip is the sauce Wikipedia describes as 'similar to the East Carolina sauce with the addition of tomato paste, tomato sauce, or ketchup'.

Where exactly it lives is argued. Kovacik and Winberry's 1987 geography set the four regions; the tourism office gives light tomato the Pee Dee and the 'upper middle part' of the state; Wikipedia gives it the Upstate; Robert Moss says the state has only two sauces, sweet mustard and spicy vinegar, and the tomato sauces are variations. Union County, in the upper middle, once had nearly fifty hash houses; Midway BBQ at Buffalo, opened around 1941 by Jack O'Dell, is the one left, cooking shoulders and hams over hickory, and its hash is beef, butter, onion, salt and pepper stewed down in a pot — 'Without hash,' its manager Jay Allen told the Southern Foodways Alliance in 2012, 'we're done. We're closed.'
text.how: Vinegar, salt, black and red pepper, and ketchup enough to color it, thinned with water; cayenne or a bottled hot sauce for heat; a little sugar in some houses. It is warmed, not cooked down. It goes on chopped or pulled pork at the block and stands on the table; on a Pee Dee buffet it sits beside the vinegar-and-pepper bottle, and in the upper Midlands it comes with beef hash and rice.
text.today: Midway BBQ at Buffalo, Union County, sells chopped pork in its house 'Original Sauce', pulled pork with none, and its beef hash; the tourism office still draws the light-tomato band across the Pee Dee and the upper Midlands, and mustard has spread into these counties from the middle of the state.

text.what: Pork — whole hogs at some pits, hams or shoulders at others — cooked over hardwood coals or on cookers, chopped or pulled, and dressed with a yellow sauce of prepared mustard, vinegar, sugar and spices. Hash, a stew of pork and onions that in the Midlands often takes mustard too, comes over white rice beside it, and the meal is often a buffet. The style belongs to the Midlands, the counties around Columbia: a belt the geographers Charles Kovacik and John Winberry drew in 1987 from Newberry and Lexington counties down through Orangeburg toward Charleston, the German-settled country whose fork of the Saluda and Broad rivers is called the Dutch Fork.
text.story:
German Protestants took up land between the Saluda and Broad rivers from the 1730s, in what became Lexington, Newberry and Richland counties — the Dutch Fork, 'Dutch' from deutsch — and at Orangeburg, where a colony of Swiss, German and Dutch families settled in 1735. The state's accounts lay the mustard sauce at their door: the tourism office says they 'brought their love of mustard', and the South Carolina Barbeque Association's history names the families who sell it — Bessinger, Shealy, Hite, Sweatman, Dukes. *Tradition holds —* the sauce was on farm tables long before any bottle; the earliest name attached to it is Joe Bessinger, who served it with pit-cooked pork at Holly Hill from 1939, and some accounts credit him with inventing it.

His sons carried it out of Orangeburg County. Maurice opened Maurice's Piggie Park at West Columbia in 1953 with his brother Joe Jr.; Thomas opened Bessinger's in Charleston, and Melvin opened Melvin's in Mount Pleasant in 1982; the Dukes family opened buffet restaurants from the 1950s — the two families, Charleston Magazine says, brought Midlands barbecue to the Lowcountry after the war. Maurice bottled the sauce as Carolina Gold, sold it in supermarkets nationwide in the 1990s, and by 1999 ran the largest barbecue business in the country.

The name also carries a civil-rights case. In 1964 Anne Newman, the wife of a Black minister, was refused entry to a Piggie Park drive-in and sued under the Civil Rights Act; Bessinger argued that his religion forbade serving Black customers. The Fourth Circuit ordered the restaurants opened to all, and in 1968 the Supreme Court, in Newman v. Piggie Park Enterprises, held that a plaintiff who wins such an injunction ordinarily recovers attorney's fees. On July 1, 2000, the day the Confederate flag came down from the State House, he raised it over his restaurants and handed out tracts arguing that slavery was not inherently evil; grocery chains dropped Carolina Gold, his $50 million suit against them failed at the state Supreme Court in 2007, and his children took down the last flag in 2013. He died in 2014.
text.how: At Sweatman's, whole hogs cook twelve to fourteen hours over oak and hickory coals and are basted with the mustard sauce as they go; at Maurice's, hams cook sixteen hours over hickory and the chopped meat is coated with the sauce for the plate; at Hite's, whole hogs and hams go over oak and hickory coals rendered from a wood fire. The sauce is prepared yellow mustard, vinegar, sugar or brown sugar and pepper — Bessinger's supermarket bottle listed soy sauce too. It goes on at the block, stands on the buffet line, and in the Midlands goes into the hash pot; some Orangeburg places blend it with ketchup into a 'rust' sauce.
text.today: Mustard sauce has spread from the Midlands to menus across the state this century. Maurice's is open in West Columbia — its offices, pits and side factory burned on October 26, 2024; the restaurant and its sign survived — with Bessinger's in Charleston, Sweatman's at Holly Hill and Hite's in West Columbia on Fridays and Saturdays, Shealy's at Batesburg-Leesville, and Dukes restaurants around Orangeburg.

names.name: Pee Dee whole-hog barbecue
names.said: In the Pee Dee a place 'cooks hogs'. The sauce is 'the sauce' or 'pepper vinegar'; Brown's in Kingstree calls its own 'barbecue gravy'.

text.what: Whole hogs cooked overnight over hardwood coals, pulled or chopped, and dressed with a thin sauce of vinegar, salt, black pepper and red pepper — the same sauce as eastern North Carolina's across the state line. The skin is taken off and fried into skins sold by the bag. Hash over rice, chicken bog, slaw and white bread fill the plate, often from a buffet. The style belongs to the Pee Dee, the northeast of South Carolina along the Pee Dee and Black rivers — Hemingway, Kingstree, Manning, Florence — and runs down the coast, where the state tourism office marks vinegar-and-pepper as the sauce of the shore.
text.story:
The vinegar-and-pepper sauce is the oldest in the Carolinas; the state tourism office calls it 'the oldest sauce, perhaps the oldest in the nation'. The South Carolina Barbeque Association ties it to the Scots who settled Williamsburg County, and Wikipedia's history of barbecue sauce credits enslaved African cooks with popularising the vinegar, black pepper and chili-flake sauce of the eastern Carolinas. *Tradition holds —* the Pee Dee's whole hog is the same cooking as the Coastal Plain's north of the line, one tradition with a border through it.

The pits that carry it are family stores. Theron Burrows opened an Esso station and country store on the new Highway 521 between Manning and Georgetown in 1937; George and Adalyn Cooper took it over in 1974, and Russell Cooper cooks whole hogs there beside the hardware and the hams with a sauce he calls 'downright vinegar and salt and pepper'. Roosevelt and Ella Scott opened a gas station and variety store in an oak grove at Hemingway in 1972 and cooked a hog or two on weekends; their son Rodney cooked his first at eleven, and by 2012 the store cooked eight to ten a night. Thomas Brown, a farmer, began selling plates from a window on his farm outside Kingstree in 1981 and built a dining room a decade later. Kingstree holds a Pig Pickin' Festival each fall, judged on vinegar-based barbecue, and Hemingway a Bar-B-Q Shag Festival each spring.

Rodney Scott left the family business after a quarrel with his father in 2016 and opened Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ in Charleston with Nick Pihakis in February 2017; in 2018 the James Beard Foundation named him Best Chef: Southeast, the second pitmaster to win a chef award, and after his Chef's Table episode in 2020 the restaurant set sales records three days running. Roosevelt Scott died in 2010 and Ella in 2023; the Hemingway store closed for five months and reopened in May 2024 under Ella's brother Sam Wilson and grandson Dominic Scott. In May 2026 the Charleston company's locations were reported closed temporarily under lawsuits and liens.
text.how: At Scott's the wood — freshly cut hickory, pecan and oak — burns down in a barrel of sheet metal with old truck axles for a grate; the embers are scooped from the bottom and hauled into the pit house under cinder-block-and-brick pits to hold the heat for twelve hours or more while the hog cooks overnight. Cooper's cooks chickens on one half of the pit and hogs on the other. The meat is pulled at Scott's, chopped at Brown's, 'picked and mixed' at McCabe's after up to twelve hours; at Brown's the vinegar-and-hot-pepper 'gravy' is mopped on as the hog smokes. It is served as a sandwich on white bread or a plate with beans and slaw, with skins sold on the side.
text.today: Scott's Bar-B-Que at Hemingway is open Wednesday to Saturday; Cooper's Country Store sells gasoline, groceries, hardware and whole-hog barbecue on Highway 521; Brown's in Kingstree and McCabe's in Manning cook whole hogs for their buffets. Rodney Scott's Charleston restaurants were reported closed temporarily in May 2026.

text.what: A Raleigh line of bottled sauces, of which the one that built the brand is Sweet Southern: cane sugar first, tomato puree second, water third, apple cider vinegar fourth, at six grams of sugar to the tablespoon. The house also bottles an Eastern Vinegar sauce, whose label puts apple cider vinegar and distilled vinegar first and tomato paste sixth, and a mustard whose seven ingredients name no tomato at all. One maker, three readings of the same state's shelf.
text.story:
The company dates the sauce to Raleigh in 1992 and calls the recipe a family one; the Sweet Southern page describes that bottle as the flavor the brand launched with. The mustard's page quotes Mr. Ford, of Ford's Foods, on making a sweet version of the house's sweet-and-spicy mustard without the heat.

The interesting part is on the backs of the bottles. Sweet Southern reads sugar, tomato, water, vinegar — the order of a Kansas City sauce, made in the eastern half of North Carolina, where the sauce a pit puts on a chopped hog has neither sugar nor tomato in it. The Eastern Vinegar bottle, sold alongside it, inverts that: two vinegars, then water, then cane sugar, with tomato paste down at six. The maker's own page for that bottle describes the tomato and molasses in it as a light hint behind the vinegar. *Inference —* a house that sells both is not choosing between the styles; it is selling the distance between them as two products.

names.name: Carolina Treet
names.said: Treet, in Wilmington; spelled with two e's.

text.what: A Wilmington sauce that fits none of the four Carolina bases. Its label reads water, vinegar, wheat flour, salt, soybean oil, paprika, garlic, onion, xanthan gum, spices — no tomato, no mustard, no sugar. The wheat flour does what tomato paste does elsewhere: it thickens. What it tastes of is vinegar, smoke and salt, and it carries 536 milligrams of sodium in a tablespoon, the highest figure among the sixty-eight bottles this project measured. The bottle calls itself a cooking barbecue sauce, meaning it goes on during the cook rather than at the table.
text.story:
The label is the document. Ten ingredients, and the four that name a Carolina style — tomato, mustard, sugar, pepper — supply only the pepper, as paprika. A sauce built on vinegar and flour is a gravy's method applied to a barbecue sauce, and it is the only bottle in the harvest that works that way.

The brand is made by Legacy Family Foods, and carolinatreet.com now forwards to that company's site, which sells the Original alongside other lines. *Tradition holds —* the sauce is a Wilmington and Cape Fear fixture, poured over chicken as often as pork; the project has not found a dated founding on the record and does not assert one.
text.how: Brushed on chicken, pork and ribs during cooking, which is what the words on the label direct. It is thin and it browns, and because there is no sugar in it there is nothing to burn.
text.today: Sold in eastern North Carolina groceries and from Legacy Family Foods.

names.name: George's Barbecue Sauce
names.said: George's, on shelves across eastern North Carolina; the label says George's Barbecue Sauce.

text.what: A bottled sauce from Nashville, North Carolina, a Nash County town on the edge of the Coastal Plain, sold in three strengths: Original, Hot and Special. The Original's label reads vinegar, water, tomato concentrate, tomato paste, sugar, apples, salt, high fructose corn syrup, corn syrup, red pepper and spices — vinegar leading, tomato third and fourth, and a sweetening that runs to three separate entries. It carries 3.5 grams of sugar in a tablespoon and 180 milligrams of sodium. The Special reverses the first four: tomato concentrate and tomato paste come before the water and the vinegar, and jalapenos join the list.
text.story:
The company dates itself to 1975 and names George Stallings as its founder, who worked the recipe out in his outdoor garage; after it caught on at home, he and his brother cooked, bottled and sold it by hand. The maker's own page says the sauces are still made by hand in small batches to that recipe, and that 4,500 bottles a day are poured, packed and shipped by hand from Womble Road in Nashville.

*Inference —* the label is worth reading against the map. Nashville sits in the eastern half of the state, where the sauce that goes on a chopped hog is vinegar and pepper with no tomato in it. George's pours vinegar first, then puts tomato third — the order of the Piedmont dip, not the Coastal Plain's — and sells it as an eastern-style sauce. A bottle that has to keep on a shelf and please a wide market is not the same object as a sauce mixed in a bucket behind a pit, and the reading here describes the bottle.
text.how: Poured over chopped or pulled pork, brushed on chicken and ribs, used as a mop while a shoulder cooks. It is thin enough to soak rather than coat. Three strengths sit beside each other on the same shelf: Original, Hot, and Special, which is the tomato-first one with jalapenos.
text.today: Made and shipped from Nashville, North Carolina. The three bottles are sold from the company's site and through eastern North Carolina grocers.

names.said: Golding Farms on the retail label; Golding Blends on the company's own site.

text.what: A Winston-Salem sauce manufacturer, the second of that city's two, and one whose output mostly reaches a table under someone else's name. It sells a retail line under the Golding Farms label — the Honey Mustard dipping sauce reads distilled vinegar, canola oil, sugar, honey, water, mustard seed, at 3.5 grams of sugar to the tablespoon — and blends and packs sauces for brands, food service and industrial customers.
text.story:
The company says it has been bringing flavor forward since 1972 and describes fifty years of blending for brand, food service and industrial buyers from Winston-Salem, with an in-house development team of a chef, scientists and technicians.

*Inference —* Winston-Salem holds both ends of the bottled-sauce trade. T.W. Garner makes Texas Pete under its own name and sells it in every grocery in the state; Golding blends and packs, and the name on the bottle is often a customer's. Between them the city puts more sauce in circulation than any pit town, which is a fact about the sauce shelf rather than about the pits. No Golding Farms barbecue sauce label turned up on 16 September 2026, so the retail reading on this page is of the honey mustard dipping sauce, which the label does not call a barbecue sauce.

text.what: A thick red sauce built on tomato — ketchup, paste or sauce — sweetened with brown sugar or molasses, soured with vinegar and seasoned with spices, cooked down until it clings. It is the sauce of the western and northwestern corner of South Carolina on the state's four-sauce map: the tourism office's 'tomato-and-sugar sauce', the one it says you are most likely to find on a grocery shelf. It goes on after cooking — on the plate, on the bun, on ribs and chicken — and sits on the meat rather than soaking in.
text.story: This is the national sauce at the state's edge. Heinz put out the first major bottled barbecue sauce in 1940, General Foods' Open Pit followed, Kraft came in around 1960 and advertised its way to first place, and after the war the sugar and the ingredient count of sauces climbed; the typical commercial sauce is the Kansas City kind, 'thick, reddish-brown, tomato-based, and made with sugar, vinegar, and spices', which Wikipedia's sauce history places downstream of the Piedmont's thin dip and Memphis's sauce. The South Carolina Barbeque Association says the heavy tomato sauce 'evolved only recently, that is, in the last sixty or so years', pushed by commercial brands, and Wikipedia's South Carolina article calls it 'more similar to sauces popular in other states'. *Inference —* a sauce that arrived by bottle would settle where the older sauces were thinnest on the ground, at the state's western edge, farthest from the whole-hog coast and the German Midlands. Henry's Smokehouse in Greenville makes its own tomato-based mild sauce by hand and sets a mustard-based spicy one beside it.
text.how: Simmer tomato with brown sugar or molasses, vinegar, salt, black pepper and spices until it thickens. It is a finishing and table sauce: brushed on ribs and chicken near the end of cooking or served alongside, spooned over chopped pork on the plate. It is the one Carolina sauce that coats rather than soaks.
text.today: Henry's Smokehouse in Greenville serves its tomato-based mild sauce beside a mustard one; national bottles fill the western shelves. Greenwood's July Festival of Discovery judges Carolina barbecue and hash under Kansas City Barbeque Society rules.

names.name: Lexington dip
names.said: 'Dip' is the Piedmont's word; a Lexington counter will not correct you for 'sauce', but the menu says dip.

etymology.root: English dip (n.), from the verb dip, Old English dyppan, Proto-Germanic *daupejanan, a causative of *deup- 'deep'. The noun 'act of dipping' is recorded from the 1590s and the sense 'a liquid into which something is dipped' by 1825.
etymology.first_attested: the noun sense 'liquid into which something is dipped' by 1825 (etymonline, dip n.1); no dated first use of 'dip' for the Lexington sauce found by this project
etymology.note: *Tradition holds —* the name is from the use: the chopped meat is dipped in it, and it is thin enough to dip into rather than spread. Etymonline notes that the sense 'thick, savory sauce for dunking pieces of raw vegetables' (by 1962) is a modern re-coinage, so the barbecue dip keeps the older, thinner sense.

text.what: The Piedmont's sauce: the east's vinegar, salt, pepper and red pepper with ketchup or tomato and water added, sometimes sugar, so that it comes out thin and reddish — tangy, a little sweet or hot by the house, and every restaurant's recipe its own. It is the sauce of pork-shoulder barbecue in Lexington, Greensboro, Salisbury, Shelby and the rest of the Piedmont. It is basted on the shoulders as they cook, goes on the chopped meat at the block, stands on the table, and, in place of mayonnaise, dresses the red slaw.
text.story:
The dip came out of the Lexington tents. Sid Weaver sold barbecue by the old courthouse from 1919 and Jess Swicegood beside him; Warner Stamey learned from both and carried the sauce to Shelby and Greensboro, and the men he taught — Wayne Monk at Lexington Barbecue among them — carried it further. *Tradition holds —* the tomato came in with cheap ketchup after the First World War, the same years Wikipedia's sauce history gives for ketchup and sugar entering barbecue sauces generally; the South Carolina Barbeque Association dates the same vinegar-and-ketchup idea to about 1900 in the Pee Dee and the North Carolina Piedmont.

The ketchup is what the columnists fought over. Jerry Bledsoe of the Greensboro Daily News took the Piedmont's side — 'America loves ketchup' — and Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer the east's: 'People who would put ketchup in the sauce they feed to innocent children are capable of most anything.' The joke ran for decades and reached the General Assembly over the Lexington Barbecue Festival's title in 2005–07. In Lexington the sauce is also the slaw dressing: red slaw is cabbage, vinegar, ketchup and black pepper, no mayonnaise, and the Southern Foodways Alliance's note on Bar-B-Q Center says it plainly — in Lexington, barbecue eaters don't squirt sauce, they dip.
text.how: Vinegar, ketchup, water, salt, pepper and other spices, in the town's own description; red pepper flakes and sugar in many kitchens; simmered and kept warm. On the pit it is a baste for the shoulders through a ten-hour cook. At the block it is spooned into the chopped meat; at the table it comes in a bottle. For red slaw, chopped cabbage is dressed with it — the same vinegar, ketchup and pepper — instead of mayonnaise, so the slaw matches the meat.
text.today: Every Lexington pit keeps its own recipe; the town's Wikipedia article calls each one 'a closely guarded secret'. Red slaw dressed with it goes on hot dogs across the Piedmont as well as on trays.

recipes.title: Eastern North Carolina Barbecue Sauce
recipes.text:
1. Start with apple cider vinegar in saucepan over medium heat.
2. Add salt, ground black pepper, crushed red pepper, molasses, and honey.
3. Let mixture heat up, but not quite boil.
4. Mix well.
5. Return sauce to the jug that the vinegar came in to cool.
recipes.note: The base the dip is built on: to make a Piedmont dip from it, a house adds ketchup or tomato and water and cuts the pepper back.

recipes.title: The dip, as described
recipes.note: Ingredients only: the parts are a fact and may be repeated; the proportions are each pit's own and are not published. The same mixture dresses the red slaw.

recipes.title: Barbecue Sauce (Sweet)
ingredients: Garlic powder or minced garlic to taste (optional)
recipes.text:
1. Combine all ingredients together and bring to a boil. Reduce heat and simmer 10 to 15 minutes, until it thickens slightly.
2. Arrange chicken pieces or pork chops in a greased baking dish.
3. Pour half of sauce over and bake at 350°F (175°C) for 30 to 40 minutes.
4. Pour remaining sauce over before serving.
recipes.note: Thicker and sweeter than a dip — a cup of ketchup to three quarters of a cup of cider vinegar, with brown sugar, mustard and Worcestershire. A dip runs the other way: mostly vinegar, with the ketchup a colouring.

recipes.title: Sauce for Barbecues (receipt 335)
recipes.author: Mrs. A. P. Hill
recipes.text: Melt half a pound of butter; stir into it a large tablespoonful of mustard, half a teaspoonful of red pepper, one of black, salt to taste; add vinegar until the sauce has a strong acid taste. The quantity of vinegar will depend upon the strength of it. As soon as the meat becomes hot, begin to baste, and continue basting frequently until it is done; pour over the meat any sauce that remains.
recipes.note: An ancestor rather than the thing: the vinegar-and-pepper mop that the Piedmont later reddened. No tomato in it.

ingredients: MUSTARD (DISTILLED VINEGAR, WATER, MUSTARD SEED, SALT, TURMERIC, PAPRIKA, SPICE, GARLIC POWDER)
CONTAINS LESS THAN 2%: APPLE JUICE CONCENTRATE
profile.note: No Lexington pit publishes a Nutrition Facts panel for its dip: Lexington Barbecue, the Bar-B-Q Center, Stamey's, Red Bridges, Hursey's, Kepley's, Little Richard's, Cook's and Short Sugar's all sell bottles and none printed a label this search could read on 2026-09-16. What can be measured is the bottle that wears the style's name from outside it. Lillie's Q of Chicago sells No. 40 Western North Carolina Tomato, and it reads tomato first and brown sugar second, at 5 g of sugar per tablespoon — the Kansas City order, under the Piedmont's name. text.what: Vinegar-and-pepper sauce with ketchup added — enough to redden and sweeten it a little, not enough to thicken it — and often cayenne or a bottled hot sauce. The state tourism office's description is the whole recipe: 'a vinegar-and-pepper sauce with ketchup added for a little sweetness'. It is the sauce of South Carolina's Pee Dee and upper Midlands on the state's four-sauce map, and the same idea as the Lexington dip across the line, which the South Carolina Barbeque Association counts as the same sauce. It goes on chopped pork at the block and stands on the table.
text.story: The South Carolina Barbeque Association dates the light tomato sauce to about 1900, 'vinegar and pepper with tomato ketchup added'; Wikipedia ties it to the affordability of mass-produced ketchup in the early twentieth century and to North Carolina's influence. The barbecue-sauce article's timeline agrees: sugar, ketchup and Worcestershire entered sauces in the 1920s. Kovacik and Winberry's 1987 geography of the state drew the four regions the tourism office still publishes, and Robert Moss answers that there are really two sauces, mustard and vinegar, of which this is a variant. *Inference —* the sauce is the vinegar tradition's own sweetening, made in the same kitchens that kept the older sauce, which is why on the map it shares the Pee Dee with vinegar-and-pepper rather than displacing it.
text.how: Cider vinegar, salt, black pepper, crushed red pepper; ketchup by the spoon until it colors; water to thin; cayenne or hot sauce; sugar if the house likes. Warmed, not cooked down. On the block it goes into the chopped meat; on the table it is the second bottle beside vinegar-and-pepper or mustard.
text.today: On the table at Pee Dee and upper-Midlands pits under the house name; Texas Pete's bottled Eastern Carolina BBQ Sauce — apple cider vinegar, tomato paste, red pepper flakes, sugar — is, by this map's terms, a light tomato sauce.

recipes.title: Eastern North Carolina Barbecue Sauce
recipes.text:
1. Start with apple cider vinegar in saucepan over medium heat.
2. Add salt, ground black pepper, crushed red pepper, molasses, and honey.
3. Let mixture heat up, but not quite boil.
4. Mix well.
5. Return sauce to the jug that the vinegar came in to cool.

ingredients: Garlic powder or minced garlic to taste (optional)
recipes.text:
1. Combine all ingredients together and bring to a boil. Reduce heat and simmer 10 to 15 minutes, until it thickens slightly.
2. Arrange chicken pieces or pork chops in a greased baking dish.
3. Pour half of sauce over and bake at 350°F (175°C) for 30 to 40 minutes.

text.what: The mustard sauce of Maurice's Piggie Park at West Columbia, sold in bottles, half gallons and gallons alongside the family's Hickory Red, Vinegar and Hot Pepper sauces. It is the bottle that carried the South Carolina mustard sauce onto national supermarket shelves in the 1990s, then off them again in 2000. No ingredient list or Nutrition Facts panel is published for it, so this page can name the sauce and its history but cannot measure it.
text.story:
Maurice Bessinger and his brother Joe Jr. opened Maurice's Piggie Park at West Columbia in 1953; by 1968 there were four drive-ins, by 2002 nine restaurants, and the mustard sauce went into supermarkets nationwide in the 1990s under the name Carolina Gold. The chain's refusal to serve Black customers produced Newman v. Piggie Park Enterprises, decided by the Supreme Court in 1968. On 1 July 2000, the day the Confederate flag came down from the South Carolina State House, Bessinger raised it over his restaurants and handed out tracts arguing that slavery was not inherently evil; nine grocery chains dropped the sauce, and his suit against them failed at the state Supreme Court in 2007. His children took down the last flag in 2013 and he died in 2014. The family sells the sauce as Southern Gold. The mustard sauce record carries that history in full; this page is about the bottle.

*Inference —* the measurement gap has a shape. Of the sixty-eight bottles read on 16 September 2026, every mustard sauce with a published Nutrition Facts panel was made outside South Carolina — in Maryland, Pennsylvania, Illinois, California, North Carolina. Maurice's, Bessinger's, Dukes, Sweatman's, Shealy's, Hite's, Jackie Hite's, Cannon's, Hudson's and Melvin's all sell the sauce the state is known for, and none of them prints the label a chart can read.

ingredients: ¼ tsp freshly ground black pepper
recipes.text:
1. Heat olive oil in a large slope-sided skillet over medium high heat. Add shallot and sauté until golden.
2. Meanwhile, combine broth and starch. Set aside.

4. Once sauce heats to just below a simmer, add broth mixture. Cook, whisking continuously, until sauce thickens slightly.
5. Whisk in butter 1 tbsp at a time, waiting for the one before it to fully melt before adding another.

text.what: The mustard sauce of Melvin's Bar-B-Que in Charleston, sold in 16-ounce glass bottles, half gallons and gallons, beside the house's Southern Red, Sweet Red and Vinegar sauces. The maker publishes no ingredient list and no Nutrition Facts for any of the four, so what this page can give is the history the family tells and the shape of its line, not a measurement.
text.story:
The maker's account dates the sauce to 1933 and to Melvin Bessinger's father, Joe Bessinger — Big Joe on the bottle's copy — and says the recipe passed down spoken and was never written. Joe Bessinger's mustard sauce at Holly Hill is the same sauce the mustard record carries as the Midlands origin story, and his sons carried it out of the Midlands in four directions: Maurice to West Columbia, Melvin and Thomas to Charleston, Robert to Charleston too.

The present line is four sauces and reads as a map of the whole subject. Golden is the family mustard. Southern Red the house calls a tangy tomato sauce blending vinegar and tomato. Sweet Red the current owner describes as a Kansas City style he worked out in his own kitchen. Vinegar, the newest, the house says its pitmaster made for the owner's wife, who grew up in North Carolina on vinegar barbecue. *Inference —* a Charleston counter selling all four is not unusual now; what is unusual is that it sells them as four named things rather than as one house sauce.

etymology.root: Carolina Gold: Maurice Bessinger's supermarket brand name for his mustard sauce, from the sauce's colour and the state. 'Carolina Gold' is also the name of the Lowcountry's rice variety, popularised in South Carolina in the 1780s and named for the golden colour of its unhulled grain; the sauce and the rice are unrelated, and the rice's name is the older by two centuries.
etymology.first_attested: no dated first use of 'Carolina Gold' for the sauce found by this project; the rice carries the name from the 1780s
etymology.note: The Bessinger family's restaurants now sell the sauce as Southern Gold, and 'Carolina Gold' has become a generic name for any South Carolina mustard sauce, used that way by Wikipedia's articles on the state's barbecue and on the barbecue sandwich.

text.what: Prepared yellow mustard thinned with vinegar and sweetened with sugar or brown sugar, with black and red pepper and whatever else the house keeps to itself — Bessinger's bottled version listed mustard, brown sugar, soy sauce and vinegar. It is yellow to gold, pourable, sweet-sour with a mustard bite. It belongs to the Midlands of South Carolina, the belt of German-settled counties from Newberry and Lexington through Orangeburg toward Charleston, and is the sauce the state is known for elsewhere. It goes on chopped or pulled pork at the block, is basted on whole hogs at some pits, and goes into hash.
text.story:
German settlers took land along the Broad, Saluda and Congaree from the 1730s — Orangeburg's colony of Swiss, German and Dutch families arrived in 1735 — and the mustard sauce is credited to them by the state tourism office, the South Carolina Barbeque Association and Wikipedia alike, on the evidence of the names on the bottles: Bessinger, Shealy, Hite, Sweatman, Dukes. Wikipedia adds a colonial belief that mustard kept off mosquitoes. *Tradition holds —* the sauce was a farm and church-supper sauce long before anyone bottled it; Joe Bessinger served it with pit-cooked pork at Holly Hill from 1939, and some accounts name him its inventor.

Maurice Bessinger made it a product. He and his brother Joe Jr. opened Maurice's Piggie Park at West Columbia in 1953; by 1968 there were four drive-ins and by 2002 nine restaurants, and the sauce went into supermarkets nationwide in the 1990s as Carolina Gold, until by 1999 his was the largest barbecue business in the country. The same restaurants had refused Black customers until Anne Newman's 1964 suit under the Civil Rights Act; Bessinger argued that his religion required segregation, lost in the Fourth Circuit, and lost again at the Supreme Court in 1968, where Newman v. Piggie Park set the rule that a winning civil-rights plaintiff ordinarily recovers attorney's fees. On July 1, 2000, the day the Confederate flag came down from the State House, he raised it over his restaurants and distributed tracts arguing that slavery was not inherently evil; Bi-Lo, Food Lion, Harris Teeter, Kroger, Piggly Wiggly, Publix, Sam's Club, Wal-Mart and Winn-Dixie dropped the sauce, his $50 million suit against them failed at the state Supreme Court in 2007, and his children took down the last flag in 2013. He died in 2014. The family sells the sauce today as Southern Gold.
text.how: Whisk yellow mustard with cider vinegar, brown sugar, salt, black and red pepper — and, in Bessinger's bottle, soy sauce — and simmer briefly; it keeps. At Sweatman's it is basted on whole hogs through a twelve-to-fourteen-hour cook over oak and hickory; at Maurice's the chopped ham is coated with it for the plate; at Hite's the base flavour is a stronger yellow mustard without the sweetness. In the Midlands it is stirred into hash; in Orangeburg it is mixed with ketchup into a 'rust' sauce.
text.today: Restaurants bottle it — Maurice's Southern Gold, Shealy's sold online — and the mustard sauce has become more popular across the state this century, by Wikipedia's account. Henry's Smokehouse in Greenville keeps a mustard-based spicy sauce beside its tomato one.

recipes.title: Sauce for Barbecues (receipt 335)
recipes.author: Mrs. A. P. Hill
recipes.text: Melt half a pound of butter; stir into it a large tablespoonful of mustard, half a teaspoonful of red pepper, one of black, salt to taste; add vinegar until the sauce has a strong acid taste. The quantity of vinegar will depend upon the strength of it. As soon as the meat becomes hot, begin to baste, and continue basting frequently until it is done; pour over the meat any sauce that remains.
recipes.note: The nearest thing to a mustard barbecue sauce in a nineteenth-century Southern cookbook: a large tablespoonful of mustard in half a pound of butter, sharpened with vinegar and both peppers, and mopped on. Sugar, which the Midlands sauce depends on, is not in it.

recipes.title: Savory Mustard Sauce
ingredients: ¼ tsp freshly ground black pepper
recipes.text:
1. Heat olive oil in a large slope-sided skillet over medium high heat. Add shallot and sauté until golden.
2. Meanwhile, combine broth and starch. Set aside.
3. Once shallot has cooked, add mustard, salt, and pepper to pan. Decrease heat to medium low heat.
4. Once sauce heats to just below a simmer, add broth mixture. Cook, whisking continuously, until sauce thickens slightly.
5. Whisk in butter 1 tbsp at a time, waiting for the one before it to fully melt before adding another.
6. Once all butter has been used, remove sauce from heat.
7. Serve with a steak or some pork tenderloin, or use as a grilling baste.
recipes.note: A modern mustard baste built on Dijon, broth and butter rather than the prepared yellow mustard, vinegar and sugar of an Orangeburg bottle; the page names grilling among its uses.

recipes.title: Barbecue Sauce (Sweet)
ingredients: Garlic powder or minced garlic to taste (optional)
recipes.text:
1. Combine all ingredients together and bring to a boil. Reduce heat and simmer 10 to 15 minutes, until it thickens slightly.
2. Arrange chicken pieces or pork chops in a greased baking dish.
3. Pour half of sauce over and bake at 350°F (175°C) for 30 to 40 minutes.
4. Pour remaining sauce over before serving.
recipes.note: Mustard here is two or three tablespoons in a cup of ketchup — the proportion a South Carolina mustard sauce reverses.

ingredients: MUSTARD (DISTILLED VINEGAR, WATER, MUSTARD SEED, SALT, TURMERIC, PAPRIKA, SPICES, GARLIC POWDER)
KETCHUP (TOMATO CONCENTRATE, SUGAR, DISTILLED VINEGAR, SALT, ONION POWDER, SPICE, NATURAL FLAVORS)
WORCESTERSHIRE SAUCE (DISTILLED VINEGAR, MOLASSES, SEA SALT, SUGAR, SPICES [CELERY], TAMARIND)
profile.note: None of the Midlands pits — Maurice's, Bessinger's, Dukes, Sweatman's, Shealy's, Hite's, Jackie Hite's, Cannon's, Hudson's, Melvin's — publishes a panel for its mustard sauce, so the measured mustard bottles in data/harvest/sauces.json are all made outside the state. This one is named for it. Mustard first, brown sugar second, ketchup fourth and tomato paste sixth: tomato is in the bottle, four and six places behind the mustard. The six measured mustard-base bottles run from 3.5 to 6.5 g of sugar per tablespoon, a median of 5.3; the seven heavy-tomato bottles run from 3.0 to 6.0, a median of 5.0. Those two groups sit above every other base in the file. USDA FoodData Central record 2584569.

text.what: A bottled line from the whole-hog house Sam Jones opened at Winterville in 2015, third generation of the Skylight Inn family at Ayden. The Sweet bottle's Nutrition Facts give 10 grams of total sugars and 210 milligrams of sodium in a 2-tablespoon serving, which is 5 grams of sugar and 105 milligrams of sodium to the tablespoon, but the record carries no ingredient list, so its order cannot be read and its base is recorded as other.
text.story:
The Jones family cooks whole hogs over wood at Ayden and has since Pete Jones opened the Skylight Inn in 1947, in a line the family traces to Skilton Dennis in 1830. The sauce a whole-hog pit of that kind puts on chopped pork is vinegar, pepper and salt, mixed by the bucket at the block.

*Inference —* the bottle is a separate object from the bucket. A sweet sauce at five grams of sugar to the tablespoon is not what goes on the meat at the pit; it is what a customer takes home, and what ships. The distance between a pit's own sauce and the pit's bottled sauce is one of the things this project can only measure on one side.
text.today: Sold from the restaurant's online store at Winterville. The Sweet bottle's panel is recorded in Open Food Facts; no ingredient list is published with it.

1. Start with apple cider vinegar in saucepan over medium heat.
2. Add salt, ground black pepper, crushed red pepper, molasses, and honey.

recipes.title: Eastern North Carolina Barbecued Pig
ingredients: Your favorite vinegar-based Eastern NC sauce
recipes.text:
1. Salt hams, ribs/midsection and shoulders liberally and place skin side up on either a gas or charcoal grill or a BBQ pit.
2. Keep lid closed, and aim for a heat of approximately 275–350°F.
3. Allow 1 hour per 10 pounds cooking time (gas or charcoal).
4. 2 hours before being done, place pig with the skin side down. As soon as it is flipped, pour BBQ sauce on meat side.
5. Close lid and allow skin to crisp.
6. The pig will be done to perfection when the ham bone can be twisted freely.
7. Lift lid and allow guests to pick/pull meat, or the chef can remove meat and chop to their liking on a chopping block.
recipes.note: The whole hog the sauce is made for, at a size a home pit can manage.

names.name: Scott's Barbecue Sauce
names.said: The label says Scott's Barbecue Sauce; in Goldsboro it is Scott's.

text.what: A bottled eastern North Carolina sauce — vinegar-based, the recipe kept secret, sold as sugar-free and fat-free — made by the Scott family of Goldsboro since the mid-1940s from a recipe the Rev. Adam Scott, a Black Holiness minister who began selling barbecue there in 1917, said came to him in a dream. His son A. Martel Scott Sr. patented it in 1946. The North Carolina Arts Council's trail page calls it 'believed to be the oldest commercially available barbecue sauce in the country'. It is sold in Harris Teeter and Food Lion and from the family's website, and the label offers it for meats, seafood, poultry and vegetables.
text.story:
Adam Scott was born in Goldsboro in 1890, the grandson of Charles and Mary Scott, who had been enslaved in Johnston County, and the son of Joseph Scott, born in Oberlin, Ohio. He cooked at an Atlantic City hotel in 1911, married Bessie Bright that September, and by 1917 was in the barbecue business at home — cooking whole pigs in his back yard and, as the Arts Council's page puts it, selling chopped 'cue with his vinegar sauce through the back door to white men who knocked. He catered for the Algonquin Club, a whites-only social club. Between 1931 and 1933 the family home on Brazil Street became a restaurant: two hogs a week at first, then four to seven a day. David Cecelski's account has him catering a barbecue for President Franklin Roosevelt in the White House Rose Garden in 1933. He was a minister of the United Holy Church of America and by 1938 pastored three churches.

The sauce came, he said, in a dream, and took three years to work out — sugar-free and fat-free because, his grandson A. Martel Scott Jr. recalled, 'Daddy never believed in putting sweet stuff on meat'. It dressed the restaurant's barbecue for nearly thirty years before A. Martel Scott Sr., who had joined the business in the 1930s, adjusted it and took out a patent in 1946; the Arts Council's page dates the bottling to 1945. The restaurant moved from the house to its own building in 1951. Adam Scott died in 1983 at 93. In June 2001 the restaurant cut back to two lunch days a week and later closed; the sauce, run by A. Martel Scott III, sells about 750,000 bottles a year by the Arts Council's count.
text.how: It is used as the eastern sauce is used: poured over chopped pork at the block or the table, as a mop on a cooking hog, and — the label's own list — on meats, seafood, poultry and vegetables. It has no sugar to burn, so it can go on early. It is a family recipe, not published; what is known is what it leaves out.
text.today: Made and shipped from Goldsboro; on the shelves of Harris Teeter and Food Lion and sold from the family's website. The restaurant on the Arts Council's trail is closed.

recipes.text: Get one dozen pods of pepper when ripe, take out the stems, and cut them in two; put them in a kettle with three pints of vinegar, boil it away to one quart, and strain it through a sieve. names.said: Asked for by name at the table: 'pass the Texas Pete'.

etymology.root: Texas + Pete: 'Texas' for a state known for hot food, chosen over a marketing adviser's 'Mexican Joe' because Sam Garner wanted an American name; 'Pete' was the nickname of his son Harold Garner.
etymology.first_attested: 1929, when the sauce was introduced (Wikipedia)
etymology.note: The sauce has never had anything to do with Texas; it has been made in Winston-Salem since 1929.

text.what: A cayenne-pepper hot sauce made by the T.W. Garner Food Company of Winston-Salem, North Carolina, since 1929 — mild as hot sauces go, 747 on the Scoville scale — in a flip-top bottle with a red cowboy on a white-and-yellow label. It is not a barbecue sauce and is on this list because of where it stands: on the table at eastern North Carolina barbecue houses beside the vinegar, and, at Skylight Inn in Ayden, in the dressing itself, where the chopped hog is seasoned with vinegar, salt, pepper and Texas Pete.
text.story: Sam Garner ran the Dixie Pig, a barbecue stand in Winston-Salem, with his sons Thad, Ralph and Harold. Customers asked for a spicier sauce, and the family made one from cayenne peppers and put it out in 1929. A marketing adviser proposed 'Mexican Joe', to suggest Mexico's spicy cooking; Sam Garner wanted an American name, so Texas — a state known for hot food — was joined to Pete, Harold's nickname. Thad W. Garner founded the T.W. Garner Food Company the same year, and the company still makes the sauce in Winston-Salem, twenty miles north of Lexington, in dip country. *Inference —* a Piedmont barbecue stand's table sauce became the east's hot sauce because it was the one made in the state and stocked everywhere in it; the bottle joined the vinegar on Coastal Plain tables at some point this project has no date for, and Skylight Inn, cooking whole hogs since 1947, names it in its own seasoning. The company has since made an Eastern Carolina BBQ Sauce of its own — apple cider vinegar, tomato paste, red pepper flakes and sugar — along with a sriracha, 'Cha!', in 2013 and a Mexican-style sauce, Sabor!, in 2016; it dropped its hot-dog chili sauce in 2015.
text.how: Shaken over chopped pork at the table for the heat the vinegar sauce lacks; stirred into the house dressing at some pits — Skylight Inn's is vinegar, salt, pepper and Texas Pete; and, *Tradition holds —* the pepper of choice in home versions of the eastern sauce, a few dashes into a cup of vinegar.
text.today: The seventh-best-selling hot sauce in the United States in 2022 by Instacart's count, in 6-, 12- and 24-ounce bottles, with a Hotter Hot Sauce, a garlic sauce, a sriracha and the Eastern Carolina BBQ Sauce beside it. Still made in Winston-Salem.

names.name: vinegar-and-pepper sauce
names.said: In the east it is 'the sauce' or just 'vinegar'; Brown's in Kingstree calls its own 'barbecue gravy'.

text.what: Vinegar — cider or white — with salt, black pepper and crushed red pepper, and nothing else in its plainest form; some houses add sugar, a bottled hot sauce or lemon. It is thin enough to pour, tart, and as hot as the cook likes. It is the sauce of whole-hog barbecue on the Coastal Plain of both Carolinas, from Rocky Mount to the Pee Dee and the coast: used as a mop while the hog cooks, tossed through the chopped meat at the block, and set on the table for more. Wikipedia's history of barbecue sauce calls it the earliest American barbecue sauce and the root of most of the others.
text.story:
Early home barbecue sauces were vinegar, salt and pepper, and stayed so until sugar, ketchup and Worcestershire came in during the 1920s. The sauce of the eastern Carolinas, Wikipedia says, was popularised by enslaved African cooks who also shaped American barbecue itself; the South Carolina tourism office calls vinegar-and-pepper 'the oldest sauce, perhaps the oldest in the nation'; the South Carolina Barbeque Association gives it the coastal plains of both Carolinas and a share in Virginia and Georgia. *Tradition holds —* vinegar was the English kitchen's preservative and its seasoning, and the sauce is what that kitchen did to a pig.

Its recipes are short. Ed Mitchell of Wilson uses apple cider vinegar, crushed red pepper, salt, sugar and black pepper. Skylight Inn dresses its chop with vinegar, salt, pepper and Texas Pete. Russell Cooper at Cooper's Country Store calls his 'downright vinegar and salt and pepper', with black, crushed and ground red pepper in it. Adam Scott of Goldsboro sold his from 1917, and his son patented it in 1946 as a sugar-free, fat-free bottle — 'Daddy never believed in putting sweet stuff on meat'. Rodney Scott's Charleston restaurant serves whole hog with a 'spicy vinegar sauce'. What none of them contains is tomato, and that absence is the whole of the east's argument with Lexington: Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer said of the sauce, 'It doesn't need anything else'.
text.how: Stir salt into vinegar until it dissolves, add black pepper and crushed red pepper, and let it sit; heat is optional. On a whole hog it is mopped on in the last hours or not at all — many pits season only at the block — and the chopped meat, skin and all, is tossed with it and salt until it tastes right. On the tray it sits in a squeeze bottle or a shaker beside the Texas Pete. It soaks into chopped meat and cuts the fat; it is not a glaze and does not thicken.
text.today: Every eastern pit has its own. Bottled versions include Scott's of Goldsboro, sold in Harris Teeter and Food Lion, and Texas Pete's own Eastern Carolina BBQ Sauce, which lists apple cider vinegar, tomato paste, red pepper flakes and sugar — a tomato paste the tradition's own recipes leave out.

recipes.title: Eastern North Carolina Barbecue Sauce
recipes.text:
1. Start with apple cider vinegar in saucepan over medium heat.
2. Add salt, ground black pepper, crushed red pepper, molasses, and honey.
3. Let mixture heat up, but not quite boil.
4. Mix well.
5. Return sauce to the jug that the vinegar came in to cool.
recipes.note: Cider vinegar, salt, black pepper and red pepper flakes, with molasses and honey for sweetening; three quarters of a gallon at a time, returned to the vinegar jug to cool.

recipes.title: Pepper Vinegar
recipes.author: Mrs. Mary Randolph
recipes.text: Get one dozen pods of pepper when ripe, take out the stems, and cut them in two; put them in a kettle with three pints of vinegar, boil it away to one quart, and strain it through a sieve. A little of this is excellent in gravy of every kind, and gives a flavour greatly superior to black pepper; it is also very fine when added to each of the various catsups for fish sauce.
recipes.note: The sauce's oldest written part: a dozen ripe pepper pods boiled down in vinegar until a quart is left. Printed in the first cookbook of the American South, under the condiments rather than the barbecue.

recipes.title: To Barbecue Shoat
recipes.author: Mrs. Lettice Bryan
recipes.text: Take either a hind or fore quarter, rub it well with salt, pepper, and a small portion of molasses, and if practicable, let it lie for a few hours; then rinse it clean, and wipe it dry with a cloth, and place it on a large gridiron, over a bed of clear coals. Do not barbecue it hastily, but let it cook slowly for several hours, turning it over occasionally, and basting it with nothing but a little salt-water and pepper, merely to season and moisten it a little. When it is well done, serve it without a garnish, and having the skin taken off, which should be done before it is put down to roast, squeeze over it a little lemon juice, and accompany it with melted butter and wine, bread sauce, raw sallad, slaugh, or cucumbers, and stewed fruit. Beef may be barbecued in the same manner.
recipes.note: The plainest eastern mop in print, 1839: the meat is basted 'with nothing but a little salt-water and pepper, merely to season and moisten it a little.'

recipes.title: Sauce for Barbecues (receipt 335)
recipes.author: Mrs. A. P. Hill
recipes.text: Melt half a pound of butter; stir into it a large tablespoonful of mustard, half a teaspoonful of red pepper, one of black, salt to taste; add vinegar until the sauce has a strong acid taste. The quantity of vinegar will depend upon the strength of it. As soon as the meat becomes hot, begin to baste, and continue basting frequently until it is done; pour over the meat any sauce that remains.
recipes.note: Vinegar, salt and both peppers, with butter and mustard added — the Georgia mop of 1867, between the eastern vinegar sauce and the South Carolina mustard one.

profile.maker: Wikibooks Cookbook, from the contributor's friend and brother Chip Crumpler
profile.note: Measured from a recipe, not a bottle: six ingredients, vinegar first, no tomato and no mustard, with the sweetening at position five. names.name: Wells Hog Heaven Barbecue Sauce
names.said: Hog Heaven, in Pender County.

text.what: A vinegar-based sauce made at Burgaw, the seat of Pender County in southeastern North Carolina, and sold in that corner of the state. The maker gives no ingredient list and no Nutrition Facts on its site, so what is on record is the description rather than the measurement: a vinegar sauce for seasoning chopped and pulled pork.
text.story:
The maker's account sets the sauce in the hog-killing calendar of southeastern North Carolina, when farming families processed several hogs at one event in the autumn and winter, and barbecued pigs between spring and fall for occasions and gatherings. Farmers made their own vinegar sauce to season the pork, and the choice at the grill was pulled or chopped. Wells Hog Heaven Barbecue Sauce began in 1982 at Burgaw with the Wells family. The present owners bought the business in 2008 and have since parted from the original meat store, keeping the sauce.

*Inference —* the bottle sits in a gap the harvest file makes visible. Of sixty-eight bottles read on 16 September 2026, the ones a reader can measure are the ones a supermarket chain or a national manufacturer put on a shelf; the ones a pit or a family sells locally almost never publish a panel. Wells is in the second group.

recipes.title: Pepper Vinegar
recipes.author: Mrs. Mary Randolph
recipes.text: Get one dozen pods of pepper when ripe, take out the stems, and cut them in two; put them in a kettle with three pints of vinegar, boil it away to one quart, and strain it through a sieve. A little of this is excellent in gravy of every kind, and gives a flavour greatly superior to black pepper; it is also very fine when added to each of the various catsups for fish sauce.
recipes.note: Peppers boiled down in vinegar and strained: the oldest written form of a Coastal Plain vinegar sauce. The maker's own formula is not published; these are free-to-use recipes of the same family, for a cook who wants to make a jar.

recipes.title: Sauce for Barbecues (receipt 335)
recipes.author: Mrs. A. P. Hill
recipes.text: Melt half a pound of butter; stir into it a large tablespoonful of mustard, half a teaspoonful of red pepper, one of black, salt to taste; add vinegar until the sauce has a strong acid taste. The quantity of vinegar will depend upon the strength of it. As soon as the meat becomes hot, begin to baste, and continue basting frequently until it is done; pour over the meat any sauce that remains.

recipes.title: Eastern North Carolina Barbecue Sauce
recipes.text:
1. Start with apple cider vinegar in saucepan over medium heat.
2. Add salt, ground black pepper, crushed red pepper, molasses, and honey.
3. Let mixture heat up, but not quite boil.
4. Mix well.
5. Return sauce to the jug that the vinegar came in to cool.

names.name: baked beans
names.said: 'Beans' on a Carolina barbecue board means these, sweet and brown, not the field peas or butter beans of a vegetable buffet.

text.what: White beans — navy or pea beans — cooked slow in a sweet brown sauce of molasses or brown sugar with pork in it, and served hot in a cup or a compartment of the tray. On a Carolina barbecue plate they usually come from a large can, warmed and doctored at the pit with more sugar, mustard, onion or a handful of chopped barbecue; the traditional form is dried beans parboiled and then baked for hours in a covered pot, and the canned form is cooked through steam rather than baked at all. They belong to the pig pickin' — the outdoor party where guests pull the meat off a whole hog — as much as to the counter.
text.story: The dish is North American before it is Southern. Native peoples of the northeast cooked beans with bear fat and maple syrup; British colonists in New England put molasses or brown sugar in place of the syrup and bacon or ham in place of the fat, and simmered the pot over the fire rather than under the ground, and by the nineteenth century each colony had its own bean — navy in Massachusetts, Jacob's Cattle in Maine, yellow-eye in Vermont. Molasses, used from the eighteenth century partly to dodge British sugar duty, is what ties the sweet brown style to Boston. Mrs. A. P. Hill printed a Southern version in 1867 that parboils the beans three times and buries a scored pound of pickled pork in them. What put beans on the barbecue tray was the can: H. J. Heinz began mass canning them in Pennsylvania in 1895, and by the early twentieth century canned beans were among the first convenience foods. *Tradition holds —* the pit adopted them because a number ten can feeds a crowd and needs no cook. *Inference —* the sweet-and-smoky seasoning most pits add is a way of making a Northern factory bean taste like it came off the pit.
text.how: Dried beans are soaked overnight, parboiled until tender, then baked slowly in a ceramic or cast-iron pot with salt pork, molasses or brown sugar, onion and mustard, until the liquid thickens and the top darkens. The pit version starts from the can: the beans go in a hotel pan with brown sugar, mustard, onion, sometimes ketchup and a scoop of chopped barbecue or the burnt ends of the shoulder, and sit at the back of the pit or in a low oven until the sauce reduces and a skin forms on top. Served hot, in a cup beside the meat or a compartment of the tray.
text.today: On the tray at Piedmont pits beside hushpuppies and red slaw. At Brown's Bar-B-Que in Kingstree, South Carolina, a whole-hog plate with bread, baked beans and slaw is the take-out order. Beans, slaw and hushpuppies are the standing list for a pig pickin'.

recipes.title: Baked Pork and Beans (receipt 184)
recipes.author: Mrs. A. P. Hill
recipes.text: Wash a quart of good white beans early in the morning; put them in a kettle with sufficient water to cover them; place the kettle upon the fire, and when the water becomes boiling hot — but it should not boil — pour the water and beans into a colander, until the water drains from them. Put them again into the kettle, and cover with cold water, adding a piece of soda, or saleratus, as large as a bean. Scald and again drain the water from them, and put the beans in cold water. Soak a pound of pickled pork of the lean part of the middling, in water enough to cover it, three hours. Put the pork and beans to stew in separate kettles. Half an hour before the beans are done, put them in a deep earthen pan, clear of the water they were boiled in. Take up the pork; score it across in gashes or slits, a quarter of an inch apart. Season it highly with pepper, and put it down in the dish of beans, until only the rind is visible; pour in a pint of warm water, and bake until the beans are soft and the meat entirely done. The water in which they were boiled makes a wholesome soup.
recipes.note: Saleratus is the old name for baking soda; the middling is the side of the hog, the cut bacon comes from. A Southern baked bean of 1867, with the pork sunk in the pot to the rind.

recipes.title: Baked Beans
ingredients: 2 pounds (900 g) Navy, Great Northern, or Pea beans, though black, kidney, or lima beans may be used for a different taste.
recipes.text:
1. Soak dry beans overnight, or use 4 cans cooked beans.
2. Preheat oven to 350°F (175°C).
3. Stir all ingredients together, then pour into casserole dish, bean pot or Dutch oven.
4. Add water from beans, or preferably stock or fresh water. Just enough to barely cover. Canned beans may need less water. Beans will absorb more water as they cook.
5. Bake 2½ hours. Check after an hour for moisture level, add more water as needed to keep appropriate moistness. If beans have too much liquid, remove lid and cook a bit longer.

recipes.title: Boston Baked Beans
ingredients: 6 rashers thick cut bacon, sliced (or 5 drops liquid smoke)
4 cups canned kidney beans, rinsed and drained
¼ cup blackstrap molasses, plus more as needed
recipes.text:
1. Cook bacon. Separate the meat from the fat, and chop the bacon.
2. Place 1 tbsp of the bacon fat into a large stainless steel pan. Add kidney beans and sauté over medium-high heat.
3. Add rum and tilt to ignite. If you do not have a gas stove, simply light with a fire stick.
4. Add remaining ingredients and chopped bacon and fold to combine.
5. Bake in a 325°F oven for 1 ½ hours, adding blackstrap molasses occasionally to prevent drying.
recipes.note: The molasses-and-salt-pork form the sweet canned bean descends from.

names.name: banana pudding
names.said: Ordered by the small or large cup at the counter; at Allen & Son it was the Friday dessert.

text.what: Layers of sweet vanilla custard, vanilla wafers and sliced bananas built up in a dish and topped with meringue or whipped cream, then chilled until the wafers soften and the layers run together. It is the barbecue house's dessert in both Carolinas, whole-hog pits and shoulder pits alike: the Barbecue Center in Lexington sells it by the small or large cup, Sam Jones BBQ lists it beside the whole hog, Sweatman's in Holly Hill serves it after hash and rice, and Rodney Scott's in Charleston listed it with the catfish and ribs. It needs no oven, scales up to a crowd and keeps — one theory of how a dessert with no early Southern tie became Southern.
text.story: The pudding is older than its Southern accent. Recipes for banana pudding were popular across the United States in the 1890s, most of them built on sponge cake; the vanilla wafer first replaces the ladyfinger in 1920, in a recipe from Mrs. Laura Kerley in the Bloomington, Illinois Pantagraph, and in the 1940s the National Biscuit Company began printing a banana pudding recipe on the Nilla Wafers box, and the box did the rest. Wikipedia finds no consensus on how it became Southern; one theory is the church picnic, the family reunion and the barbecue, where a dessert that needs no cooking, scales to a crowd and keeps has the advantage. *Inference —* the barbecue house is that gathering made permanent, and the pudding came in on the same logic: a pit kitchen has no pastry oven, but it has a cooler. At Buxton Hall in Asheville, which cooked whole hog until it closed in November 2023, the pudding went out under meringue and Our State said its regulars would swear by that; at Allen & Son outside Chapel Hill, where Keith Allen baked the pies and rolled the cobbler crusts himself, banana pudding was the Friday dessert. Clyde Cooper's in Raleigh, which opened in 1938 without it, added it later and calls it a good old Southern thing. Centerville, Tennessee holds a National Banana Pudding Festival on the first weekend of October.
text.how: A vanilla custard is cooked and cooled. In a deep dish the cook lays wafers, then banana slices, then custard, and repeats to the top; the dish is chilled for hours so the wafers absorb the custard and the layers merge, which is the point. The top is meringue browned in the oven, or whipped cream. Counters sell it by the cup — 10 or 16 ounces at the Barbecue Center — and it comes after the tray, not with it.
text.today: The Barbecue Center, Lexington: homemade banana pudding, small (10 oz) $4.00, large (16 oz) $6.25 on its online menu (September 2026). Sam Jones BBQ lists it in Winterville and Raleigh; Sweatman's keeps it with hash and rice; Clyde Cooper's keeps it in Raleigh. Lexington Barbecue's dessert list is pies and cobbler, with no pudding.

recipes.title: Banana Pudding
ingredients: 1 cup + 2 Tablespoons (200 g + 25 g) granulated sugar
1 teaspoon vanilla extract or vanilla sugar
recipes.text:
1. [Custard] In a saucepan, stir together the milk, 1 cup (200 g) of sugar, butter, salt, and vanilla extract and cook over medium heat until the butter melts.
2. [Custard] Whisk the egg yolks in a separate container (a coffee mug will do), then whisk two tablespoons of the hot milk mixture into the egg yolks to temper them so they don’t curdle.
3. [Custard] When the egg mixture is smooth, whisk it into the milk mixture.
4. [Custard] Add 2 tablespoons of cold water to the cornstarch and stir until smooth; then whisk it into the milk mixture and cook until thickened, stirring constantly so it doesn’t burn.
5. [Custard] Remove the custard from heat.
6. [Meringue] Whip the egg whites and 2 Tablespoons (25 g) sugar in a bowl until stiff peaks form.
7. [Assembly] Cut the bananas into thin slices (about ¼ inch or 5 mm thick).
8. [Assembly] In a large bowl with a flat bottom, place a layer of vanilla wafers or ladyfingers on the bottom.
9. [Assembly] Pour half of the lemon juice and spread half of the custard over these, then layer half of the banana slices on top of the custard.
10. [Assembly] Add another layer of cookies, the rest of the lemon juice, the rest of the custard, and the rest of the banana slices.
11. [Assembly] Top with the meringue and sprinkle the coconut on top.
12. [Assembly] Refrigerate for several hours before serving.
recipes.note: Custard cooked from scratch, wafers, bananas and a meringue — the built-from-scratch form, before the box-pudding-and-whipped-topping version most pits serve now.

recipes.title: Banana Custard
recipes.author: Emma and William McKinney
recipes.text: Cook in double boiler until thick. When cool, add one teaspoonful of vanilla. Bake on a nice crust. When cool, cover pie with thin slices of banana, then the meringue, and bake a delicate brown.
recipes.note: A pie, not a layered pudding, and there are no wafers in it: the vanilla wafer only reaches the dish after the National Biscuit Company began printing a banana recipe on the Nilla box. The custard, the bananas and the meringue are already here in 1922.

recipes.title: Banana Custard Pie
recipes.author: Mrs. M. E. Porter
recipes.book: Mrs. Porter's New Southern Cookery Book
recipes.text:
Same, except you take full-ripe bananas mashed to a paste; flavor with rose.

[The receipt it refers to, Lemon Custard Pie, No. 2, printed just above it:] Grate one-half outside of a lemon and squeeze out the juice, yolks of two eggs, two tablespoonsful heaped of sugar, half a cup of water, one teaspoonful of butter; stir well, and bake in a deep dish lined with crust; beat the whites of the eggs to a stiff froth; stir in two tablespoonsful of pulverized sugar and spread over the top of the pie as soon as it is baked; set in the oven till the top is nicely browned.
recipes.note: Four words long in the book, because it is written as a variation. The receipt it points back to is quoted in brackets so it can be cooked; the brackets are this site's, everything inside them is the book's. An early printed pairing of banana with a meringue-topped custard.
