names.name: barbecue chicken
names.said: In the Carolinas it is chicken, not barbecue: 'barbecue' alone means the pork, so the bird keeps its own name.

text.what: Half a chicken, cooked on the pit beside the pig or on its own cooker until the skin chars, brushed with the house sauce — vinegar and pepper in the east, a thin tomato-and-vinegar dip in the Piedmont — and sold by the half or the whole bird. At eastern pits it is the one other meat: B's in Greenville sells out of chicken halves by early afternoon, and Skylight Inn lists it beside the whole hog. Keaton's in Cleveland, Rowan County, does it the other way round, frying the chicken and dipping it in a hot vinegar-tomato barbecue sauce. NCpedia notes that North Carolinians seldom use 'barbecue' alone for chicken.
text.story: Burette Walker Keaton was laid off by the railroad in 1953 and started selling chicken from a cinder-block shack on Cool Springs Road outside Cleveland, in Rowan County. He fried it, then dipped it in a barbecue sauce he said he had worked out 'like a football huddle' with a ninety-two-year-old man, a sauce meant to penetrate the chicken and then the bone; the legend at the counter is that Schlitz offered him $10,000 for the recipe and he said he would think about it at $100,000. He turned down offers to build a proper restaurant in Statesville or Charlotte, and he died in 1989; his niece Kathleen Murray has run Keaton's since 1991, cash only, on hours that change with the season, with the hot vinegar slaw — cabbage in vinegar, tomato, cayenne and celery seed — beside the chicken. In the east the bird is the pit's second meat. Bill and Peggy McLawhorn opened B's in a former convenience store just inside Greenville in 1978; their three daughters run it now with the pitmaster Dexter Sherrod, the hogs cook eight hours on charcoal in metal pit cookers, the chicken halves cook on their own, and the food is gone by early afternoon. *Tradition holds —* many eastern pits cook chicken only on certain days, and the regulars know which.
text.how: The chicken is split into halves and laid bone-side down over the coals or on the cooker, turned once, and cooked until the skin blisters and the joints run clear; at B's it gets a light brushing of the vinegar sauce, and in the Piedmont the dip does the same work. Keaton's fries or bakes it first, then dips the whole piece in the hot sauce so the sauce goes through the crust. A half is the portion; it comes on a tray with slaw and the house bread, or by the whole bird to take away.
text.today: B's Barbecue: chicken half $7, whole $11.50 (Our State, January 2016); the food sells out by early afternoon. Keaton's: closed Sunday and Monday, open Tuesday to Saturday on hours that vary between lunch and an evening sitting, no cards (Our State, 2017). Sam Jones BBQ lists a chicken tray and slow-cooked chicken plates (2026).

recipes.title: North Carolina Style BBQ Chicken
ingredients: 3 each skinless bone-in chicken thighs and drumsticks
recipes.text:
1. Season chicken liberally with the barbecue rub. Gently massage into meat and refrigerate for at least 1 hour.
2. Meanwhile, combine the vinegar, honey, and Worcestershire sauce.
3. Place enough charcoal briquets to fill the charcoal compartment of a large chimney starter. Wad up some oil-moistened newspaper, stick under the compartment, and light. Wait 15 minutes.
4. Once coals are heated, disperse evenly along the bottom of the grill. Toss in soaked hickory chunks and reapply the grate.
5. Grill chicken over medium low, turning often and brushing with vinegar mixture when turned, until internal temperature reaches 165°F.
6. Remove and let rest for 7 minutes.
7. While chicken is resting, boil remaining vinegar mixture on high for 5 minutes. Drizzle over chicken and serve warm.
recipes.note: Thighs and drumsticks over charcoal and soaked hickory, mopped with cider vinegar, honey and Worcestershire each time they are turned.

recipes.title: To Barbecue Any Kind of Fresh Meat (receipt 200)
recipes.author: Mrs. A. P. Hill
recipes.text: Gash the meat. Broil slowly over a solid fire. Baste constantly with a sauce composed of butter, mustard, red and black pepper, vinegar. Mix these in a pan, and set it where the sauce will keep warm, not hot. Have a swab made by tying a piece of clean, soft cloth upon a stick about a foot long; dip this in the sauce and baste with it. Where a large carcass is barbecued, it is usual to dig a pit in the ground outdoors, and lay narrow bars of wood across. Very early in the morning fill the pit with wood; set it burning, and in this way heat it very hot. When the wood has burned to coals, lay the meat over. Should the fire need replenishing, keep a fire outside burning, from which draw coals, and scatter evenly in the pit under the meat. Should there be any sauce left pour it over the meat. For barbecuing a joint, a large gridiron answers well; it needs constant attention; should be cooked slowly and steadily.
recipes.note: 'Any kind of fresh meat' takes in the half chicken; the basting sauce is receipt 335, below. A few characters in this paragraph are damaged in the scan and are read from context; the line 'Gash the meat' runs straight into 'Broil slowly' in the printing.

recipes.title: Sauce for Barbecues (receipt 335)
recipes.author: Mrs. A. P. Hill
recipes.text: Melt half a pound of butter; stir into it a large tablespoonful of mustard, half a teaspoonful of red pepper, one of black, salt to taste; add vinegar until the sauce has a strong acid taste. The quantity of vinegar will depend upon the strength of it. As soon as the meat becomes hot, begin to baste, and continue basting frequently until it is done; pour over the meat any sauce that remains.
recipes.note: Butter, mustard, red and black pepper and vinegar — a mop rather than a finishing sauce, brushed on from the first heat.

names.name: barbecue sandwich
names.said: Ordered as 'a barbecue' or 'a chopped sandwich'; the slaw is on it unless you say otherwise.

text.what: Chopped pork on a soft white bun with slaw laid on the meat. In North Carolina it is the commonest form of the sandwich: whole-hog barbecue dressed with vinegar and pepper in the east, chopped or sliced shoulder with dip and red slaw in the Piedmont. In South Carolina the meat is pulled or chopped and the sauce is mustard, vinegar-pepper or tomato by region, with slaw a common topping. The bun is a plain hamburger roll — at Skylight Inn a white bread roll — and the bread keeps the meat warm and catches the sauce.
text.story: The whole-hog sandwich is a twentieth-century form: the older barbecue was a plate, or the pig itself, and the bun came with the roadside stand. At Melton's in Rocky Mount a sandwich cost 15 cents in 1929, against 45 cents for a plate with boiled potatoes. Lexington's version has a name of its own, the 'Lexington Barbecue Sandwich', and its mark is the red slaw — cabbage in vinegar and ketchup with no mayonnaise — that sits on the meat. Slaw on the sandwich is a habit the Carolinas share with Memphis, where Leonard Heuberger's restaurant, opened in 1922, put chopped shoulder, tomato sauce and slaw on a bun and other houses followed; the Carolina sandwich is the same idea with its own sauce under the slaw. *Inference —* the slaw goes on the meat rather than beside it because the sandwich was built to be eaten in one hand at a stand or in a car; the tray, with its slaw in the other half of the boat, is the sandwich opened up for people who sat down.
text.how: The meat is chopped on the block and seasoned there; a spoonful of slaw goes on top and the bun closes over it. Eastern pits use white slaw, Lexington pits red slaw; at Keaton's in Cleveland the hot vinegar slaw goes on. Lexington Barbecue sells a chopped and a sliced sandwich, both with slaw, and a pork skin sandwich with slaw besides; the Barbecue Center adds a coarse chopped one. On a South Carolina buffet the pork comes with loaves of white bread, and the eater builds the sandwich at the table.
text.today: Lexington Barbecue: chopped sandwich with slaw $5.70 cash, $5.85 card; sliced $5.90 cash (September 2026). The Barbecue Center: chopped $6.00, sliced or coarse chopped $6.35 (September 2026). B's Barbecue in Greenville charged $3.75 in January 2016.

recipes.title: Pulled Pork Sandwiches
ingredients: 2 tbsp cayenne pepper (more if you like)
recipes.text:
1. Combine water, salt, and honey in a 6-quart cooler. Add pork and refrigerate or place a large bag of ice on top for 8–12 hours.
2. Remove pork from brine and pat dry with paper towels. Combine remaining seasonings and rub on pork.
3. Light a few chunks of apple wood and place in the firebox of a smoker. Keep temperature in smoker around 210°F.
4. Place in a smoker and cook for 8–12 hours, changing wood as needed. The meat should be tender at this point—if not, continue smoking.
5. Let rest 1 hour, then shred with two forks. Serve on hamburger buns.
recipes.note: Slaw on the meat, on a soft bun; the Carolina order.

recipes.title: Eastern North Carolina Barbecued Pig
ingredients: Your favorite vinegar-based Eastern NC sauce
recipes.text:
1. Salt hams, ribs/midsection and shoulders liberally and place skin side up on either a gas or charcoal grill or a BBQ pit.
2. Keep lid closed, and aim for a heat of approximately 275–350°F.
3. Allow 1 hour per 10 pounds cooking time (gas or charcoal).
4. 2 hours before being done, place pig with the skin side down. As soon as it is flipped, pour BBQ sauce on meat side.
5. Close lid and allow skin to crisp.
6. The pig will be done to perfection when the ham bone can be twisted freely.
7. Lift lid and allow guests to pick/pull meat, or the chef can remove meat and chop to their liking on a chopping block.
recipes.note: An 80-pound pig on a home pit or a covered grill, skin up all night and turned at the end; the meat that goes on the bun.

recipes.title: Eastern North Carolina Barbecue Sauce
recipes.text:
1. Start with apple cider vinegar in saucepan over medium heat.
2. Add salt, ground black pepper, crushed red pepper, molasses, and honey.
3. Let mixture heat up, but not quite boil.
4. Mix well.
5. Return sauce to the jug that the vinegar came in to cool.
recipes.note: The sauce the chopped meat is dressed with before it reaches the bread.

names.name: barbecue tray
names.said: In Lexington you order a tray, chopped, coarse chopped or sliced; in the east you say plate or tray and the counter knows what comes with it.

text.what: The unit of ordering at a Carolina barbecue counter: a paper boat or a plate with the chopped pork on one side and slaw on the other, and no bun. In Lexington the meat is pork shoulder and the order names the cut — chopped, coarse chopped (small chunks) or sliced — and the size, tray or large tray; in the east it is whole hog, and the tray or plate carries white slaw with cornbread, a corn stick or hushpuppies. A plate adds french fries and a choice of hushpuppies or rolls. A sandwich is the same meat and slaw on a bun.
text.story: The tray is a counter word. At Melton's in Rocky Mount, the first sit-down barbecue restaurant in the state, a plate of barbecue with boiled potatoes cost 45 cents in 1929 and a sandwich 15 cents; the plate was the eastern form from the start. In Lexington the vocabulary grew around the shoulder. A regular quoted in Carolina Country in 2018 counted ten ways to order — coarse chopped, fine chopped, chopped, chopped brown, sliced — each dressed with the house dip, and the hushpuppies 'round, thin, fat, oblong, dense or light'. Regulars keep the order light, a paper tray with nothing but pork and slaw; the plate with fries is for visitors and big appetites. *Tradition holds —* the tray began as the cheapest way to sell barbecue from a tent or a curb-service window, and the cardboard boat is still the vessel at Lexington Barbecue and the Barbecue Center. In the east the whole hog gives the counter another set of choices: some pits chop the whole pig together, others let the customer ask for white meat, dark meat, or the 'middlin' from the belly, and Jane and Michael Stern wrote that the sound of the cleavers on the block is one of the pleasures of a Carolina whole-hog house.
text.how: The order names the cut first, then the form. Lexington Barbecue lists chopped, sliced and coarse chop trays in two sizes; the Barbecue Center fills a plate with two sides and hushpuppies or a potato bun. The meat is dressed on the block — with dip in the Piedmont, with the vinegar-pepper sauce in the east — and more comes in a cup on the side. Slaw goes beside the meat, not under it. At Skylight Inn the tray is barbecue, slaw and a square of cornbread; at B's in Greenville a plate is pork, slaw, potatoes, green beans and corn sticks; at Sam Jones BBQ the family tray is pork, cornbread and one side.
text.today: At Lexington Barbecue in September 2026 a chopped tray is $8.00 cash, a large chopped tray $13.40 and a chopped plate $13.40; sliced and coarse chop run a little more. At the Barbecue Center a small chopped tray is $9.00, a large $12.00 and a chopped plate $13.00. B's Barbecue's dinner was $7.75 in January 2016.

recipes.title: To Barbecue Shoat
recipes.author: Mrs. Lettice Bryan
recipes.text: Take either a hind or fore quarter, rub it well with salt, pepper, and a small portion of molasses, and if practicable, let it lie for a few hours; then rinse it clean, and wipe it dry with a cloth, and place it on a large gridiron, over a bed of clear coals. Do not barbecue it hastily, but let it cook slowly for several hours, turning it over occasionally, and basting it with nothing but a little salt-water and pepper, merely to season and moisten it a little. When it is well done, serve it without a garnish, and having the skin taken off, which should be done before it is put down to roast, squeeze over it a little lemon juice, and accompany it with melted butter and wine, bread sauce, raw sallad, slaugh, or cucumbers, and stewed fruit. Beef may be barbecued in the same manner.
recipes.note: The tray, written down in 1839: the meat cooked slowly over clear coals, mopped with nothing but salt water and pepper, and sent to table with slaugh — slaw — and cucumbers beside it.

recipes.title: To Barbecue Any Kind of Fresh Meat (receipt 200)
recipes.author: Mrs. A. P. Hill
recipes.text: Gash the meat. Broil slowly over a solid fire. Baste constantly with a sauce composed of butter, mustard, red and black pepper, vinegar. Mix these in a pan, and set it where the sauce will keep warm, not hot. Have a swab made by tying a piece of clean, soft cloth upon a stick about a foot long; dip this in the sauce and baste with it. Where a large carcass is barbecued, it is usual to dig a pit in the ground outdoors, and lay narrow bars of wood across. Very early in the morning fill the pit with wood; set it burning, and in this way heat it very hot. When the wood has burned to coals, lay the meat over. Should the fire need replenishing, keep a fire outside burning, from which draw coals, and scatter evenly in the pit under the meat. Should there be any sauce left pour it over the meat. For barbecuing a joint, a large gridiron answers well; it needs constant attention; should be cooked slowly and steadily.
recipes.note: The pit and the cloth swab on a foot-long stick, from a Georgia book of 1867. A few characters in this paragraph are damaged in the scan and are read from context; the line 'Gash the meat' runs straight into 'Broil slowly' in the printing.

recipes.title: To Barbecue Shote
recipes.author: Mrs. Mary Randolph
recipes.text: This is the name given in the southern states to a fat young hog, which, when the head and feet are taken off, and it is cut into four quarters, will weigh six pounds per quarter. Take a fore quarter, make several incisions between the ribs, and stuff it with rich forcemeat; put it in a pan with a pint of water, two cloves of garlic, pepper, salt, two gills of red wine, and two of mushroom catsup, bake it and thicken the gravy with butter and brown flour; it must be jointed and the ribs cut across before it is cooked, or it cannot be carved well; lay it in the dish with the ribs uppermost; if it be not sufficiently brown, add a little burnt sugar to the gravy, garnish with balls.
recipes.note: Mrs. Randolph's footnote to the title: 'Shote being a Provincial term, and not a legitimate English word, Mrs. R. has taken the liberty of spelling it in a way that conveys the sound of the pronunciation more clearly than shoad, the usual manner of spelling it.' A shoat is a young hog. This one is baked in a pan rather than cooked over coals — the word 'barbecue' in 1824 still meant the animal and the occasion as much as the fire.

recipes.title: To Barbecue Shoat
recipes.author: Marion Cabell Tyree, editor
recipes.text: Lay the shoat in water till ready for use; if small, it will cook in an hour. Put in the oven with two spoonfuls of water, a piece of lard, and dredge with flour. When ready for use, pour in half a teacup of walnut catsup, and, if not fat, a piece of butter.
recipes.note: An oven receipt under the barbecue name, in a Virginia book of 1879 — the word had by then loosened away from the fire.

names.name: Blenheim Ginger Ale
names.said: Ordered by the cap: pink cap for the hot one, gold for Not As Hot, white for diet.

etymology.root: named for Blenheim, Marlboro County, South Carolina, the town that grew up around the mineral spring the drink was first mixed with
etymology.first_attested: 1903, when Dr. C. R. May and A. J. Matheson opened the Blenheim Bottling Company (Wikipedia)
etymology.note: Bottling moved to Hamer, in Dillon County, in 1993; the name stayed with the spring.

text.what: A ginger ale bottled at Hamer, in Dillon County, South Carolina, made with Jamaica ginger and sugar in mineral water from a spring in Marlboro County, and hot enough that the heat is the point of it. It comes in three strengths: #3 Hot with a pink cap, #5 Not As Hot with a gold cap, and #9 Diet with a white cap. It was made first as a stomach tonic rather than a soft drink, and it sits on Pee Dee barbecue tables the way Cheerwine sits on Piedmont ones.
text.story: *Tradition holds —* in 1781 a Patriot named James Spears, running from the British, lost a shoe in the mud of a natural spring; when he came back for it he found the hollow full of water, tasted it and found it strongly mineral. Word spread, and by the late 1800s a small town had grown up at the spring. In the late 1890s Dr. C. R. May began sending patients with stomach trouble to drink the water, and because they complained about its iron taste he mixed in Jamaica ginger and sugar. He went into partnership with A. J. Matheson and they opened the Blenheim Bottling Company in 1903; the plant beside the springs was built in 1920, and for ninety years the company made as little as eighteen or twenty cases a day. In 1993 Alan Schafer, who owned the South of the Border roadside attraction at Hamer, bought Blenheim and moved the bottling to a new plant next to it rather than refurbish the old one. Charles Kuralt filmed a segment on it for CBS on 26 June 1983. In February 1998 William Grimes of the New York Times described the first swallow as bringing on a four-sneeze fit.
text.how: The recipe is the company's and has not changed in over 110 years: Jamaica ginger and sugar in the mineral water, carbonated and bottled. A ginger ale made at home is a ginger syrup — grated ginger boiled with sugar and water, strained — mixed with carbonated water, or a brewed one, in which the sugar solution is fermented briefly with yeast in a sealed vessel until it carbonates itself. The Blenheim heat is in the quantity of ginger rather than in any added pepper.
text.today: Bottled at Hamer, next to South of the Border. Distribution stayed inside the Carolinas for most of the company's life; the company now ships to 44 states and three international distributors.

recipes.title: Ginger Ale
ingredients: ½ cup (120 ml) fresh or frozen ginger in ½ in (1.25 cm) dice
recipes.text:
1. Combine the 1 cup (240 mL) water with the ginger in a saucepan. Bring to a boil, then remove from the heat and strain the liquid.
2. Combine the ½ cup (120 ml) water with the sugar in a saucepan. Bring to a boil, and simmer until reduced to about 5 oz (150 ml). Remove from the heat.
3. Combine the ginger liquid, the syrup, and the lime juice.
4. To make the finished soda, combine 1 volume of ginger syrup with 1 volume of carbonated water.
recipes.note: A ginger ale made at home from ginger, sugar and water; Blenheim's own formula has never been published.

recipes.title: Ginger Beer
recipes.author: Mrs. Mary Randolph
recipes.text: Pour two gallons of boiling water on two pounds brown sugar, one and a half ounce of cream of tartar, and the same of pounded ginger; stir them well, and put it in a small cask; when milk warm, put in half a pint of good yeast, shake the cask well, and stop it close—in twenty-four hours it will be fit to bottle—cork it very well, and in ten days it will sparkle like Champaigne—one or two lemons cut in slices and put in, will improve it much. For economy, you may use molasses instead of sugar—one quart in place of two pounds. This is a wholesome and delicious beverage in warm weather.
recipes.note: The Southern household ginger drink of 1824, fermented in a cask rather than carbonated in a plant: an ounce and a half of pounded ginger to two gallons, which is the proportion that makes a ginger drink hot. 'Champaigne' is the book's spelling.

recipes.title: Uncle Remus Mint Julep
recipes.author: Emma and William McKinney
recipes.text: Boil sugar and water ten minutes, and cool; add strained lemon juice, mint leaves bruised, and ginger ale; half fill glasses with crushed ice and pour the mixture over it.
recipes.note: Included for what it shows rather than what it is: bottled ginger ale is already an ordinary Southern pantry item by 1922, sold by the pint and mixed into a non-alcoholic punch. The book's title for it is a minstrel one; the quantities are transcribed as printed, including the quotation marks in the last line.

names.name: boiled potatoes
names.said: 'Potatoes' on an eastern plate means these, boiled whole or in halves — not fries and not potato salad.

text.what: Potatoes boiled whole or in halves until they are soft and served beside chopped whole hog on the eastern North Carolina plate — the side the Piedmont does not have. At Parker's in Wilson and, by Bob Garner's account, most eastern restaurants they are stewed rather than plainly boiled: peeled potatoes, often with onion, simmered in water with ketchup or red sauce, hot sauce, paprika, sugar, salt, pepper and a spoon of bacon grease, so the broth seasons them through. They come on the plate with slaw and the plate's bread, a corn stick or hushpuppies, and they have been there since Melton's in Rocky Mount charged 45 cents for barbecue with boiled potatoes in 1929.
text.story: The potato is the eastern plate's own vegetable, and the first record of it is a price. When Bob Melton's shed on the Tar River in Rocky Mount — the state's first sit-down barbecue restaurant, Wikipedia says — printed its prices in 1929, a plate of barbecue with boiled potatoes was 45 cents and a sandwich 15; by 1988 the plate came with slaw, hushpuppies and Brunswick stew, and the potatoes stayed on the side list with the corn sticks until the restaurant closed in 2005. Clyde Cooper's in Raleigh opened on New Year's Day 1938 with boiled potatoes, French fries, coleslaw and Brunswick stew beside the pork, and the core of that menu has not changed. Bob Garner's North Carolina Barbecue: Flavored by Time (1996) prints Tad Everett's barbecue potatoes — potatoes and onions in chunks, bacon drippings, catsup, Texas Pete and a little sugar, covered with water and simmered until soft — as a variation on the boiled potatoes of most eastern restaurants, and places the dish around Palmyra, Hobgood and Oak City. *Tradition holds —* the seasoned broth is the pit's idea of a potato: the pepper and a spoon of ketchup in the pot, so the side tastes of the same table as the meat. A Barbecue Bros writer touring the whole-hog pits in 2022 called B's potatoes a simple side not really found in the Piedmont; in Lexington the tray's starch is the hushpuppy.
text.how: Small potatoes, scrubbed, whole or halved, or larger ones peeled and cut in chunks, go into a pot with cold water and salt and boil until a fork slides in. The stewed way, as Mandy Rivers reconstructs Parker's version and as Garner prints Tad Everett's, adds onion, a quarter-cup of hot sauce, smoked or sweet paprika, black pepper, bacon grease and half a cup of red sauce or a quarter-cup of ketchup, with a little sugar, and simmers twenty to forty minutes until the potatoes are soft and have drunk the broth. *Inference —* the ketchup and paprika are what tint them. They are served hot beside the slaw and the bread, and take the pork's vinegar sauce spooned over.
text.today: On the plate at B's in Greenville, where the sides are slaw, potatoes or green beans and the barbecue dinner was $7.75 in 2016; on Bum's buffet in Ayden with the collards and black-eyed peas; by the bulk order at Parker's in Wilson; on the menu at Clyde Cooper's in Raleigh (2026). Melton's closed in 2005 and its 1929 price survives on Wikipedia.

recipes.title: To Boil Irish Potatoes
recipes.author: Marion Cabell Tyree, editor
recipes.text: Old potatoes must be nicely peeled and dropped in boiling water, covered with a lid and boiled hard half an hour. Then drain off the water and set by the fire. This makes them mealy. — Mrs. S. T.

recipes.title: Boiled Irish Potatoes
recipes.author: Mrs. Barringer, of North Carolina
recipes.text:
If they are young, put them in a bucket of cold water, scrape off the skins, wash them, and drop into boiling water. When soft, dress with cream and melted butter.

If you wish to have them mashed, pare them, and put into plenty of boiling water until half done. Then renew the boiling by pouring over fresh hot water, and when barely done, pour off the water, and let them steam ten minutes, when they must be mashed, and dressed with butter and salt, and served in a hot water dish. Or you may put the potatoes in a steamer over boiling water, and boil till tender; press one by one in a napkin to remove all the moisture, and lay on a hot water dish with a lid, and serve.

recipes.title: Stewed Irish Potatoes
recipes.author: Mrs. Barringer, of North Carolina
recipes.text: Slice thin, and boil in water till tender; pour off the water and put in some butter, salt, pepper, and rich cream and a dust of flour. Before taking up, stir in the beaten yolk of an egg, with some chopped parsley. It is a nice breakfast dish.
recipes.note: The eastern pits stew them rather than boil them dry, in butter and a little liquid; this is that method, from a North Carolina book of 1867, without the barbecue plate around it.

names.name: Brunswick stew
names.said: On an eastern North Carolina menu it is 'Brunswick stew' or just 'stew'; a cup or a bowl beside the plate.

text.what: A thick tomato stew of chicken or pork with corn, butter beans (lima beans), onion and, in the east, potatoes, cooked in big pots and served in a cup beside the barbecue. Virginia and Georgia both claim it; North Carolina makes it without argument at barbecue houses, church suppers and fundraisers, where it holds the place that hash holds in South Carolina. The name is a county in Virginia or a city in Georgia, both named for the German duchy of Brunswick. The squirrel of the first recipes has given way to chicken, and at a barbecue house some of the chopped pork goes into the pot.
text.story: Two states keep the argument. In Brunswick, Georgia, a twenty-five-gallon iron pot on a plaque is called the vessel in which the stew was first cooked, in 1898, on St. Simons Island; the Virginia General Assembly answered in 1988 with a proclamation that Jimmy Matthews, a Black cook, made a squirrel stew for Creed Haskins in Brunswick County in 1828 and gave it the county's name. The Virginia Writers' Project guide of 1941 tells it as a hunting-camp story — the cook left behind throws everything into the pot — and Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings passed on the tale in 1942 that it was a favourite of Queen Victoria and came from Braunschweig. None of the claims traces to the ground. North Carolina stays out of the fight and eats the stew. Kennedy's Barbecue in Greensboro was advertising 'Barbecue, Brunswick stew, slaw and hush puppies' in 1949, the plate that became the state's standard. Our State printed Mary Scott's recipe on November 10, 1951: the governor's wife's pot held a five-pound chicken, corn, lima beans, tomatoes, onion, potato, okra and chopped barbecue. At Melton's in Rocky Mount the stew sat beside boiled potatoes, slaw, corn sticks and hushpuppies until the house closed in 2005. *Tradition holds —* the eastern stew has potatoes in it and the Piedmont's may not, and church stew-masters cook it overnight in iron pots for the fall fundraisers, with a paddle and a crowd.
text.how: A whole chicken, or chicken and pork, boiled until it falls apart and picked from the bone; the stock takes tomatoes, corn cut from the cob, butter beans, onion and, in the east, potatoes, and simmers for hours with a long paddle going round until the meat has shredded into the vegetables and a spoon stands up in it. Salt, black and red pepper; at a barbecue house a ladle of chopped pork and its sauce. Served hot in a cup or bowl beside the tray, or by the quart to take home.
text.today: A standing side at eastern barbecue houses and at the Greensboro-line pits of the Piedmont; Melton's priced a plate with slaw, hushpuppies and Brunswick stew in 1988. *Tradition holds —* churches and fire departments across the Piedmont sell it by the quart at fall stews.

recipes.title: Old Virginia Brunswick Stew
recipes.author: Emma and William McKinney
recipes.text: Boil one chicken and one rabbit or squirrel in two or three quarts of water. When about half done add one quart of lima beans, one quart of tomatoes, one quart of corn and butter the size of two eggs. Season to taste with salt and pepper and cook until thick enough to eat with a fork.
recipes.note: The squirrel is in the older Virginia line of the stew; Carolina pits cook it with chicken or pork and, in the east, potatoes. 'Thick enough to eat with a fork' is the test a Carolina stew is still held to.

recipes.title: Circuit Hash (recipe 152)
recipes.author: Mrs. Abby Fisher
recipes.book: What Mrs. Fisher Knows About Old Southern Cooking
recipes.text:
One dozen tomatoes, one quart of butter beans, one dozen ears of corn cut off from cob, quarter pound of lean and fat pork cut in fine pieces, if pork is not liked, use two tablespoonfuls of butter; put on in a sauce-pan and stew one hour.

Note. Five minutes before dinner put in the corn to cook with the rest of stew.
recipes.note: Abby Fisher's dish is called a hash, not a stew, but its parts are the stew's: tomatoes, butter beans, corn and pork, cooked down together. She was born into slavery in South Carolina about 1832.

recipes.title: Vegetable Soup
recipes.author: Mrs. Barringer, of North Carolina
recipes.text: Put a pint of Lima beans, a half a dozen large tomatoes, two teacupfuls of corn cut from the cob, a few snap beans, and two teaspoonfuls of dried ochra, into five quarts of water, with three slices of lean ham. Boil for two hours, and season with salt and pepper. Remove the ham before sending to table. Thicken with yellow of egg and a little flour.
recipes.note: An ancestor rather than the thing: a North Carolina book of 1867, the same beans, corn and tomatoes in the same pot, without the name. Ochra is okra.

names.name: Cheerwine
names.said: One word, capital C. It is a soda with no wine in it; the name is for the burgundy colour and the cheer.

etymology.root: cheer + wine: named, the company says, for its burgundy-red colour and cheery disposition — wine for the colour, cheer for the taste; it contains no alcohol
etymology.first_attested: 1917, Salisbury, North Carolina; registered as a trademark in 1926 (Wikipedia)
etymology.note: The company's own line, as Wikipedia quotes it: 'it made sense to name a burgundy-red, bubbly, cherry concoction — Cheerwine.'

text.what: A cherry-flavoured soft drink — burgundy-red, sweet, with a strong black-cherry note and more carbonation than most sodas — made in Salisbury, Rowan County, North Carolina by the Carolina Beverage Corporation since 1917, and run by founder L.D. Peeler's family throughout. On a Piedmont barbecue counter it is the soda beside the tea: Lexington Barbecue lists Cheerwine and Diet Cheerwine with the Cokes, and the Barbecue Center sells it by the 10-, 16- and 32-ounce cup. It is bottled in glass with cane sugar as Retro or 'Original 1917 Formula' Cheerwine, comes as ice cream and sherbet in Food Lion, and has had its own festival in Salisbury each year since its centennial in 2017.
text.story: Two accounts of 1917 survive, and they agree on the man and the town. Wikipedia's: when the Maysville Syrup Company of Maysville, Kentucky went bankrupt that year, L. D. Peeler, Hughston Kirby, Kurt Weinmann and other investors bought its assets, moved them to North Carolina as the Carolina Syrup Company, and the same year bought a cherry-soda recipe from a St. Louis flavor salesman and sold it as Cheerwine. The company's own: Peeler made it during the wartime sugar shortage from a wild-cherry flavour a St. Louis salesman brought him, and named it for its burgundy-red colour and cheery disposition. The trademark was registered in 1926. Peeler's son Clifford took over in 1931 and kept the company profitable through the Depression; the plant moved to its present Salisbury site in July 1967; Clifford's grandsons Cliff and Mark Ritchie joined in the late 1970s, and Cliff Ritchie has headed the parent company since 1992 by Wikipedia's account, since 2007 by the company's — which makes it, by its own claim, the oldest soft-drink company still run by its founding family. The rest is reach: Pepsi distributors bottling it outside the Carolinas from 2005, a Krispy Kreme Cheerwine doughnut in July 2010, a New York Times piece on 'The Expanding Cult of Cheerwine' in 2011 with a plan the same year to be nationwide by the centennial, and a festival in downtown Salisbury from 2017 that drew over 100,000 people in 2025 and, the Salisbury Post says, $5.9 million to Rowan County.
text.how: Carbonated water, high-fructose corn syrup (cane sugar in the glass-bottle Retro line), caramel colour, phosphoric acid, natural and artificial flavours, caffeine, citric acid, sodium benzoate and Red 40, as the label read in 2021; the flavour is cherry with a black-cherry edge and the fizz is high. It is sold in glass bottles, cans, 12-packs and two-litre bottles, and as a fountain drink at some restaurants and convenience stores, Cook Out and Bojangles among them. At the barbecue counter it comes in a cup over ice with the tray; at home it goes into a Cheerwine cake — a commercial one has been baked in Salisbury since 2008 — and into a float, and with Captain Morgan rum it is a 'Captain Cheerwine'.
text.today: Lexington Barbecue: Cheerwine or Diet Cheerwine $2.90 cash, $3.00 card (September 2026); the Barbecue Center: 10 oz $2.50, 16 oz $2.90, 32 oz $3.75. Sold from Maryland to Florida and in specialty-soda shops beyond. The 2026 Cheerwine Festival was Saturday, May 16, in downtown Salisbury; Cheerwine Zero Sugar arrived in 2021 and a Cheerwine Ale with NoDa Brewing in 2023.

recipes.title: Cherry Shrub
recipes.author: Mrs. Mary Randolph
recipes.text: Gather ripe morello cherries, pick them from the stalk, and put them in an earthen pot, which must be set into an iron pot of water; make the water boil, but take care that none of it gets into the cherries; when the juice is extracted, pour it into a bag made of tolerably thick cloth, which will permit the juice to pass, but not the pulp of your cherries; sweeten it to your taste, and when it becomes perfectly clear, bottle it—put a gill of brandy into each bottle, before you pour in the juice—cover the corks with rosin. It will keep all summer, in a dry cool place, and is delicious mixed with water.
recipes.note: The household ancestor of a bottled cherry drink: juice drawn from the fruit, sweetened, bottled and mixed with water to drink. A morello is a sour cherry; the brandy is the keeping agent and can be left out, in which case the syrup must be kept cold.

recipes.title: Cherry Shrub
recipes.author: Mrs. Lettice Bryan
recipes.text: Break up some fine ripe cherries, press out all the juice, and put it in a preserving kettle, with a pound of loaf sugar to each quart of the juice. Break up a few of the cherry seeds, boil them in a very little water, till the flavor is extracted, and strain the liquid into the juice and sugar. Boil it for eight or ten minutes, skim it, and cool it. Have ready some small bottles, washed clean, and dried; put in each a wine glass of brandy; fill them with the syrup, and cork them securely. It makes very delicate ice, frozen over twice, as directed for ice creams, and is also fine, mixed with iced waters.
recipes.note: A pound of sugar to a quart of juice, and the cherry stones boiled separately for the almond note that a black-cherry flavouring still carries. 'Fine, mixed with iced waters' is what a cherry soft drink does.

names.name: chicken bog
names.said: 'Bog' to the people who cook it; 'chicken bog' on the sign at the Loris Bog-Off.

etymology.root: English bog 'wet, soft, spongy ground', c. 1500, from Gaelic and Irish bogach 'bog', from bog 'soft, moist'; applied to the dish for its wet rice
etymology.first_attested: The Loris historical marker (2022) says the dish fed crowds by the 1920s. No source this project has read gives a first print date for the name; Stan Woodward, who filmed the dish in 2002, found it 'never well documented by its users'.
etymology.note: Two accounts, both reported in the South Carolina Encyclopedia. The documented one: James Villas writes that a bog, unlike a pilau, is any stew with wet, soggy rice, and Karen Hess that a pilau cooked in a big batch always ends up wet. The folk one: that the dish is named for the boggy ground of the Pee Dee where it is cooked. Wikipedia calls the wetness the likelier reading.

text.what: Chicken, rice and smoked sausage cooked together in the chicken's own broth until the rice has taken up the liquid and sits wet and plump — a pilau (rice cooked in stock) that is deliberately wetter than a pilau. It belongs to the Pee Dee, the northeast of South Carolina from Horry County west to Florence, and to the Lowcountry beyond it; Loris, a town of about two thousand north of Myrtle Beach, has held a Bog-Off cook-off every October since 1979. The pot is a fifty-gallon wash pot and the dish is cooked for crowds: tobacco crews, church suppers, the stump meeting at Galivants Ferry.
text.story: The rice came first. South Carolina grew more rice than any other state from the 1700s until the Civil War — Carolina Gold, planted and worked by enslaved people in the Lowcountry — and the culinary historian Damon Lee Fowler reads chicken bog as a localized pilau, 'probably of African provenance', found nowhere else in the country. The name was never written down by the people who used it; Stan Woodward, who made a documentary on the dish in 2002, concluded it went unrecorded because it was a commonplace high-protein meal that fed a lot of people in a poor place. The marker that Loris put up in 2022 says the dish fed crowds by the 1920s and was eaten after gathering tobacco in the northeast of the state: the crew that had primed and strung the leaves all day sat down to a wash pot of bog. The Democratic stump meeting at Galivants Ferry, on the Little Pee Dee, serves it with snap beans, white rolls and Pepsi, and Loris, which calls itself the chicken bog capital of the world, made it the theme of an October festival in 1979; by 2001 the Bog-Off drew about twenty thousand people. To the south, in Georgetown County, the same pot is cooked drier and called chicken pilau.
text.how: An old hen past laying is the first choice, a fat rooster the second. The bird is poached whole with onion, salt and plenty of black pepper; the meat is pulled from the bone, not chopped, the fat is skimmed from the broth, and the rice, chicken, smoked sausage and onion go back in to simmer until the rice is done and still wet. Woodward's bogmaster's test: the rice is plump and moist, holds together, sits up above a little gravy in the bottom, and does not cling to the chicken. Fork or spoon depends on the cook. Green peppers and other vegetables appear in some recipes; the Loris standard is chicken, sausage, rice, salt, pepper and perhaps onion.
text.today: The Loris Bog-Off runs every October; the town's marker, put up by the William G. Pomeroy Foundation in 2022, stands on Main Street outside the library. Bog is a church-supper and fundraiser dish across Horry County and the Pee Dee, and the Galivants Ferry stump meeting still serves it.

recipes.title: Chicken Bog I
ingredients: 1 small onion (about the size of a lemon or smaller)
1 small green bell pepper, chopped small
2 lb uncooked long grain white rice (not instant rice)
recipes.text:
1. Put chicken in heavy aluminum pot and cover with hot water. Be sure there is enough water so that there will be at least 6 cups of broth after cooking chicken. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat, cover, and simmer until chicken is very tender (an hour or more).
2. While the chicken is cooking, put 4 cups of rice into a bowl, cover with cold water, and let soak.
3. When chicken is very tender, remove pot from stove and let cool until the chicken can be handled.
4. Take chicken from pot, and pull meat from bones in large pieces; do not cut it up. Discard any fat-heavy skin.
5. Pour broth from pot into a bowl. If chicken was very fat and broth is very fatty, pour off about 1 cup of fat from broth.
6. Wash pot, then put bacon in pot and cook slowly until bacon is crisp.
7. Take bacon from pot and drain; leave bacon grease in pot.
8. Put in chopped onion, green pepper and brown slightly.
9. Add 6 cups chicken broth to pot, and season to taste with salt and pepper (at least a tablespoon of each—use a heavy hand since rice will absorb salt).
10. Increase heat, bring broth to a boil, and put chicken in pot.
11. Drain rice and put rice in pot.
12. Add a stick of butter and mix well. Reduce heat, cover with lid, and simmer very slowly for about an hour. To avoid gooey rice, avoid stirring.
13. When rice is tender and has absorbed the liquids, remove from stove. Serve hot. You can crumble bacon for a topping, according to taste.

recipes.title: Chicken Bog (Grand Strand)
recipes.text:
1. Boil chicken and onions in 4 cups of water until tender. If desired, debone chicken.
2. Slice sausage into ½-inch pieces. Add sausage, pepper and rice to chicken.
3. Simmer until all broth is absorbed and rice is cooked.

recipes.title: Chicken Bog II
recipes.text:
1. Put water, salt, onion, and chicken in pot. Boil until tender (about 1 hour).
2. Remove chicken, let cool, and remove bones.
3. Chop meat into bite-sized pieces.
4. Skim off fat from juices. Measure 3 ½ cups of this broth into a 6-quart saucepan. Add rice, chicken pieces and smoked sausage, herb seasoning and "chicken and herb" seasoning.
5. Cook these ingredients for 30 minutes. Bring to a boil and reduce heat and simmer, keeping covered the entire time. If rice mixture is too wet, cook uncovered until desired consistency.

recipes.title: Perlean
recipes.author: Emma and William McKinney
recipes.text: Dress and cut up one chicken as for frying. Boil until very tender, then add two cups of rice, half a cup of butter, some salt and plenty of pepper. Cook until it can be eaten with a fork.
recipes.note: 'Perlean' is one of the spellings of perloo, the Lowcountry word for a rice pilau; the dish is the bog with the sausage left out.

recipes.title: A Chicken Pilau
recipes.author: Mrs. Lettice Bryan
recipes.text: Take a fat young fowl, that has been nicely cleaned, skewer the legs to the body, chop the liver and gizzard small, with two onions and two boiled eggs; season them with salt, pepper and mace, and put them into the fowl, having moistened them with butter. Skewer some thin slices of ham to the breast, put it in a pan, with just enough water to cover it well, and boil it for half an hour, carefully removing the scum as it rises. Then put in a pint of rice, which has been picked and washed clean; boil them together till all are done; then serve it up, covering the fowl entirely with the rice, and send with it to table a boat of drawn butter, seasoned with pepper and nutmeg.
recipes.note: The pilau the bog descends from: one bird, its own broth, rice cooked in it. The fowl is left whole here; a bog is pulled off the bone.

names.name: collards
names.said: 'Greens' on a Carolina buffet usually means these; when a house cooks turnip or mustard greens in with them it says mixed greens.

text.what: Broad flat leaves of a loose-headed cabbage, stripped from the stem, cut in ribbons and stewed a long time with a piece of smoked pork until they are dark and soft, in a salty broth the South calls pot liquor. They are a staple of Southern cooking and one of the vegetables a Carolina barbecue buffet is judged by; cornbread is used to soak up what is left in the bowl. Eaten with black-eyed peas and cornbread on New Year's Day for wealth in the year to come.
text.story: The collard is an old non-heading cabbage, and the varieties grown in the United States thinned out after the Second World War as people left the land — five kinds in common cultivation by the end of it, with the rest kept alive by individual growers and seed savers and, since the early 2000s, by projects set up to bring them back. In the Appalachian counties the cabbage collard, yellow-green and part-heading, is the one grown; the coastal South grows the dark non-heading kind. The green carries meaning past the plate: Thelonious Monk wore a collard leaf in his lapel, Alice Walker wrote with collards, the first Obama state dinner had them on the menu, and the Latibah Collard Greens Museum opened in Charlotte in 2010. In eastern North Carolina the barbecue connection runs through the garden rather than the market — Bum's in Ayden cooks collards grown by the family and keeps a vegetable table few other eastern pits keep, and Grady's in Dudley stews them for a plate whose vegetables are peeled and chopped by hand that morning.
text.how: The leaves are washed several times to get the grit out, the thick centre rib is pulled or cut away, and the leaves are rolled and sliced into ribbons. They go into a pot with smoked or salted pork — ham hock, smoked turkey neck, pork neckbones, fatback — with diced onion, vinegar, salt and black, white or crushed red pepper, and some cooks add a little sugar. They cook down for an hour or more until soft. The broth left in the pot is the pot liquor and is served with them. The leaves may also be sliced thin and fermented into a collard sauerkraut, which is then cooked with flat dumplings.
text.today: On the buffet at Bum's in Ayden from the family garden; stewed at Grady's in Dudley; on the line at Dukes Bar-B-Que in Orangeburg; at Jackie Hite's in Leesville they were remembered as sweet and smoky; among the sides at Shealy's in Batesburg-Leesville and at Lewis Barbecue in Charleston, which is a Texas house that lists collards as the local one.

recipes.title: Boiled Collard Greens
ingredients: 2 tablespoons pork fat or some type of oil (optional)
1.5–2 lbs (700–900 g) smoked pork neck bone (optional, or, may substitute a much smaller amount of sausage)
¼ teaspoon cayenne pepper (powder or flakes; optional)
1 medium onion (optional), diced, chopped, or sliced
recipes.text:
1. Thoroughly wash the collard greens with very slightly soapy water, and rinse clean with plain water. Rinse at least twice to ensure removal of all grit and soap.
2. Leaves may be stripped from stems or left on if preferred. If left on, cut stems in small length (under 1 inch / 2.5 cm) for ease.
3. Chop leaves into bite-sized pieces. They may be folded lengthwise or widthwise to facilitate this.
4. Place chopped leaves into pot of boiling water—use just enough water to keep the greens off of the bottom of the pot; or else your greens will be watery and will have no flavor. Leaves will reduce in size while cooking, though not significantly. Depending on the size of the pot in which they're cooked, it may be necessary to cook some, then add more leaves after a brief time.
5. Add remaining ingredients.
6. Boil for approximately 20 minutes or until they reach desired tenderness. If overcooked, their taste will not be affected, but they'll be mushy.

recipes.title: Braised Collard Greens
recipes.text:
1. Place ham hocks, garlic cloves and a healthy pinch of sea salt in the 2 quarts of water, and slowly bring to a boil in a large stew pot until the ham hocks become tender.
2. Meanwhile, wash the greens thoroughly with cold water to remove dirt, and then wash them once in the vinegar (do not pat dry after vinegar wash). Next, remove the stems and shred the leaves into thin strips.
3. When the water is boiling, add the greens by the handful and turn the temperature down to medium. Simmer the greens uncovered until they are quite tender and the broth has reduced.
4. Serve with hot pepper vinegar, Tabasco, or red pepper flakes.

recipes.title: Greens (receipt 385)
recipes.author: Mrs. A. P. Hill
recipes.text: Kale, or cole, mustard, cabbage sprouts, turnip tops, to any of which may be added a few beet tops, the young shoots of the poke plant, all make good spring greens. Pick and wash them; let them lie in cold water at least an hour before they are used. Put them on in plenty of boiling water salted; boil briskly twenty minutes; they will sink to the bottom when done. Take them up in a colander; press the water from them; put upon a hot dish; cut across the leaves in several places with a sharp knife; pour over melted butter; dress with poached eggs, either placed upon the dish of greens or served in a separate dish. They are not good unless served hot. Some persons prefer greens boiled with a piece of bacon or hock bone of ham. No matter in what way they are cooked, poached eggs should accompany them.
recipes.note: The mixed-greens receipt: collard is not named, but cole is the same plant and the pot of several greens with a hock of ham in it is the dish. Poke shoots are the young growth of pokeweed, which is poisonous when older.

recipes.title: Bacon and Greens
recipes.author: Marion Cabell Tyree, editor
recipes.text:
The middling is generally used for this purpose: cut a piece about a foot square, boil three hours.

Take a good head of cabbage, cut, quarter, and wash clean; press the water out as dry as you can. Boil them one or two hours with half a pod of red pepper; put them on a dish and the middling on top. You can fry the cabbage next day, and make a savory dish, but it does not suit dyspeptics. The thin part of the middling is used for frying, and is called 'breakfast bacon.' — Mrs. P. W.
recipes.note: Cabbage here rather than collards, but the method is the one a collard pot still uses: a square of side meat boiled for hours, the greens cooked in its liquor, the meat laid on top. A dyspeptic is someone with a weak digestion.

recipes.title: Turnip Tops
recipes.author: Mrs. Mary Randolph
recipes.text: Are the shoots which grow out, (in the spring.) from the old turnip roots. Put them in cold water an hour before they are dressed; the more water they are boiled in, the better they will look; if boiled in a small quantity of water, they will taste bitter; when the water boils, put in a small handful of salt, and then your vegetables; they are still better boiled with bacon in the Virginia style: if fresh and young, they will be done in about twenty minutes—drain them on the back of a sieve, and put them under the bacon.
recipes.note: Turnip greens rather than collards, and the oldest of these: 'boiled with bacon in the Virginia style' in 1824.

names.name: cornbread
names.said: 'Bread' on an eastern menu board means the corn stick or the cornbread square; the sandwich roll is light bread.

etymology.root: corn (American English for maize) + bread. The bread is Native American in origin — the Hidatsa call baked cornbread naktsi, the Choctaw bvnaha — and the English name is the settlers' description of it
etymology.note: Corn pone, the egg-less and milk-less dough baked in an iron pan, keeps the older name; in the Appalachians a round of cornbread baked in a skillet is still a 'pone'.

text.what: A quick bread of cornmeal — meal, water or buttermilk, salt, fat, often egg and soda — baked in a pan, a skillet or a stick mould. It comes with eastern North Carolina barbecue in two forms. At the Skylight Inn in Ayden it is a flat, dense cake of stone-ground cornmeal, water, salt and the day's hog drippings, spread thin on a sheet pan, baked and cut in squares; Our State calls it more grit cake than bread. At Parker's, B's, Bum's and a third of the pits in six Coastal Plain counties it is the corn stick, an eight-inch baton of meal, fat and boiling water, baked, then deep-fried. West of the Coastal Plain the bread is hushpuppies.
text.story: Cornbread is the older bread of the South. Wheat withered and turned rancid in the heat and humidity, so the colonies baked ground corn and water over the fire or in the hearth, a bread learned from Native cooks; buttermilk, eggs, soda and pork fat came into it in the 1700s and 1800s, and sugar and wheat flour mostly in the 1900s, when steel roller mills replaced stone ones and the meal lost sweetness and turned from white to yellow. The Skylight Inn's cornbread stays on the old side of that line: cornmeal, water, salt and pork drippings, made the same way since Pete Jones opened in 1947, and served at his grandson Sam Jones's restaurants as 'Skylight Inn-style cornbread'. The corn stick is younger than it looks. Bob Melton's Rocky Mount restaurant, the state's first sit-down barbecue house, served cornsticks beside boiled potatoes and hushpuppies from 1924 until it closed in 2005, and NCpedia lists baked corn sticks first among the Coastal Plain's sides; but nearly every corn stick sold in the region now comes from Atkinson's Mills in Selma, which began making them in the mid-to-late 1970s. In the six counties around Wilson and Greenville about one pit in three serves them and the rest serve hushpuppies, and on B's menu board in Greenville they are simply 'bread'.
text.how: The Skylight cake is stone-ground cornmeal stirred with water and salt to a pourable batter, enriched with drippings from the pit, spread on a sheet pan and baked until it sets and browns; it comes out coarse, heavy and chewy, and is cut in squares for the tray. A corn stick is meal, fat and boiling water with a little soda, baked in an eight-inch stick and then dropped in the fryer, so that most of it is crisp and the middle soft; the grease keeps it from drying out the way a hushpuppy does, and it reheats. At B's the corn sticks are the plate's bread; at Bum's cornbread sits on the buffet with the vegetables. Skillet cornbread — batter poured into hot fat in a cast-iron pan — is the home form.
text.today: Skylight Inn serves it on every tray and sells it by the slice, a dollar each in September 2025; Sam Jones BBQ in Winterville and Raleigh lists 'Skylight Inn-style cornbread' with the Jones Family Original tray (2026). Parker's in Wilson sells cornsticks and hushpuppies both by the bulk order and puts hushpuppies on every plate. Corn sticks hold in six counties; the rest of the state fries hushpuppies.

recipes.title: Southern Cornbread
ingredients: 2 cups yellow or white self-rising corn meal
¼ cup olive oil or vegetable oil
recipes.text:
1. Preheat the oven to 425°F. If using cast-iron skillet, place it in the oven to heat. Do not preheat other types of skillets or baking pans.
2. If using non-cast-iron skillet or baking pan, coat with a non-stick spray.
3. Beat egg in the bowl. Stir in buttermilk and oil.
4. Stir in the cornmeal and mix until just moistened. The batter will be somewhat lumpy. Take care not to overmix.
5. Pour the batter into the skillet and place in the oven.
6. Bake until crust is a light golden brown and a toothpick inserted into the center comes out clean. For an 8-inch skillet this can be 25–30 minutes; for a 10-inch skillet or an 8x8-inch baking pan about 20–25 minutes.
7. Allow to cool for 5 minutes in pan before serving.
recipes.note: Unsweetened, in a cast-iron skillet; the form a Carolina kitchen bakes at home.

recipes.title: Cornbread I
ingredients: ¼ cup (60 g / 2.1 oz) shortening, melted
¼ cup (55 g / 1.9 oz) white granulated sugar (optional)
½ of a can whole corn kernels, drained (optional)
recipes.text:
1. Preheat oven to . Grease an baking pan.
2. Combine cornmeal, flour, baking powder, salt, and sugar in a large mixing bowl.
3. Add egg, milk, and shortening.
4. Beat until fairly smooth (about a minute).
5. If using corn and/or onion, fold in these ingredients.
6. Pour the mixture into the baking pan.
7. Bake for 20–25 minutes or until a toothpick inserted in center comes out clean. If corn is added to batter, increase time by ~50%
8. Serve hot!

recipes.title: Corn Meal Bread
recipes.author: Mrs. Mary Randolph
recipes.text: Rub a piece of butter the size of an egg, into a pint of corn meal—make it a batter with two eggs, and some new milk—add a spoonful of yeast, set it by the fire an hour to rise, butter little pans, and bake it.
recipes.note: A yeast-risen cornmeal bread, from the first cookbook of the American South. The dash is Mrs. Randolph's punctuation.

recipes.title: Batter Bread
recipes.author: Mrs. Mary Randolph
recipes.text: Take six spoonsful of flour and three of corn meal, with a little salt—sift them, and make a thin batter with four eggs, and a sufficient quantity of rich milk; bake it in little tin moulds in a quick oven.
recipes.note: Batter bread is the loose, spoonable cornbread — the ancestor of spoonbread; 'little tin moulds' are the forerunner of the stick mould that makes an eastern corn stick.

recipes.title: Indian Hoe Cakes
recipes.author: Mrs. Lettice Bryan
recipes.text:
Sift a quart of Indian meal, mix with it a large teaspoonful of salt, two large spoonfuls of butter, and make it a thin dough with sweet milk. Bake them as the pumpkin hoe cakes, and butter and eat them warm.

[Pumpkin Hoe Cakes, the receipt it refers to:] Heat your griddle rather brisk, place it over a bed of clear coals, grease it well with lard or butter, put on your dough in small thin cakes, and bake them hastily, turning them over once. As soon as both sides have a thin crust, and are of a light brown, send them to table, that they may be split and buttered while warm.
recipes.note: Indian meal is cornmeal. The method is borrowed from the receipt for pumpkin hoe cakes on the same page, which is quoted here in brackets so the receipt can be followed; the brackets are this site's, everything inside them is the book's.

names.name: Duke's mayonnaise
names.said: Said as the brand, not the ingredient: a Carolina cook asks for Duke's the way another asks for mayonnaise.

etymology.root: the founder's married surname: Eugenia Thomas Slade Duke of Greenville, South Carolina, who put her own name on the sandwiches she sold from 1917
etymology.first_attested: 1917 for the sandwiches; about 1923 for the bottled mayonnaise (Wikipedia)
etymology.note: No connection to Duke University, to Dukes Bar-B-Que of Orangeburg, or to the Duke family of Durham tobacco.

text.what: A bottled mayonnaise made in Mauldin, South Carolina, outside Greenville: egg yolks, oil and cider vinegar, with more yolk than most brands and no added sugar, which is where the tang comes from that the company sells it on. In the Carolinas it is the jar a white slaw, a potato salad, a deviled egg, a pimento cheese and a tomato sandwich are made with, and it is the third-largest mayonnaise brand in the United States, behind Hellmann's and Kraft, after a long stretch when it was sold mostly in the South.
text.story: Eugenia Thomas Slade Duke was born in Columbus, Georgia in October 1881, married Harry Cuthbert Duke at eighteen and moved to Greenville. In August 1917 she and her daughter Martha began selling sandwiches at Army canteens run by the YMCA, to bring money into the family; the soldiers at Camp Sevier, a National Guard training camp nearby, and her other customers kept asking about the mayonnaise, and by about 1923 she was bottling it on its own. She spoke at the Mayonnaise Manufacturers' Convention in Boston in November 1928. Demand outran her, and in 1929 she sold the business to the C. F. Sauer Company of Richmond, Virginia, where it became the flagship product; she followed Martha to California and opened the Duchess Sandwich Company and a catering company there. She worked for the passage of the Nineteenth Amendment, which gave women the vote. She died in 1968. The South Carolina legislature marked the brand's centenary in 2017. Falfurrias Capital Partners bought C. F. Sauer and the brand in 2019 and sold Sauer Brands, Duke's with it, to Advent International in 2025.
text.how: It is bought, not made, and the household use is as a binder: folded into shredded cabbage for a white slaw, into diced boiled potato and egg for potato salad, into mashed yolk for deviled eggs, into grated cheddar and pimento for pimento cheese. Made by hand, a mayonnaise is egg yolk with oil beaten in a drop at a time until it thickens, then faster, with vinegar or lemon juice and salt; mustard whisked into the yolk first makes it hold together more readily.
text.today: The plant is at Mauldin, southeast of Greenville, and was filmed for a How It's Made episode about mayonnaise in 2011. The brand is sold across the United States and in New Zealand, Australia and the Middle East, with Latin American sales announced in 2017.

recipes.title: Basic Mayonnaise
ingredients: 2½ teaspoons (12.5 mL) lemon juice and/or vinegar
recipes.text:
1. In a large bowl, beat the egg yolk with a wire whisk for about a minute.
2. Then add the mustard, salt, and half the lemon juice. Whisk for another minute - the mixture should thicken very slightly.
3. Then, very slowly, add half the oil with one hand whilst whisking with the other.
4. Start drop by drop, incorporating each drop before adding the next, and build up to a trickle.
5. Keep going until the oil is whisked in.
6. Add the rest of the lemon juice, whisk to combine.
7. Add the rest of the oil in the same manner as before.
8. Keep going until all the oil is whisked in.
9. If desired, stir in flavourings such as crushed garlic, or use the mayonnaise as a base for other sauces.
recipes.note: How the jar's contents are made from scratch, if a cook wants to.

recipes.title: Sana Mayonnaise
recipes.author: Marion Cabell Tyree, editor
recipes.text:
The yolks (raw) of two eggs.

Stir in oil, a drop at a time, until it begins to thicken, and then pour it in slowly still, but in greater quantities, stirring continually. Add cayenne pepper, salt, and vinegar to the taste.

If mustard is liked in the sauce, it must be mixed with the yolks of the eggs before dropping the oil.

This sauce should be nearly as thick as soft butter. It makes a delicious dressing for lettuce, celery, cold poultry or game; and also for cold boiled fish or pickled salmon. — Mrs. E. P., Cin.
recipes.note: A hand-made mayonnaise in a Southern cookbook of 1879, forty years before Eugenia Duke began bottling hers: two raw yolks, oil beaten in a drop at a time, cayenne, salt and vinegar.

recipes.title: Mayonnaise Dressing (Without Oil)
recipes.author: Emma and William McKinney
recipes.text: Mix together two tablespoonsful of flour, one teaspoonful of mustard, one teaspoonful of salt, one tablespoonful of sugar. Add this to two eggs well beaten, and lastly one cup of vinegar. Put on to cook in a double boiler and cook until thick, stirring frequently.
recipes.note: The cooked, oil-less kind — flour, egg, vinegar, sugar and mustard thickened over water — which is what many Southern kitchens meant by 'dressing' when oil was dear. Sweet, and close to what a boiled slaw dressing is.

names.name: fried okra
names.said: Taken by the scoop; a plate of it eats like a snack, which is why it gets called Southern popcorn.

text.what: Okra pods sliced into rounds, rolled in cornmeal and fried until the outside is crisp. It is the commonest way okra is cooked in the South and a standing side at barbecue houses and meat-and-three counters, eaten most in summer when the pods are in. Cutting the pods small keeps the outside crisp and leaves the inside slippery; whole pods can be fried too.
text.story: Okra came to the Americas on slave ships, and the method of frying it is thought to have roots in the Congo or West Africa before it arrived here. Fried vegetables and fritters spread through Southern cooking in the middle of the nineteenth century, and fried okra spread with them; the dish belongs to soul food, to Cajun cooking and to Gullah Geechee cooking, and is part of the Oklahoma state meal. In the Carolinas the barbecue connection is a farm one as much as a kitchen one: Brown's Bar-B-Que in Kingstree grows the okra it serves, along with corn, squash, butter beans, collards and cabbage, and McCabe's in Manning puts it on a buffet beside the hash and rice. Older Southern cookbooks cook it wet rather than dry — boiled and finished with cream and butter, or cut into a soup — and the frying is the newer habit.
text.how: The pods are topped and cut into rounds about half an inch thick. They are tossed or dredged in cornmeal, or dipped first in beaten egg or buttermilk and then in cornmeal, or cornmeal and flour, and fried in butter or vegetable oil, deep or in a pan, until browned. The batter may be seasoned with black pepper and cayenne. Drained and salted, and sometimes given a dipping sauce.
text.today: On the buffet line at Dukes Bar-B-Que in Orangeburg with the collards and corn nuggets; at McCabe's in Manning with the tomatoes and butter beans; at Brown's in Kingstree, grown on the family's own farm.

recipes.title: Fried Okra
ingredients: Spices as desired (e.g. salt, pepper, cayenne, thyme, etc.)
recipes.text:
1. Wash and drain a couple of handfuls of fresh okra.
2. Cut each okra into three or four slices, about ¾–1 inch (2–2.5 cm) long. Discard the stem.
3. Soak the okra in buttermilk or plain milk, drain, then dredge in seasoned flour and corn meal. A quick way to do this is to put ½ cup flour and 1 cup of corn meal in a plastic bag, add the spices you like, put in the okra, and shake.
4. Let the okra rest a few minutes. If any pieces look soggy, dredge them again in a flour/corn meal mix.
5. Deep fry the okra in hot oil until a light to medium brown. They're done in 2–3 minutes.
6. Drain, and enjoy!

recipes.title: Spicy Fried Okra
recipes.text:
1. Combine salt, peppers, and ½ cup flour. Coat okra with flour mixture.
2. Dip okra into hot sauce and dredge in remaining flour, adding more as needed. Let rest 2–3 minutes.
3. Heat oil in a large pot or a deep-fryer to 375°F. Add okra, 6 at a time, and fry 3–4 minutes until golden brown and crispy. Drain on a cooling rack and repeat until all okra has been fried.
4. Sprinkle fried okra with additional kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper and serve warm.

recipes.title: Okra
recipes.author: Marion Cabell Tyree, editor
recipes.text: Boil young okra till tender, in salt and water. Drain, add half a teacup of cream, and a heaping tablespoonful butter. Let it boil up, turn it out in a dish, sprinkle salt and pepper over it and serve hot.
recipes.note: The wet way, 1879: boiled and finished with cream and butter, with no cornmeal and no fat to fry in. An ancestor of the side rather than the fried dish.

names.name: green beans
names.said: 'Beans' on an eastern plate means these when the board also lists baked beans; Parker's in Wilson prints them as string beans.

etymology.root: green + bean; the older Southern names are string beans, for the fibre pulled off the pod before cooking, and snaps, for the sound the pod makes when broken
etymology.first_attested: 'snaps, string beans' as a recipe heading in Mary Randolph's The Virginia House-Wife, 1824
etymology.note: Modern varieties are bred stringless, so the first name describes a job the cook no longer has.

text.what: Whole or broken pods of the common bean, stewed slow with a piece of pork until they give up their squeak and take on the meat's salt, and served in a cup or a compartment beside the barbecue. They are the plain vegetable on a Carolina barbecue plate — a house that keeps one vegetable and no buffet usually keeps these — and the Southern way with them is long cooking rather than short, so the pod goes soft and olive rather than staying bright.
text.story: The pod bean has been in Southern cookbooks as long as there have been Southern cookbooks, under the names the field gave it. Mary Randolph heads the receipt 'Ragout of French Beans, Snaps, String Beans' in 1824 and boils them fifteen minutes before finishing them in brown gravy — the short French method. Maria Massey Barringer, writing at Concord, North Carolina in 1867, gives an hour and a half in salt water and then butter and cream, and adds that the more common way is to boil them with a piece of thin middling, the side of the hog. That second sentence is the Southern one, and the one the barbecue plate inherited. On barbecue menus the bean is the mark of a short kitchen: when Beau Hammond opened Henry's Smokehouse in Greenville, South Carolina, the whole side list was coleslaw and simmered green beans.
text.how: The pods are snapped or cut into lengths and the strings pulled off, where there are any. They go into a pot with a piece of streak-of-lean, fatback, ham hock or bacon and enough water to cover, and simmer an hour or more until soft; new potatoes are often dropped in with them for the last stretch. Salt, black pepper, sometimes a little sugar or a splash of the pot's own vinegar. The pot liquor goes into the bowl with them. A shorter method — fifteen or twenty minutes, then butter and cream — is in the old books and is not what a pit serves.
text.today: On the plate at B's Barbecue in Greenville, North Carolina, where the sides are slaw, potatoes or green beans; the whole side list at Henry's Smokehouse in Greenville, South Carolina, with the coleslaw; on the buffets at McCabe's in Manning and Shealy's in Batesburg-Leesville; printed as string beans on the menu at Parker's in Wilson.

recipes.title: Beans
recipes.author: Mrs. Barringer, of North Carolina
recipes.text: String, and break them in halves; boil in salt and water, and throw in a piece of soda the size of a pea, if they are old, or you wish them a fine color. Boil them for an hour and a half; pour off the water, and dress with butter and cream, and sprinkle over some pepper. But a more common way is to boil them with a piece of thin middling.
recipes.note: A North Carolina book of 1867. The last sentence is the method the barbecue plate kept: the beans cooked with a piece of the side of the hog. Soda in the water was used to hold the green, and is not used now.

recipes.title: Ragout of French Beans, Snaps, String Beans
recipes.author: Mrs. Mary Randolph
recipes.text: Let them be young and fresh gathered, string them, and cut them in long thin slices; throw them in boiling water for fifteen minutes; have ready some well seasoned brown gravy, drain the water from the beans, put them in the gravy, stew them a few minutes, and serve them garnished with forcemeat balls; there must not be gravy enough to float the beans.
recipes.note: The short French method, 1824, with all three names for the bean in the title. A ragout is a stew; forcemeat balls are seasoned minced meat rolled and cooked.

recipes.title: Lima Beans
recipes.author: Mrs. Barringer, of North Carolina
recipes.text: Let them boil about an hour, and when the water is poured off, season with salt, pepper, and butter. Send to table hot. Dried Lima beans must be soaked over night, and boiled two hours, or until they are soft, and should have some cream added to the dressing.
recipes.note: Butter beans, on the same page — the other bean a Carolina buffet keeps, and the one in a Brunswick stew.

names.name: hash and rice
names.said: Just 'hash'. The rice is understood; 'hash and rice' is how the menu writes it.

etymology.root: French hacher 'to chop up' (from Old French hache 'axe') → English hash, verb, 1650s, 'to hack, chop into small pieces' → hash, noun, 1660s, 'a stew of meat cut into small pieces'
etymology.first_attested: English verb 1650s, noun 1660s (Online Etymology Dictionary). The South Carolina dish is in print by 1854, when the Abbeville Press and Banner reported 'rich hash' at a barbecue at Matthews' Spring (Moss, 2020).
etymology.note: Robert Moss traces the dish's name to 'haslet', an old English word for the viscera of a butchered animal — the head, liver and lights that went into the first hash pots. That is a claim about the dish; the dictionary word is the French chopping verb, and the two may have met in the pot. Folk — a Huguenot 'hachis' brought to Charleston is proposed on Destination BBQ without a citation.

text.what: A thick stew, or gravy, of pork cooked down with onions until it can be eaten with a spoon, ladled over white rice beside the barbecue. It is South Carolina's side the way Brunswick stew is Georgia's, Virginia's and North Carolina's, and it is barely known outside the state. The old hash was made from what the whole hog left after the barbecue — the head, the liver and the lights (the lungs) — simmered for a day in an iron pot; most restaurants now use shoulder or ham. Three loose regions: mustard in the Midlands, vinegar and liver in the Lowcountry, beef and onions in the Upstate.
text.story: Hash was on the table before the Civil War in the counties along the Savannah River. Robert Moss found it in the Abbeville Press and Banner — 'rich hash' at a barbecue at Matthews' Spring in 1854, 'smoking hash' at Robinson's Spring in 1858 — and at an 1861 barbecue for the Edgefield Riflemen, and Estella Jones, who had been enslaved on plantations near Augusta, remembered the men cooking hash and rice there. The cooks were Black, the pots were iron, the fire was wood and the cooking took a day; what went in was the head, the liver and the lights that the whole hog left behind, which Moss reads in the name itself, haslet, the old word for the viscera. Howard Conyers, who grew up with it in the Black churches of the Midlands, calls it liver-and-lights hash and says it is now nearly impossible to get unless you kill your own hog, because federal rules keep lungs out of commercial processing. Hash houses stood across the Upstate, some set up by textile-mill owners to draw farmers to town. The Post and Courier reported in 2020 that hash was fading from the state's restaurants; Moss answered in Southern Living that new places were adding it to their menus. *Tradition holds —* the pot is stirred all night, and some say it must be cooked by the light of the moon; Lake High of the South Carolina Barbeque Association calls the finished thing 'liquid sausage'.
text.how: The meat — shoulder, ham, or the head and liver where a pit still uses them — is boiled until it falls from the bone, picked, then ground through a hand-crank grinder or chopped, and returned to the pot with onions and its own stock to simmer until it thickens to gravy. The seasoning marks the region: mustard in the Midlands and the Dutch Fork, vinegar and ketchup in the Lowcountry, beef with onions and butter and no dominant base in the Upstate (called white hash), a red hash around Sumter. Potatoes go in at some pits and never at others. Served by the ladle over white rice, beside the pork, on a buffet plate or in a styrofoam bowl.
text.today: Hash is on the buffet at Dukes in Orangeburg and Walterboro, at Sweatman's in Holly Hill, at Midway in Buffalo and at True BBQ in West Columbia; Big T in Gadsden and Brown's in Kingstree still put hog's head and liver in the pot (Moss, 2020). A survey found it most common around Columbia. Fire departments and civic clubs cook it in big pots for fundraisers.

recipes.title: To Hash Pig's Head
recipes.author: Marion Cabell Tyree, editor
recipes.text:
Take head, feet, and haslet of pig; boil them until done, then cut them up fine, taking out the bones.

Put it back in the same vessel with liquor and cook till done, then thicken with a little flour. Add two hard-boiled eggs and one cup walnut catsup. — Mrs. Dr. G.
ingredients: Black pepper, salt, a little sage.
recipes.note: The haslet is the heart, liver and lights (lungs). This is the head-and-organ hash that South Carolina pits still cook, written down in 1879 without the state's name on it; the rice is not in the receipt, because in Virginia it was eaten on its own.

recipes.title: Southern Hash
recipes.author: Emma and William McKinney
recipes.text: Put vegetables through the meat chopper, using coarse cutter; cook in the stock, covered, until tender; add beef, salt, and pepper, and when hot turn on a platter and garnish with toast points. If corned beef and stock are used, use salt with care.
recipes.note: A beef hash, not a hog's-head hash, and served on toast rather than rice; printed in 1922 as the Southern one.

recipes.title: To Make Hash (receipt 123)
recipes.author: Mrs. A. P. Hill
recipes.text: Meats that have been once done, only require to be warmed over. To cook them again renders them tough and insipid. Cut up the vegetables to be used for seasoning — onions, potatoes, tomatoes, etc., as may be preferred. Put the butter, flour, salt, pepper, and vegetables (or spices if preferred as seasoning) into the stew-pan with all the cold gravy that may have been saved; essence of ham answers a good purpose; a few inches of portable soup is very good if there should not be sufficiency of gravy; a teacup of boiling water for a pound of meat; very little water should be used. Cover the stew-pan and let this stew gently a quarter of an hour, shaking the stew-pan frequently. Have the meat minced fine, removing all bones and gristle, add to the gravy, stirring it in well. Let it remain until the meat is thoroughly hot, and serve. Use catsup upon the plate for extempore dressing. Very little cooking is necessary and very little gravy. When there is stuffing, a small quantity may be used.
recipes.note: Hash in its older, wider sense — cooked meat minced and warmed in its own gravy. A few words in this paragraph are damaged in the scan and are read from context.
