names.name: hushpuppies
names.said: One word on the Carolina menu; the pit fries them to order and puts a handful in the tray.

etymology.root: hush + puppy. 'Hush puppy' was slang for something that keeps a thing quiet — hush money in a 1738 British account of smuggling, and from 1879 the gravy or pot liquor that kept the hounds from growling, meaning a growling stomach — and was applied to deep-fried cornmeal by 1899; current in Georgia by 1927 (Moss)
etymology.first_attested: 1899 for the fried cornmeal sense (Online Etymology Dictionary; Wikipedia). Moss's earliest Georgia example is the Macon Telegraph, 1927, a Methodist church fish fry; the South Carolina forerunner, 'red horse bread', is in the Augusta Chronicle in 1903.
etymology.note: Folk, all of them: that hunters and fishermen tossed fried batter to their dogs to hush them; that Confederate soldiers silenced camp dogs with it; that escaping enslaved people threw it to tracking hounds; that Ursuline nuns brought croquettes de maïs to New Orleans in the 1720s. Robert Moss finds no nineteenth-century source calling fried cornbread hushpuppies and reads the name as a joke about stopping a growling stomach. The shoe brand is a 1961 trademark.

text.what: Balls or fingers of cornmeal batter — meal, a little flour, egg, buttermilk or water, salt, soda, often onion — dropped by the spoonful into hot oil and fried until the outside is crisp and dark gold and the inside soft and steaming. In the Carolinas they are the bread of the fish fry and, since the 1940s, of the barbecue tray: Lexington pits serve them with the shoulder and red slaw in place of rolls, and most eastern pits give them with whole hog, though a third of the pits in the Wilson–Greenville counties give corn sticks instead. Sweeter and lighter than a corn stick, and fried, not baked.
text.story: The first of them had a fish in the name. Romeo Govan, born into slavery in the 1840s, settled after Emancipation near Cannon's Bridge on the Edisto River, five miles from Bamberg, South Carolina, and by the early 1900s ran a club house where the state's political and civic clubs came for his fish fries; the Augusta Chronicle wrote in 1903 of his never-to-be-forgotten 'red horse bread' — cornmeal, water, salt and egg dropped by spoonfuls into the lard the fish had fried in, named for the red horse, a river fish. Govan died in 1915; red horse bread lived on at fish fries in Bamberg, Orangeburg and Dorchester counties through the 1920s. Across the Savannah the same fritter was picking up another name: the Macon Telegraph in 1927 has a church fish-fry chairman cooking 'the hushpuppies', in quotation marks, a word still strange, and by 1940 a Chronicle fishing columnist could write that red horse cornbread is often called hush puppies on the Georgia side. Florida fishing camps fed them to Northern visitors and the name won. In North Carolina the hushpuppy walked from the fish camps of the Piedmont rivers into the barbecue houses in the 1940s: Kennedy's in Greensboro advertised barbecue, Brunswick stew, slaw and hushpuppies in 1949, and Warner Stamey — whose son Keith says he picked the idea up from a friend's fish camp, the Friendly Road Inn in Greensboro — made them the bread of Lexington-style barbecue.
text.how: Self-rising cornmeal, or meal with soda and a little flour, salt, an egg, buttermilk or water, and chopped onion for the savoury kind; some pits sweeten the batter and some add beer or jalapeño. The batter rests thick enough to hold a spoon, is dropped into oil at frying heat — in the old way, the oil the fish came out of — and fried until it floats and browns. Lexington houses fry them to order and shape them round, oblong or as fingers, dense or light, house by house. Served hot in the tray or in a paper bag as a side.
text.today: Lexington Barbecue: hushpuppies small $3.10, large $3.90 cash (September 2026); the Barbecue Center gives a choice of hushpuppies or a potato bun with every plate. House-Autry Mills of Four Oaks still sells the Original Recipe Hushpuppy Mix descended from Walter Thompson's post-war Swansboro business.

recipes.title: Hush Puppies
recipes.text:
1. Pour oil 3–4 inches (7.5 cm to 10 cm) deep in a pan and preheat to 370°F (~190°C).
2. In bowl mix cornmeal, flour, baking powder, baking soda, salt, and cayenne.
3. Mix in eggs, green onions, milk, and ¼ cup vegetable oil.
4. Spoon 6–7 tablespoons of the batter into preheated oil.
5. Fry, stirring constantly for overall browning, until golden brown.
6. Remove from heat and drain on paper towels.

recipes.title: Corn Fritters
recipes.author: Mrs. Lettice Bryan
recipes.text: Having removed the shucks and silks from a dozen young tender ears of corn, grate or scrape the grains fine from the cobs, mix with it the beaten yolks of four eggs, two spoonfuls of flour, a salt-spoonful of salt, and a teaspoonful of pepper; mix the whole together, stirring it till it is well intermingled; then drop it by spoonfuls into a pan of boiling butter or lard, making them all as nearly the same shape and size as possible; turn them over once, and when both sides are of a light brown, serve them up. It is a breakfast dish, and is quite an agreeable relish.
recipes.note: An ancestor, not the thing: the hushpuppy's name is not printed anywhere before the 1890s, but the method — a stiff batter dropped by the spoonful into deep hot fat and turned once — is the fritter's, and it is already in print in this form.

names.name: mac and cheese
names.said: Said as one word on a menu board — 'mac and cheese' — and counted as a vegetable on a meat-and-three line.

text.what: Macaroni in a cheese sauce, most often cheddar, baked in a dish until the top browns. On a Carolina barbecue buffet it sits with the vegetables and is taken as one, cut in squares from a hotel pan rather than spooned; a stovetop version bound with a white sauce is the other common form. In the Lowcountry and in Black Southern kitchens the baked, custard-set kind is often called macaroni pie.
text.story: The dish reaches the South through the first cookbook written here. Elizabeth Raffald printed a baked macaroni with cream, butter and Parmesan in England in 1769; one account has James Hemings, enslaved by Thomas Jefferson and trained as a cook in France, bringing the method to the United States, and Jefferson served 'a pie called macaroni' at a state dinner in 1802. Mary Randolph's The Virginia House-Wife of 1824 carries a recipe under the name macaroni and cheese: three things, macaroni, cheese and butter, layered and baked in a hot oven. Mrs. A. P. Hill's Southern cookbook of 1867 gives the same layering and then a custard version with three beaten eggs poured over. Factory macaroni and factory cheese put it within reach of every household, and by then it had stopped being a rich person's dish. On a Carolina barbecue menu it is a late arrival and a well-established one: at Luella's in Asheville it is on the board because the daughter the restaurant is half named for likes it.
text.how: Macaroni is boiled in salted water until just tender and drained. For the baked kind it is layered in a dish with grated cheddar, salt and pieces of butter, covered with milk or cream, and baked until the top browns; for the custard kind beaten eggs and evaporated or whole milk are poured over the layers so the dish sets and can be cut. A stovetop version makes a Mornay — a white sauce with cheese melted into it — and stirs the macaroni through. At a pit it is baked in a hotel pan in the morning and held warm on the line.
text.today: On the buffet at Dukes Bar-B-Que in Orangeburg, at Shealy's in Batesburg-Leesville, at Brown's in Kingstree, and at Jackie Hite's in Leesville while it ran. Among the sides at Lewis Barbecue in Charleston. At Luella's in Asheville it is the daughter's recipe. Barack Obama ate it at 12 Bones in Asheville on April 23, 2010, with ribs, corn pudding and sweet tea.

recipes.title: Macaroni
recipes.author: Mrs. Mary Randolph
recipes.text:
Boil as much macaroni as will fill your dish, in milk and water, till quite tender; drain it on a sieve, sprinkle a little salt over it, put a layer in your dish, then cheese and butter as in the polenta, and bake it in the same manner.

[The polenta receipt it points back to, from the page before:] …slices of cheese and butter, put the dish in a quick oven; twenty or thirty minutes will bake it.
recipes.note: Three things — macaroni, cheese, butter — layered and baked, in the 1824 book that carries the first American recipe under this name. The brackets are this site's; the words inside them are the book's.

recipes.title: Macaroni (receipt 564)
recipes.author: Mrs. A. P. Hill
recipes.text: Wash half a pound of macaroni; boil it in plenty of water until tender; lay in a shallow earthen dish a layer of the macaroni (the pieces should be broken the same size), one of grated cheese, and salt to taste. Lay over slices of butter; cover with sweet milk or cream. Bake in a moderate oven, ten or fifteen minutes. Serve hot. Another way is, to arrange alternate layers of boiled macaroni and grated cheese. Pour over a custard made of three well beaten eggs, two tablespoonfuls of stale grated bread, one tablespoonful of butter, and half a teacup of cream or sweet milk. Bake half an hour, or until the custard is set. If boiled too long, it will lose its shape; if baked too much, it will be dry and tough.
recipes.note: The second method — eggs poured over the layers and baked until set — is the macaroni pie that cuts in squares.

recipes.title: Aunt Katy's Macaroni
recipes.author: Emma and William McKinney
recipes.text: Put macaroni on to boil in water with a little salt. When tender drain off water. Put in a baking dish first a layer of macaroni, then cheese, crumbs and butter. Pour milk over it and bake.
ingredients: One-half small sized package of macaroni,
Butter the size of a walnut.

recipes.title: Macaroni and Cheese I
ingredients: ½ cup (8 tbsp / 1 stick / 125 g / 4.4 oz) butter
1 cup (125 g / 4.4 oz) Parmesan or Monterey Jack cheese
½ tsp cayenne pepper, or to taste
1 pound (450 g) macaroni noodles, boiled and drained
recipes.text:
1. Make a roux using the butter and flour.
2. Add the heated milk, and whisk until smooth to complete the white sauce.
3. Mix in the cheese and cayenne pepper.
4. Mix the cheese sauce into the cooked macaroni noodles until well-coated.

recipes.title: Macaroni and Cheese (Baked)
ingredients: [Base] ½ lb (227 g) dry elbow macaroni
recipes.text:
1. Preheat oven to 350 °F.
2. In a large pot of boiling, salted water, cook the pasta until it is al dente.
3. While the pasta is cooking, melt the butter in a separate pot.
4. Whisk in the flour and mustard and keep it moving for about five minutes. Make sure it is free of lumps.
5. Stir in the milk, onion, bay leaf, and paprika. Simmer for ten minutes and remove the bay leaf.
6. Temper in the egg.
7. Stir in ¾ of the cheese.
8. Season with salt and pepper.
9. Fold the macaroni into the mix and pour into a 2-quart casserole dish.
10. Top with remaining cheese.
11. Melt the butter in a sauté pan, add breadcrumbs, and toss to coat.
12. Top the macaroni with the bread crumbs.
13. Bake for 30 minutes.
14. Remove from oven and rest for 10 minutes before serving.

names.name: outside brown
names.said: Ask for it 'brown', or for 'extra outside brown'; some counters chop it in, some set it aside for the order.

text.what: The dark crust from the outside of a pork shoulder — the bark, where ten hours of smoke and dip have cooked into the surface — ordered by name at Lexington pits. Regulars ask for extra outside brown on a tray or sandwich; ordered 'brown', the meat comes chopped from that crust rather than from the pale inside. The word marks the Piedmont. Eastern pits chop the whole hog together, skin and all, and have no order for it, though NCpedia notes that some North Carolinians follow South Carolina in separating skin, the dry 'outside meat' and the juicier 'inside meat'.
text.story: Bob Garner, writing about Lexington Barbecue in 2012, watched the shoulders roast ten hours over oak coals, hickory when it could be had, the attendants shovelling fresh coals from the fireboxes under the dripping meat every half hour; when the shoulders came off, that outside 'brown', as it is called, was lifted off the meat and saved for special orders. A regular quoted by Carolina Country in 2018 counted 'chopped brown' among the ten ways to order. When Southern Living's readers named Lexington Barbecue the best in the state in 2026, the News & Observer explained the house words to newcomers: regulars ask for extra outside brown, the caramelized, heavily smoked end bits, and the pork comes dressed in a thin vinegar-and-ketchup dip. Barbecue Bros, in 2019, corrected a New York pitmaster who had called it an off-menu item: it is the bark from the shoulders, which locals know to ask for. *Tradition holds —* the crust is prized because it carries the most smoke and dip, and because a shoulder yields little of it; one shoulder feeds many trays and the brown runs out first. *Inference —* the word does for the Piedmont what the chopped skin does for the east: it puts the pit's crust, not only its meat, into the order.
text.how: Order the tray or sandwich and add the word: 'brown', 'outside brown' or 'extra brown'. The counter takes the crust set aside from the morning's shoulders and chops it in, or chops the whole order from it. It is darker and drier than the inside meat and has taken more of the dip. Coarse chopped shows it best; fine chopping hides it. *Tradition holds —* the supply is finite and late in the day the answer is often no.
text.today: Lexington Barbecue's menu (September 2026) lists chopped, sliced and coarse chop trays and sandwiches and no brown; the order is spoken at the counter. The News & Observer's 2026 guide to the house treats it as the thing regulars ask for.

recipes.title: Eastern North Carolina Barbecued Pig
ingredients: Your favorite vinegar-based Eastern NC sauce
recipes.text:
1. Salt hams, ribs/midsection and shoulders liberally and place skin side up on either a gas or charcoal grill or a BBQ pit.
2. Keep lid closed, and aim for a heat of approximately 275–350°F.
3. Allow 1 hour per 10 pounds cooking time (gas or charcoal).
4. 2 hours before being done, place pig with the skin side down. As soon as it is flipped, pour BBQ sauce on meat side.
5. Close lid and allow skin to crisp.
6. The pig will be done to perfection when the ham bone can be twisted freely.
7. Lift lid and allow guests to pick/pull meat, or the chef can remove meat and chop to their liking on a chopping block.
recipes.note: Step five is where the brown comes from: the pig is turned skin down for the last two hours and the lid kept shut so the outside crisps.

recipes.title: To Barbecue Any Kind of Fresh Meat (receipt 200)
recipes.author: Mrs. A. P. Hill
recipes.text: Gash the meat. Broil slowly over a solid fire. Baste constantly with a sauce composed of butter, mustard, red and black pepper, vinegar. Mix these in a pan, and set it where the sauce will keep warm, not hot. Have a swab made by tying a piece of clean, soft cloth upon a stick about a foot long; dip this in the sauce and baste with it. Where a large carcass is barbecued, it is usual to dig a pit in the ground outdoors, and lay narrow bars of wood across. Very early in the morning fill the pit with wood; set it burning, and in this way heat it very hot. When the wood has burned to coals, lay the meat over. Should the fire need replenishing, keep a fire outside burning, from which draw coals, and scatter evenly in the pit under the meat. Should there be any sauce left pour it over the meat. For barbecuing a joint, a large gridiron answers well; it needs constant attention; should be cooked slowly and steadily.
recipes.note: Constant basting over coals is what builds a crust on the outside of a joint. A few characters in this paragraph are damaged in the scan and are read from context; the line 'Gash the meat' runs straight into 'Broil slowly' in the printing.

recipes.title: To Barbecue Shoat
recipes.author: Mrs. Lettice Bryan
recipes.text: Take either a hind or fore quarter, rub it well with salt, pepper, and a small portion of molasses, and if practicable, let it lie for a few hours; then rinse it clean, and wipe it dry with a cloth, and place it on a large gridiron, over a bed of clear coals. Do not barbecue it hastily, but let it cook slowly for several hours, turning it over occasionally, and basting it with nothing but a little salt-water and pepper, merely to season and moisten it a little. When it is well done, serve it without a garnish, and having the skin taken off, which should be done before it is put down to roast, squeeze over it a little lemon juice, and accompany it with melted butter and wine, bread sauce, raw sallad, slaugh, or cucumbers, and stewed fruit. Beef may be barbecued in the same manner.
recipes.note: The contrary instruction, 1839: the skin is taken off before the meat goes down, so there is no browned outside to ask for. A Lexington shoulder is cooked with the skin on and the outside is the part regulars order by name.

names.name: peach cobbler
names.said: 'Cobbler' on a Carolina dessert board usually means peach in summer and whatever fruit was put up the rest of the year.

text.what: Sliced peaches sweetened and thickened in a deep dish and covered with a crust — pastry, biscuit dough or a batter — then baked until the top browns and the fruit bubbles at the edge. It is a barbecue dessert of the same family as banana pudding, ordered by the cup or the square after the tray, and served warm, often with ice cream. The Southern kind is frequently closer to a deep-dish pie, with a bottom crust as well as a top.
text.story: Cobbler is what English settlers made when they could not make a suet pudding: with Dutch ovens, they covered a stewed filling with a layer of pastry, and later with plain biscuits, scone batter or dumplings fitted together. The first recorded recipe may be in The Kentucky Housewife, Lettice Bryan's book of 1839, where it is 'A Peach Pot-Pie' and the text says cobler is what it is often termed. Abby Fisher, born into slavery in South Carolina and dictating her book in San Francisco in 1881, gives it with two layers of pastry, peaches cut to the size of a plum, and cinnamon. The name's origin is not settled — it may come from the archaic cobeler, a wooden bowl, or from the cobbled look of the crust. North Carolina has its own deep-dish version under its own name, the sonker, made in and around Surry County. At Allen & Son outside Chapel Hill, Keith Allen rolled the cobbler crusts from his grandmother's recipe and the desserts were the second reason people came.
text.how: Peaches are peeled and sliced, tossed with sugar and a thickener — cornstarch or flour — and sometimes lemon juice and cinnamon, and either put straight into a buttered baking dish or brought to a boil in a pan first so the syrup thickens. The topping is rolled pastry, spoonfuls of biscuit dough, or a batter poured over; a Southern deep-dish version lines the bottom of the dish as well, cuts air-holes in the top and bakes it brown. Forty to fifty minutes in a hot oven. Served warm, with cold sweet milk in the old books and with vanilla ice cream now.
text.today: On the dessert board at Lexington Barbecue, whose list is pies and cobbler with no pudding on it; at Allen & Son in Chapel Hill it was made in the house from a family recipe, with ice cream churned daily.

recipes.title: A Peach Pot-Pie
recipes.author: Mrs. Lettice Bryan
recipes.text:
A peach pot-pie, or cobler, as it is often termed, should be made of clingstone peaches, that are very ripe, and then pared and sliced from the stones. Prepare a pot or oven with paste, as directed for the apple pot-pie, put in the prepared peaches, sprinkle on a large handful of brown sugar, pour in plenty of water to cook the peaches without burning them, though there should be but very little liquor or syrup when the pie is done. Put a paste over the top, and bake it with moderate heat, raising the lid occasionally, to see how it is baking. When the crust is brown, and the peaches very soft, invert the crust on a large dish, put the peaches evenly on, and grate loaf sugar thickly over it. Eat it warm or cold. Although it is not a fashionable pie for company, it is very excellent for family use, with cold sweet milk.

[An Apple Pot-Pie, pages 267–268, for the paste it refers to:] Rub the bottom and sides of a porridge-pot, or small oven, with butter, and then with dry flour. Roll out some pieces of plain or standing paste about half an inch thick, line the sides of the pot or oven with the pieces of paste, letting them nearly touch in the bottom.
recipes.note: Possibly the first recorded cobbler recipe, and it spells the word cobler. Loaf sugar is refined sugar broken from a cone. The brackets are this site's, everything inside them is the book's.

recipes.title: Peach Cobbler (recipe 143)
recipes.author: Mrs. Abby Fisher
recipes.book: What Mrs. Fisher Knows About Old Southern Cooking
recipes.text: Peel the peaches (freestones) and make a pastry the same way as for pie, and roll out the dough as thin as for pie crust. Put one layer at the bottom of the dish, and cut the peaches into pieces the size of a plum and fill the dish with them, sprinkling them freely with fine sugar. Cover them over with another layer of pastry, cut with a knife two or three air-holes on the top and put to bake. Let it bake brown. It makes a delicious luncheon or dessert. Season the peaches with powdered cinnamon to taste. See recipe for all kinds of pastry.
recipes.note: Two crusts and air-holes: the deep-dish Southern form. Freestone peaches part from the stone; Lettice Bryan's receipt calls for clingstones instead.

recipes.title: Sweet Peach Cobbler
recipes.text:
1. [Filling] Preheat oven to 400°F.
2. [Filling] Combine granulated sugar and cornstarch in a mixing bowl.
3. [Filling] Stir in peaches and lemon juice to make a sugary-brown syrup.
4. [Filling] Bring the peach mixture to a boil in a saucepan, and simmer until it thickens. Transfer to a 2-quart casserole dish, and put into the oven.
5. [Topping] Combine the flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt in a mixing bowl. Stir, until well mixed.
6. [Topping] Add shortening, and cut with a pastry blender until well mixed.
7. [Topping] Mix in milk to make a ball of dough.
8. [Assembly] Remove casserole dish from the oven. Add dough in spoon-sized dollops on top of fruit.
9. [Assembly] Return to 400°F oven. Bake for 25–30 minutes, until topping turns brown.
10. [Assembly] Serve.

recipes.title: Easy Peach Cobbler
recipes.text:
1. Preheat oven to 375°F.
2. Melt margarine in quart size baking pan or dish. Set aside.
3. Mix baking powder, flour, sugar, and milk. Pour this batter over the melted margarine, and do not stir.
4. Arrange peaches over the batter.
5. Bake 20–30 minutes.

recipes.title: Basic Cobbler
ingredients: Salt (optional; add only if butter is unsalted)
1 cup fresh fruit (e.g. peaches, blackberries, cherries, etc.)
recipes.text:
1. Preheat oven to 350°F (175°C).
2. Place the butter in a deep 9½ x 12-inch baking dish. Put dish in oven to melt butter while preparing other ingredients. If butter is unsalted, add a touch of salt to the pan as well.
3. Add flour and sugar to a bowl and sift together lightly. Create a well in the center of the mixture, and pour the milk into the well. Mix together with a wire whisk until smooth.
4. Remove pan from oven. Pour batter into dish on top of melted butter. Do not stir. Spoon the fresh fruit out evenly across the top, but again, do not stir.
5. Place cobbler in oven and bake uncovered until golden brown.
recipes.note: The method without the fruit named, for whatever is in season.

names.name: pickles
names.said: 'Pickle' on a Carolina plate means cucumber unless the board says chow-chow.

text.what: Cucumbers held in brine or vinegar until they sour, sliced into rounds or spears and put on the plate beside the meat, with the sandwich, or loose in a dish on the table. Sweet pickle — cucumbers in a vinegar-and-sugar syrup with spices — is the common Carolina one; chow-chow, a chopped relish of cabbage, green tomato, onion and pepper, does the same job in a spoonful. The point of them on a barbecue plate is acid and salt against fat.
text.story: The pickled cucumber is old and worldwide, and the sweet Southern one is a strand of it: cucumbers marinated in vinegar, sugar and spices rather than left to sour in salt. The bread-and-butter pickle — sweeter than most, spiced with coriander — is credited to Omar and Cora Fanning, Illinois cucumber farmers who trademarked the name in 1923 after bartering pickles made from their undersized cucumbers with their grocer for staples. North Carolina's pickle industry started the same way, out of a surplus. In the mid-1920s Shikrey Baddour, a Lebanese immigrant from Goldsboro, saw farmers around Mount Olive wasting cucumber crops and began buying them, brining them in tanks and offering the brine stock to pickle firms; nobody bought it. In 1926 the Mount Olive business leader I. F. Witherington relaunched the idea as a company that would pack and sell the pickles itself, and thirty-seven shareholders put in $19,500 — a community proposition, they called it. The plant stands where the board bought an acre from the farmer J. A. Westbrook for $1,000, at the corner of Cucumber Boulevard and Vine Street. Mt. Olive now sells more than 230 million jars a year and employs more than 1,200 people in North Carolina. In 1999 the Farm Labor Organizing Committee called a boycott over the pay and conditions of cucumber pickers; it ended in 2004 when the company agreed to raise what it paid for cucumbers and growers pledged higher wages.
text.how: For a sweet pickle the cucumbers are cut, soaked, and cooked or steeped in vinegar with sugar, turmeric, celery seed, mustard seed and whole spices, then sealed in jars; for a sour or dill pickle they are packed in a crock or barrel with garlic, dill heads, mustard seed, leaves and salt, covered with cooled boiled water, weighted under the brine and left to ferment for weeks. Chow-chow is chopped cabbage, green tomato, onion and pepper salted overnight, drained, then simmered in vinegar with sugar, mustard seed and celery seed. On the plate they are cut in rounds or spears; on a chopped sandwich they go under the slaw or on top of it, by the house's habit.
text.today: Pickles are part of the standing list of fixins in both states, and the South Carolina plate — pork, rice, hash, coleslaw, sweet pickles, white bread, iced tea — carries them by default. Mt. Olive, in Wayne County, was the top-selling pickle brand in the South in an analysis of 2024 nationwide consumption by the delivery service Instacart.

recipes.title: Cucumber Pickle
recipes.author: Emma and William McKinney
recipes.text: Take enough cucumbers to fill a two-gallon jar. Cut into lengthwise pieces and soak until fresh. Cover with equal parts of water and vinegar, and boil an hour and ten minutes. Then take them out and boil one and one-half hours in one gallon of fresh vinegar, two pounds of sugar, one tablespoonful of celery seed, one tablespoonful of tumeric, one teaspoonful each of cloves, mace and ginger, one tablespoonful of black pepper, and one of horse radish. When cold add one-half teaspoonful of cayenne pepper.
recipes.note: A sweet pickle in the Southern proportion — two pounds of sugar to a gallon of vinegar. 'Tumeric' is the book's spelling.

recipes.title: Tar Heel Chow Chow
recipes.author: Emma and William McKinney
recipes.text:
Chop one head of cabbage, one gallon of green tomatoes, and one quart of onions. Add one-half cup of salt, put in a bag and let it drain for twenty-four hours.

Then put in kettle and add about two pounds of brown sugar, one cup of white mustard seed, and one-half cup of celery seed. Cover with good apple vinegar and cook until done, about three or four hours. To the above add one or two pods of chopped red pepper.
recipes.note: North Carolina's relish under North Carolina's nickname, printed in Chicago in 1922.

recipes.title: Aunt Caroline's Own Pickle
recipes.author: Emma and William McKinney
recipes.text: Chop fine one-half gallon of green tomatoes, one pint of onions, one pint of green and red peppers with seeds taken out, and one gallon of cabbage. Mix well and sprinkle two tablespoonsful of salt over it and let stand all night. Add three quarts of vinegar, two pounds of sugar, three teaspoonsful of celery seed, three of mustard seed two of spice, and one of cloves. Let simmer two hours.
recipes.note: The punctuation is the book's.

recipes.title: To Pickle Cucumbers
recipes.author: Mrs. Mary Randolph
recipes.text: Gather them full grown, but quite young — take off the green rind, and slice them tolerably thick; put a layer in a deep dish, strew over it some chopped onion and salt; do this until they are all in; sprinkle salt on the top, let them stand six hours, put them in a colander — when all the liquor has run off, put them in a pot, strew a little cayenne pepper over each layer, and cover them with strong cold vinegar; when the pot is full, pour on some sweet oil, and tie it up close; at the end of a fortnight, pour off the first vinegar, and put on fresh.
recipes.note: No sugar in it: a plain sour pickle of 1824, peeled and sliced rather than left whole.

recipes.title: Cucumbers
recipes.author: Mrs. Barringer, of North Carolina
recipes.text: Make a strong salt and water, and let the cucumbers lie in it for two weeks. Then soak all night in fresh water. The next day put them into a bright brass kettle, with a little alum, and water enough to cover them. Put grape-leaves on top, and a plate to keep in the steam. Simmer gently for a half a day. Let them get entirely cold, and then put them into fresh alum water, over the fire, and continue doing this, until they are quite fresh. Then, if they are a fine green, put them into a jar, and boil some vinegar and spices in a porcelain kettle, and pour over them. Have plenty of vinegar to cover the pickles, and cork them up tightly.
recipes.note: A North Carolina receipt of 1867. The alum and the brass kettle were used to hold the colour; neither is used now.

names.name: pig pickin' cake
names.said: Named for the party, not an ingredient: a pig pickin' is the whole-hog gathering where guests pick the meat off the pig, and this is the cake that comes after.

etymology.root: pig pickin' (the whole-hog party, named for picking the meat off the cooked pig) + cake
etymology.first_attested: 1975, a recipe in the Raleigh News & Observer, the oldest KC Hysmith could name (2024); a 1980 reference in the Boca Raton News
etymology.note: Folk: that the orange and pineapple are there to cool the mouth after vinegar barbecue (Coastal Review, 2017). 'Pea pickin' cake' is a reshaping by ear; Coastal Review calls it a mistake, Chowhound records it as a second name. John Shelton Reed, quoted by Hysmith, says North Carolinians did not say 'pig-picking' before the 1970s. *Inference —* the name is no older than the expression.

text.what: A layer cake of convenience-food parts: yellow or butter-golden cake mix beaten with eggs, oil and a can of mandarin oranges, juice and all, baked in three eight-inch pans and frosted with a can of crushed pineapple folded into instant vanilla pudding and whipped topping, sometimes with pecans or coconut on top, and served cold. It is North Carolina's barbecue dessert by name — the pig pickin' being the whole-hog party where guests pick the meat off the pig — and it is carried to those parties; Hysmith places it at barbecue restaurants too, though it is a home cake first. Our State calls it an essential companion to any good barbecue, noun not verb.
text.story: The cake has no founding story that anyone has documented, and two writers have looked. KC Hysmith, tracing it in 2024, found the oldest recipe she could name in the Raleigh News & Observer in 1975 and a reference in the Boca Raton News in 1980; every ingredient but the eggs comes from a can or a box, which reads like a brand's test kitchen, but she could not find which brand, and the 'Nancy Ware's cake' some sources credit stays a mystery. She reads it as a variation of the Pineapple Dream Cake of the convenience-food years. John Shelton Reed told her North Carolinians did not say 'pig-picking' until the 1970s, so the name is a child of that decade; *Inference —* the cake is older than its name, renamed for the party it was carried to. Liz Biro, in Coastal Review in 2017, gives the folk reason the state claims it — the name, and the way orange and pineapple cool the mouth after tangy pork — and notes that when Google sorted Thanksgiving searches by state in 2014, the New York Times reported pig pickin' cake as North Carolina's first. Our State printed Mavis Brannon of Mooresville's version the same year, sent in by her daughter, who remembered her yeast rolls as well. Chowhound records pea pickin' cake and sunshine cake as other names; Biro calls the first a mistake.
text.how: One box of yellow or butter-golden cake mix, four eggs, a quarter to three-quarters cup of oil and an 11-ounce can of mandarin oranges, chopped and undrained, beaten together and divided among three greased and floured 8-inch pans; 350 degrees for 15 to 20 minutes, then cooled through. The frosting is a 16- or 20-ounce can of crushed pineapple, drained, stirred into a small box of instant vanilla pudding, with two 8-ounce tubs of whipped topping folded in and, in Biro's version, a cup of chopped pecans. The layers are stacked and covered, top and sides, and the cake goes into the refrigerator; it is served cold and keeps there, loosely covered, a few hours by Our State's count. Some cooks bake it as a single layer or as cupcakes and finish it with orange segments, coconut or toasted pecans.
text.today: A home cake, carried to pig pickins and Thanksgiving tables: the dish North Carolinians searched for most in November 2014, by Google's count as the New York Times reported it. Recipes in Our State (2017) and Coastal Review (2017); Hysmith (2024) and Chowhound (2025) on the name. The barbecue-house menus read for this record — Lexington Barbecue, the Barbecue Center, Sam Jones, Parker's — do not list it.

names.name: pork skins
names.said: 'Skins' at the eastern counter; 'cracklins' when they come off a whole hog at a pig pickin or out of the lard pot at a hog killing.

text.what: The pig's hide, cooked until it blisters and cracks. On an eastern whole hog the skin faces up through the night and is turned to the coals at the end to crisp; at Skylight Inn it is chopped into the meat, where the crunch and the salt are part of what 'barbecue' means. Sold on their own, skins are a side or a snack: fresh fried squares with pimento cheese at Sam Jones BBQ, a pork skin sandwich with slaw at Lexington Barbecue. In the Pee Dee the hog is sometimes skinned before cooking and the skin fried on its own. A crackling keeps a little fat and meat under the skin; a rind is skin alone.
text.story: The skin is the pit's own by-product. At a hog killing the fat is rendered for lard and the cracklings are what is left in the pot, and *tradition holds —* crackling bread, cornbread with cracklings baked in, was the winter bread of the farm. On the eastern pit the same crust comes off the barbecue: the small hogs of the Carolinas are cooked hot enough for the skin to crisp, and the skin takes up more of the smoke than the meat does, so the chopped skin carries the flavor of the fire into every bite. At a pig pickin some cooks wipe the ash from the skin with paper towels or a whisk broom before the hog is turned, to keep the cracklings clean. Tennessee cooks larger hogs at lower heat and the skin never crisps — one of the marks that separate the Carolina hog from the Memphis one. At Skylight Inn the chop takes in tenderloin, inner meat and crisped skin together, which NCpedia records as the eastern habit: in some areas bits of skin are integral to the finished product. South of the line the Pee Dee sometimes strips the hide before the pig goes on and fries it apart, and NCpedia notes North Carolinians who follow that lead, sorting skin from outside meat from inside meat.
text.how: On the pit: the hog cooks skin-up, is turned skin-down at the end, and the blistered skin is chopped with cleavers into the meat, or lifted, salted and broken into pieces. Fried: the skin is cut into squares, rendered slowly, then fried hot so it puffs. Commercial rinds are dried pellets rehydrated and fried in pork fat at 200–210 °C, which swells them to five times their size; the pink or purple spot on a bagged rind is a USDA inspection stamp. Eaten with the fingers, salted, with hot sauce, or with pimento cheese.
text.today: Sam Jones BBQ lists fresh fried pork skins with housemade pimento cheese (September 2026). Lexington Barbecue sells a pork skin sandwich with slaw at $4.50 cash, $4.65 card (September 2026). Bagged rinds from the gas station are the same thing at a distance.

recipes.title: To Try the Fat (receipt 215)
recipes.author: Mrs. A. P. Hill
recipes.text: The lard for cooking is made from the leaf fat, the fat from the chine, head and trimmings of the joints, etc. Wash it well, and soak twelve hours; if put to soak in the evening let it remain until next morning; wash it in tepid water, changing it twice; cut it in small pieces; pour a little water in the bottom of the kettle to prevent the fat from scorching (very little water is necessary); boil briskly until the oil from the meat is nearly extracted, and the process almost completed; then reduce the fire; stir frequently, turning the meat up from the bottom; when done, the cracklings will be a good brown, and float to the top and break crisp. Great care must be taken after the oil begins to look clear, to prevent its burning (the least taste of that kind will injure its quality); at the same time the cracklings must be thoroughly done, the water entirely evaporated, or the lard will turn sour. Strain first through a colander, pressing the oil out; then place a muslin or other thin cloth over the mouth of the jar, and strain again.
recipes.note: Cracklings as a by-product of rendering lard at hog-killing, which is where most of them came from: fried out of the fat rather than crisped on a pit. 'When done, the cracklings will be a good brown, and float to the top and break crisp' is the test. The running head is unreadable in the scan, so no page is given; the receipt number locates it.

recipes.title: To whiten Lard
recipes.author: Mrs. Barringer, of North Carolina
recipes.text: To twelve gallons of lard add a pint of lye. Put the lye in when the lard is first put on. When the cracklings are a light-brown the lard is done. Strain through a thin cloth put inside of a colander.
recipes.note: From the household chapter rather than the cookery, and included for the same test by another hand: the cracklings tell you when to stop. The lye is for the lard, not for eating. No page is legible in the scan.

recipes.title: Eastern North Carolina Barbecued Pig
ingredients: Your favorite vinegar-based Eastern NC sauce
recipes.text:
1. Salt hams, ribs/midsection and shoulders liberally and place skin side up on either a gas or charcoal grill or a BBQ pit.
2. Keep lid closed, and aim for a heat of approximately 275–350°F.
3. Allow 1 hour per 10 pounds cooking time (gas or charcoal).
4. 2 hours before being done, place pig with the skin side down. As soon as it is flipped, pour BBQ sauce on meat side.
5. Close lid and allow skin to crisp.
6. The pig will be done to perfection when the ham bone can be twisted freely.
7. Lift lid and allow guests to pick/pull meat, or the chef can remove meat and chop to their liking on a chopping block.
recipes.note: The skin crisped on the pit rather than in a kettle: turned down to the coals for the last two hours with the lid closed.

names.name: potato salad
names.said: Ordered as a side at the counter; in the east it is the cold one, against the hot boiled potatoes on the same plate.

text.what: Boiled potatoes cut up cold and dressed with mayonnaise, with hard-boiled egg, onion, celery, sweet pickle or relish and often a spoon of yellow mustard that colours the whole bowl. It is served cold beside the barbecue, and in the Carolinas it is the mayonnaise side that answers to the vinegar of the meat. Mustard in the dressing is common enough in South Carolina that a bowl of it can read as the same yellow as the sauce.
text.story: American potato salad came in with German immigrants in the nineteenth century, and the earliest American recipes are the German kind: cooked potatoes dressed with oil, vinegar and herbs, served warm. The north German version — cold, with mayonnaise, hard-boiled egg and sweet or sour pickle — is the one the American bowl most resembles. Mayonnaise made the change possible on this scale, and in the Carolinas that means Eugenia Duke, who began bottling hers in Greenville, South Carolina around 1923. Aunt Caroline's Dixieland Recipes, printed in Chicago in 1922, already gives the Southern shape of it: five cold boiled Irish potatoes diced, three hard-boiled eggs, parsley, celery, salt and both peppers, bound with an oil dressing made at home. *Inference —* the sweet pickle and the mustard that distinguish a Carolina bowl from a German one are the same two things that distinguish the region's slaw and its sauce.
text.how: Potatoes are boiled in their skins, peeled and diced while still warm so they take the dressing, then cooled. Hard-boiled eggs are chopped in, with onion, celery and sweet pickle relish; the dressing is mayonnaise, sometimes cut with a little of the pickle liquor, and yellow mustard to taste. Salt, black pepper and paprika finish it. It is made in the morning and kept cold, and at a pit it is dished with an ice-cream scoop.
text.today: On the plate at Grady's in Dudley, where the day's vegetables are peeled and chopped by hand that morning; on the buffet at Brown's in Kingstree; among the sides at Lewis Barbecue in Charleston, which lists it as creamy potato salad; on the Dukes buffets in the Orangeburg family of houses.

recipes.title: Potato Salad
recipes.author: Emma and William McKinney
recipes.text:
Five medium sized, cold, boiled Irish potatoes, diced; three hard boiled eggs and a few pieces of parsley chopped fine, and one cup of diced celery. Season with salt, black and red pepper and mix well with oil dressing.

[Wesson Oil Dressing, the dressing it calls for, printed with it:] Yolks of three eggs, one-half teaspoon of salt, one-fourth teaspoon of mustard, one-fourth teaspoon of red pepper, juice of one lemon, pint of Wesson Oil. Beat yolks until thick; then add salt, pepper, mustard and part of lemon juice. Lastly add the oil one drop at a time at first, then slowly until dressing is thick, and then the remainder of the lemon juice.
recipes.note: The dressing is a hand-made mayonnaise; the brackets are this site's, everything inside them is the book's. Irish potato is the old Southern name for the white potato, said against the sweet potato.

recipes.title: Potato Salad
ingredients: ½ cup (120 g) finely-chopped yellow onion
recipes.text:
1. Cook bacon strips, cut into small pieces, and set aside for later.
2. Boil potatoes for 5–10 minutes or until softened; cut into small chunks or thick slices.
3. Place potatoes in a large bowl and let them come to room temperature.
4. In a bowl combine flour, celery seed, parsley, chopped onion, salt, and pepper.
5. Pour the water and vinegar into a pot, stir in sugar and bring to a boil. Add the dry mixture and stir until thickened.
6. In the original bowl place potatoes and bacon, pour on thickened mixture.
7. Break apart eggs and stir lightly into the bowl to combine.
8. Place in large serving bowl and sprinkle with paprika.
9. Serve

recipes.title: American Potato Salad I
recipes.text:
1. Peel and cut potatoes into ¾ inch cubes.
2. Cover potatoes with an inch of water in a large saucepan and bring to a boil.
3. Add 1 tablespoon salt to boiling water and reduce heat to medium.
4. Simmer about 8 minutes, stirring gently once or twice, until potatoes are tender. Taste a piece—don't overcook.
5. Drain potatoes and place in a large bowl.
6. Toss potatoes gently with vinegar using a rubber spatula.
7. Cool potatoes. They must be no more than barely warm to mix.
8. Chop celery fine.
9. Stir together celery, celery seeds, mayonnaise, dry mustard, onion, parsley, pepper, and ½ teaspoon salt.
10. Gently fold together dressing mix and potatoes.
11. Cover and refrigerate at least an hour, until thoroughly chilled.

recipes.title: American Potato Salad II
ingredients: 3 pounds small white potatoes (use waxy or red potatoes)
½ cup freshly-squeezed lemon juice (from 2–3 lemons)
recipes.text:
1. Place potatoes and 2 tablespoons of salt in a large pot of water. Bring the water to a boil, and cook for 15–20 minutes, until the potatoes are tender when pierced with a knife. Drain the potatoes in a colander.
2. Place the chopped eggs in a large bowl.
3. Sauté the onions until light golden brown and add to the bowl with the eggs.
4. When the potatoes are cool enough to handle, cut them in quarters, or smaller, depending on their size. Place the potatoes in the bowl with the eggs. Add the corn along with some salt, pepper and pasta seasoning to the potato and egg mixture. Set aside.
5. In a small bowl add the lemon juice while whisking in olive oil slowly. Add to the potatoes, mix all ingredients. Chill for 30 minutes before eating.

names.name: red slaw
names.said: 'Slaw' in Lexington means this one; you ask for white slaw if you want the other.

etymology.root: Dutch koolsla 'cabbage salad' (kool 'cabbage', from Latin caulis, + sla 'salad') → American English coleslaw, 1794 → slaw, the American clipping; 'red' is the Lexington marker for the ketchup or dip in the dressing, against 'white' for mayonnaise
etymology.first_attested: coleslaw 1794 in American English (Online Etymology Dictionary); the 1667 Dutch cookbook De Verstandige Kock already has cabbage strips dressed with melted butter, vinegar and oil (Wikipedia, Coleslaw)
etymology.note: Folk: 'cold slaw', a reshaping by ear, was the common spelling until about the 1860s, when cole was restored.

text.what: Finely chopped green cabbage dressed with vinegar, ketchup, sugar, salt and black pepper — or with the pit's own dip — and no mayonnaise. It is the slaw of Lexington and the Piedmont, red-pink in the boat beside the chopped shoulder, on the sandwich under the meat, and on hot dogs as a relish; it is what the counter means by 'slaw' from Lexington to Shelby. Because it carries no mayonnaise it keeps without refrigeration, which suits an outdoor pit. Across the rest of the state the pale mayonnaise slaw is the default and this one is called barbecue slaw.
text.story: The dressing is the dip. In Lexington the thin sauce of vinegar, ketchup, water, salt and pepper that dresses the shoulder also goes into the cabbage, so the slaw is coloured by the same bottle as the meat; NCpedia records it as red coleslaw, 'barbecue slaw', coloured with ketchup or dip. The Lexington sandwich is defined by it — the town's own account calls red slaw the sandwich's most distinguishing feature — and it goes on hot dogs as a relish, where the Carolina hot dog's chili, slaw and onions are the same three things in a bun. *Tradition holds —* the slaw went red because the first pits were tents and curb stands without ice, and a vinegar dressing holds where mayonnaise will not; it was also the dressing a pit already had on the block. In the late 1990s Wendy's put red slaw on a 'Carolina Classic' burger with chili, onions and American cheese and trademarked the name, which is as far as the slaw has travelled under its own. At Keaton's in Rowan County the house slaw is the same idea run hot: cabbage in vinegar, tomato, cayenne and celery seed.
text.how: Green cabbage chopped fine — finer than a Northern slaw, close to minced — and dressed with vinegar, ketchup, sugar, salt and black pepper, or with a ladle of the house dip; some pits add hot sauce, mustard seed or onion. It is made ahead and kept cold, and the vinegar keeps it. Served in the second half of the tray, on the sandwich under the meat, and on a hot dog with chili and onions; the Barbecue Center and Lexington Barbecue both put it on the sandwich unless you ask for none.
text.today: Every Lexington pit serves it and most keep a mayonnaise white slaw for the asking. It rides in the boat with a chopped tray at $8.00 cash at Lexington Barbecue and on the $5.70 chopped sandwich (September 2026). Outside the Piedmont, red slaw on the tray is the sign of a pit cooking in the Lexington manner.

recipes.title: Cold Slaw
recipes.author: Mrs. Barringer, of North Carolina
recipes.text:
Take vinegar and water in equal proportions (unless the vinegar is very strong); add butter, the size of an egg, and a little flour. Pour into a saucepan over the fire, and stir until it is thick; then pour in the beaten yolks of two eggs, and some salt. When it has been on the fire ten minutes more, stir in the cabbage, nicely shreded with a cabbage-cutter. The cabbage must be taken up, as soon as it is hot.

You may add a saltspoonful of mustard to the sauce, if you like it. Salt the cabbage.
recipes.note: The word is the old one: before mayonnaise reached the Southern kitchen, 'cold slaw' meant shredded cabbage under a cooked dressing of vinegar, butter and egg. This is the ancestor of the barbecue slaws, not the thing itself. Barringer cooked in Concord, Cabarrus County, thirty miles from Lexington; her dressing is vinegar, butter, egg and mustard, with no mayonnaise in it.

recipes.title: Cold and Hot Slaws
recipes.author: Mrs. M. E. Porter
recipes.book: Mrs. Porter's New Southern Cookery Book
recipes.text:
To make cold-slaw, take a nice, fresh cabbage, wash and strain it (after submitting it to the insect-destroying process); cut off the stalk, shave down the head into very small strips with a cabbage-cutter or very sharp knife. It must be done evenly. Put it into a deep china-dish and prepare for it the following dressing: Melt in a sauce-pan a quarter of a pound of butter, with half pint of water, a large tablespoonful of vinegar, a saltspoonful of salt and a little cayenne. Give this a boil, and pour it hot on the cabbage. Send to the table cold.

To prepare warm-slaw, cut the cabbage as for cold-slaw (red cabbage is best); put it in a deep dish, cover closely, and set it on the top of the stove for half an hour or till warm all through; do not let it boil. Then make a dripping as for cold-slaw. Boil this mixture in a sauce-pan, and pour it hot over the warm cabbage; send to table immediately.
recipes.note: The warm slaw is the one that calls for red cabbage; the colour in a Lexington red slaw comes from ketchup instead, and that ingredient is not in this book.

recipes.title: Cold Slaw (receipt 366)
recipes.author: Mrs. A. P. Hill
recipes.text: Cut a head of hard white cabbage into very fine shavings. It is seldom shaved fine enough. For a quart of the cabbage take the yolks of three eggs, beat them well; stir into a tumbler and a half of vinegar two teaspoonfuls of loaf sugar, a tablespoonful of olive oil, one of thick, sweet cream, or a piece of butter as large as a walnut, a heaped teaspoonful of mustard, salt and pepper to taste; mix with the egg, and put this sauce into a stew-pan; when hot add the cabbage; stew until thoroughly hot, which will only require four or five minutes. Toss it up from the bottom with a silver or wooden fork. Take it up and set where it will become perfectly cold, on ice is best. The quantity of vinegar will depend upon its strength.
recipes.note: The word is the old one: before mayonnaise reached the Southern kitchen, 'cold slaw' meant shredded cabbage under a cooked dressing of vinegar, butter and egg. This is the ancestor of the barbecue slaws, not the thing itself.

names.name: sweet tea
names.said: 'Tea' on a Carolina barbecue menu means this: iced, and sweetened while hot. Lexington Barbecue prints it as 'Iced Tea (Unsweet on Request)'; the unsweetened glass is the one you ask for.

text.what: Black tea brewed strong, sweetened with sugar while hot — so it dissolves, rather than being stirred into a cold glass — and poured over ice. It is the drink of the Carolina barbecue house in both states and every sauce region: sold by the glass, the quart and the gallon, brewed on the stove at Grady's in Dudley, named by Dukes in Orangeburg among the five things people come for, and served, Wikipedia says, wherever whole hog is. Some cooks temper it with a pinch of baking soda against bitterness; lemon is the usual addition. Its presence on a menu is one sign used to tell whether a place counts as the South.
text.story: Sweet tea began as a luxury of three shipped-in things — tea, sugar and ice, the ice the dearest — and became cheap when all three did. The oldest known recipe for it is in Housekeeping in Old Virginia, a community cookbook compiled by Marion Cabell Tyree (copyright 1878, and dated 1879 by the historian Robert Moss): ice, sugar, hot green tea, lemon. Green tea was the tea of the 19th-century South; the Second World War cut off its sources and black tea from British India took its place, and by the war's end black tea was the American tea. Moss, checking Summerville, South Carolina's 2013 claim to be 'The Birthplace of Sweet Tea' — a trademarked tagline, a Sweet Tea Trail and billboards on I-26 and I-95, resting on Dr. Charles Shepard's Pinehurst Tea Plantation of 1888–1915, the first successful tea farm in the country — found the Boston Journal recommending iced tea in July 1868, twenty years before Shepard planted, and Fannie Farmer's 1896 Boston Cooking-School Cook Book telling readers to pour tea over cracked ice and sweeten to taste. Summerville answered with a jar: 'Mason', fifteen feet tall, filled on National Tea Day 2016 with 2,524 gallons of sweet tea, the world's largest, a record traded since 2010 among Chick-fil-A, Summerville and Lipton. In 2003 a Georgia House bill, apparently an April Fool's joke, would have made selling iced tea without offering sweet tea a misdemeanor; it never came to a vote.
text.how: Tea bags or loose black tea steep in a pot of boiling water — some cooks add a pinch of baking soda — and the sugar goes in while the tea is hot; cold water and ice bring it down. At Grady's, Gerri Grady brews it on the stovetop for the day's service; at Allen & Son Keith Allen brewed it himself and sold it by the litre. It is served in a tall glass over ice, with lemon if you want it. Pits sell it to go by the pint, quart, half gallon and gallon — Parker's in Wilson lists all four — and the Barbecue Center in Lexington prices it from a 10-ounce cup to the gallon jug. The sugar can run to 22 degrees Brix, twice a Coca-Cola.
text.today: Lexington Barbecue: 'Iced Tea (Unsweet on Request)', $2.90 cash, $3.00 card (September 2026). The Barbecue Center: 10 oz $2.50, 16 oz $2.90, 32 oz $3.75, half gallon $6.00, gallon $8.50. Summerville holds a Sweet Tea Festival each September and keeps the record jar.

recipes.title: Iced Tea
recipes.author: Emma and William McKinney
recipes.text: Use one scant teaspoonful of tea to one cup of boiling water. Pour boiling water over tea leaves and let stand until milk warm. Then strain and sweeten to taste while tea is still warm, as it requires less sugar. Serve with crushed ice, green mint leaves, and sliced lemon and orange.
recipes.note: The sweetening rule the Carolina glass still follows, printed in 1922: sugar goes in while the tea is warm, because warm tea takes less of it.

recipes.title: Tea — Southern Style
recipes.author: Emma and William McKinney
recipes.text: Take one-half teaspoonful of tea to one cup of boiling water. Put the tea in the pot, pour the boiling water upon it and let stand where it will keep hot for five minutes. Then serve. Tea should never be boiled for it makes it bitter.
recipes.note: The hot brew on the facing column, at half the strength of the iced one: iced tea is made stronger because the ice waters it down.

recipes.title: Iced Tea
ingredients: 2 teaspoons citric acid crystals (or malic / tartaric / citric blends)
recipes.text:
1. Fill a drip coffee maker with cold water and place the tea bags in the basket.
2. Place the stevia, acid, and sugar in the pot, and place the pot in the machine.
3. Let it run through its cycle, then chill the product. This is a concentrate and will make several litres of iced tea.
4. Place some ice in a tall glass and fill 80–90% with cold water. Pour in some iced tea nectar. You may reduce the water and add some fruit juice if desired.
recipes.note: A concentrate brewed through a drip coffee maker and diluted in the glass; sweetened with stevia and a little sugar rather than the Carolina cup of it.

names.name: white slaw
names.said: In the east it is just 'slaw'; 'white slaw' is what a Lexington counter calls it when it offers both.

text.what: Finely chopped cabbage in a dressing of mayonnaise or whipped salad dressing, sweet and pale: the slaw of eastern North Carolina and of most of South Carolina. It goes on the tray beside the chopped whole hog and on the bun of the sandwich, where its sweetness sets off the vinegar and pepper of the meat. Eastern pits use mayonnaise almost universally; NCpedia lists white or yellow coleslaw among the eastern sides, the yellow taking mustard. The name exists only where the red slaw does. Everywhere else in the state this is coleslaw, from the Dutch koolsla, cabbage salad.
text.story: Coleslaw came to the colonies with the Dutch — the 1667 cookbook De Verstandige Kock gives a landlady's recipe of cabbage strips in melted butter, vinegar and oil — and the word is Dutch too, koolsla, cabbage salad, in American English by 1794 and spelled 'cold slaw' by ear until the 1860s. The mayonnaise version is younger than the word, since mayonnaise itself dates from the mid-eighteenth century, and it is the version the South took up, with buttermilk slaw a Southern variant. In North Carolina the coleslaw is fine-chopped and vinegary and served with barbecue; in the east it is dressed with mayonnaise or whipped salad dressing almost without exception and put on the bun of the sandwich, the way Memphis puts slaw on its pork sandwich. The South Carolina plate — pork, rice, hash, coleslaw, sweet pickles, white bread, iced tea — carries the same slaw beside mustard-sauced pork. *Tradition holds —* the sweetness is the point: against a whole hog dressed with vinegar and pepper, the slaw is the sweet thing on the tray.
text.how: Cabbage chopped fine, often with a little carrot or onion, dressed with mayonnaise or whipped salad dressing, sugar, vinegar, salt and pepper, and chilled until it weeps a little. Eastern pits chop it nearly as fine as the meat so the two mix on the bun. A yellow slaw takes mustard in the dressing. Served cold beside the hot pork on the tray, spooned on the sandwich, and on hot dogs across the Coastal Plain.
text.today: Sam Jones BBQ lists a sweet slaw (2026); Skylight Inn serves its tray with slaw and cornbread; the Lexington pits keep a white slaw for those who ask. South Carolina buffets put it beside hash and rice.

recipes.title: Coleslaw I
ingredients: 4 tablespoons mayonnaise or 2 dL olive oil
recipes.text:
1. If adding cider vinegar, add it to the mayonnaise and mix together well.
2. Slice or shred the cabbage, as coarsely or finely as desired.
3. In a large bowl, mix cabbage and onion together with mayonnaise.
4. Set aside to allow the flavours to merge at least 20 minutes but preferably for a couple of hours.
recipes.note: The plain mayonnaise-and-cabbage form; a Carolina barbecue house chops the cabbage far finer than 'as coarsely or finely as desired' allows, and most sweeten the dressing.

recipes.title: Coleslaw II
recipes.text:
1. Toss cabbage with a few big handfuls of kosher salt. Place in a colander in a bowl and let sit at room temperature 2 hours.
2. Drain cabbage. Rinse with clean water and let them go for a spin in your salad spinner until relatively dry.
3. Combine vinegar and spices. Microwave on high until mixture comes to a boil.
4. Fold in mayonnaise and cabbage. Chill until cold.
recipes.note: A vinegar-and-mayonnaise slaw with celery seed and dry mustard, chilled.

recipes.title: Salad for Slaw
recipes.author: Marion Cabell Tyree, editor
recipes.text: Stir well over the fire until as thick as custard. Let it cool and pour over cabbage. — Mrs. R. A.
ingredients: Pepper and salt to your taste.
recipes.note: A boiled dressing — egg, sugar, mustard, milk and vinegar cooked to a custard — which is what a sweet white slaw was made with before jarred mayonnaise. The initials are the book's: each receipt is signed by its contributor.

recipes.title: Dressing for Cold Slaw
recipes.author: Marion Cabell Tyree, editor
recipes.text:
Mix together the butter, salt, pepper, sugar, mustard; add the eggs last.

Have the vinegar boiling and pour it on, stirring all the time. Then pour it back in the saucepan and boil a few minutes. Pour on the slaw when cold. — Miss W.

recipes.title: Cold Slaw
recipes.author: Mrs. Barringer, of North Carolina
recipes.text:
Take vinegar and water in equal proportions (unless the vinegar is very strong); add butter, the size of an egg, and a little flour. Pour into a saucepan over the fire, and stir until it is thick; then pour in the beaten yolks of two eggs, and some salt. When it has been on the fire ten minutes more, stir in the cabbage, nicely shreded with a cabbage-cutter. The cabbage must be taken up, as soon as it is hot.

You may add a saltspoonful of mustard to the sauce, if you like it. Salt the cabbage.
recipes.note: The word is the old one: before mayonnaise reached the Southern kitchen, 'cold slaw' meant shredded cabbage under a cooked dressing of vinegar, butter and egg. This is the ancestor of the barbecue slaws, not the thing itself.

text.what: An open pit built above ground of cinder blocks — concrete blocks — wide and shallow, a little longer than a split hog, with a rack across the top on which the pig lies and a bed of charcoal below; brick or steel are the alternatives, and the charcoal is made in a fireplace or a burn barrel beside it. It is the whole-hog pit of the Carolinas, the one a farm, a fire department or a family can lay in an afternoon. *Tradition holds —* the blocks go up dry, without mortar, two or three courses high, a gap is left for the shovel, and a sheet of tin or plywood closes the top.
text.story: The trench came first. *Tradition holds —* the farm barbecue of the Carolinas was cooked over a pit dug in the ground, and Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church in Charlotte cooked its 1929 barbecue that way, hickory coals shoved under whole hogs in ditches; by the 1980s metal cookers had replaced the church's dirt pits, with some meat still cooked on open pits inside a screened building. NCpedia records that few commercial pits today are dug in the ground. The cinder block — cheap, fireproof, stackable — is what the open pit became when it climbed out of the ditch. It is the pit of the pig pickin' and the cook-off, and the pit the whole-hog restaurants of the east grew from: the Skylight Inn's hogs cook over charcoal made in fireplaces beside the pits, and Rodney Scott's over hardwood charcoal shoveled from a burn barrel. The Cuban roasting box, by contrast, is a closed box of concrete blocks and steel mesh with the coals on top.
text.how: Blocks are laid in a rectangle a little longer and wider than the split hog; a rack spans the top, the hog goes on skin-side up, and a lid holds the heat. Coals from the burn barrel are shoveled in and spread beneath the carcass on a regular round through the night — *Tradition holds —* heavier under the hams and shoulders, thinner under the loin. The fat that drips hisses on the coals, and a flare-up is the danger the cook watches for; an uncontrolled pit fire can take the pit and the building. After eight to twenty-four hours the hog is flipped once, skin down, to crisp.
text.today: The block pit is the pit of the yard, the church lot, the fire station and the competition; restaurants that cook whole hog mostly cook in masonry or steel pits under a roof, and the form — a bed of coals, a rack, a hog, a lid — is the same.

names.name: brick pit
names.said: In Lexington the pits are 'the pits', and the hand on them is 'firing the pits'.

text.what: The masonry pit of the Piedmont: a closed brick chamber with a rack for the shoulders and a chimney through the roof to carry off the smoke. Coals made from oak and hickory go in through the door and are spread on the floor under the meat; the door shuts and the shoulders cook nine to twelve hours at about 200 to 225 degrees. The Barbecue Center in Lexington describes its pit as a brick oven with three chambers, 'comparable to an oversized smoker', and Lexington Barbecue's roof carries a row of smoking stacks. The line of chimneys on a Lexington roof is how you know a wood pit from the road.
text.story: The closed pit is the restaurant's answer to the trench. *Tradition holds —* the Lexington style began under tents on the courthouse square in the 1910s and moved indoors as its cooks built permanent pits, and the pits they built were brick because brick holds heat and a chimney takes the smoke out of a dining room. NCpedia's entry records that few commercial pits today are dug in the ground, and that economy, fastidiousness and health rules keep most Piedmont pits from basting with the ketchup-and-vinegar sauce, which flares; it goes on at the table instead, hence its name, dip. The Barbecue Center has cooked in its pit since 1955 under the Conrad family, and Lexington Barbecue, founded in 1962, cooks 'with wood, not gas' over oak and hickory coals only; a new pit hand there trains for a year before working the pits alone, and the heat from the fires, one visitor wrote, is overwhelming as the coals are turned. The North Carolina Historic Barbecue Trail admits only pits that cook on grates over wood or charcoal, so its Piedmont stops — Stamey's in Greensboro, Short Sugar's in Reidsville, the Bar-B-Q Center, Red Bridges in Shelby — are brick pits by definition.
text.how: Oak and hickory logs burn to coals in a fireplace or burner at the end of the pit house; a crew member shovels the coals through the pit door and spreads them evenly under the shoulders — the round Lexington calls 'firing the pits' — then shuts the door. The shoulders sit on the rack, salted but not basted or marinated, for nine to twelve hours at 200 to 225 degrees; the Barbecue Center puts three hundred a week through its three chambers. The smoke leaves by the chimney. Finished shoulders come off to the block to be chopped, coarse chopped or sliced.
text.today: The brick pit is still the plant of the Lexington restaurants — Lexington Barbecue, the Barbecue Center — and of the Piedmont stops on the Historic Barbecue Trail. Lexington Barbecue's site says it cooks with wood, not gas.

text.what: A repurposed steel drum — or, at Scott's in Hemingway, two 55-gallon drums welded together — in which logs are burned down to coals: the wood goes in at the top, the coals are pulled out from below and carried by shovel to the pit. It is the coal-maker of the wood pit, the reason a whole hog can sit over a steady bed of coals for twelve hours with no flame under it. Older pit houses use a fireplace for the same job — the Skylight Inn burns its oak and hickory in fireplaces beside the pits — and the barrel is the version anyone can weld.
text.story: The barrel is the modern form of an older arrangement. *Tradition holds —* the trench pit of the farm barbecue had a fire burning at one end and coals raked down its length under the meat; when the pit climbed above ground into blocks and brick, the fire moved into a fireplace or a drum beside it. Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church in Charlotte cooked its first barbecues, from 1929, in ditches with hickory coals shoved underneath the whole hogs. At Scott's Bar-B-Que in Hemingway, Rodney Scott feeds hunks of hickory, oak and pecan through the top of the welded drums and pulls hot coals from below to stoke the pit. In November 2013 the family's wooden cookhouse caught fire — 'shooting like a torch', the fire department told him — and Scott took his hogs on the road to raise at least $100,000, part to rebuild and part for a fund to preserve the region's food traditions.
text.how: Split logs go in at the top and burn with the draft from the bottom; as they collapse into coals the cook rakes them out with a flat shovel and spreads them in the pit under the meat. *Tradition holds —* the bed goes heavier under the hams and shoulders and thinner under the loin, and a hog cooked through a night takes a fresh shovelful on a regular round, so the barrel is kept fed the whole time. Lexington crews call the same round, in a brick pit, 'firing the pits'.
text.today: Every wood-fired whole-hog pit keeps a barrel, a fireplace or a burner going through the night; the drum is the standard beside a block pit and at Scott's. Gas and electric cookers do without it, and the labor it stands for is the reason owners give for switching.

names.name: chopping block
names.said: 'Chopped', 'coarse chopped' and 'sliced' are the three words on a Lexington menu; in the east the only word is 'barbecue', and it comes chopped.

text.what: A thick wooden block and a pair of cleavers, on which cooked pork is turned into barbecue. The whole hog is pulled from the bones onto the block and chopped, skin and all, until the meat is fine enough to hold a thin vinegar sauce; the salt and the sauce go on at the block — at the Skylight Inn, vinegar, salt, pepper and Texas Pete. A Lexington shoulder is chopped fine, chopped coarse into small chunks, or sliced, and at Lexington Barbecue never pulled. Jane and Michael Stern called the sound of cleavers on the block one of the most alluring aspects of whole hog barbecue in the Carolinas.
text.story: The chop is the Carolinas' answer to a question other regions answer with a knife or a fork. *Tradition holds —* the eastern chop comes from the whole hog itself: light meat, dark meat, fat and skin from one animal are one dish only once they are chopped together, and the chop is what lets the crisp skin be eaten in every bite. Eastern-style meat is chopped after it is pulled from the bone, for a finer texture and so that it holds the thin vinegar sauce; Lexington-style is served pulled or lightly chopped, with larger strands of muscle, and the Lexington restaurants add the sliced tray. NCpedia records a South Carolina habit that has crossed the state line: separating the skin, the dry 'outside meat' and the juicier 'inside meat', so the customer chooses; some whole-hog restaurants let the customer choose white meat, dark meat or both, and prize the 'middlin' from the belly and the 'catfish' from under the tenderloin. The three cuts of the Piedmont are a price list. At Lexington Barbecue in September 2026 a chopped tray was $8.00 cash, a sliced tray $8.20 and a coarse-chop tray $8.60, with slaw and rolls or hush puppies; at the Barbecue Center a chopped tray was $9 small and $12 large, sliced or coarse chopped $10 and $13, dip on the meat, slaw included, hush puppies or a potato bun.
text.how: The cooked meat is pulled from the bones by hand and heaped on the block; the cook works the cleavers across the heap, folding the pile back on itself, adding the crisp skin in pieces once the meat is broken down, and seasoning on the block. For a Lexington shoulder the meat is chopped fine, chopped coarse for 'chunks', or sliced, and the dip goes on before it is trayed. A sandwich takes the chop and slaw on a soft bun.
text.today: The block and cleavers are in use at the Skylight Inn and in most whole-hog kitchens; Lexington menus carry the three cuts, and 'chopped' is the ordinary order on both sides of the state.

text.what: The Carolina way of putting fire to meat: a bed of hardwood coals directly beneath the hog or the shoulders, with no flame and no separate firebox. The coals are made elsewhere — in a burn barrel or a fireplace — and shoveled in, so the meat sits over glowing charcoal and its own dripping fat rather than in a stream of smoke. The contrast is the offset smoker of Central Texas: a cylinder with a smaller firebox attached at one end, whose burning post-oak fire sends heat and smoke sideways through the chamber past the meat — indirect heat. The whole-hog article, the Mallard Creek church and the Barbecue Center all describe the coals going under the meat.
text.story: The word carries the method. The Wikipedia article on barbecue draws its line between the indirect barbecues of the United States — meat roasted or smoked over wood or charcoal at low temperature for hours — and the direct grilling of most of the world, done over hot coals for minutes; in a typical American home barbecue the coals are dispersed to the sides. The Carolina pit sits across that line: the coals are directly under the meat, as on a grill, but far enough below and slow enough that the cook is barbecuing, not grilling. True 'Cue quotes a federal meat-labeling rule that defines barbecued meat as 'cooked by the direct action of dry heat resulting from the burning of hard wood'. Texas divides the same way: Central Texas cooks with indirect heat from a pecan, post-oak or mesquite fire, and West Texas over direct mesquite heat 'in a method very similar to grilling'. *Inference —* in geometry the Carolina pit is closer to the West Texas cowboy fire than to the Austin smoker, and the reason both Carolina styles burn their wood to coals first is that flame under a fat hog is a fire. Ed Mitchell in Wilson cooks 'hot and fast' with a bank of coals surrounding the hog, starting at 500 degrees and letting it fall to 250; Rodney Scott shovels coals under a hog lying belly-down for eight to twelve hours; the Barbecue Center in Lexington 'fires the pits' by distributing coals evenly beneath the shoulders.
text.how: Coals go in under the meat in a thin, even bed and are renewed from the burn barrel through the cook; the meat is never over flame. *Tradition holds —* the bed goes heavier under the hams and shoulders of a whole hog and thinner under the loin. Fat drips onto the coals and vaporizes — *Inference —* the source of much of what the Carolinas call wood flavor — and a flare-up from that fat is the whole-hog cook's constant danger. The pit is closed with a lid or a door to hold the heat, and a hog is flipped once near the end.
text.today: Every pit on the North Carolina Historic Barbecue Trail and every True 'Cue certificate cooks this way by definition — on grates over pits with wood or charcoal. *Tradition holds —* the offset smoker has arrived too: Lewis Barbecue in Charleston cooks Central Texas brisket in offset smokers, and is described here the same way as a wood pit.

text.what: The cookers most Carolina barbecue is cooked in: steel ovens fired by propane, natural gas or an electric element, with a thermostat and racks, and often a box for wood chips or a log to put smoke on the meat. A gas smoker lights a burner directly under a box of wood or charcoal; an electric one runs a heating element that holds any temperature from a cold smoke to about 275 degrees. New barbecue restaurants mostly open on them and many older ones switched. They cook overnight unattended, hold a set temperature, make no soot and need no one to shovel coals at three in the morning, and they are the machine behind a great deal of what both states call barbecue, sauce and slaw included.
text.story: The argument has two sides and each states its reasons. The cooks who switched say it plainly: gas and electricity are cheaper and easier and the product is more consistent — John Shelton Reed grants all three — and a wood pit needs someone awake through the night, produces soot, and burns more fuel and labor for the same meat. Many owners also say the health department made them do it. Reed and the True 'Cue campaign he co-founded put a Challenge in the Raleigh News & Observer on April 23, 2014, offering a prize to anyone who could name the regulation; two years on no one had, and Daniel Vaughn in Texas and Robert Moss in South Carolina had reported the same from their states. Reed writes that one state official mentioned environmental concerns and that the actual motives remain unclear. On the other side stands the billboard at the Skylight Inn, whose four tenets include that barbecue must be cooked with wood, and the True 'Cue Pledge for those who hold that if it is not cooked with wood it is not barbecue; the campaign's wood page calls smoke 'the umami of barbecue', quotes Pete Jones, Rodney Scott and Wilber Shirley among its witnesses, and Alton Brown's joke that with gas 'you can control the heat. But you're going to go to hell.' Reed draws the line with care: the campaign has 'no beef' with cooks who use gas or electricity for ignition and temperature control so long as wood smoke reaches the meat, and reserves 'faux 'cue' for meat cooked with no smoke at all. The pig pickin' article records the same split at the backyard: propane for a steady temperature, charcoal 'touted as producing better-tasting meat'. Jim Early, searching a hundred counties for pits still cooking over wood coals, found fewer than thirty.
text.how: Shoulders or a split hog go on the racks in the evening with the smoke box loaded, the thermostat holds the temperature overnight, and in the morning the meat comes off to the block. There is no burn barrel, no shoveling round and no chimney; the cook's labor is loading, unloading and chopping. The sauce, the slaw and the chop are the same as at a wood pit, which is why the customer often cannot tell and the campaigns exist to tell them.
text.today: Wood pits are a counted minority: about seventy North Carolina restaurants held True 'Cue certificates in January 2018, and the Historic Barbecue Trail listed about two dozen. *Inference —* the rest of the barbecue sold in both states comes off gas or electricity.
