text.what: The hardwoods of the Carolina pit. Hickory and oak are the woods a Carolina cook burns, usually together and usually burned down to coals before they go under the meat: Lexington pits cook over oak and hickory coals, the Skylight Inn burns oak and hickory logs in fireplaces beside its pits, and Scott's in Hemingway feeds hickory, oak and pecan through the top of a burn barrel. South Carolina's barbecue is smoked over hickory or oak; Lexington's over a hardwood fire, usually hickory. Both are dense, slow-burning and abundant in the eastern forest, and both give the strong smoke that pork carries. Pecan is itself a hickory — Carya illinoinensis — with a sweeter, milder smoke.
text.story: Wood smoke flavors the meat, so the woods a region has decide how its barbecue tastes; hickory, oak and mesquite give a strong smoke, and pecan, maple, alder and the fruit woods a milder, sweeter one, which is why the strong woods go with pork and beef. Pecan, a hickory native to the south-central United States, is sold as a smoking wood for a 'sweet and nutty flavor stronger than many fruit woods'; Rodney Scott burns it with hickory and oak. Skin takes up more of the smoke than meat does, which is one reason the eastern chop keeps its skin. Ed Mitchell in Wilson burns oak and hickory logs and adds charcoal briquettes. *Inference —* in a Carolina pit the wood is burned to coals before it reaches the meat, so most of the flame's smoke is spent; what the meat then breathes is largely its own fat and juices vaporizing on the coals, and that is the flavor Carolina cooks call 'wood' rather than 'smoke' — the same log gives a different result in a Texas offset smoker, where the meat sits in the smoke of a burning fire. True 'Cue, the campaign that certifies wood-cooked pits, calls wood smoke 'the umami of barbecue' and 'barbecue's soul'.
text.how: Logs burn down to coals in a fireplace or a burn barrel; the coals are shoveled into the pit under the meat, and Lexington crews 'fire the pits' by spreading them evenly beneath the shoulders. At a pig pickin' the fuel is often bagged charcoal with chunks of blackjack oak or hickory added for flavor, or a separate stove of hardwood whose coals are shoveled under the grate; Ed Mitchell adds charcoal briquettes to his oak and hickory.
text.today: Hickory is the sign-painter's word across both states and oak the workhorse beside it; every pit on the North Carolina Historic Barbecue Trail and every True 'Cue certificate is a wood fire of one or both. Scott's in Hemingway burns pecan with the other two.

names.name: hog killing
names.said: 'Hog killin'' in speech. A hard frost is still 'hog-killing weather'.

text.what: The winter slaughter of the farm's hogs, done on the first cold day of autumn or winter, when the meat would keep. In rural North Carolina neighbors gathered before dawn; water was heated with fire-hot stones dropped into barrels; the penned and fattened hogs were killed with knives, bled, scalded, hung on a gambrel — a spreader bar through the hind legs — and scraped clean of hair; the carcasses cooled overnight and were cut up the next day, the hams, sides, shoulders, jowls and heads salted down in the smokehouse. Lard was rendered, the fat cooked down to cracklings, the trim ground for sausage. It is the farm year's pork day, and the social form the pit barbecue grew up beside.
text.story: William S. Powell's entry in the Encyclopedia of North Carolina (2006) describes the day as farms kept it: as many as a hundred hogs penned and fattened on peas, potatoes, corn gleaned from the harvested fields or mast from the woods; workers from the neighborhood gathered well before dawn; stones heated in an open fire and dropped into barrels to heat the scalding water; the hogs killed with large knives, bled, scalded, hung and scraped; cooled overnight, cut up and salted the next day on a tilted platform in the smokehouse, the dripping brine caught in troughs and boiled down to save the salt for the stock. The weeks after were spare ribs, liver and sausage; the hams came a month or two later. Carolina Country followed the Jackson family of Hopkins through a January hog killing in 2019: Terry Jackson directing, his son in training, neighbors and friends at the scalding vat; sausage seasoned with salt, red pepper and sage and a patty fried over the wood fire for approval; lard rendered and cracklings saved; hams and shoulders carried to the salt room; chitterlings, feet and bones for broth; a pot of homemade soup at midday for everyone who came. The pit's relation to the day is old: George Washington raised pigs for slaughter in November at Mount Vernon and, once the enslaved people had cured the hams and bacon, whole pigs were pit-roasted over coals 'as a treat'. John Shelton Reed writes that barbecue was never home cooking, and until the early twentieth century was reserved for harvests, fundraisers and political rallies. *Tradition holds —* the hog killing and the pit shared a season and a crowd, and a pig set aside from the killing was the cheapest way to feed the neighbors who came to help.
text.how: Cold weather first. The hog is stuck and bled, scalded in a vat or barrel of water just under the boil and scraped clean of hair, then hung head-down from a gambrel, gutted, and left overnight to cool and firm. Next day it is cut into hams, shoulders, sides for bacon, loins and ribs; the trim is ground and seasoned for sausage, the fat rendered in a kettle for lard with the crisp bits kept as cracklings, the intestines cleaned for chitterlings, and the feet and bones boiled for broth. Hams and shoulders are salted or smoked to keep.
text.today: The community hog killing survives on some farms — Carolina Country followed one in 2019 — and the pig for a pit comes from a processor: the Skylight Inn buys most of its hogs from meat processors in Ayden. *Tradition holds —* the word survives in the weather: a hard frost is hog-killing weather.

text.what: A steel box on a trailer chassis, long enough for a split hog, with a hinged lid, a grate, and either a row of propane burners underneath or a bed for charcoal: the cooker of the pig pickin', towed to the church lot, the tailgate or the fire station and home again. Carolina Cooker of Micro, North Carolina, builds one of 12-gauge steel with four propane burners on a leaf-spring trailer, listed at $2,599.99 in September 2026; BQ Grills of Elm City builds towable charcoal-and-wood cookers of eighth-inch steel in five- and six-foot lengths at $7,200 to $9,800. The article on the pig pickin' calls the grills 'as varied as the methods of producing them', some homemade, some custom-made.
text.story: The pig pickin' moved the whole hog off the farm pit and onto wheels. *Tradition holds —* welded cookers appeared in eastern North Carolina after the Second World War, when propane and a cutting torch put a pit within reach of anyone with a trailer hitch, and the rental cooker followed. What the article on the pig pickin' records is the argument the cooker started: propane 'is said to maintain a consistent temperature, whereas charcoal or charwood are often touted as producing better-tasting meat', and the cooks who run charcoal add chunks of blackjack oak or hickory for the smoke, or keep a separate stove of hardwood to make coals and shovel them under the grate. The cooking is communal and 'usually directed by an authority figure' — the host, helped by friends and family — and the pig goes on meat-side down for four to eight hours and is flipped once when it stops dripping fat. Ed Mitchell learned on a family cooker in Wilson: at fourteen or fifteen he tended the fire after the men, having passed the moonshine, fell asleep, and his grandfather woke to a cooked pig and poured him his first glass.
text.how: The split hog goes on the grate meat-side down; on gas the burners run low, on charcoal the coals are lit in the bed or shoveled in from a hardwood stove; the lid comes down for four to eight hours until the dripping slows, and the hog is flipped once, skin down, to crisp. Some cooks wipe the ash from the skin with paper towels or a whisk broom before the flip so the cracklings come out clean. Off the cooker the meat is chopped, pulled, or picked straight off the bones by the guests.
text.today: Cookers are built and sold across the Coastal Plain — Micro and Elm City among the makers — and every pig pickin', tailgate and fire-department plate sale runs on one. Gas is the ordinary choice and charcoal the argued-for one.

names.name: pork shoulder
names.said: Lexington menus say 'pork shoulders'; 'butt' means the upper shoulder, not the rear of the animal.

etymology.root: Boston + butt, a barrel: in colonial and Revolutionary-era New England butchers stored and shipped this shoulder cut in barrels called butts, and the Boston-area method of cutting it gave the cut its name. Picnic (the lower shoulder): cured on the bone it is a 'picnic ham'; no origin for the name is cited here.
etymology.first_attested: 'Boston butt' in print, 1915, in Hotel Monthly; a 1912 University of Illinois Agricultural Experiment Station bulletin records the barrels still in use for export to Germany and Denmark
etymology.note: Folk: that the butt is the animal's hindquarter. It is not; the cut is the upper shoulder, above the picnic, and may contain the blade bone.

text.what: The front leg and shoulder of the pig, sold as one primal — a primal being one of the large first divisions of a carcass — or split in two: the butt, the upper half with the blade bone, and the picnic, the lower arm half, which cured on the bone is a 'picnic ham'. The butt's name is a barrel, not an anatomy. In the North Carolina Piedmont, shoulder is the only cut that counts as barbecue: Lexington pits salt it, lay it over oak and hickory coals for nine to twelve hours, and serve it chopped, coarse chopped or sliced under a red dip. It is darker meat than the loin and stays moist through a long cook, and it is what packers ship when they will not ship a carcass.
text.story: New England butchers of the colonial and Revolutionary era stored and shipped pork in barrels called butts, and the shoulder cut they packed that way took the name of the port; a 1912 University of Illinois bulletin notes the barrels still going to Germany and Denmark, and 'Boston butt' first appears in print in 1915. In the Carolinas the cut's rise is the whole hog's decline. The Piedmont settled on shoulders early — *Tradition holds —* because a shoulder fit a small brick pit and a lunch counter's day in a way a carcass did not. By the 1980s the corporate farms replacing independent hog farms shipped butchered shoulders and hams rather than whole pigs, which pushed restaurants elsewhere the same way. Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church in Charlotte, which began in 1929 by cooking three or four pigs and a goat, told Our State in 2016: 'Now we just use the butt.' South Carolina hash, once made from heads and liver, is now mostly made from leftover shoulder.
text.how: Lexington pits cook shoulders only, salted but not basted or marinated, on racks over oak and hickory coals for nine to twelve hours at about 200 to 225 degrees; the Barbecue Center puts three hundred a week through its pit. Elsewhere a butt is rubbed, smoked until it reaches 195 to 205 degrees inside, and shredded. Off the pit the Piedmont serves it three ways — chopped fine, coarse chopped in small chunks, or sliced; never pulled, at Lexington Barbecue — and dresses it with dip. *Tradition holds —* the crusted outer meat is sold apart as outside brown.
text.today: Shoulder is the cut of the Piedmont's pits — Lexington Barbecue, the Barbecue Center, Stamey's, Red Bridges, Short Sugar's — and of most new restaurants in both states, because it arrives boxed from the packer; a pulled-pork menu anywhere in the country means this cut. At Lexington Barbecue a chopped tray was $8.00 cash and $8.25 by card in September 2026.

names.name: whole hog
names.said: Eastern cooks 'cook a pig' or 'put on a hog'; what comes off the block is just 'barbecue'.

text.what: The entire dressed pig — dressed meaning gutted and scraped of hair, the head sometimes left on — split open along the backbone, laid flat over coals and cooked as one piece, then pulled from the bones and chopped together: ham, shoulder, loin, belly and, in the Carolinas, the crisped skin. It is the oldest form of open-pit barbecue in the United States and the cut that defines eastern North Carolina and the Pee Dee of South Carolina. A hog of 80 to 120 pounds dressed weight is the usual size for a pig pickin'; restaurants choose small hogs and cook them hot so the skin crisps, and a whole animal can run to 300 pounds.
text.story: Robert Moss finds the ritual barbecue of whole hogs established in the British colonies by the eighteenth century; the communal feast of whole pigs or sheep spread from Virginia into the Carolinas in the mid-1700s and fed fundraisers, church gatherings and political rallies. The Oxford Encyclopedia of Food and Drink in America calls whole hog the oldest style of open-pit barbecue in the country. The first sit-down restaurant built on it was Bob Melton's, opened at Rocky Mount in 1924; for most of the twentieth century such places had white owners and Black cooks, and new pits were founded by cooks trained at older ones. In Hemingway, South Carolina, the Scott family's variety store cooked one hog a week when Rodney Scott started at eleven and grew to seven or eight a day. The hazards are in the method: fat renders and pools in the cavity, so the meat cooks in its own fat, and a lean 'bacon hog' such as the American Yorkshire is chosen because a fat one feeds the fire. Pit fires are the common disaster; Scott's wooden cookhouse burned in November 2013 — 'shooting like a torch', the fire department told him — and the family took its hogs on the road to raise at least $100,000 to rebuild. In 2017 Daniel Vaughn of Texas Monthly counted the whole-hog restaurants of the country and found them falling: packers ship shoulders and hams, not carcasses; a whole hog costs more labor, fuel and soot than a shoulder; and much of its weight is bone and fat that cannot be sold.
text.how: The carcass is split so it lies flat; the backbone may be cracked and the head split. It goes on the rack skin-side up — meat-side down, in the east's phrase — over a bed of coals and cooks for eight to twenty-four hours, most of that time unturned, before one flip to crisp the skin; at Scott's the flip comes at the eight-to-twelve-hour mark and a full-size mop bathes the meat in the family's vinegar-and-pepper sauce. The meat is not basted before the flip, though some cooks season it with a dry rub. Turning a heavy carcass takes several hands. Off the pit the meat is picked from the bones and chopped fine or pulled into threads; the eastern chop takes the crisp skin in, and the Pee Dee sometimes skins the pig first and fries the skin separately.
text.today: Whole hog is the restaurant cut of the Coastal Plain and the Pee Dee — the Skylight Inn, B's, Grady's, Parker's and Wilber's in North Carolina; Scott's in Hemingway and Rodney Scott's in Charleston in South Carolina — and the cooking of most pig pickin's. Vaughn's 2017 count found fewer whole-hog restaurants each year; cooks who keep it say their customers come for the ritual.

text.what: A mountain barbecue house now trading from Hendersonville Road in Arden, south of Asheville, after Hurricane Helene took its River Arts District room in September 2024. Tom Montgomery and Sabra Kelley opened the first one in 2005 in a cinder-block shack on an Asheville floodplain; Bryan and Angela King have owned it since about 2012. Ribs are the signature — blueberry-chipotle and other glazes that are not Carolina orthodoxy — with pulled pork alongside. Barack Obama ate here in April 2010, which is the thing most often said about it.
text.story: The first 12 Bones was a cinder-block shack in a floodplain in the River Arts District, opened in 2005 by Tom Montgomery and Sabra Kelley. Bryan and Angela King bought it — 2012 by two 2024 accounts, 2011 by a 2017 one — and Explore Asheville's profile puts the ownership plainly in Bryan King's own words, that he owns 12 Bones with his wife Angela. On April 23, 2010 Barack Obama came in and ate ribs, mac and cheese, corn pudding and sweet tea; accounts differ on whether he visited twice or three times. In January 2017 the original Riverside Drive building was closed and demolished for a road project and a roundabout, and the business moved to Foundy Street beside Wedge Brewing. Then on September 27, 2024 Helene put the floodplain under water. Bryan King described going inside to find mud in the attic and the building almost completely submerged, and called it a very long recovery. By April 2025 the business had told Blue Ridge Public Radio it would not rebuild on Foundy Street. Arden is what is left, open seven days now rather than the weekday lunches the Asheville room kept.
text.how: Ribs are the thing: a dry rub and a run of glazes, the blueberry-chipotle the one people name, which is not how a Piedmont or a Coastal Plain pit finishes pork. Pulled pork, sides and a brewing operation fill the rest. An Explore Asheville listing says the meats are smoked long and slow over oak and cherry; that reads as the restaurant's own copy and could not be confirmed on the company's site, which is why the fuel here is left unknown.
text.today: Open seven days, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., at 2350 Hendersonville Road, Arden — the only location the company lists. The Foundy Street room in Asheville's River Arts District closed with Helene in September 2024 and will not be rebuilt.

text.what: The hickory-fired pork-shoulder restaurant on Millhouse Road at N.C. 86 north of Chapel Hill that Keith Allen opened in 1971 at nineteen and closed in the first week of December 2018, quietly, to avoid a long goodbye. Allen split the hickory himself, fired the pit every half hour for nine hours, and dressed the chopped shoulder with the hot vinegar sauce he had from his father — an eastern sauce on Piedmont meat. His wife Tammy waited tables for thirty years and made the ice cream; the pies, cobblers and banana pudding were the second reason to come. A separate Allen & Son in Pittsboro, under a licensing agreement, stayed open.
text.story: Keith Allen's father James ran an Allen & Son in Chatham County, and Keith was cooking at twelve or thirteen after his father bought the business; his father died at 51 or 52. In 1971 Keith opened the Chapel Hill restaurant with $3,000, Our State reported in 2017. He started work at 2:30 in the morning five days a week, split hickory logs by hand for the heat and the flavor — 'I keep cooking with wood because I'm chasing that flavor' — and cooked sixteen-pound shoulders down to nine or eleven over nine hours. 'Nobody's hands but mine touch my barbecue, until the customer's do.' The authors of Holy Smoke interviewed him at length; the Southern Foodways Alliance gave him its Guardian of the Tradition award in 2007. He had no son to take it on; his daughter went to graduate school in geospatial science. In early December 2018 he closed without notice, and Chapelboro reported on December 6 that the Pittsboro Allen & Son on U.S. 15-501 would continue under a separate licensing agreement. UNC Press published a closing interview with him two weeks later.
text.how: Sixteen-pound shoulders over hickory Allen split himself, the pit fired every thirty minutes for nine hours, the meat chopped and dressed with a vinegar sauce he called hot and spicy. Chicken, catfish and cheeseburgers filled out the menu, and the desserts — ice cream made daily, cobblers from his grandmother's recipe, coconut chess and peanut butter pies, pecan pie, banana pudding — were made in the house, with sweet tea.
text.today: Closed since December 2018. The building at 6203 Millhouse Road, Chapel Hill, is not the Pittsboro Allen & Son, which continued separately; this record is the Chapel Hill restaurant only.

text.what: The Shelby pork-shoulder house of the other Bridges family, on East Grover Street in Cleveland County, where Alston Bridges and his wife Mabel bought the property in 1955. Alston learned the trade from his brother-in-law Warner Stamey, managing Stamey's Log Cabin Barbecue in Lexington for two and a half years first. About fifty shoulders a day go through the kitchen; the tray is chopped or coarse-chopped pork with red slaw and hushpuppies. What is under the meat is disputed: three accounts describe electric cookers or gas, one promotional listing says wood-smoked.
text.story: Two Bridges families cook barbecue in Shelby and they are not related — a shared ancestor somewhere in the 1700s is as close as the local history will put them. Warner Stamey trained both Red Bridges and Alston Bridges in the 1940s, and Alston's apprenticeship is the documented one: he and Mabel moved to Lexington, he managed Stamey's Log Cabin Barbecue for two and a half years, and then they came to Shelby and bought 620 East Grover Street. The county history gives the year as 1955 and a visiting writer gives 1956. Alston died in 1970; his son Kent and Kent's wife Linda took it on, and the county history says Kent and Linda's children operate the business now. Our State found Alston's grandson Reid Bridges behind the counter in 2013, explaining the difference between chopped and coarse-chopped. The fuel is where the sources part. Our State wrote in 2013 that he starts the pork on electric cookers and finishes it in a pit. A visiting writer in March 2024 found the smoke missing and put it down to a move from pit to gas some years earlier. The NC Pork Council's listing calls it wood-smoked. Neither the Historic Barbecue Trail nor the Campaign for Real Barbecue lists the house, and both exclude gas and electric.
text.how: About fifty pork shoulders a day, from a short-shank cut the kitchen buys through a Gastonia distributor. Our State's account of the method has the pork starting on electric cookers and finishing in a pit. The meat is chopped or coarse-chopped to order and served with red slaw, the cabbage cut fine and dressed with the Piedmont dip, and hushpuppies. The menus read: Pigs are Beautiful.
text.today: Open at 620 East Grover Street, Shelby. Hours differ across three listings, and the restaurant's own site was posting a Labor Day closing and a September 8 return when read on September 16, 2026. Check before driving.

text.what: A Black-owned barbecue restaurant on N.C. 55, the Apex Highway, in southeast Durham, opened in April 2007 by Fabianne and Melvin Simmons, who bought a struggling restaurant and made it a neighborhood institution: chopped barbecue and sandwiches, ribs, smoked chicken and oxtails, cooked over wood coals and made from scratch. Its later years were hard — a $50,000 GoFundMe in 2023, a change of owners, eight months dark for renovations before a March 2024 reopening, and in April 2026 a report that it was weeks from closing unless a buyer came. Its status in September 2026 is not confirmed on this disk.
text.story: Melvin Simmons ran the pit for more than sixteen years, Fabianne with him, from the April 2007 opening through recessions and the pandemic. In 2023 the family asked the public for $50,000 to keep the doors open. The reports on disk then part: Spectacular Magazine wrote in April 2026 that Angela McLean had taken the restaurant over in 2023, while CBS 17 reported in March 2024 that Damien Holloway, as new owner, had redone 'every single thing in the building' — equipment, floors, walls, ceilings, bathrooms — over eight closed months and was set to reopen, the grand opening slipping for weather. The Assembly, surveying the state's Black-owned pits in February 2026, found the restaurant exploring a sale, its future uncertain. By April 2026 McLean told Spectacular that customers were choosing between a meal and gas for the car, and that without a buyer the restaurant could close by the end of the month.
text.how: Barbecue chopped and sandwiched, ribs, smoked chicken and oxtails, cooked over wood coals and made from scratch, by the owners' accounts to the Durham press. Which cut, which sauce and which sides are not described in the sources on this disk, and no price is recorded.
text.today: Status unknown as of September 2026: the last reports on this disk, from February and April 2026, had it for sale and near closing. The address is 5122 N.C. Highway 55 (Apex Highway), Durham.

text.what: A pork-shoulder pit and ice-cream counter on North Main Street in Lexington, Davidson County, that began in 1955 as a dairy bar, put a shoulder on a pit one slow winter, and has been the Conrad family's since: Sonny Conrad (1938–2013), who started on curb service there as a teenager in 1955 and became owner in 1969, his wife Nancy, and their sons Michael and Cecil. Shoulders cook over hickory; the barbecue comes chopped, sliced or 'brown' — the smoky outside of the shoulder — with the dip and red slaw. The ice cream never left: about 200 gallons a week, much of it in a banana split of three and a half pounds.
text.story: The dairy bar of 1955 sold ice cream on Main Street, and in the 1960s the strip was a cruising street for hot rods; Sonny Conrad later put up metal railings to keep the place a family one, Our State wrote in 2014. Ice cream sales dip in winter, so one winter a pork shoulder went on a pit, and the restaurant's own history says it moved to its present building at 900 North Main in the late 1950s. Conrad had begun as a curb-service boy in 1955; in 1969 he married Nancy, a waitress there, and became the owner. He told the Southern Foodways Alliance in November 2011 that the kitchen made a hundred gallons a week each of dip and red slaw, that four customers in ten still ate in their cars, and that 'red slaw. That's a good vegetable.' He died in 2013; Nancy still worked, and the sons ran the day to day. Southern Living and Good Morning America have both come for the banana split. New airtight pits went in around 2013, glowing orange with coals; the dining room seats about a hundred at booths and a counter.
text.how: Pork shoulders cook over hickory coals with the family's spice blend; the meat is chopped or sliced, or served brown from the smoky outside, with the Lexington dip — thin, vinegar-based, reddened with ketchup — and red slaw, hushpuppies, baked beans and cornbread. Curb service brings the tray to the car. The banana split weighs three and a half pounds and is built for a table.
text.today: Open Monday to Saturday 11 to 9, at 900 North Main Street, Lexington, per OpenStreetMap (2026), which tags the address to Thomasville in error; the 27292 postcode and the restaurant's own site say Lexington. Dine-in and curb service.

text.what: A Bessinger family barbecue house at 1602 Savannah Highway in Charleston's West Ashley. Thomas Bessinger came from Holly Hill to Charleston with his brother Melvin in 1955, opened his own restaurant in 1960, and in 1961 the brothers opened Piggy Park Drive-In on the highway; renamed Bessinger's in 1971, it is run by Thomas's sons Tommy and Michael. It serves chopped pork in the family's mustard sauce, ribs, hash and rice, and a buffet on weekend evenings, and the South Carolina Barbeque Association lists it as 100-Mile Barbecue — a house worth a hundred-mile drive. It is the Charleston branch of the family whose Columbia branch is Maurice's Piggie Park.
text.story: Joseph Jacob 'Big Joe' Bessinger traded the family cow, a mule and fifty dollars for the Holly Hill Café in 1939 and served mustard-sauced barbecue there. After the war his son Melvin put his Army pay into a second Holly Hill restaurant, Eat At Joe's, in 1946, and the younger Thomas — born in Orangeburg in 1931 — started cooking there at fourteen. Thomas joined the Army after school and cooked two years overseas for soldiers. In 1955 Melvin closed Eat At Joe's and moved to Charleston, bringing Thomas; Thomas opened his own restaurant there in 1960, and in 1961 the brothers opened Piggy Park Drive-In on Savannah Highway together. After ten years they renamed it Bessinger's — The Barbecue Family. In 1982 Melvin crossed the Cooper River to open Melvin's in Mount Pleasant, and the brothers went their own ways. When their brother Maurice raised Confederate flags over his Columbia restaurants in July 2000, the press described the Charleston brothers' businesses as independent concerns, 'sans the politics'; grocery chains that dropped Maurice's sauce stocked Melvin's, and Maurice stopped speaking to him. Thomas Bessinger Sr. died on November 10, 2023, at ninety-two, with the restaurant in his sons' hands.
text.how: Chopped pork dressed in the family's yellow mustard sauce, from a pit behind the building; ribs, St. Louis cut, wet with the same sauce; hash over rice that the Barbeque Association's listing rates 'very, very good'; and onion rings the size of a doughnut. The buffet runs Friday and Saturday evenings and Sunday midday.
text.today: Open seven days, 10:30 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., with the buffet Friday and Saturday 5:30 to 8:30 p.m. and Sunday noon to 8, per the Barbeque Association's listing; OpenStreetMap recorded 11 to 9 in November 2023. 1602 Savannah Highway, Charleston. Checked September 15, 2026.

text.what: A Black-owned wood-burning pit on Congaree Road at Gadsden, in lower Richland County below Columbia, run by Larry Brown, known as Teddy and as Big T, who has sold barbecue to the Columbia area for more than thirty years. Logs burn down in a warped burn box behind the smokehouse and the coals are shovelled into low metal pits under pork shoulders. Hash goes over rice, made with pork and offal in the Midlands way. A second house on Garners Ferry Road in Columbia serves the same barbecue from a buffet.
text.story: Neither the founding year nor a founding date is on this disk; what the listings agree on is that Larry Brown has been at it in this part of Richland County for over thirty years. He is not a Sweatman, and Big T has no connection to Sweatman's Bar-B-Que at Holly Hill, though the two names travel together in loose accounts of South Carolina barbecue. The evidence that the business is Black-owned is the directory kind rather than the profile kind: EatOkra, which indexes Black-owned restaurants, carries it, and the chef Todd Richards put it in his guide to Black-owned barbecue. A 2019 newspaper profile that would have said it in a reporter's words could not be fetched for this record. The South Carolina Barbeque Association's own page files Big T under Worth the Trip and describes the method — slow over coals and wood at the Gadsden operation — while saying the hash there is a little mild for the writer's taste, which is the sort of judgement a project like this one records rather than adopts. Brown's son Travis works the pits. The Gadsden house closes Sunday, Monday and Tuesday; the Columbia house runs a buffet.
text.how: Logs burn down to coals in a large warped burn box behind the smokehouse, and the coals are shovelled into low metal pits under pork shoulders — not whole hogs. The hash is the Midlands kind, pork and offal cooked down and ladled over white rice. Cards and cash are both taken. The Garners Ferry Road house in Columbia serves from a buffet; Gadsden does not.
text.today: Open at 2520 Congaree Road, Gadsden, closed Sunday, Monday and Tuesday, with a second house at 7535 Garners Ferry Road, Columbia. The map point is the Congaree Road centreline rather than the building: the geocoder returned the road, not the house number.

text.what: A Black-owned barbecue counter on Statesville Road in north Charlotte, opened in 2008 by Bob Steven Roberts after four years working on his sauce. The board runs to pulled pork, ribs, brisket and wings rather than whole hog, and the room is counter service with online ordering. Roberts's niece Chloria Chandler is his business partner. It is one of the few barbecue businesses in Mecklenburg County that the Black-owned business directories carry, and the only one in this project's Charlotte records.
text.story: Bob Steven Roberts spent four years on the sauce before he opened. He had lived in California and New Jersey before coming to North Carolina more than thirty years ago, cooked in Fayetteville and Raleigh, and landed in Charlotte. His niece Chloria Chandler works with him as his business partner; she told QCity Metro in November 2021 that her favourite is the ribs, because she had been eating them since she was in her mother's stomach. The Black-owned business directories carry him: EatOkra lists the restaurant, NBA.com put it first in a list of ten Black-owned Charlotte restaurants in February 2023, and the chef Todd Richards included it in his guide to Black-owned barbecue, updated May 2025, with a note that this is the place for a sampler plate. What is under the meat is not settled. A 2024 lifestyle listing says hickory; a barbecue blog reported second-hand in 2016 that the kitchen ran a cabinet smoker and was not trying for wood smoke, and its own 2012 visit found no smoker in sight. The restaurant's site says nothing about fuel, so no wood tag is set here. *Inference —* the sauce, not the fire, is what every account of this kitchen is actually about.
text.how: Counter service and online ordering: pulled pork, ribs, brisket and wings by the plate or the pound, with the house sauce that took four years to settle. There is no whole hog on the board in any source read, and no hash. Cards are taken. The room keeps long hours by barbecue standards, into the evening six nights and to eight on Sunday.
text.today: Open, on the listings read, at 9401 Statesville Road, Suite C, Charlotte; an earlier address on Old Statesville Road appears in accounts from 2012. No closure notice was found and no news-grade source confirms trading in 2026, so treat the status as reported rather than checked.

text.what: A Texas-leaning smokehouse on North Main Street in Fountain Inn, Greenville County, owned by Octavius Nelson, called Tay, and his wife Sarah. Brisket, pulled pork, ribs, turkey and house-made sausage come off the pits; there is no hash and no buffet, which sets it apart from most South Carolina barbecue houses. The name is for Tay's father Bobby Nelson Sr. and his brother Bobby Jr., both dead before the business began. A seasoning line came first, in 2010; the restaurant followed.
text.story: Tay Nelson started working with his father in a Greenville restaurant at twelve. Bobby Nelson Sr. died in 2008 and Bobby Jr. in 2009, and what Tay built next was assembled out of what they left him: he blended a seasoning from the spices his father had used, sold it from 2010, and taught himself to smoke from tutorials on the internet. The restaurant opened in 2018, though the business's own page dates the barbecue side to 2014 and the seasoning to 2010, so the anniversary depends on which thread is counted. The ownership line is unusually plain, in the business's own words: Bobby's BBQ is owned by Tay Nelson and his wife Sarah. That is the sentence the woman-owned tag here rests on. What the record does not carry is a Black-owned tag. Nothing on the business's own pages uses the phrase, EatOkra does not list it, and a Post and Courier piece that might have settled it returned an error on two attempts. The press the business does have is broad and national — ABC News in 2020, Tamron Hall in 2021, a Forbes gift guide, a Google economic impact report — rather than the barbecue-world kind.
text.how: Brisket, pulled pork, ribs, turkey and house-made sausage, in the Central Texas manner rather than the Midlands one: no hash on the menu, no mustard tradition, no buffet. The seasoning blend that started the business in 2010 is still sold. Cards and cash are both taken. The kitchen runs four days, Thursday to Saturday, and the smoke is wood, on the strength of the certification rather than any published description of the fire.
text.today: Open Thursday to Saturday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., closed Sunday to Wednesday, at 1301 North Main Street, Fountain Inn. Both the restaurant's own site and the OpenStreetMap harvest agree on the address.

text.what: A farm family's buffet house on the Williamsburg County Highway north of Kingstree, in the Pee Dee, opened in 1981 as a take-out window by Thomas M. Brown Jr., a row-crop farmer, with a dining room added about ten years on. Whole hogs are cooked and chopped, mopped on the pit with a vinegar-and-hot-pepper sauce the family calls barbecue gravy, and set on a long buffet with ribs, smoked ham, barbecued and fried chicken, barbecued and baked turkey, perloo, liver hash and rice, and vegetables the Browns grow themselves — corn, squash, okra, butter beans, collards, cabbage. The Barbeque Association names it among the state's top barbecue houses.
text.story: Thomas Brown learned to cook as a teenager laid up after a motorcycle accident broke his leg, working a hot plate within reach of the bed. He farmed — soy, wheat, hay and oats for market — and in 1981 opened a take-out window on the highway; the dining room came a decade later. The farm feeds the buffet: corn, squash, zucchini, broccoli, okra, butter beans, collards and cabbage in season. When the Southern Foodways Alliance came through the Pee Dee in June 2012, Rien Fertel recorded the Browns, and Angela Brown told him, 'We always take barbecue everywhere we go.' Kingstree is a whole-hog town — its Pig Pickin' festival each fall draws cooking teams, seventy of them in 2010, to compete on the county's vinegar-based barbecue — and Brown's is its standing barbecue house, more than forty years on. In April 2024 a visiting writer paid $14.95 for the buffet and ate liver hash over rice with salt, pepper and Texas Pete.
text.how: Whole hogs on the pit, mopped as they cook with the barbecue gravy — vinegar and hot pepper — then chopped. The buffet runs the length of the room: chopped barbecue, ribs, smoked ham, barbecued and fried chicken, barbecued and baked turkey, perloo (rice cooked with chicken), white rice, liver hash — hash with the liver in it, as the name says — macaroni, sweet potatoes, coleslaw, potato salad, the farm's vegetables, a salad bar and pecan pie. Buffet $14.95 in April 2024; a whole-hog plate with bread, baked beans and slaw is the take-out order.
text.today: Open Wednesday to Saturday 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. and Sunday 11 to 3, closed Monday and Tuesday, per Destination BBQ; 809 North Williamsburg County Highway (US 52), Kingstree. Checked September 15, 2026.

text.what: A whole-hog and chicken pit on the edge of Greenville, Pitt County, in a converted country store on a road the county named for it. Bill McLawhorn, the B, opened it in 1978 with his wife Peggy; their daughters Judy Drach, Tammy Godley and Donna McLawhorn have run it since his death in 2007. There is no telephone, no take-out menu and no closing time: the doors open at nine in the morning and shut when the day's barbecue and chicken are gone, usually early afternoon. Cash or check only. The line forms before opening.
text.story: Bill McLawhorn gave up farming in 1978 and bought a convenience store just inside Greenville's city limits; he and Peggy worked out the sauce together and cooked out back, selling up front. He refused a telephone — 'If you need me, come get me' — and the refusal outlasted him. Bob Garner wrote it up for Our State in 2012 as a place of red picnic tables and cafeteria-style counter service with no promise the food would still be there at noon. Judy Drach told the Southern Foodways Alliance in 2009 that the family could have built something bigger with more staff and a day off, 'but when you start doing all that, then it's like any other restaurant and that's not what we wanted it to be.' Bill died in 2007 and the sisters took it on. The pits were once wood-fired brick; after fires the family went over to charcoal, and the pigs go on around nine at night to be ready by nine in the morning. The county renamed the road B's Barbecue Road.
text.how: Whole hogs and chickens cook overnight over charcoal, the hogs going on about 9 p.m. The pork is chopped by hand, never ground, and dressed with the McLawhorns' vinegar sauce; the chicken is sold by the half or the whole bird. In 2016 Our State printed the board: barbecue dinner $7.75, sandwich $3.75, a pound $8.50, half a chicken $7, a whole one $11.50. The customer orders at the counter and eats at a picnic table or in the car.
text.today: Open Tuesday to Saturday from 9 a.m. until sold out, at 751 B's Barbecue Road, Greenville. No phone. Cash or check. Hours pattern from Our State (2012 and 2016); check before driving.

text.what: A wood-fired whole-hog restaurant in downtown Ayden, Pitt County, opened in 1963 by Latham 'Bum' Dennis, of the family that counts Skilton Dennis's 1830 wagon as the start of barbecue for sale here, and run by his son Larry, who cuts the wood, burns the coals and starts around four in the morning. Unlike most eastern pits it keeps a buffet of vegetables cooked that day — collards from the family garden, cabbage pastry, stewed rutabaga, black-eyed peas, boiled potatoes — beside the chopped barbecue. The sign is modest; the smell does the advertising.
text.story: Latham Dennis opened Bum's in 1963. The family's claim runs back to Skilton Dennis, who *tradition holds —* sold smoked hog meat commercially from 1830, a date the Southern Foodways Alliance recorded from the Dennises themselves, and to Otter Dennis, whom the family connects to the founding of Ayden; the Skylight Inn's Joneses paint the same 1830 on their billboard. Bum told the Alliance's Rien Fertel in December 2011, with Larry beside him, that in this kind of restaurant 'what you got to do you got to love it and it's a way of life.' Our State in April 2014 found Larry cutting oak and pecan and burning it down to embers before dawn, and Shirley Dennis, the family's matriarch, decorating the overflow dining room with Gone with the Wind memorabilia, a parking space reserved for her outside. Bum Dennis died in December 2022; Larry runs the restaurant. The vegetable buffet is what the writers single out: collards grown by the family, cabbage pastry, rutabaga, black-eyed peas, boiled potatoes, a table few other eastern pits keep.
text.how: Whole hogs cook over embers burned down from oak and pecan; the pork is chopped and dressed eastern-style, with vinegar and pepper. The barbecue is one station of a cafeteria line: the rest is the day's vegetables — collards from the family garden, cabbage pastry (cabbage stewed with strips of flat dumpling dough), rutabaga, black-eyed peas, boiled potatoes — and the plate is built by pointing.
text.today: Open, at 566 East Third Street, Ayden; Larry Dennis runs it. Hours are not recorded on this disk, and the last press confirmation read is from 2022; check before driving.

text.what: A whole-hog restaurant that ran from August 2015 to November 22, 2023 in a 1930s roller rink on Banks Avenue in Asheville's South Slope, opened by pitmaster Elliott Moss with Meherwan Irani's Chai Pani restaurant group. Pasture-raised pigs from western North Carolina farms smoked over wood from ten at night to eight in the morning; the plate carried South Carolina hash over rice — the pig's organs and fatty trimmings cooked down to a gravy — beside the chopped hog, with a fried-chicken sandwich, smoked baked beans and pimento cheese, lard-crust pies and banana pudding under meringue. The rink's murals stayed on the walls.
text.story: Elliott Moss grew up watching his grandfather smoke whole hogs, and brought that South Carolina whole hog to the mountains. He and Meherwan Irani, both James Beard nominees, opened Buxton Hall in August 2015 in a building that had been a roller rink in the 1930s and then the Standard Paper Sales Company. Bon Appétit ranked it ninth among the country's new restaurants in 2016 and named its fried chicken sandwich the sandwich of the year. The pandemic closed it from March to July 2020; a fire later forced another closure and new equipment. Moss left as pitmaster in July 2022 and chef Nick Barr took the kitchen. The Smoke Sheet reported on November 8, 2023 that the last day of service would be November 22. Chai Pani, Irani's Indian restaurant, moved from Battery Park Avenue into the 8,000-square-foot space and reopened there on May 21, 2024.
text.how: Whole hogs from pasture farms smoked overnight, ten to eight, over wood, then were chopped in the eastern way. The hash — organs and trimmings cooked to a gravy — went over rice as it does in the Pee Dee. The kitchen fried chicken for a sandwich, smoked the baked beans and the pimento cheese, baked pies on lard crusts and topped the banana pudding with meringue.
text.today: Closed since November 22, 2023. Chai Pani, its co-owner's Indian restaurant, has occupied the rink at 32 Banks Avenue, Asheville, since its reopening there on May 21, 2024.

text.what: A small barbecue house in a converted mobile home at a five-way crossroads in Little Mountain, Newberry County — the Dutch Fork, the German-settled land between the Broad and Saluda rivers where the Midlands mustard sauce is at home. The Cannons cooked over wood coals they burned down themselves and chopped the pork for a sauce with a concentrated yellow-mustard taste; the ribs fell off the bone, and the hash — the Midlands' stew of pork and onion, here tinged bright yellow with mustard — is what Robert Moss remembered it for. It has closed: Moss, writing in March 2020, called it recently closed.
text.story: Little Mountain sits off Interstate 26 at exit 91, and Cannon's sat a few miles from the exit in a modified mobile home at a 'five points' intersection, with an overfilled dumpster and wood strewn about the lot when Destination BBQ came in March 2014 — the wood being the point, since the Cannons burned their own coals. The reviewers found the pork chopped finer than they liked, the ribs falling off the bone, the hash good and the sauce 'typical of the Midlands: mustard based', with a very concentrated yellow-mustard flavor. Robert Moss, telling the story of hash and rice in 2020, used it as his example of the mustard-yellow hash: 'At the recently-closed Cannon's BBQ in Little Mountain, S.C., the hash was tinged bright yellow with mustard.' *Tradition holds —* the Cannon brothers ran it about fifteen years and served the last plates on July 4, 2019, a closing the Columbia station WLTX reported that June.
text.how: Pork chopped and sauced with a yellow-mustard sauce, ribs that fell from the bone, and hash — pork and onion cooked down to a spoonable stew — tinged bright yellow with mustard and served over rice, all cooked over wood coals the family burned down on the lot. The building was a mobile home fitted out as a dining room, the lot a woodyard.
text.today: Closed. Robert Moss described it as recently closed in March 2020; no reopening is recorded in this project's sources as of September 15, 2026. The coordinates here are the town's, not the building's.

text.what: A mustard-sauce buffet house on South Main Street in New Ellenton, Aiken County, founded by Willie Mae Walker and her son Jess. She was born Willie Mae Baltzegar, daughter of the Rowesville pitmaster Willie Baltzegar, which puts a pit-cooking line behind the place two generations deep. Pork shoulders cook over wood in smokers out back — not open-pit whole hog. The buffet was twelve dollars in April 2025 and the hash is rust-orange and thick enough to lift on a fork. Thomas Zeigler has run it since about 2022.
text.story: Willie Mae Walker came out of Rowesville, where her father Willie Baltzegar cooked, and she and her son Jess opened in New Ellenton — 1969 by two accounts, 1968 by a third. Naming her as a founder is not a courtesy: the sources put her first, with her son second, which is unusual enough in this trade to be worth saying once. Jess 'Bubba' Walker carried it on. Then the place slipped. Michael Stern, writing for The Food Section on April 22, 2025, said it had been losing its footing four or five years earlier — the food not up to standard and the staff getting cranky — before Thomas Zeigler took the business over about three years before he wrote, tweaked a few recipes and turned it round. Destination BBQ's page, updated April 2025, still names Bubba Walker as the owner, so the two listings disagree and the later, purpose-built piece is followed here. Southern Living put it on the South's Top 50 barbecue list in 2016, a list Robert Moss compiled, and the Barbeque Association gives it the hundred-mile designation. The Campaign for Real Barbecue certified it. Destination BBQ traces the hash recipe to the Dukes family tradition, which is the Orangeburg line reaching west.
text.how: Pork shoulders only — no ribs — cook over wood in smokers behind the building, which is not the open-pit whole-hog method of the Pee Dee and is described that way by the writers who visit. The sauce is the Midlands mustard. The buffet is all you can eat, twelve dollars in April 2025. The hash is rust-orange, thick, with an organ-meat sweetness, ladled over rice; one writer put it slightly thicker than Maurice's and a little less tart.
text.today: Open Wednesday 11 to 1:30 and Thursday to Saturday 11 to 8, closed Sunday to Tuesday, at 109 South Main Street, New Ellenton. Cards and cash. A search result circulating a South Main address in the eight hundreds is not supported by any page read here.

text.what: Raleigh's downtown barbecue house since New Year's Day 1938, when Clyde Cooper opened on East Davie Street with fifty dollars borrowed from a brother-in-law; it moved around the corner to 327 South Wilmington Street in 2014 when the old building was lost to development, carrying the awning and the front door with it. It cooks pork shoulders — hand-trimmed, never whole hog — in pits on the upper floor, chops them and dresses them with Cooper's tangy sauce, which the city's tourism office calls a blend of eastern and Lexington ways. Fried chicken, Brunswick stew, collards, hushpuppies, boiled potatoes and banana pudding fill out the board; fried pork skins ride on the tray.
text.story: Clyde Cooper opened on January 1, 1938 in an 1884 building at 109 East Davie Street, and for fifty years he alone held the key. He cooked at first behind his house on Chapel Hill Road until the health department stopped him and the pits went upstairs, built to order by Nunnery-Freeman. The restaurant's own history says he was among the first Raleigh business owners to let Black customers in through the front door, in the early 1960s. After decades of being asked, he sold around 1988 to a builder named Tony; Debbie Holt, who had managed the place for him for five and a half years, took it over around 2008. Clyde Cooper died on February 12, 1998, short of a hundred. Holt told the Southern Foodways Alliance in November 2011 that she was fighting a developer's plan for a multistory apartment building on the Davie Street site — 'Ain't all about the money. It's about saving it for people and generations to come.' The building was lost; in 2014 the restaurant moved to South Wilmington Street, where the old awning hangs over the lunch counter and the old door hangs on the wall. In 2023, marking 85 years, Visit Raleigh noted it had at last begun taking credit cards.
text.how: Pork shoulders are trimmed by hand and cooked in the upstairs pits, then served chopped, sliced or coarse; the sauce is tangy rather than sweet, on Cooper's recipe. A tray — barbecue, slaw, hushpuppies and fried pork skins — cost $11 in 2023. Fried chicken, ribs and brisket, Brunswick stew, collards, boiled potatoes, several kinds of fried pork skins and banana pudding are the rest of the menu.
text.today: Open Monday to Saturday 10 to 6, at 327 South Wilmington Street, Raleigh, per OpenStreetMap (2026). Cards accepted since 2023.

text.what: A pork-shoulder pit off Valiant Drive south of Lexington, Davidson County, built by hand in 1969 by Doug Cook on a cul-de-sac plot down the road from his house — a pit and kitchen, a wooden chopping block, a drive-up window — with a dining room he framed from oaks felled on the lot. His son Brandon, born a year after the restaurant, came back as pitmaster in 2001 and kept the original brick pit and the hickory coals. In an October report DavidsonLocal recorded that the restaurant, by then trading as Cooks & BBQ Still Smoking, had announced on July 28 that it was closed indefinitely and would be sold; no reopening is on this disk.
text.story: Doug Cook built his stand in 1969 with his own hands; when customers wanted somewhere to sit he cut trees from the oak grove around it and framed a dining room. Brandon Cook grew up in the place — crawling into the fireplace as a child, flirting with the waitresses as a teenager — and learned under his father to tend the pits, shovel the cherry-red hickory coals and cook Lexington-style shoulders. He returned in 2001 as pitmaster and told the Southern Foodways Alliance's Rien Fertel in November 2011, 'Believe it or not, I'm related to half of the people around here that run the barbecue places, so yeah, I eat a bunch of it.' Customers dip their plates rather than pour sauce. DavidsonLocal, in an October roundup of Davidson County barbecue houses changing hands, reported that Cooks & BBQ Still Smoking on Valiant Drive had posted on July 28 that it was closed 'indefinitely' and was to be sold, with no buyer announced.
text.how: Shoulders cook over hickory coals in the original brick pit, the coals shoveled in from the fireplace; the meat is chopped on the wooden block and served Lexington style, with the dip beside the plate for dipping rather than poured over.
text.today: Closed. DavidsonLocal reported the indefinite closure and a planned sale; listings still showed it closed in September 2026 and no reopening is recorded on this disk. The building sits at 366 Valiant Drive, Lexington.

text.what: A whitewashed general store on US 521 near Salters, south of Kingstree in Williamsburg County, that sells hardware, groceries, gasoline, diesel, propane, plow points, cast-iron cookware, live crickets — and, from a small meat counter at the back, whole-hog barbecue cooked over wood embers, hash, boiled peanuts and salt-cured country hams. Theron Burrows opened it as an Esso station in 1937; George Cooper built the pit after 1974; his nephew Russell Cooper has run it since 2003. It is a store, not a restaurant, and the barbecue is one more thing it keeps.
text.story: In 1937 the federal government built Highway 521 from Manning to Georgetown, and Theron Burrows, a tobacco and cotton farmer, opened an Esso service station and store on the new road. When he died in 1974 his daughter Adalyn and her husband George Cooper took it over as Cooper's Country Store. George watched families along the highway selling barbecue from car trunks and built his own pit — chickens on one half, hogs on the other. He ran the store twenty-nine years and in 2003 sold it to his nephew Russell Cooper, who told Rien Fertel of the Southern Foodways Alliance in June 2012: 'We keep all the meats. We keep all the hams. We got a full line of groceries and we got a full line of hardware. We got gasoline. We got propane. We got diesel fuel. You name it, we got it.' Garden & Gun sent Hunter Kennedy in 2014 and found the two-storey porte cochère over the pumps, the wood-panelled aisles, the plow points and cant hooks, and the Southampton-style country hams the same family has cured for the store for nearly sixty years, sold by the slice or whole and shipped across the country. A lunch buffet was added in March 2024.
text.how: Whole hogs cook over wood embers until the meat pulls with tongs; when the hog is flipped, the pitmaster Laverne Darby — more than thirty-five years at the pit — mops it with the vinegar sauce, which Russell Cooper describes as 'downright vinegar and salt and pepper', with black pepper, crushed pepper and ground red pepper. The hash is not ground but stringy, pulled meat cooked down. Barbecue and hash are sold from the meat counter at the back, with the hams, house-cured bacon, smoked tails and hocks; barbecue sandwiches and boiled peanuts too. The lunch buffet runs Wednesday to Saturday, 10:30 to 2.
text.today: Open Monday to Saturday, 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., closed Sunday; lunch buffet Wednesday to Saturday, 10:30 a.m. to 2 p.m. 6945 SC Highway 521, Salters. The coordinates here are the highway at Salters Depot, not the building. Checked September 15, 2026 against Destination BBQ.

names.name: Dukes Bar-B-Que
names.said: Dukes, no apostrophe, on the family's signs; the Whitman Street site now writes Duke's.

text.what: The name on a dozen or more buffet houses across the Midlands and Lowcountry, all descended from the sons of Manuel Dukes of Orangeburg County, who learned pit cooking from a Rowesville pitmaster and catered the county's gatherings. In Orangeburg itself the line is Earl Duke's: he opened downtown at Chestnut Street and Columbia Road in 1955 and later moved to Whitman Street, and his sister's family runs a second Dukes on Chestnut Street. Both sell from a buffet line: chopped pork in a mustard-and-ketchup 'rust' sauce, hash over rice — the Midlands' stew of pork and onion — fried and barbecued chicken, and a loaf of sliced white bread at the end.
text.story: Manuel Dukes was born in rural Orangeburg County around 1875. His sons became the county's pitmasters, catering barbecues, and historians have suggested that their German descent explains the mustard in the sauce. Willie Baltzegar, a Rowesville pitmaster, taught them. In the 1950s the sons and daughters opened restaurants: Danny Dukes first, in Cope and Branchville; Earl Duke in Orangeburg in 1955, at Chestnut Street and Columbia Road, later moving to Whitman Street beside the Pepsi plant; a sister, Elma, and her husband Harry Ott on Spruill Street in North Charleston; and others in Aiken, Elloree, Smoaks, Ridgeville, Blackville and New Ellenton. The name spread past the family, and by 2017 some Dukes were family-owned and others sold. Earl's Whitman Street house passed to Harold Kittrell, a carpenter, and then to his son Tony, who told the Southern Foodways Alliance in June 2012 that 'the barbecue, hash, and rice, our sauce, sweet tea, and sliced bread are just what people come here for' and gave the sauce its name: rust gravy — sweet, ketchup-based, orange-yellow, thicker than most. The Otts opened in St. Matthews in 1965 and moved to Chestnut Street in Orangeburg ten years later; their descendants cook fifty to fifty-five pigs a week in the pit out back, Wednesday to Friday, for a buffet that is 'just barbeque, hash, rice and slaw with loaves of bread at the end'.
text.how: A buffet, all you can eat, paid at the register; in March 2011 the Charleston City Paper gave the price as $10 for adults and $6 for children. Chopped pork from shoulders and hams is dressed with the rust sauce; hash — pork simmered down with onion into a reddish stew — is ladled over white rice; fried chicken, barbecue chicken, collards, butter beans, black-eyed peas, mac and cheese, fried okra, hushpuppies, corn nuggets and a loaf of Sunbeam bread fill the rest of the line. Most Dukes houses stopped burning logs decades ago and cook on gas-fired cookers with wood chips for smoke; the Chestnut Street house cooks its hogs in a pit behind the building, and takes cash only.
text.today: Two houses in Orangeburg. Chestnut Street (789 Chestnut Street NE) opens Thursday to Saturday, 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. Whitman Street (1298 Whitman Street SE) lists Thursday to Saturday, 11 to 8, but its own site on September 15, 2026 reads 'temporarily closed. We plan to reopen soon.'

text.what: A pork-shoulder house on Highway Street in Madison, Rockingham County, opened in 1954 by T.H. 'Fuzzy' Nelson and in the Nelson family since. Shoulders cook over hickory coals in pits behind the building; the tray is the Piedmont tray, chopped or coarse-chopped pork with the dip — the thin vinegar-and-ketchup sauce of the region — red slaw and hushpuppies. It holds True 'Cue certification, which turns on wood or charcoal being the only heat under the meat, and it is a stop on the North Carolina Barbecue Society's Historic Barbecue Trail. Breakfast is served from early morning, which few barbecue houses do.
text.story: T.H. Nelson, called Fuzzy, opened on the road through Madison in 1954, and the family kept it. The restaurant's own page calls itself a Nelson family restaurant operated by Fuzzy's son and daughter, Phil and Debbie, with Hilda Vestal managing after more than seventeen years; a visitor writing in April 2016 instead named a son, Fred, as the one running it, and the two accounts are not reconciled here. The building was rebuilt around 1978 and photographs of the first one hang inside. The pits stayed outdoors and the wood stayed in them. Both rosters of the Historic Barbecue Trail read for this project carry Fuzzy's — the older twenty-three-stop list and Visit NC's twenty-stop page of 2026 — which makes it one of the few pits to survive every revision of that list, while the Campaign for Real Barbecue certified it separately. *Inference —* the double listing is why Fuzzy's appears in nearly every written account of the trail, though its own advertising runs to one page and a telephone number. That page also claims notice from The New Yorker, from PM Magazine and from a Congressional barbecue contest. No issue, date or citation is given for any of the three, and none is repeated here as established.
text.how: Pork shoulders cook over hickory coals in pits behind the building, the fire tended through the cook rather than set and left. The meat is chopped or coarse-chopped and dressed with the dip; red slaw — cabbage cut fine and dressed with the same sauce, which is why it is red — and hushpuppies fill the tray. The kitchen serves breakfast from early morning as well, so the room is working hours before the barbecue houses down in Lexington open their doors.
text.today: Open at 407 North Highway Street, Madison. Three sources give three sets of hours: the restaurant's page says Monday to Saturday from seven in the morning and Sunday from seven, the NC Pork Council says Tuesday to Saturday from six and closed Sunday and Monday, and it lists a different street besides. Check before driving.

text.what: A whole-hog pit at a country crossroads in Dudley, Wayne County, south of Goldsboro, opened on July 4, 1986 by Steve and Gerri Grady and run by Gerri and their son Scottie since Steve's death in August 2025. Hogs cook over oak and hickory coals; the barbecue is chopped by hand and served with stewed collards, cabbage, slaw and potato salad, and tea Gerri brews on the stove. The Assembly reported in February 2026 that it is, by most accounts, the one Black-owned brick-and-mortar whole-hog restaurant at the top of North Carolina's best-of lists, and one of the last of its kind. It opens four days a week.
text.story: Steve Grady's brother started the restaurant on a Friday in 1986 and quit by Saturday; he disliked the smoke. Steve and Gerri, married that same year, bought it with bank loans and the backing of the boss at the sawmill where Steve worked. Both had grown up on farms at Seven Springs. Steve had learned whole hog from his father and grandfather, who cooked a couple of pigs a year in pits dug in the ground for holidays; Gerri learned to cook at nine or ten from her mother and grandmother and then her mother-in-law, and told ABC11 in 2021, 'This is cooking the old fashioned way. It's a dash of this and a dash of that. There are no measurements.' Steve cut oak and hickory from storm-downed trees across Wayne County and stacked it beside the building where customers could see it. USA Today and GQ wrote the place up; the Gradys spoke for the North Carolina Barbecue Society and gave the Southern Foodways Alliance an oral history in December 2011. In June 2020 Steve was hospitalized with COVID-19; the restaurant reopened that July on its 34th anniversary. In 2024 the NC BBQ Hall of Fame and the American Royal both inducted him. Stephen Grady died on August 26, 2025; Gerri and Scottie kept the pit going.
text.how: Steve started the charcoal fires at eleven at night and came back at four in the morning to put the hogs on over hickory and oak; by eight the barbecue was ready. The meat is hand-chopped and dressed with a spicy vinegar sauce, and the plate carries slaw, hushpuppies — fried cornmeal fritters — and the day's vegetables, stewed collards, cabbage and potato salad, peeled and chopped by hand that morning.
text.today: Open four days a week at 3096 Arrington Bridge Road, Dudley, run by Gerri Grady and her son Scottie since Steve Grady's death in August 2025. Days and hours are from Our State (2013) and The Assembly (February 2026); check before driving.

text.what: An Upstate barbecue house at 240 Wade Hampton Boulevard on the edge of downtown Greenville, opened by Beau Hammond — in 1991 by the company's own account, in 1992 by the Greenville Journal's — in a small building that had been other eateries before. It cooks pork butts twelve hours and ribs six to eight over hickory logs in open pits, hand-pulls and chops the pork, and serves it with two sauces, a mild tomato-based one in the Piedmont manner and a spicy mustard one, with hash and rice on the side. A second house is in Simpsonville and a food truck, Henry's Hog Hauler, travels; the Barbeque Association lists it as 100-Mile Barbecue.
text.story: Beau Hammond opened Henry's with a menu so short that the sides were coleslaw and simmered green beans, and a rule he kept repeating: 'You want to be fair to the customer first. The money will come after that.' The house grew, added stores in Simpsonville and on Woodruff Road, and passed to Tiger O'Rourke and Bo Wilder, partners who added hand-cut fries in O'Rourke's years. Playboy ranked it first in the world in June 2002, a line the house still quotes; it took the Upstate readers' award seventeen years running; and in 2024 Southern Living picked it for the state. John Malik, writing in the Greenville Journal in October 2025, found a pulled-pork sandwich with fries and half-and-half tea at about $13 and the fire still built every day: 'You have to baby great barbecue. The fire changes every day... The result of great smoked pork should stay the same.'
text.how: Pork butts cook twelve hours and ribs, St. Louis cut, six to eight, in open pits over hickory logs — cured oak and pecan too, by Malik's account — at low temperatures, the fire built and tended all day. The pork is pulled by hand from the bone and chopped; the sauces are a mild tomato-based one and a spicy mustard; hash and rice, a stew of pork over rice, is on the menu with the hand-cut fries. About $13 for a sandwich, fries and tea in October 2025.
text.today: Open Monday to Saturday 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. and Sunday 11 to 3 at 240 Wade Hampton Boulevard, Greenville, with the same hours at 123 North Main Street, Simpsonville, per the company's site on September 15, 2026.

text.what: A take-out barbecue stand on Dreher Road in West Columbia, open only on Friday and Saturday, where the Hite family has cooked whole hogs and hams over oak and hickory coals since 1957. It sells chopped pork, ham, ribs, pork skins, chicken, hash and rice and slaw by the plate and the pound, with a yellow mustard sauce applied lightly; there is no dining room, only picnic tables by a pond. The hash — the Midlands' stew of pork and onion — is made in cast-iron kettles over wood embers. It is not Jackie Hite's of Batesburg-Leesville, some twenty-five miles west, which closed in 2018.
text.story: John D. Hite farmed on Dreher Road — minnows, hogs, corn and sweet potatoes — and in 1957 began selling barbecue as a side project, a farmer looking for extra income. The stand stayed a two-day business beside the farm and passed to his grandson David Hite, who runs it with the family recipes and, in the words of the restaurant's site, 'the age-old process for cooking barbeque'. Destination BBQ describes that process: coals rendered in a modified campfire fashion, then shoveled, 'payload after smoky payload', under whole hogs and hams until the meat is lacquered with smoke. The hash is cooked the old way in cast-iron kettles over wood embers, and the stand makes an onion sausage that Destination BBQ calls unique to the Midlands. *Inference —* the Dreher Road Hites and Jackie Hite of Leesville share a Lexington County surname and a mustard sauce; no source in this project links the two businesses.
text.how: Whole hogs and hams cook on a pit over oak and hickory coals. The meat is chopped and lightly dressed with a mustard sauce whose base is a strong yellow mustard. Orders are plates — pork, rib or chicken with hash, rice, slaw and rolls — or sandwiches, or meat by the pound, all to go; picnic tables by the pond are the only seating. Hash simmers in cast-iron kettles over wood embers; pork skins and onion sausage are the extras.
text.today: Open Friday and Saturday only. The restaurant's site gives 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. both days; Destination BBQ recorded 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. Friday and 8 to 6 Saturday. Take-out only. 240 Dreher Road, West Columbia. Checked September 15, 2026.

text.what: A Charleston barbecue company that began in November 2006 when Aaron Siegel, a Culinary Institute-trained cook from Atlanta, turned Bunch's, a mid-century gas station at 1205 Ashley River Road in West Ashley, into Fiery Ron's Home Team BBQ. It cooks pulled pork, ribs, brisket and smoked chicken wings with an Alabama white sauce, runs a bar known for American whiskey and frozen drinks — the Game Changer is its signature — and books live Americana, blues and bluegrass. Seven locations by 2026: West Ashley, Sullivan's Island (2009), downtown Charleston (2016), Aspen (2016), Columbia (2019), Greenville (2021) and north Mount Pleasant (2022), with more than six hundred employees.
text.story: Aaron Siegel grew up in Atlanta without barbecue, went to the University of Georgia and then, in January 1997, to the Culinary Institute of America at Hyde Park; he interned at Nava in Atlanta under Kevin Rathbun, cooked in Aspen at a white-tablecloth restaurant and a burrito shop, and moved to Charleston in 2002. In 2006, with little money and much help from friends and family, he and his partners Taylor Garrigan, Tony McKie and Madison Ruckel opened in the old gas station on Ashley River Road; Garrigan was the opening sous chef and is an operating partner now. Sullivan's Island came in 2009; downtown at 126 Williman Street and Aspen, Colorado, in 2016; Columbia in 2019, Greenville in 2021, north Mount Pleasant in 2022. McKie curates the music. The company gives to Hogs for a Cause, has run the Rock the Block fundraiser since 2017 and started the Holy Smokes festival in 2021. 'There wasn't a place where you could go have a good time and hang out for a few hours, watch a game, catch a music show' with the family, Siegel told the City Paper before the twentieth anniversary in July 2026.
text.how: Low and slow, in the company's phrase, on smokers at each store: pulled pork, ribs, brisket, smoked wings tossed in Alabama white sauce — *Tradition holds —* a mayonnaise-based sauce from north Alabama — pulled-pork sandwiches, barbecue tacos, tots and queso, a kids' menu. The bar carries a wide American whiskey list, frozen cocktails and craft beer; live Americana, blues and bluegrass play at several stores.
text.today: Open at seven locations: the original at 1205 Ashley River Road, Charleston (West Ashley); Sullivan's Island; 126 Williman Street downtown; north Mount Pleasant; Columbia; Greenville; and Aspen, Colorado — per the company's site and the City Paper in July 2026. Checked September 15, 2026.

text.what: The Burlington, Alamance County, barbecue business of the Hursey family: Sylvester and Daisy Hursey began smoking pork over a backyard pit in 1945 with a sauce of their own, moved to a cafe in Gibsonville with two big pits behind it, and built a Burlington restaurant on Rauhut Street in 1957; their son Charles took over the Burlington trade in 1966, and his sons Chuck and Chris manage it now, a fourth generation coming on. It smokes more than 1,200 pork shoulders a week over hickory, plus hams, for five restaurants, a catering house and a wholesale trade; broasted chicken and hot apple turnovers are the other things it is known for.
text.story: The family's telling starts in the mid-1940s with Sylvester Hursey and a friend cooking their first pig after a night out; in 1945 he and Daisy set up a homemade pit in the yard and sold to neighbors, using his father's way with hickory-smoked pork and a sauce they kept to themselves. When the yard was too small they bought a cafe on Piedmont Street in Gibsonville and built two large pits behind it. The family says the state issued them its first license to wholesale barbecue — in 1949 by the company's history, in 1945 by Our State's 2014 account. Sylvester built the Rauhut Street restaurant in Burlington in 1957; Charles Hursey went full-time in 1960 out of high school and took over Rauhut Street in mid-1966, expanding the wholesale plant on Highway 87 North. Our State in 2014 found Charles, about seventy, and his wife Ellen at the register, and counted five addresses in Burlington, Graham and Mebane. The company lists a win at a North and South Carolina cook-off held in Washington, D.C., and a National Golden Chicken Award among its credentials.
text.how: Pork shoulders, more than 1,200 a week, and hams are hickory-smoked and served chopped or sliced with the family's Old-Fashioned Barbecue Sauce and hushpuppies; broasted chicken — pressure-fried — and hot apple turnovers are the other things people drive for. The wholesale kitchen also makes hot-dog chili by the ton: Our State reckoned 200,000 hot dogs' worth in ten days.
text.today: Open daily 11 to 9 at 1834 South Church Street, Burlington, per OpenStreetMap (2026); four more Hursey's stand in Burlington, Graham and Mebane (Our State, 2014).

text.what: A Black-owned whole-hog counter on South Main Street in Farmville, Pitt County, that Jack Cobb and his son Rudy built as a cinder-block storefront in 1971 and closed in the autumn of 2018. Hogs cooked all night over oak, pecan and hickory coals banked around them; Rudy Cobb shovelled glowing coals in from the hearth and would not use gas. There were no chairs and no tables, only a counter, three days a week. Barbecued chicken and barbecued turkey shared the board with the pork.
text.story: Jack Cobb made tobacco hogsheads for A.C. Monk & Co. for about fifty years and cooked barbecue on Saturdays. When his son Rudy came home from Vietnam in 1966 — North Carolina A&T, then combat — the business faced the plain arithmetic of a segregated town. Our State put it in 2013: white customers wanted Jack's barbecue but would not walk into a Black-owned business. So Jack and Rudy carried it out to the cars. A hundred plates a trip, barbecue and cornbread and slaw, sixty-five cents each. Rudy dated the turn to 1966 or 1967 and remembered how he ended the deliveries: he used to carry it to their houses, and when there got to be too many he told them they had to come get it — nobody would bother them, he would be there. He told Rien Fertel for the Southern Foodways Alliance on November 30, 2011 that he was the principal owner, born September 1941, and that he still cooked with wood and did not use gas. Jack died in September 1989, having blessed his son's decision to stop turning the hogs overnight. Rudy's own sons did not want it and no buyer came. He closed in 2018: it was like losing a wife or a son, he told WRAL.
text.how: Whole hogs — always whole hogs — cooked overnight on oak, pecan and hickory, the wood banked around the pit so it lit through the night, the coals shovelled in from the hearth. Decades of it stained the white walls grey. The pork came chopped with a vinegar sauce, and the hushpuppies were made to Rudy's stepmother Lillian Blunt Cobb's recipe. Barbecued chicken and barbecued turkey were the other meats. There was nowhere to sit: you took your food and went.
text.today: Closed. The last service was in the autumn of 2018 — WNCT reported in August that the closing had been put off to October 18 while buyers were sought, and WRAL confirmed the closure the following July. The building stands at 3883 South Main Street, Farmville.

text.what: A whole-hog buffet house on East Railroad Avenue in Leesville, across the tracks from the town, that James Lee 'Jackie' Hite opened in May 1979 and ran until his death in September 2016; his family closed it in 2018. Hogs cooked whole over hickory coals, the coals made in a burn barrel — a steel drum in which the logs burn down — and the chopped meat was dressed with a mustard, vinegar and pepper sauce and set on a buffet with fried chicken, hash and rice, collards, field peas and creamed corn, paid for on the way out. Hite was also Leesville's mayor and fire chief.
text.story: Jackie Hite's father was a plumber, a fisherman and a part-time barbecue man, and the son learned the pit helping him cook for the annual Firemen's Ball. Hite went into Leesville's public life from 1966 — fire chief, water commissioner, councilman, magistrate, and three terms as mayor — and in May 1979 opened the restaurant across the railroad tracks. He cooked hogs whole over hickory as his father had, and told Rien Fertel of the Southern Foodways Alliance in June 2012, five years after open-heart surgery and with constituents asking him to run for mayor again: 'Once you been there, you can't get it out of your blood', and 'We just never done nothing but what we're doing and that's why it's so hard.' He died in September 2016 after weeks of failing health; WIS called him a Midlands barbecue legend, and the restaurant had then been open more than thirty-five years. *Tradition holds —* his family kept the pits going two more years and closed the doors on September 23, 2018, the anniversary of his burial, saying it was what Jackie Hite himself would have wanted.
text.how: Whole hogs over hickory coals, the wood burned down in a burn barrel and shoveled under the meat — *Tradition holds —* on pits of concrete block. The chopped pork got a sauce a visitor called 'like straight mustard': mustard seed and vinegar. Service was a buffet: fried chicken, hash and rice, coleslaw, collards sweet and smoky, salad, creamed corn, mac and cheese, field peas. Guests ate first and paid on the way out. The last listed hours were Wednesday and Thursday 9 to 2, Friday and Saturday 9 to 3, Sunday 9 to 2, cash or card.
text.today: Closed since 2018. The building stands at 460 East Railroad Avenue, Leesville (Batesburg-Leesville); Destination BBQ marks it permanently closed. Nothing continues under the name as of September 15, 2026, so far as this project's sources show.
