text.what: Latham Wade 'Bum' Dennis (June 12, 1937 – December 9, 2022) opened Bum's Restaurant in downtown Ayden in 1963 with his wife Shirley and cooked whole hogs over wood coals there for the rest of his working life, with a table of vegetables beside the barbecue that few eastern pits keep. He was of the Dennis family that counts Skilton Dennis's 1830 wagon as the start of the trade, and a kinsman of Pete Jones of the Skylight Inn. His son Larry, at the pit since he was nine, runs the restaurant.
text.story: His mother could not settle on a name for weeks, and people said a man without a name would grow up to be a bum; she named him Latham, and Bum stuck. He was born in Pitt County on June 12, 1937, finished Ayden High School in 1956 and joined the Navy that year. In 1963 he and Shirley opened the restaurant that carries his nickname; he cut the wood for the pits, opened for breakfast at 5:30 and closed at nine every day but Sunday. The family's barbecue, he and Larry told Rien Fertel for the Southern Foodways Alliance in December 2011, runs back through six generations of Dennises to the wagon of 1830. 'People have been cooking with wood for 500,000 years,' Larry told Our State. 'We just never stopped.' Bum's own account of the trade, as he gave it to Fertel: 'In this type restaurant business, what you got to do you got to love it and it's a way of life. You get up every morning and that's what you do.' When Daniel Wallace visited for Our State in 2014 Bum had retired but came in to serve breakfast around five, silver handlebar moustache and all, and Shirley sat at her table with her friend Hilda Worthington; Larry arrived at four to burn oak and pecan down to coals and did everything but kill the pig. Bum died at his home, Raven Hall, on December 9, 2022, at eighty-five.
text.today: Dead: December 9, 2022, at home in Ayden, aged eighty-five. Larry Dennis runs Bum's Restaurant at 566 East Third Street; the Dennis family's whole hog and vegetable table continue there.

text.what: Dennis Rogers (October 10, 1942 – August 8, 2020), a News & Observer columnist for more than thirty years, raised in Wilson and an Army veteran, who wrote about small-town eastern North Carolina and its soldiers and, in barbecue, spoke for the east: whole hog with vinegar and pepper and nothing else. He called himself the 'oracle of the holy grub' in a long mock war of columns with Jerry Bledsoe of Greensboro over ketchup in the sauce. His columns were collected in Home Grown (1979), Second Harvest (1981), Crossroads (1984) and It's Bad News When the Bartender Cries (1988).
text.story: The war ran in print for decades, Rogers from Raleigh for the whole hog of Wilson, Greenville and Goldsboro, Bledsoe from Greensboro for the Piedmont's shoulder and red dip, each with a self-conferred title. Rogers's line, in one column, was that people who would put ketchup in the sauce they feed to innocent children are capable of most anything, and that the eastern purveyors of pure barbecue would not be roadkill for their western kin. When the 2005 bills over the Lexington Barbecue Festival's title brought the argument to the General Assembly, ABC's World News Tonight put the two men on air: Rogers said of the eastern sauce, 'It doesn't need anything else', and that somebody who would put ketchup on barbecue and give it to a child was capable of pretty much anything; Bledsoe answered that America loves ketchup and that Rogers had ruined any chance of the state being distinguished in its barbecue. In January 2007, after thirty years as a columnist, Rogers gave up the column at 64 for a new beat — the home front and the war's weight on eastern North Carolina, reported from Sanford — telling WRAL, 'I'm not dead yet!' and that he could not walk away with the soldiers' stories untold. He retired later that year, kept a website of his and his wife's RV travels, wrote a novel, acted in local theatre and rode motorcycles. He died in his sleep on August 8, 2020, at 77, after a long illness.
text.today: Died August 8, 2020, at 77. His column collections, published by the News & Observer between 1979 and 1988, survive in libraries and used bookshops; his family promised a barbecue in his memory once the pandemic allowed.

text.what: Ed Mitchell (born 1948 or 1949) is a whole-hog pitmaster from Wilson who began cooking pigs behind his family's grocery store in the early 1990s, turned the store into Mitchell's Ribs, Chicken & Bar-B-Q, co-founded The Pit in Raleigh in 2007, and has argued for pasture-raised heritage hogs since the 2000s. The Southern Foodways Alliance recorded him in 2007; the American Royal put him in its Barbecue Hall of Fame in 2022. His book, Ed Mitchell's Barbeque, written with his son Ryan Mitchell and Zella Palmer, came out from Ecco in 2023.
text.story: He cooked his first pig at fourteen or fifteen, at a family gathering in Wilson where the men had passed the moonshine and fallen asleep; his grandfather woke to a cooked hog, asked who had done it, and poured him a glass. 'Growing up, all our lives on any celebration... it had to be accompanied by barbecue,' he told Amy Evans of the Southern Foodways Alliance in September 2007. After his father died — in 1991, by his own account in WALTER magazine; 1990 by the Alliance's — his mother asked for barbecue, he cooked a pig behind Mitchell's Grocery, customers asked for it, and by 1992 the store was Mitchell's Ribs, Chicken & Bar-B-Q. From 2002 he headlined New York's Big Apple Barbecue Block Party each year; in 2003 he began cooking free-range pigs. The Wilson restaurant closed in 2004 or 2005 amid a state tax case. In 2007 he opened The Pit in Raleigh with a real-estate developer and left it in May 2011; Que, in Durham's American Tobacco campus, ran less than a year from 2014. He cooks hot and fast, a bank of coals around the hog, 500 degrees falling to 250, with a rub of salt, black and red pepper and onion powder and a sauce of cider vinegar, crushed red pepper, salt, sugar and black pepper; he wants the whole hog because a sandwich needs shoulder, ham and belly together. With Ryan he has worked with True Made Foods on sauces since 2018 and announced The Preserve, a Raleigh restaurant with LM Restaurants, in 2019. 'I barbeque not because I love hoisting 150-pound hogs over my shoulders, but because I want to keep the tradition of my African American ancestors alive,' he wrote in 2023.
text.today: Living. He has not run a restaurant since Que closed in 2015; he ships barbecue from a smokehouse in Micro, Johnston County, through Goldbelly, sells sauces with True Made Foods, and works with his son Ryan. The Preserve, announced for Raleigh in 2019, had not opened as of July 2024.

text.what: Elliott Moss is a chef and whole-hog pitmaster from Florence, in the Pee Dee of South Carolina, who grew up watching his grandfather smoke hogs, moved to Asheville in 2007 to open The Admiral, and in August 2015 opened Buxton Hall Barbecue there with Meherwan Irani's Chai Pani group, bringing wood-cooked whole hog and South Carolina hash to the mountains. He left Buxton Hall in July 2022; it closed in November 2023. In 2025 he and his wife Jennifer opened Elliott's Barbecue Lounge inside Seminar Brewing in Florence, which Southern Living named the South's best new barbecue restaurant for 2026.
text.story: Moss, 'a son of the low country of Florence, S.C.' in the Asheville chamber's words, learned smoke from his grandfather's whole hogs. He came to Asheville in 2007 to help open The Admiral, whose cooking put him on the James Beard Foundation's semifinalist list for Best Chef: Southeast in 2013. A first deal for a barbecue place fell through; Meherwan Irani of Chai Pani reached out within forty-eight hours, and Buxton Hall Barbecue opened in August 2015 in a 1930s roller rink on Banks Avenue on the South Slope: pasture-raised hogs from western North Carolina farms smoked over wood from ten at night to eight in the morning, hash and rice made from the pig's organs and trimmings, a fried chicken sandwich, pies on lard crusts. 'When I'm in here, I cut all the lights off except this little lamp,' he told Our State in 2016, 'and it's just like I'm outside, cooking a pig, standing in front of the burn barrel.' Bon Appétit put the restaurant ninth among the country's new restaurants in 2016 and named the sandwich its fried chicken sandwich of the year; the Beard Foundation listed him as a semifinalist again in 2017. He left Buxton Hall in July 2022, opened two West Asheville restaurants, Regina's and Little Louie's, in the summer of 2023 and left them within six weeks, and in March 2024 announced on Instagram that after seventeen years he and Jennifer were leaving Asheville to keep cooking whole hog somewhere else. The somewhere was home: Elliott's Barbecue Lounge opened inside Seminar Brewing at 551 West Lucas Street, Florence, in the spring of 2025 — pasture-raised whole hog 'cooked Pee Dee burn barrel-style', in Robert Moss's words for Southern Living, with collards, hash and rice and a buttered, grilled bun.
text.today: Living. He and Jennifer Moss run Elliott's Barbecue Lounge in Florence, South Carolina, open since spring 2025; Southern Living ranked it 36th among the South's fifty barbecue restaurants in 2025 and its best new barbecue restaurant in 2026.

text.what: Jerry Carroll Bledsoe (July 14, 1941 – December 31, 2025), a Greensboro newspaper columnist and author, born in Danville, Virginia and raised in Thomasville, who wrote for the Greensboro Daily News, later the News & Record, for twenty-three years and became a true-crime writer with Bitter Blood (1988), a number-one New York Times bestseller. In barbecue he was Lexington's man: the self-styled 'world's leading, foremost barbecue authority' in a decades-long mock war of columns with Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer over ketchup in the sauce.
text.story: Bledsoe delivered the Thomasville Tribune at nine, served three years in the Army after high school, and worked at papers in Kannapolis and Charlotte before the Greensboro Daily News, where his columns of the 1970s and 1980s made his name; he was later a contributing editor at Esquire. The barbecue war was one of those columns' running jokes: Bledsoe for the Piedmont's chopped shoulder with its red dip, Rogers for the east's whole hog and clear vinegar, each claiming a title — Bledsoe the world's leading, foremost barbecue authority, Rogers the oracle of the holy grub. Bledsoe wrote that Rogers had ruined any chance of the state being distinguished in its barbecue; Rogers wrote that people who would put ketchup in sauce fed to innocent children were capable of most anything. The joke outlived the columns. When bills to make the Lexington Barbecue Festival the state's official barbecue festival divided the General Assembly in 2005, ABC's World News Tonight came to Greensboro, and Bledsoe gave them 'America loves ketchup' and called vinegar an astringent thing that ruins the taste buds. In 1996 he wrote 'Slaw Crazy', an essay holding that barbecue is always served with slaw in North Carolina and always has been. Bitter Blood, on the Lynch–Newsom–Klenner murders of 1984–85, was followed by Blood Games (1991), Before He Wakes (1994) and Death Sentence (1998); he founded Down Home Press to publish books about North Carolina, and in later years wrote for the Rhino Times, including a long series on the Greensboro police. He died on December 31, 2025, at 84.
text.today: Died December 31, 2025, at 84. The Rhino Times, where he last wrote, marked his death the next day; The Assembly's tribute, 'A Hell of a Writer', ran on January 12, 2026.

text.what: Jess Swicegood ran a barbecue stand a few yards from Sid Weaver's tent by the Lexington courthouse in the 1920s, taught Warner Stamey pit cooking alongside Weaver, and sold Stamey the business in 1938 — for $300, by Robert Moss's account — when Stamey came back from Shelby and renamed it Stamey's. Through that sale the Swicegood stand is the ancestor of Stamey's in Greensboro and, through Stamey's pupil Wayne Monk, of Lexington Barbecue. He is spelled Jess and Jesse in the sources, and no dates of birth or death are on record here.
text.story: The sources agree on the order: Weaver's tent in 1919, Swicegood's stand beside it within the decade, then the two of them together. Moss's history, as the Barbecue Bros relay it, says Weaver 'later teamed up with Jess Swicegood and those two men perfected Lexington-style barbecue and helped spread the technique across the Piedmont of North Carolina'. Stamey's history and the American Royal's 2020 bio put Swicegood first in the pair that taught Warner Stamey when he was a high-school boy boarding with his sister, and the Southern Foodways Alliance's note on Stamey's calls the two 'pit-cooking pioneers'. In 1938 Stamey moved back to Lexington, bought out his mentor and renamed the operation Stamey's; Wayne Monk worked under Stamey in downtown Lexington for several years before he opened Lexington Barbecue in 1962. *Inference —* a stand that changed hands for $300 was a tent or a shed, not a building; the first permanent barbecue restaurant in town was Alton Beck's, in 1938, the same year.
text.today: Dead, on no date this record can name. The Lexington stand he sold in 1938 carried the Stamey name into the 1950s; the Stamey family's restaurants are in Greensboro, and Lexington Barbecue, opened by Stamey's pupil Wayne Monk in 1962, cooks a mile or two from where his stand stood.

text.what: James Howard Early Jr. (1939–2021), a Winston-Salem lawyer and cook who founded the North Carolina Barbecue Society in 2006 and led it until his death. His self-published guide, The Best Tar Heel Barbecue: Manteo to Murphy (2002), came out of a search through all hundred counties for pits still cooking pork over wood coals; the society's Historic Barbecue Trail is that list under rules he wrote — wood or charcoal on grates, a house sauce, fifteen years' cooking, no more than two stops in a town.
text.story: Early was born in Henderson, grew up in Winston-Salem, took his bachelor's and law degrees at Wake Forest, and practiced law for years before barbecue took over. The search behind the book covered 22,000 miles and about 4,000 hours across the state's hundred counties; he found fewer than thirty restaurants still cooking over wood coals, six of them Black-owned and three owned by women. The society he founded in 2006 set itself to preserve the state's barbecue history and, in its own words, to secure North Carolina's place as the Barbecue Capital of the World; the less formal motto was to cook and eat barbecue as often as possible, preferably among friends. It ran two-day cooking boot camps three times a year — Tanglewood Park in May, Sugar Mountain in July, Castle Hayne in September — teaching whole hog, pork butt, ribs, chicken, brisket and Early's pimento cheese; CNN put the school on a 2012 list of ten cooking schools worldwide, the only one in the United States. He published a monthly magazine, Pigtails, and a second book, Jim Early's Reflections: The Memories and Recipes of a Southern Cook. In September 2017 he closed his law office to run the society full time. He took no side in the east–west argument, and told Our State in 2016 that '99.99 percent of places' now cooked with gas or electricity; the Trail bypasses all of them. He died on June 21, 2021, at 82, weeks after a stroke.
text.today: Died June 21, 2021. The society's two web addresses did not resolve when this project checked on September 15, 2026; its Facebook page carries on as a forum, and the Trail's list is reprinted by Our State and others. His 2002 guidebook is held by libraries and sold used.

text.what: Joseph Jacob 'Big Joe' Bessinger, a farmer from Orangeburg County, traded the family cow, a mule and fifty dollars for a cafe in Holly Hill and opened it in 1939 serving pork with a mustard-based sauce — the Golden Secret, his family calls it, worked out with the Sweatman family on shared German roots. Five of his sons opened barbecue restaurants on it: Maurice and Joe Jr. at West Columbia in 1953, Melvin and Thomas in Charleston from 1955, and, by two accounts, Robert. Some name him the inventor of South Carolina's mustard sauce; the evidence names no one.
text.story: Big Joe was one of fourteen children of Mack Bessinger and raised eleven of his own — Maurice was the eighth — on a farm near Orangeburg with his wife Genora. In 1939 he gave up farming, sold a cow, and opened the Holly Hill Café; Melvin, ten, was taught to make the sauce, and Maurice, nine, went to work in the restaurant. Robert Moss's 2011 history in the Charleston City Paper puts the move to Holly Hill in the 1940s; the family's own dates say 1939. After the war Melvin's Army pay went into a second Holly Hill restaurant, Eat At Joe's, in 1946, where Thomas started cooking at fourteen. Then the sons scattered with the recipe. Maurice and Joe Jr. opened Maurice's Piggie Park at West Columbia in 1953; Melvin closed Eat At Joe's in 1955 and moved to Charleston with Thomas, where Thomas opened his own place in 1960 and the brothers opened Piggy Park Drive-In on Savannah Highway in 1961, renamed Bessinger's in 1971; Melvin crossed the Cooper River to Mount Pleasant in 1982. Moss writes that three sons — Melvin, Thomas and J.D. — opened Piggy Park drive-ins around Charleston; West Of lists Thomas, Melvin, Maurice, J.D., Woodrow and Robert as owners of competing restaurants, with Robert's Bar B Que in North Charleston. The businesses were separate: when Maurice raised Confederate flags in 2000 the Charleston brothers were reported as independent concerns, 'sans the politics'. His grandson David Bessinger told the Southern Foodways Alliance in 2012: 'It's just in our blood.' *Inference —* the 'Joe Jr.' of Wikipedia and Maurice's obituary and the 'Joe David' or 'J.D.' of the Charleston writers are one son.
text.today: Dead; no source read for this record gives the year. The sauce he served in 1939 is on the tables of Maurice's Piggie Park, Bessinger's and Melvin's, and bottled by Maurice's heirs as Southern Gold.

text.what: A sociologist of the American South, born 1942, who taught at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill from 1969 until 2000 and retired as William Rand Kenan Jr. Professor. With his wife Dale Volberg Reed and William McKinney he wrote Holy Smoke: The Big Book of North Carolina Barbecue (UNC Press, 2008); alone, Barbecue: A Savor the South Cookbook (2016) and On Barbecue (2021). In 2013 he and Dan Levine founded the Campaign for Real Barbecue, which certifies restaurants that cook their local style over wood alone. He lives in Chapel Hill.
text.story: Reed came to barbecue after a career on the South itself: MIT, a Columbia doctorate in 1971, the Center for the Study of the American South, which he helped found, and the quarterly Southern Cultures, which he co-edited. Holy Smoke, written with Dale and William McKinney, gives North Carolina's two styles their history, their recipes and their people, and in it the Reeds lamented how much of the state's barbecue was cooked on gas. In 2011 he wrote the introduction to the Southern Foodways Alliance's North Carolina barbecue oral histories, opening with George Washington's diary for May 27, 1769 — a barbecue in Alexandria and a night away — and the point that until the early twentieth century barbecue was for harvests, fundraisers and rallies, never home cooking. The campaign came two years later: a retired professor 'with time on my hands', in his words, and Dan Levine, 'Porky LeSwine' of the blog BBQJew, set out to find and list the places still cooking entirely with wood, Levine as Chief Smoke Detector, Reed as Éminence Grease. On April 23, 2014, in the Raleigh News & Observer, they offered a prize — an apron, later a cap as well — to anyone who could name the statute, regulation or official that forbade a restaurant to cook with wood, since owners so often said the health department had made them switch; two years on nobody had claimed it, and Daniel Vaughn in Texas and Robert Moss in South Carolina had found the same in their states. Reed allows that gas is cheaper, easier and more consistent. Dale Volberg Reed died in 2018. On Barbecue (University of Tennessee Press, 2021) collects his essays, reviews and op-eds on the subject, and in 2023 the governor gave him the Order of the Long Leaf Pine.
text.today: Retired, in Chapel Hill; co-founder and Éminence Grease of the campaign, whose site listed about seventy North Carolina restaurants in January 2018 and remains active in 2026. His own site lists The Ramos Gin Fizz (LSU Press, 2025) and a revised 1001 Things Everyone Should Know About the South, due in 2027.

text.what: Lake E. High Jr. of Columbia, a wine judge and, in his own account, a born critic, who founded the South Carolina Barbeque Association with the psychologist Walter Rolandi in 2004 to train judges and promote the state's barbecue, and wrote its history: A History of South Carolina Barbeque (The History Press, 2013). His account gives South Carolina all four of the barbecue sauces he counts — vinegar-and-pepper, mustard, light tomato and heavy tomato — each with a region and a date, and the association publishes them as a map.
text.story: High was 74 when South Carolina Living profiled him in September 2015 as 'the guru of 'que': a master judge of the association he founded, certified as well by the Kansas City Barbeque Society, the Memphis Barbecue Network and the American Wine Society, who said he had probably eaten more barbeque than anyone in the state. When he and Rolandi founded the association the state had two cook-offs a year; by 2015 it had thirty-seven, more per head than any other state, and the association had certified more than 800 judges. His book, published in June 2013 while he was the association's president, runs from the 1500s — Native Americans cooking pork on frames after the Spanish brought the pig, and, in his telling, Europeans learning barbecue at the sixteenth-century colony of Santa Elena at what is now Port Royal — through the 1920s, when the craft settled into restaurants, to the cook-off era. The sauce account, posted on the association's site over his name as founder, runs in order of age: vinegar-and-pepper first, hundreds of years old; mustard from the German settlers of the 1730s to 1750s, distinct to South Carolina; light tomato, vinegar-and-pepper with ketchup, from around 1900; heavy tomato, the newest, of the last sixty years. Only South Carolina, he holds, has all four. Robert Moss, another South Carolinian, counts two: sweet mustard and spicy vinegar. In 2015 High told the magazine, 'Barbeque is a noun, not a verb. It's something Southerners eat, not do.' In August 2018 the co-founders named Jim Wellman of Lexington president and Don Adkins of Seneca vice president.
text.today: The association is active in 2026 with a full cook-off calendar; its site names High as founder and 'a professional wine judge' and lists no current officers. His book remains in print with The History Press. No later interview with High was found for this record (checked September 15, 2026).

text.what: Lloyd Maurice Bessinger Sr. (July 14, 1930 – February 22, 2014) opened Maurice's Piggie Park, a drive-in, in West Columbia in 1953 with his brother Joe Jr., built it into a chain, and bottled his father's mustard sauce as Carolina Gold for supermarkets nationwide. He refused Black customers until the suit that became Newman v. Piggie Park Enterprises (1968), ran for the legislature in 1964 and for governor in 1974, and raised the Confederate flag over his restaurants on July 1, 2000, the day it came off the State House dome. His children took the last flags down in 2013.
text.story: Bessinger was born on the family farm near Orangeburg on July 14, 1930, the eighth of eleven children of Joseph Jacob and Genora Thomas Bessinger, and started cooking at nine in his father's Holly Hill restaurant in 1939. He served in the Army in the Korean War, came home in 1952, and with Joe Jr. opened the first Piggie Park drive-in in West Columbia in 1953; there were four by 1964. That year Anne Newman, the wife of a Black minister, was refused entry, and Matthew J. Perry filed a class action under Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964; Bessinger answered that his religious beliefs compelled him to oppose integration. The district court held the Act reached his sandwich shop but not the drive-ins; the Fourth Circuit reversed; and in 1968 the Supreme Court held 8–0 in Newman v. Piggie Park Enterprises, 390 U.S. 400, that a plaintiff who wins such an injunction ordinarily recovers attorney's fees. He chaired George Wallace's 1964 campaign in the state, lost a House race that year by about a hundred votes, and took 2.5 percent in the 1974 Democratic primary for governor. By 1999 the sauce — mustard, brown sugar, soy sauce and vinegar, sold as Carolina Gold — had made his the largest barbecue business in the country. On July 1, 2000 he raised Confederate flags over them and called the flag a Christian symbol; his restaurants distributed a tract arguing that slavery is not inherently evil; Bi-Lo, Food Lion, Harris Teeter, Kroger, Piggly Wiggly, Publix, Sam's Club, Wal-Mart and Winn-Dixie dropped the sauce, and his $50 million suit against them failed at the state Supreme Court in 2007. He published an autobiography, Defending My Heritage, in 2001. He died on February 22, 2014, at eighty-three.
text.today: Dead: February 22, 2014, West Columbia, aged eighty-three. His sons Lloyd and Paul, his daughter Debbie and his grandchildren run Maurice's Piggie Park; the flags came down by 2013 and the sauce is sold as Southern Gold.

text.what: Walter B. 'Pete' Jones (died 2006) opened the Skylight Inn in Ayden, Pitt County, in the summer of 1947 — at seventeen by his family's count, eighteen by Wikipedia's — and cooked whole hogs over wood coals there for nearly sixty years. He learned the trade at his uncle Emmitt Dennis's City Cafe, counted his barbecue back to a Dennis ancestor's wagon, and put a copy of the U.S. Capitol dome on his roof after National Geographic called the place the barbecue capital of the world. The James Beard Foundation made the restaurant an America's Classic in 2003.
text.story: Pete Jones told Bob Garner that he sat in school as far back as the fifth or sixth grade and daydreamed about having his own barbecue place. He got it at seventeen: he built the Skylight while working for his uncle Emmitt Dennis at the City Cafe, where he cooked whole hog, and opened on July 8, 1947. He gave the place beer and a jukebox to set it apart from Ayden's other barbecue stands, thought about adding a dance hall, and ran late with rowdy crowds until the town's 7 pm curfew ended the late nights. The cooking did not change: whole hogs, heads on, over coals burned down from oak and hickory in fireplaces beside the pits, chopped with the crisp skin through the meat. He could not read or write, Kathleen Purvis records in Garden & Gun. In 1979 a National Geographic article called the restaurant the barbecue capital of the world; the dome went up in 1984, silver-painted wood, so that people could find the place — 'A place like this don't need any sign,' he told Garner. By the restaurant's own account he cooked at a congressional event attended by President Reagan and Vice President Bush in 1982, and in 2003 the James Beard Foundation named the Skylight an America's Classic. His line on fuel — 'If it's not cooked with wood, it's not barbecue' — is the one the Campaign for Real Barbecue prints on its wood page. He died in February 2006; his son Bruce, his nephew Jeff and his grandson Sam kept the pits.
text.today: Dead. Pete Jones died in February 2006 by the restaurant's account; Wikipedia gives the year, and Bob Garner's 2012 profile prints 2005. The Skylight Inn is run by his son Bruce, his nephew Jeff and his grandson Sam Jones.

text.what: A New Orleans writer and historian — a Tulane doctorate in history, 2013 — who recorded the Southern Foodways Alliance's barbecue oral histories in North Carolina in 2011 and South Carolina in 2012, then spent five years following the whole-hog pitmasters of Tennessee and the Carolinas for The One True Barbecue (Touchstone, 2016): part travelogue, part memoir, about the cooks who fire, flip and chop 200-pound pigs in smoke-filled pit houses, from Rodney Scott of Hemingway and Sam Jones of Ayden to Ricky Parker of Lexington, Tennessee.
text.story: Fertel's first bite of whole hog was at Siler's Old Time BBQ in Henderson, Tennessee, in 2008, and the cook who held his attention was Ricky Parker of Scott's-Parker's in Lexington, Tennessee, who died of liver disease at fifty-one; Fertel went back to see Parker's sons at the pits. For the Southern Foodways Alliance he recorded the North Carolina set in November and December 2011 — Chip Stamey in Greensboro, Sonny Conrad at the Barbecue Center, David Wilson at Short Sugar's, Brandon Cook at Cook's, Debbie Holt at Clyde Cooper's, the Parker's crew in Wilson, Samuel Jones at the Skylight Inn on November 29, Bum and Larry Dennis in Ayden, Stephen and Gerri Grady in Dudley — and the South Carolina set in June 2012: Douglas Oliver at Sweatman's, Tony Kittrell at Dukes, Jay Allen at Midway, Jackie Hite, Russell Cooper at Cooper's Country Store, the Browns in Kingstree, David Bessinger at Melvin's, and Rodney Scott in Hemingway, where the pits were turning eight to ten hogs a night. The One True Barbecue follows the whole-hog line from those pits: Scott, who went on to a Charleston restaurant and a James Beard award; Jones, the Skylight's grandson; Keith 'Pop' Ward, who tends Wilber's pits through the night in Goldsboro; Oliver at Sweatman's; three places named Scott's; and a new generation, Tyson Ho at Arrogant Swine in Brooklyn and Elliott Moss at Buxton Hall in Asheville. Robert Moss reviewed it for Southern Living, and John Shelton Reed wrote that it 'should be read by anyone who thinks barbecue is about sticky red sauce'. Fertel holds that most barbecue writing is hyperbole.
text.today: Visiting professor of history at Tulane and book critic for the Times-Picayune/Advocate; his fourth book, Brown Pelican (LSU Press, 2022), left barbecue behind. He calls New Orleans home and lives part of the time in a century-old church in St. Martinville, Louisiana.

text.what: A food writer and historian in Charleston — a Furman graduate with a doctorate in English from the University of South Carolina — who is contributing barbecue editor for Southern Living and was restaurant critic for the Post and Courier. Barbecue: The History of an American Institution (University of Alabama Press, 2010; revised and expanded 2020) is a documentary history of the subject built from newspapers, letters, diaries and travel narratives; Barbecue Lover's the Carolinas (2015) is his guide to both states. He counts South Carolina's sauces as two, mustard and vinegar, where the state's association counts four.
text.story: Moss's history reads the colonial and early-republic barbecue out of the record: whole hogs cooked as a ritual in the British colonies by the eighteenth century, the communal feast spreading from Virginia into the Carolinas in the mid-1700s, the political barbecue as an institution of the new republic, and the restaurants of the twentieth century. The second edition, published October 6, 2020, added colonial material, profiles of early restaurateurs and African American cooks, and a final chapter, 'The Second Golden Age of Barbecue', on the wood-cooked places that opened across the country in the 2010s. On South Carolina hash he went to the newspapers — 'rich hash' at a barbecue at Matthews' Spring, in the Abbeville Press and Banner of 1854 — and traced the name to haslet, the old word for the viscera: the head, liver and lights the whole hog left behind. When the Post and Courier reported in 2020 that hash was fading, he answered in Southern Living that new places were putting it on their menus, and used the recently closed Cannon's in Little Mountain as his example of the Midlands' mustard-yellow kind. He has tested Summerville's claim to sweet tea (2013) and told the story of hushpuppies (2023). When John Shelton Reed's campaign asked in 2014 for any regulation that forbade wood cooking in North Carolina, Moss looked in South Carolina and reported in the Columbia Free Times that there was none there either. He reviewed Rien Fertel's The One True Barbecue for Southern Living in 2016. His other books are Southern Spirits (2016), The Lost Southern Chefs (University of Georgia Press, 2022) and The Roffignac (LSU Press, 2024).
text.today: Based in Charleston; contributing barbecue editor for Southern Living and a frequent contributor to Charleston Magazine, Garden & Gun, Serious Eats and The Local Palate. His site, robertfmoss.com, carries his features on hash, hushpuppies and the revised history.

text.what: Rodney Scott (born November 1, 1971) is a whole-hog pitmaster from Hemingway, in the Pee Dee of South Carolina, who cooked his first pig at eleven at his parents' store, took the business over in 2011, and in February 2017 opened Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ in Charleston with Nick Pihakis. In 2018 the James Beard Foundation named him Best Chef: Southeast, the second pitmaster to win a Beard chef award. His book with Lolis Eric Elie, Rodney Scott's World of BBQ, came out in 2021. Every Rodney Scott's location closed in May 2026; he cooks pop-ups as Pitmaster Scott.
text.story: Roosevelt and Ella Scott moved from Philadelphia to the Pee Dee in 1972 with their infant son, farmed and raised hogs near Nesmith, and opened a gas station and variety store on the Hemingway highway; the barbecue began as a weekend hog. Rodney cooked his first at eleven and was full time at seventeen, when the store cooked four to six a week. 'My whole life has been barbecue,' he told Rien Fertel for the Southern Foodways Alliance in June 2012, by which time the pits held eight to ten hogs a night. John T. Edge had profiled the store in 2009, and Nick Pihakis of the Jim 'N Nick's chain, a customer, told him he was undercharging. On November 27, 2013 the wooden cookhouse burned; Scott took his hogs on the road — the Bar-B-Que in Exile Tour, staged with Pihakis's Fatback Collective — to rebuild in metal. After a quarrel with his father in 2016 he left Hemingway, and in February 2017 he and Pihakis opened Rodney Scott's Whole Hog BBQ in a former fried-chicken house on upper King Street, Charleston. In May 2018 the James Beard Foundation gave him its Best Chef: Southeast award; the Chef's Table: BBQ episode about him in 2020 set the restaurant's sales records three days running. Birmingham followed in 2019, Atlanta and a second Alabama town in 2021, and the book with Lolis Eric Elie the same year. On May 3, 2026 the King Street restaurant closed 'until further notice' amid suits and liens against Pihakis Restaurant Group, and the other locations with it; in June he cooked at Munkle Brewing under a new name, Pitmaster Scott. Roosevelt Scott died in 2020 and Ella in 2023; the Hemingway store reopened in May 2024 under her brother Sam Wilson and Rodney's son Dominic.
text.today: Living. His Charleston restaurant has been closed since May 3, 2026; he cooks pop-ups in Charleston as Pitmaster Scott, has said that reopening there is his first priority, and was announced in July 2026 as a headliner of the Pair'd Margaret River Region Festival in Western Australia.

text.what: Samuel 'Sam' Jones is the grandson of Pete Jones and a third-generation pitmaster of the Skylight Inn in Ayden, where he sold chopped pork as a child. With Michael Letchworth he opened Sam Jones BBQ in Winterville on November 10, 2015, and a second restaurant in Raleigh in February 2021. His book with Daniel Vaughn, Whole Hog BBQ: The Gospel of Carolina Barbecue (2019), writes the family method down. He was a James Beard semifinalist for Best Chef: Southeast in 2018, and Sam Jones BBQ holds a Michelin Bib Gourmand from the first Michelin Guide American South (2025).
text.story: At four, Sam Jones told a reporter that he wanted to be a trash man and the Prince of Barbecue; his father Bruce joked about putting hog grease in his milk bottle. He grew up in the Skylight Inn, quit it at fifteen, and came back after a college paper on barbecue told him what his work was. He described the return to Rien Fertel of the Southern Foodways Alliance in November 2011 as a flag-bearer's job, keeping the standard up on the field: 'I don't want our style of barbecue to be one of them things where you read about it in the history books. I want it to be one of them things where you can go get it and taste it and see it.' Southern Living put him among ten Southern pitmasters in 2012. A cooking event in Charleston in 2013 turned him toward a place of his own; in 2014 he and Michael Letchworth signed for a loan, and Sam Jones BBQ opened in Winterville on November 10, 2015, with a longer menu than the Skylight's — ribs, turkey, chicken, banana pudding — around the same wood-cooked hog. The James Beard Foundation listed him as a semifinalist for Best Chef: Southeast in 2018; Whole Hog BBQ, written with Daniel Vaughn of Texas Monthly, came out from Ten Speed Press in 2019. The Raleigh restaurant opened in a former garage on West Lenoir Street in February 2021. He has served as Ayden's fire chief, lives on the farm he grew up on with his wife Sarah and two daughters, and told Garden & Gun in 2019: 'Today I'm proud to be from Ayden, North Carolina.'
text.today: Living. He runs Sam Jones BBQ in Winterville and Raleigh with Michael Letchworth and the Skylight Inn with his father Bruce and Jeff Jones; a stall in Raleigh's Morgan Street Food Hall is planned for the end of 2026, and Sam Jones BBQ holds a Bib Gourmand from the first Michelin Guide American South, November 2025.

text.what: Sid Weaver sold barbecue from a tent across from the Davidson County courthouse in Lexington from 1919 — cooked in the alley behind, sold to people on their way to court — and is the first name in every account of Lexington-style barbecue. Jess Swicegood set up beside him within the decade; the two taught Warner Stamey, and Weaver's hand Alton Beck built the town's first permanent barbecue restaurant in 1938. What is known of him is the tent, the date, the pupils and the sauce that came out of those stands: vinegar and pepper with ketchup, the Piedmont's dip.
text.story: Our State's Jeremy Markovich calls him Lexington barbecue's Abraham, 'first cooking up his barbecue in the alley outside and selling it from a tent to people heading over to the old courthouse in 1919'. Robert Moss's history, as the Barbecue Bros summarize it, has him first and Jess Swicegood joining him later, the two working out the shoulder-and-dip style and spreading it across the Piedmont. Stamey's own history puts both men 'selling pork out of tents across from the courthouse' when Warner Stamey, boarding with his sister for high school in the late 1920s, came to learn from them; the American Royal's 2020 citation for Stamey says they taught him everything there was to know about pit cooking. Alton Beck, who had worked for Weaver, opened the first bricks-and-mortar barbecue restaurant in town on West Center Street in 1938, rebuilt it in 1949, and retired after thirty-one years; the wood pits found behind a wall of Lexington's city hall in 2015 are thought to be his. *Tradition holds —* Weaver later built a small cafe of his own near the square. No birth date, death date or photograph of Weaver is in any source read for this record.
text.today: Dead, on no date this record can name. The stands are gone; Lexington counted more than twenty barbecue restaurants in 2003, and the Lexington Barbecue Festival has closed Main Street each October since 1984, a few blocks from where the tent stood.

text.what: Skilton Dennis is the ancestor the Dennis and Jones families of Ayden name as the start of barbecue for sale in North Carolina: by their account he sold smoked hog meat and cornbread from a wagon in 1830, and Otter Dennis, of the same family, founded the town. The 1830 is painted on the Skylight Inn's billboard as one of its four tenets and was recorded from Bum and Larry Dennis by the Southern Foodways Alliance; Bob Garner's 2012 profile of Pete Jones puts the covered wagon in the mid-1800s. No document has been produced.
text.story: The claim is the families'. Pete Jones, who opened the Skylight Inn in 1947, learned the trade from the Dennis side of his family and liked to say that barbecue ran in his blood; his great-great-grandfather, he told Bob Garner, sold barbecue from a covered wagon in Ayden in the mid-1800s. The billboard outside the Skylight sets the tradition at 1830. Bum Dennis and his son Larry gave Rien Fertel the same story for the Southern Foodways Alliance in December 2011: Skilton Dennis selling smoked hog meat and cornbread from a wagon in 1830, and Otter Dennis founding the 'enigmatically-named' town. John Tanner's post on Bum's death counts the wagon-seller as a great-great-great-grandfather, 'add 4 or 5 more greats' — the arithmetic of a family story, not of a record. The Alliance's page for Sam Jones says the Dennis clan's history shows them as the first in North Carolina to serve pit barbecue publicly. *Inference —* Ayden was incorporated only in 1891, around a railroad depot on William Henry Harris's farm; a wagon in 1830 would have served the farms and churches of what became southern Pitt County, not a town. *Inference —* this project has seen no census, deed or grave for a Skilton Dennis selling barbecue in 1830; the date is held here as the families' and nothing more.
text.today: Dead, on no date this record can name. The two families that tell his story cook whole hog in Ayden: the Joneses at the Skylight Inn, opened 1947, and the Dennises at Bum's Restaurant, opened 1963, a few blocks apart.

text.what: Charles Warner Stamey (born 1911), the youngest of eleven children, learned pit-cooking as a high-school boarder in Lexington from Jess Swicegood and Sid Weaver at their tents across from the courthouse, sold barbecue in Shelby through the 1930s, came back in 1938 to buy Swicegood's stand and rename it Stamey's, and in 1953 opened the Greensboro drive-in his family runs. His restaurant credits him with putting hushpuppies beside barbecue in North Carolina. Wayne Monk, Red Bridges and his brother-in-law Alston Bridges learned under him; the American Royal made him a legacy inductee of its Barbecue Hall of Fame in 2020.
text.story: Stamey was born in 1911 — in Lincoln County, by Cleveland County's local history — and moved to Lexington to live with his older sister while he attended high school. There he hooked up with Jess Swicegood and Sid Weaver, who were selling pork out of tents across from the courthouse, and they taught him pit cooking. With a diploma and $350 he went to Shelby and sold barbecue to growing crowds; he married Mary Linda Bridges in 1933, and the county history has Stamey's Barbecue at 230 South Washington Street in 1937. Her brother Alston Bridges learned smoking from him and managed his Log Cabin Barbecue in Lexington for two and a half years; Red Bridges, no relation, learned from him too and opened at the same Washington Street address about 1949. In 1938 Stamey sold the Shelby operation, went back to Lexington, bought Swicegood's and put his own name on it — for $300, Robert Moss's history says. Wayne Monk worked under him there for several years before opening Lexington Barbecue in 1962. In 1953 Stamey opened a drive-in on High Point Road in Greensboro, his sixth restaurant by the American Royal's count, with call-in service; four years later he handed it to his son Charles, and Charles's brother Keith joined in 1970. The hushpuppy — the fried cornmeal fritter of the fish camps — went onto the barbecue tray under him: Keith said his father picked the idea up from a friend's fish camp, the Friendly Road Inn in Greensboro, and the restaurant's history says he introduced it to North Carolina barbecue diners. Chip Stamey, his grandson, left another career to take the Greensboro house in 1993, and told the Southern Foodways Alliance in 2011 that his rule is to keep everything the same.
text.today: Dead; his death year is not confirmed by any source this record cites. The American Royal inducted him as a 2020 legacy member of its Barbecue Hall of Fame, and the fourth generation of Stameys runs the two Greensboro restaurants.

text.what: Wayne Monk opened Lexington Barbecue beside U.S. 29/70 in Lexington, Davidson County, in 1962, at twenty-six, after years as a carhop and then a pit hand under Warner Stamey, and he owns it with his son Rick. The pit cooks pork shoulders over oak and hickory coals and serves them with the dip, the Piedmont's thin red vinegar sauce; locals call it the Honeymonk, from his name and his early partner Sonny Hunneycutt's. He cooked for the heads of government at the 1983 economic summit in Williamsburg, and the James Beard Foundation named the restaurant an America's Classic in 2003.
text.story: Monk was a teenage carhop at a Lexington barbecue place, worked for Holland Tussey, and spent several years working directly under Warner Stamey at Stamey's in downtown Lexington — Stamey had bought Jess Swicegood's stand there in 1938 — so that his own pit stands two teachers from the courthouse tents of 1919. At twenty-six, in 1962, he bought a roadside parcel beside U.S. Highway 29/70 that had been Tussey's, built onto the small cafe on it, and opened Lexington Barbecue #1 with Sonny Hunneycutt; the partner left, and the joined name, Honeymonk, stayed on the town's tongue. In 1983 a politically connected local attorney asked whether he would cook for President Reagan, and he served barbecue to the heads of government at that year's economic summit in Williamsburg, Virginia, Margaret Thatcher and François Mitterrand among them. The James Beard Foundation made the restaurant an America's Classic in 2003, the same year as the Skylight Inn in Ayden. Garden & Gun found three generations at the pits in 2015: Wayne; Rick, who started at thirteen and is pitmaster, bookkeeper or janitor as the day requires; and Rick's son Nathan, who began in the kitchen at about sixteen. 'It's not a job. It's a way of life,' Rick said. The American Royal inducted Wayne Monk into its Barbecue Hall of Fame on September 14, 2019 — he 'set the standard that practically defines North Carolina barbecue', the citation said — and the new North Carolina Bar-B-Q Hall of Fame inducted him at Burlington on March 1, 2024.

text.what: Wilberdean 'Wilber' Shirley (1930–2021) learned barbecue at Griffin's in Goldsboro, bought the former Hill's Barbecue on U.S. 70 east of town in 1962 and put his name on it, and cooked split whole hogs over oak coals there for more than forty years. Wilber's fed presidents, governors and senators and, on a holiday weekend, up to 130 pigs. It closed in March 2019 over unpaid taxes; a group of customers bought it and reopened it in July 2020, while he lived. He died on April 5, 2021, at ninety.
text.story: 'I went to work at a place called Griffin's Barbecue... That's how I first learned to cook it,' he told John Shelton Reed and Dale Volberg Reed for Holy Smoke. In 1962 — July 24, 1961, by WRAL's obituary — he bought Hill's Barbecue on Highway 70 and renamed it. 'Split halves of whole hogs over oak coals in closed pits,' he said of his method: 'That grease hitting those coals makes the smoked flavor. You can't spray it on there, paint it on there, put it on there.' The pits ran overnight, from about ten at night to ten in the morning; in season the place cooked 100 to 125 pigs a week, and Our State counts 130 on a Labor Day weekend and dining rooms for more than 300. 'I work seven days a week,' he said. 'Some weeks I come in eight days a week.' A waitress had been there more than thirty years, a cook since before he bought the place. Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton, Governors Terry Sanford and Jim Hunt and Senator Jesse Helms ate there. The restaurant was shut in March 2019 for nonpayment of taxes. Willis B. Underwood III, an insurance salesman who had eaten there all his life, gathered other regulars into Goldpit Partners, bought it, and reopened it in July 2020 for curbside orders: 'I just didn't want to see the smoke die.' Shirley, a longtime member of First Free Will Baptist Church in Goldsboro, died at a retirement community in Kinston on April 5, 2021. The Campaign for Real Barbecue quotes him on its wood page: cooking whole hogs over hardwood coals overnight 'is not easy or cheap, but it is the right way, and something we as a community take a lot of pride in'.
text.today: Dead: April 5, 2021, at Kinston, aged ninety. Wilber's Barbecue is open under Goldpit Partners at 4172 U.S. Highway 70 East, Goldsboro, cooking whole hogs over oak; his portrait hangs in the dining room.

text.what: A campaign, founded in 2013 by the sociologist and barbecue writer John Shelton Reed and the blogger Dan Levine, that certifies restaurants which cook the barbecue style traditional to their area and rely solely on wood for heat, and gives them a certificate and a decal. It began in North Carolina — about seventy places certified by January 2018 — and has regional 'smoke detectors' for South Carolina, Kentucky, Georgia, Alabama and the Virginia–Washington region under a True 'Cue USA program. Its three stated goals are to celebrate wood-cooking, to honor the places that keep it, and to teach eaters the difference between wood-cooked barbecue and what it calls 'faux 'cue'.
text.story: Reed and his wife Dale wrote Holy Smoke (2008) and in it lamented how much North Carolina barbecue was cooked on gas. In 2013 he and Dan Levine — 'Porky LeSwine' of the blog BBQJew, the campaign's 'Chief Smoke Detector' to Reed's 'Eminence Grease' — founded the campaign to find and list the places still cooking entirely with wood or charcoal. On April 23, 2014, in the Raleigh News & Observer, they issued the True 'Cue Challenge: a prize to anyone who could name the statute, regulation or official that forbade a restaurant to cook with wood, since owners so often said the health department had made them switch. Two years on, Reed wrote, no one had claimed it, and Daniel Vaughn in Texas and Robert Moss in South Carolina had found the same in their states; one state official mentioned environmental concerns, and Reed allows that gas and electricity are cheaper, easier and more consistent. The campaign draws its line with care: it certifies only wood-for-heat, but has 'no beef' with cooks who use gas or electricity for ignition and temperature control so long as wood smoke reaches the meat, and reserves 'faux 'cue' for meat cooked with no smoke at all. Its Pledge is for those who hold that if it is not cooked with wood it is not barbecue. Its wood page quotes a federal meat-labeling rule defining barbecued meat as cooked by the direct action of dry heat from burning hardwood, and gathers witnesses from Pete Jones to Rodney Scott, Wilber Shirley and Aaron Franklin, with Alton Brown's joke that gas lets you control the heat, 'but you're going to go to hell'.
text.how: A restaurant is certified once the campaign confirms it cooks its region's style with wood as the only heat; it receives a certificate and a window decal and is listed on truecue.org by state. Eaters sign the Pledge; the site sells merchandise; regional smoke detectors handle the other states.
text.today: Active; the site lists certified places by state and runs the True 'Cue USA program. About seventy North Carolina restaurants held certificates in January 2018; no current count is posted.

text.what: A non-profit founded in 2006 in Winston-Salem by Jim Early, a lawyer and cook, to promote North Carolina's barbecue culture and, in its own words, to secure the state's place as the Barbecue Capital of the World. Its lasting work is the Historic Barbecue Trail: a route of about two dozen restaurants, some 700 miles end to end, admitted only if the meat cooks on grates over pits with wood or charcoal, the owners make their own sauce, the pits have run fifteen consecutive years, and no town has more than two. Early wrote the guidebook, The Best Tar Heel Barbecue: Manteo to Murphy, and the society ran two-day cooking boot camps three times a year.
text.story: Jim Early had a law office in Winston-Salem and a self-published guide to every barbecue place from Manteo to Murphy when he founded the society in 2006; he closed the law office in September 2017 to run it full time. Searching the state's hundred counties for pits still cooking pork slowly over wood coals, he found fewer than thirty, and the Trail is that list under its rules — Wilber's in Goldsboro, the Skylight Inn in Ayden, B's in Greenville, Allen & Son near Chapel Hill, Stamey's in Greensboro, Short Sugar's in Reidsville, the Bar-B-Q Center in Lexington and Red Bridges in Shelby among them. Wikipedia's article counts twenty-five establishments in twenty-one locales; WRAL in 2021 counted twenty. The boot camps ran at Tanglewood Park in May, Sugar Mountain in July and Castle Hayne in September, teaching whole hog, butts, ribs, chicken, brisket and Early's pimento cheese; CNN put the school on a 2012 list of ten cooking schools worldwide, the only one in the United States. The society's motto, in its less formal version, was to cook and eat barbecue as often as possible, preferably among friends, and to promote the state as the Cradle of 'Cue. It took no side in the east-west argument but recorded it: the 2006 bills that would have made Lexington's festival official, and their failure. Early died on June 21, 2021, at 82, after a stroke. In March 2024 John Tanner's barbecue blog reported that the society 'appears to have withered considerably' since, with Ben Thompson keeping its Facebook page as a forum, and that a separate group of pitmasters, Chuck Hursey among them, had started a North Carolina Barbecue Hall of Fame. Neither ncbbqsociety.com nor ncbbqsociety.org resolved when this project checked on September 15, 2026.
text.how: Membership is by dues, and the sponsors are mostly barbecue restaurants. The Trail is followed by car with the map or Early's book; a stop earns its place by its pit, its sauce and its years, not its fame. The boot camps were two-day schools open to anyone who paid.
text.today: Status unknown as of September 2026: the founder is dead, both web addresses are down, and the Facebook page carries on as a forum. The Trail's list is reprinted by Our State and others.

text.what: A judging body and booster founded in 2004 by Lake E. High Jr., a wine judge, and Walter Rolandi, a psychologist, 'to train the best BBQ judges in the world and to preserve and promote the unique nature of South Carolina Barbecue'. It runs judging seminars in Columbia that turn eaters into certified judges — more than 800 by 2015 — sanctions cook-offs across the state, eight of them listed between September 12 and October 24, 2026, and keeps a points championship for the teams. Its account of the state's barbecue is Lake High's: South Carolina as the home of all four sauces — mustard, vinegar-pepper, light tomato and heavy tomato — mapped by region.
text.story: When High and Rolandi founded the association, South Carolina had two barbecue cook-offs a year; by 2015 it had thirty-seven, more per head than any other state, and the association's judge-training system was being copied elsewhere. High is its historian as well as its founder. His A History of South Carolina Barbeque (2013) and the association's history page hold that Europeans first learned barbecue from the Native Americans at Santa Elena, the sixteenth-century colony in what is now South Carolina; that vinegar-and-pepper is the original sauce, hundreds of years old; that mustard came with the German settlers of the 1730s to 1750s; that light tomato is vinegar-and-pepper with ketchup added, from around 1900; and that heavy tomato is the newest, of the last sixty years. Only South Carolina, the page says, is home to all four. Robert Moss, another South Carolinian, counts two — sweet mustard and spicy vinegar — and the state's Wikipedia article gives both counts, along with the four-or-five-region division first drawn by Charles Kovacik and John Winberry in South Carolina: A Geography (1987). High's line, to South Carolina Living in 2015: 'Barbeque is a noun, not a verb. It's something Southerners eat, not do.' In August 2018 the association named Jim Wellman of Lexington president and Don Adkins of Seneca vice president.
text.how: Judges train at an annual seminar in Columbia and advance through levels; a team enters a sanctioned cook-off, is scored by certified judges, and earns points toward the SCBA Championship. The cook-offs are run by towns, churches, scout troops and civic groups — Troop 61's competition at Pomaria and the Hopeful Hog Festival at Lancaster were on the 2026 list — with the association supplying the judging.
text.today: Active. The 2026 calendar lists cook-offs from Mauldin to Barnwell through October 24, the judge seminars are held in Columbia each year, and the association posts from PO Box 115, Blythewood.

text.what: An institute of the Center for the Study of Southern Culture at the University of Mississippi, founded in 1999 and directed since then by John T. Edge, that documents the food of the South: oral histories, films, writing, awards and events, funded by about 800 members. For the Carolinas its work is the Southern BBQ Trail, an oral-history project begun in February 2011 across nine states, whose North Carolina set includes the Skylight Inn, Parker's, Grady's, B's, Bum's, Stamey's, Short Sugar's, Red Bridges, Cook's, Clyde Cooper's, the Barbecue Center and Ed Mitchell, and whose South Carolina set holds eight interviews: Sweatman's, Scott's, Midway, Jackie Hite's, Dukes, Cooper's Country Store, Brown's and Melvin's. Each interview is a transcript with audio, free online.
text.story: The SFA came out of a 1999 meeting called by the journalist John Egerton, with John Martin Taylor among the founders, and John T. Edge has directed it since. It gives the Ruth Fertel Keeper of the Flame award with the Fertel Foundation and the John Egerton Prize, and Corby Kummer in the Atlantic called it 'this country's most intellectually engaged (and probably most engaging) food society'. The Southern BBQ Trail went up on February 22, 2011, and the Carolina sets on April 25 of that year. The North Carolina introduction, by John Shelton Reed, opens on the point that barbecue was never home cooking — too much trouble — and until the early twentieth century was reserved for harvests, fundraisers and political rallies; the South Carolina introduction opens: 'Like everything in South Carolina, we cook barbeque cantankerously.' Rien Fertel interviewed Samuel Jones at the Skylight Inn for the project and went on to write The One True Barbecue (2016) about the whole-hog pitmasters; John and Dale Reed drew on the North Carolina interviews for Holy Smoke; in 2009 Edge himself profiled the Scott family of Hemingway. Rodney Scott's interview sits in the South Carolina set beside Bub Sweatman's and Jackie Hite's; Chip Stamey's, Sonny Conrad's of the Barbecue Center and Ed Mitchell's are in the North Carolina set.
text.how: Interviews are recorded by SFA oral historians, transcribed and posted with audio, a portrait and a short biography, under the project and the state; the site filters by state and by tag. Membership funds the work; the awards and events run alongside it.
text.today: Active at the University of Mississippi; the Carolina barbecue interviews remain online under the Southern BBQ Trail.

text.what: A three-day barbecue-and-blues festival in Uptown Greenwood each July — Thursday to Saturday of the second weekend; July 9 to 11 in 2026 — hosted by the Uptown Greenwood Development Corporation. Its cook-off is sanctioned by the Kansas City Barbeque Society, the national competition body, and is billed as a South Carolina state championship with a Black Kettle hash competition beside it; the barbecue vendors fill the Main Street parking lot between Court and Seaboard avenues, and the Blues Cruise puts bands in restaurants and venues around the uptown into the night. The organizers billed 2026 as the twenty-fifth anniversary; press accounts date the first festival to 2000.
text.story: Greenwood is a county seat in the Old 96 District on the Piedmont side of the state, and the festival is its downtown corporation's summer event rather than a pit's or a church's. The competition is Kansas City's — KCBS judges, KCBS categories, and a date the society sets rather than the town — laid over a South Carolina crowd, with a hash kettle competition to keep the state's own dish in view and the public sampling and voting on Carolina hash, and a blues program, the Blues Cruise, run under the artistic direction of the bluesman Shrimp City Slim. *Inference —* it is the Upstate's festival in the way Lexington's is the Piedmont's, and the sanctioned cook-off, not a local pit, is its center.
text.how: Thursday evening through Saturday: teams cook overnight in the Main Street lot for KCBS judging; the public samples barbecue and hash and votes; the Blues Cruise runs at venues around the uptown from late morning to midnight.
text.today: Held July 9–11, 2026; the 2027 dates are July 8–10. Contact is the Uptown Greenwood office at 104 Main Street.

text.what: The plate sale: a church, a volunteer fire department, a Ruritan club or a scout troop cooks pork — a whole hog or a stack of butts — and sells it by the plate on a Saturday to pay for a roof, a truck or a mission. In eastern North Carolina the plate is barbecue or barbecue chicken with slaw and bread; Back Swamp Volunteer Fire Department in Richlands sold pork or chicken plates for $10 on April 18, 2026, from 11 a.m. until the food ran out. In South Carolina the same money is often raised on hash: the Highway 34 Volunteer Fire Department outside Ninety Six cooks it in cast-iron pots and sells it by the quart to neighbors who read the notice in the paper and phone in an order.
text.story: The fundraiser is where the whole-hog barbecue of the colonial Carolinas went when the plantation left: barbecues for fundraisers, church gatherings and political rallies are on record in the Carolina colonies, and John Shelton Reed's line is that until the early twentieth century barbecue was reserved for harvests, fundraisers and rallies. Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church in Charlotte is the form at full scale: begun in 1929 to pay $89.50 of Sunday-school debt, it grew to 14,600 pounds of pork and 20,000 eaters by 2015 and ran ninety-three years on volunteers taking a week off work. Hillsborough's Hog Day began in 1983 as a chamber-of-commerce fundraiser and since 2014 has been the Orange County Optimist Club's, its proceeds to children's programs — Future Farmers of America, the Hillsborough 4-H and a church youth group in 2025. On the coast the volunteer fire departments own the Saturday calendar: Back Swamp's annual barbecue and raffle at the station on Catherine Lake Road is one of dozens. South Carolina's version is the hash sale: fire stations, churches and civic groups stew pork, liver and onions in iron kettles over a wood fire and sell hash by the quart; at Highway 34 VFD, Melvin Fouchee learned the recipe from Ike Berry and the department buys its equipment on the proceeds. The South Carolina Barbeque Association's cook-off calendar is much the same list under another name — Troop 61's competition at Pomaria, the Hopeful Hog Festival at Lancaster.
text.how: A Saturday, 11 a.m. until sold out. The pigs or butts cook overnight on a rented or department-owned cooker; volunteers make slaw and stew; plates are packed to go — barbecue, slaw, bread, sometimes potatoes or beans — and sold at a window or a drive-through for a set price, with a raffle beside the table. Hash is ordered by the quart in advance and picked up; Mallard Creek sold by the plate, sandwich, pound and quart.
text.today: Continuous. Back Swamp VFD's plate was $10 in April 2026; Mallard Creek's was $15 in October 2024 and is no more; the SCBA calendar listed eight cook-offs for the autumn of 2026.

text.what: A two-day barbecue festival and cook-off at River Park in downtown Hillsborough, Orange County, held since 1983 — the oldest continuing barbecue festival in North Carolina, by the Daily Tar Heel's account — and run since 2014 by the Orange County Optimist Club as a fundraiser for children's programs. A Friday evening opens it; Saturday brings the cook-off, live music, a car show, a fun run and the Pigs on Parade. In 2019 the count was 27 cooking teams, more than 100 vendors and a collective three tons of barbecue; the 2025 festival, September 13 and 14, came two months after Tropical Storm Chantal flooded the Eno riverfront and lost its 5K to the water.
text.story: Hog Day was the Hillsborough/Orange County Chamber of Commerce's festival for thirty-one years, drawing up to 35,000 people as the county's largest festival, until the chamber's board voted in January 2014 that it was not 'an adequate use of resources' for the chamber's mission. Craig Lloyd, the chamber's former executive director and a Hog Day hand since he won a design contest more than thirty years ago, gathered the volunteers into a new Orange County Optimist Club and put the festival on that June 20 and 21 at the Efland Ruritan Club under the theme 'Bringing Home the Bacon', because it was '100% developed and produced by local volunteers'; after two years in Efland it came home to River Park in 2016, the thirty-fourth festival, now in September. Hurricane Florence pushed 2018 to a make-up weekend on November 2 and 3; the pandemic cancelled 2020 and 2021; 2022 was the return. The cook-off carries a North Carolina Pork Council contest alongside the festival's own — James Catlett and Brittany Thompson took the two first places in 2025 — and the proceeds go to youth: Future Farmers of America, the Hillsborough 4-H club and a Holy Family Catholic Church youth group in 2025. Lloyd, now the club's president, is the 'Godfather of Hog Day' on the festival's site; Al Hartkopf chairs it.
text.how: Friday night music at River Park; Saturday from 10 to 5, the cook-off teams sell plates and sandwiches, vendors line the park, and the car show, the fun run along the Eno and the Pigs on Parade fill the day. Proceeds go to the Optimist Club's charities.
text.today: Open. The 2025 festival ran September 13 and 14 at River Park; the organizer is the Orange County Optimist Club, at hogday.org.

text.what: A one-day street festival on Main Street in uptown Lexington, Davidson County, each October since 1984, built on the town's pork-shoulder barbecue: up to twenty area restaurants cook and sell, several blocks close to traffic, and hundreds of other vendors sell crafts and fudge around them. Wikipedia's article says it draws as many as 200,000 people; the first festival drew 30,000 and 3,000 pounds of barbecue, and by 1994 the count was over 100,000 and 11,000 pounds. Since 2007 it holds a title from the General Assembly — Official Food Festival of the Piedmont Triad Region of the State of North Carolina. The 2026 festival is planned for October 24.
text.story: The idea came from Joe Sink Jr., publisher of Lexington's daily, The Dispatch, in 1983; the bank BB&T hired Kay Saintsing to study whether a festival could work, the study found Lexington already a weekend destination for barbecue, and the first festival was held on October 27, 1984. In 1995 the North Carolina Championship Pork Cook-Off joined it, so that Piedmont crowds could watch eastern whole-hog cooks at work in the capital of the shoulder. NC By Train sets up a temporary stop a block away for the day, served by Amtrak's Carolinian and Piedmont. The 2020 festival went virtual. The politics is the story the festival tells about itself under the heading 'Pork-Barrel Politics'. In 2006 House Bill 21 and Senate Bill 47 would have made it the official barbecue festival of North Carolina; the east read that as making Lexington the official barbecue, nearly half the state prefers the other kind, and neither bill passed. In 2007 House Bill 433 gave it the Piedmont Triad title instead — a designation that names a region and so leaves the east out of the question. Jerry Bledsoe, the 'world's leading, foremost barbecue authority' by his own account, said that Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer, the self-styled 'oracle of the holy grub', had ruined the state's chances of distinction in barbecue. Eastern vendors turn up on Main Street each year; the article calls the controversy mild, and sometimes not so mild.
text.how: One Saturday in October: Main Street closes, the restaurants set up on the street, and the plate is Lexington's — chopped or sliced shoulder with red slaw and hush puppies, the dip on the meat. Around it are four hundred or more vendors, live music on up to five stages, lumberjack games and street performers. Visitors come by car and, for the day, by train.
text.today: Held each October; the 2026 date is October 24. It is listed in 1,000 Places to See in the USA & Canada Before You Die, and in 2012 U.S. News & World Report ranked Lexington fourth among the country's barbecue cities.

text.what: The one-day church barbecue of Mallard Creek Presbyterian Church in northeast Charlotte, held on the fourth Thursday of October from 1929 to 2024 and retired in 2025 after ninety-three editions. It sold hickory-smoked chopped pork, Brunswick stew and the church's own slaw by the plate, sandwich, pound and quart — dine-in, drive-through and carry-out; a plate was $15 and a sandwich $7 in 2024 — and it was one of North Carolina's best-known political stops: a rope line in the parking field where candidates for every office from vice-president to dog catcher worked the crowd in the last weeks before an election.
text.story: In late 1928 or early 1929 the pastor, Dr. W. H. Frazer, and his brother Ben held a men's meeting with a barbecued pig; the church owed money on a Sunday-school building, and that October the deacons cooked three or four pigs and a goat to pay it. The first year cleared $89.50, enough to retire the debt with a little over. The fourth Thursday was chosen to keep clear of Halloween. The hogs cooked in ditches with hickory coals shoved underneath; by 1979, the fiftieth year, the church cooked 4,800 pounds of meat, 2,000 pounds of slaw and 250 gallons of Brunswick stew, and in the 1980s metal cookers replaced the dirt pits, with some meat still cooked on open pits inside a screened building. By 2015 Our State counted 20,000 people, 14,600 pounds of pork, 2,500 gallons of stew and two tons of slaw, and Tommy Oehler told the magazine the whole hogs were gone: 'Now we just use the butt', dressed with an eastern-style vinegar sauce. The politics grew with the plates. Dan Quayle came seeking the 2000 Republican nomination; Charlotte mayors Richard Vinroot, Pat McCrory and Jennifer Roberts worked the line; Deborah Ross came running for the Senate. No speeches: candidates set up booths, hand out fliers and court voters along a rope in the parking area. On October 1, 2025, the church announced with 'heavy hearts' that the barbecue was retired. The leaders of its four main components had stepped aside, co-chair Charles Kimrey said, and the church could not find volunteers able to take eight to ten days off work for the preparation; each prep day took about a hundred volunteers and the day itself about three hundred. 'Everything seems to have a life cycle and for the Mallard Creek BBQ, that life cycle is 93 years.'
text.how: For a week before, volunteers cooked pork butts — hickory-smoked, then chopped, cooled and seasoned — and stewed Brunswick stew in quantity; on the Thursday the church served from morning, dine-in, drive-through and walk-up, by plate (barbecue, stew, applesauce, slaw and bread), sandwich, pound or quart. Proceeds went to the church's missions and to the building debt the barbecue was founded to retire.
text.today: Retired. The last barbecue was held Thursday, October 24, 2024; the church announced the end on October 1, 2025, three weeks before the date it would have kept.

etymology.note: Pig pull and hog roast name the same event elsewhere; pig roast is the wider term, used of the Cuban, Filipino and Hawaiian roasts, which are other traditions. Kingstree, South Carolina, calls its fall cook-off the Pig Pickin' Festival.

text.what: A party at which a whole hog is cooked for the crowd and the crowd eats it off the pig — picked by hand from the split carcass, or chopped on a block beside it. A barrow, a castrated male, or a gilt of about 80 to 120 pounds dressed weight is split and laid on a large charcoal or propane cooker for four to eight hours, under the direction of the host and whoever is helping; the meat is basted or dressed in the local sauce and served with slaw, hush puppies, baked beans, Brunswick stew or, in South Carolina, hash and rice. It is the eastern Carolinas' form of the wedding, the homecoming, the tailgate, the political rally and the fire-department fundraiser.
text.story: The whole-hog feast is older than the name. Communal barbecues of whole pigs spread from Virginia into the Carolinas in the mid-1700s and fed church gatherings, fundraisers and political rallies; George Washington wrote of attending a barbecue on August 4, 1769. The pig pickin' is that feast on a trailer cooker. Its year is the church's and the college's: 'dinner on the grounds', family reunions, Thanksgiving and Christmas, graduations and weddings, and the tailgate — East Carolina University in Greenville has run a pig pickin' contest, the Pigskin Pig-Out, since 1985. Politics keeps it: local parties and candidates still use a pig pickin' to draw a crowd, and in 1983 Rufus Edmisten, running for governor of North Carolina, was overheard saying he had eaten enough barbecue, would eat no more, and was taking his stand. Ed Mitchell's first hog was a family pickin' in Wilson: at fourteen or fifteen he tended the fire after the men, having passed the moonshine, fell asleep, and his grandfather woke to a cooked pig and poured him a glass. Kingstree, in the Pee Dee, holds a Pig Pickin' Festival each fall for the vinegar-based barbecue of Williamsburg County; seventy teams competed in 2010. The name is the one thing the article is sure of: the meat is picked off the hog by the guests, and the gathering is named for it.
text.how: The host borrows or rents a cooker, buys a dressed hog, and lights charcoal or gas the morning of, or the night before for a big pig. The hog goes on meat-side down and is flipped once when it stops dripping fat; some cooks wipe the ash from the skin with paper towels or a whisk broom before the flip so the cracklings come out clean. The baste is the region's: mustard in the South Carolina Midlands, vinegar and red pepper flakes in eastern North Carolina, a ketchup base in the west. When the meat falls from the bone the pig is carried to the table and the guests pick, or a cook chops it at the block; sweet tea, beer and soft drinks alongside.
text.today: Held year-round in a mild climate; cookers are rented by the weekend across the Coastal Plain, the tailgate pickin' is a college-football fixture, and Kingstree's festival and ECU's Pigskin Pig-Out put it on a calendar.

facets.when: election years; the weeks before a vote

text.what: The free feed a candidate or a party puts on to draw a crowd: a whole hog, or these days a pile of pork butts, cooked for whoever comes, with speeches or a rope line attached. It is as old as the republic in the Carolinas — the communal whole-hog barbecue fed political rallies in the colonial Carolinas and Virginia — and it has two living forms. In South Carolina the Galivants Ferry Stump Meeting in Horry County has gathered Democratic candidates on the Holliday family's land every second spring since 1880, descended from Wade Hampton's 1876 appearance there. In North Carolina the Mallard Creek church barbecue in Charlotte was the candidates' October stop from 1929 to 2024.
text.story: Robert Moss finds the political barbecue an institution of the early republic and the whole-hog rally established in the colonies by the 1700s. In North Carolina the tradition runs through the pig pickin' — local parties and politicians still use one to draw people to meetings and rallies — and its cost is recorded in one sentence from 1983, when Rufus Edmisten, running for governor, was overheard saying he had eaten enough barbecue and was not going to eat any more. In South Carolina the form is the stump meeting. Wade Hampton, the Confederate general running for governor, spoke at Galivants Ferry in 1876 and was elected that year; in 1880 Joseph William Holliday, merchant and tobacco farmer, invited the county's Democratic candidates to speak at his store, and the meeting has been held there in the spring of every second year since, carried on by the Hollidays and grown into a statewide event with national candidates — the longest-running Democratic campaign-speech site in the country, by the county's marker and the community's own account; by 2004 it counted 128 years. *Tradition holds —* chicken bog and barbecue are the food of the day. Mallard Creek's Presbyterians did not plan a political stop; they planned to pay off a Sunday-school building in 1929, and the candidates came to the crowd. By 2015 the crowd was 20,000 and the guests had included a former vice-president; the church retired the barbecue in 2025. The Lexington Barbecue Festival's politics — two bills in 2006 to make it the state's official festival, defeated by the east, and a regional title in 2007 — are the same appetite turned on the food itself.
text.how: A hog or a pile of butts is cooked by a church, a club or a hired pit; the candidate pays, or the host does; plates are free or cheap; the speaking is from a stump, a flatbed or a stage, or there is no speaking at all and the candidates walk a rope line with fliers. The date is the calendar's: spring of an election year at Galivants Ferry, the fourth Thursday of October at Mallard Creek.
text.today: Galivants Ferry continues on its two-year cycle; Mallard Creek ended in 2025; the pig pickin' rally goes on wherever a county party has a cooker.
