names.name: barbecue
names.said: In the Carolinas the word is a noun for the cooked pork: you eat barbecue, you do not 'have a barbecue'. The grill in the yard is a grill; cooking on it is grilling.

etymology.root: Taíno (Arawakan) barbacoa, a framework of sticks set on posts → Spanish barbacoa (1526, Oviedo) → English barbecue (1660s: the frame and the method; the cooked animal and the gathering by the 1700s)
etymology.first_attested: English 1661, Edmund Hickeringill's Jamaica Viewed ('Barbacu'd'), per the OED as quoted in the Wikipedia article; 'barbecado' in 1648; as a noun 1697, William Dampier. Spanish barbacoa printed by Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo, 1526.
etymology.note: The folk etymology from French barbe à queue ('beard to tail', i.e. the whole animal) is a joke first printed in the eighteenth century and has no standing; the Taíno origin is the dictionary etymology. Spellings with -que and Bar-B-Q are twentieth-century sign-painting and are as common on Carolina signs as the dictionary form.

text.what: The cooked meat itself — in the Carolinas, pork cooked slowly over coals or in a cooker and then chopped, pulled or sliced — and, by extension, the place that sells it and the gathering that eats it. Elsewhere in the country the same word means a grill, or a cookout of any meat; here the narrower sense is the ordinary one.
text.story: The word came north from the Caribbean with the Spanish and into English by way of the colonial Atlantic: a frame of sticks first, then the method, then the meat. Samuel Johnson's dictionary of 1755 already gives the Carolina sense — 'to barbecue: a term for dressing a whole hog', and the noun, 'a hog dressed whole'. *Tradition holds —* the whole-animal feast over wood coals was the shape of the colonial Southern gathering by the eighteenth century, and the political barbecue, a free feed put on by a candidate, was an institution of the early republic. *Inference —* the Carolina insistence that barbecue is a noun for pork is a memory of that feast: what was cooked at the rally was the pig, and the pig was what you came for.

kin.as: one of the two North Carolina answers to what the word means: the whole hog, chopped, with vinegar.
the other North Carolina answer: pork shoulder with a red dip.

names.name: Carolina Gold
names.said: 'Carolina Gold' on a sauce bottle in the Midlands means mustard; on a Charleston menu it means the rice under the shrimp. Both are South Carolina's, and neither knows the other.

etymology.root: Carolina + gold. For the rice, the colour of the unhulled grain (Wikipedia); for the sauce, the colour of yellow mustard and the brand name under which Maurice Bessinger's Piggie Park sold it (Wikipedia). Two coinages, one name, no common root but the state
etymology.first_attested: rice: 'first popularized in South Carolina in the 1780s' (Wikipedia); sauce: undated — Bessinger sold sauce under the Carolina Gold brand by the 1990s, and Wikipedia says the mustard sauce 'is sometimes called Carolina Gold'
etymology.note: A third thing wears the name: Riviana Foods sells a parboiled 'Carolina Gold' under its Carolina Rice brand with, Wikipedia says, no connection to the heirloom variety. *Inference —* the sauce borrowed a name the rice had made mean the state's own treasure, and its use for any yellow mustard sauce is a brand gone generic.

text.what: Two South Carolina things with one name. The sauce: the yellow-mustard barbecue sauce of the Midlands — mustard, vinegar, sugar and spices — which Wikipedia says is sometimes called Carolina Gold and which Maurice Bessinger of Piggie Park sold in supermarkets under that brand. The rice: an heirloom variety of Oryza sativa named for the gold of its unhulled grain, grown in the Lowcountry by enslaved people from the 1780s, the staple of Lowcountry cooking, last harvested commercially in 1927 and revived from a seed bank in the 1980s.
text.story: The rice came first. Carolina Gold was popularized in South Carolina in the 1780s; at the outset of the Civil War 3.5 million of the 5 million bushels of rice grown in the United States were Carolina Gold, grown in the Lowcountry by enslaved people. The last commercial crop was harvested in 1927. In the 1980s Richard and Patricia Schulze, restoring rice ponds at Hardeeville, found a stock in a USDA seed bank in Texas, planted 14 pounds and harvested 64; by 1988 they had 10,000 pounds a year, and Anson Mills and Carolina Plantation Rice sold it to the public from 1998. The sauce's name is younger. Mustard sauce belongs to the German-settled Midlands. Maurice Bessinger, who opened Maurice's Piggie Park in West Columbia with his brother Joe in 1953, sold a sauce of mustard, brown sugar, soy sauce and vinegar under the Carolina Gold brand and by 1999 had the largest barbecue operation in the country; in 2000, when he raised Confederate flags over his restaurants, grocery chains dropped the sauce from their shelves. *Inference —* Carolina Gold for any yellow mustard sauce is the brand gone generic, wearing a name the rice made first.

names.name: chopped
names.said: 'Chopped or sliced?' is the question at a Lexington counter, and 'coarse chopped' gets it in bigger pieces. In the east nobody asks: the whole hog is chopped, and fine.

etymology.root: chop (v.), mid-14c., 'to cut with a quick blow', of uncertain origin, perhaps Old North French choper or Old French couper 'to cut'; the noun 'a slice of mutton, lamb or pork' from the 1630s. Coarse chopped: the same, in larger pieces. Minced: Old French mincier 'to chop in little pieces', in English cooking from the late 14c. Sliced: the far pole — not chopped at all
etymology.first_attested: chop, verb, mid-14c. (etymonline); the counter sense is undated in the sources consulted
etymology.note: The three-word scale — chopped, coarse chopped, sliced — is a Lexington menu's, read on 15 September 2026 at Lexington Barbecue. NCpedia gives the eastern meat as 'boned, chopped, or shredded' and the western as 'chopped or sliced pork shoulders or butts'.

text.what: The way most Carolina barbecue reaches the tray: cooked meat cut across on a block with cleavers — in the east fine enough to hold the thin vinegar sauce, in the Piedmont in larger pieces. At a Lexington counter it is an ordering word with a scale, chopped, coarse chopped, sliced, and each is a different plate from the same shoulder. 'Sliced' is the far end, the shoulder cut into slabs and not chopped at all. A whole hog is chopped all together, skin included, so that every tray gets every part.
text.story: Chop is a Middle English verb of uncertain parentage, and by the 1630s a chop was a slice of pork. The barbecue sense grows out of the whole hog: once the meat comes off the bones it goes to the block, and the food writers Jane and Michael Stern called the sound of cleavers on it among the most alluring things about Carolina whole hog. NCpedia gives the eastern meat as 'boned, chopped, or shredded' and the western as 'chopped or sliced pork shoulders or butts'; the Wikipedia article has the east chopping after the meat is pulled from the bone, for a finer texture that holds the thin sauce, and Lexington serving 'pulled' or very lightly chopped, leaving strands. Melton's in Rocky Mount chopped whole hog so fine that a 1988 magazine compared it to chopped peanut butter. At Lexington Barbecue the menu on 15 September 2026 reads Chopped BBQ, Coarse Chopped BBQ and Sliced BBQ, on plate, tray or sandwich, a chopped plate at $13.40 cash. *Tradition holds —* some eastern pits call their finest chop minced. *Inference —* the scale exists at Lexington because a shoulder can be sliced to order and a whole hog cannot.

names.name: dip
names.said: 'Dip' is what a Lexington pit calls the reddish sauce on its table; the same bottle dresses the red slaw. Say 'barbecue sauce' there and you are from somewhere else.

etymology.root: dip (v.), Old English dyppan 'to plunge, immerse', from Proto-Germanic *daupejanan, a causative of *deup- 'deep'; the noun 'act of dipping' 1590s, 'liquid into which something is to be dipped' 1825; also in the 19th century 'a sweet sauce for pudding' and 'the juices and fat left after cooking meat'; the party dip of 1962 is, etymonline says, probably a re-coinage
etymology.first_attested: noun, 'liquid into which something is dipped': 1825 (etymonline); the Lexington sense is undated in the sources consulted
etymology.note: NCpedia's explanation of the name is service: the thin tomato sauce is served at table because sauce on meat over an open fire is a hazard, so the meat is dipped after. *Inference —* the nineteenth-century sense 'juices and fat left after cooking meat' fits a sauce that began as drippings, vinegar and pepper before ketchup was cheap.

text.what: The Lexington word for its sauce: vinegar, water, ketchup or tomato, salt, black and red pepper, sugar to taste — thin enough to pour, reddish rather than red. It goes on the chopped shoulder at the counter, sits on the table in a bottle, and is the dressing of the red slaw. Each pit's recipe is its own and, the town's own article says, closely guarded; the taste runs from tangy to slightly sweet or spicy. The eastern sauce is the same idea without the tomato, and is not called dip.
text.story: Dip is Old English dyppan, to plunge, kin to deep. The Online Etymology Dictionary dates the noun for a liquid you dip something into to 1825, and records a nineteenth-century kitchen sense: the juices and fat left in the pan after cooking meat. NCpedia explains the Lexington name by service — the thin tomato sauce is served at the table, because sauce on meat over an open fire is a hazard, so the meat is dipped after cooking. *Inference —* the pan-juice sense fits as well: the first Piedmont dips were drippings, vinegar and pepper, and the Wikipedia article on barbecue sauce has the early homemade sauces as vinegar, salt and pepper, with ketchup and sugar arriving in the 1920s. The Wikipedia article on Lexington says the shoulder is basted in a sauce 'called dip locally' of vinegar, ketchup, water, salt and pepper; the North Carolina Barbecue Society's page has red slaw made with the barbecue sauce 'locally called dip' in place of mayonnaise. *Tradition holds —* the recipe line runs from the tent pits on the Lexington courthouse square in the 1910s to Warner Stamey and the pits his cooks opened.

the Lexington cook whose dip, *tradition holds*, is the ancestor of most of the others.

A dip pours and is tart; a heavy tomato sauce clings and is sweet. Dip is a Piedmont word; nobody calls the thick sauce a dip.

names.name: Down East
names.said: 'Down East' in North Carolina is where the whole hog is; a Raleigh eater 'goes Down East for barbecue'. On the coast the phrase narrows to the fishing villages east of Beaufort.

etymology.root: down + east, a sailing direction. Along the New England coast the summer wind is south-westerly, so a ship bound east from Boston runs downwind, and Maine was Down East (Wiktionary; Wikipedia). In North Carolina the same phrase names the coastal communities east of Beaufort in Carteret County and, broadened, the eastern part of the state (Wikipedia)
etymology.first_attested: 1817, nautical, for the New England sense (Wiktionary); 1810–20, an Americanism (dictionary.com); the North Carolina sense is undated in the sources consulted
etymology.note: *Inference —* the North Carolina phrase is the same logic on another coast: rivers and roads run down to the sea, and east is where the sea is. No source consulted derives it from the Maine phrase, and none needs to.

text.what: In North Carolina, the coastal plain east of Raleigh — the barbecue east, where the hog is cooked whole and the sauce has no tomato; eastern North Carolina barbecue is also called Down East barbecue. The narrow sense is the string of fishing communities east of Beaufort in Carteret County — Bettie, Otway, Straits, Harkers Island, Gloucester, Marshallberg, out to Cedar Island — and Wikipedia says the phrase has broadened to mean eastern North Carolina generally, the central coastal plain of Greenville, Goldsboro, Kinston, New Bern, Rocky Mount, Tarboro, Washington and Wilson.
text.story: The phrase is New England's first: a ship from Boston bound for Maine ran before the south-west wind, so Maine was down east, and the term is on record from 1817. North Carolina has its own. To Carteret County, Down East is the villages east of Beaufort, where the accent is the coastal 'High Tider' brogue; to Raleigh and the Piedmont the same words cover the whole coastal plain, and the towns Wikipedia lists for that broader sense are the barbecue towns — Rocky Mount, where Bob Melton opened the state's first sit-down barbecue restaurant in 1924; Wilson, where Ed Mitchell grew up; Greenville, with Ayden and the Skylight Inn just south. In the 1980s newspaper war over what barbecue meant, Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer spoke for the east and Jerry Bledsoe of Greensboro for Lexington. *Tradition holds —* in barbecue talk Down East means whole hog and vinegar, and where it begins is argued; the fall line east of Raleigh is the usual answer. *Inference —* down is the way the rivers run — Neuse, Tar, Roanoke — and east is where they go; the Carolina phrase needs no ship.

names.name: Dutch Fork
names.said: The Dutch Fork is the wedge between the Saluda and the Broad above Columbia; a mustard-sauce pit in Newberry County is in it, and the 'Dutch' are Germans.

etymology.root: Dutch, in its older English sense 'German': from the late 14th century Dutch meant German and the non-Scandinavian continental Germanic peoples generally, from Middle Dutch duutsch, cognate with German deutsch, from Proto-Germanic *theudo 'of the people'; the sense narrowed to the Netherlands around 1600 in England, but in America the older sense lasted, as in Pennsylvania Dutch (etymonline) + fork, Old English forca from Latin furca, of rivers from 1753 (etymonline): the land between the Saluda and the Broad, which join to form the Congaree at Columbia
etymology.first_attested: the name is undated in the sources consulted; the settlement it names began between 1730 and 1766 (Wikipedia) or in the 1740s (South Carolina Encyclopedia)
etymology.note: The South Carolina Encyclopedia gives the name as 'Dutch Fork for deutsch Volk (German people)'; Wikipedia gives Dutch as an anglicization of deutsch. Nobody from the Netherlands is involved — the Dutch of slaw, koolsla, is the other Dutch.

text.what: The land between the Saluda and the Broad rivers above their meeting at Columbia, in Lexington, Newberry and Richland counties, settled by German-speaking Protestants in the middle of the eighteenth century and named for them, Dutch for deutsch. It is the upstream end of the mustard belt: the yellow mustard barbecue sauce of the Midlands is linked to the German families who settled between Orangeburg County and Newberry County, and the Fork is the Newberry end of that line. Lutheran churches, place names and family names are what remains of the German; the dialect is gone.
text.story: The British colony offered incentives to foreign Protestants to settle its backcountry, and between 1730 and 1766 German-speaking families took up the fork of the Saluda and the Broad; the South Carolina Encyclopedia dates the first European settlement to the 1740s and says German language and culture lasted in the Fork's isolation into the early twentieth century. The name is English for what the settlers called themselves. Their mark on the plate is mustard. Wikipedia says South Carolina's mustard sauce may have originated with the French and German immigrants of the eighteenth century and is linked to a 'Mustard Belt' from Orangeburg County to Newberry County where Germans settled; the Dukes family of Orangeburg County, of German origin, is the example historians give; and mustard goes into the hash of the German Midlands. Newberry is still the only South Carolina county more than a tenth Lutheran. *Inference —* the Fork is not the whole belt but its upstream end; Orangeburg, the other end, lies south of the Congaree and outside it. *Tradition holds —* the Dutch Fork is claimed as the birthplace of mustard sauce; no document in the sources consulted places the first pot.

names.name: fixins
names.said: 'A plate with all the fixins' — the slaw, the hushpuppies, the potatoes, the tea. Said with no g, and spelled on Carolina menus as said.

etymology.root: fix (v.), late 14c., from Old French fixer, Latin fixus 'fastened' → fixing, verbal noun, 'act of putting in order', c. 1600 → fixings, American English, 'apparatus' 1820, 'food, garnishing' 1839 (etymonline); spelled fixin's or fixins for the g that Southern speech drops
etymology.first_attested: 1839, American English, in the food sense (etymonline)
etymology.note: Wiktionary: the necessary ingredients for something, especially food, and the side dishes or accompaniments — 'a sandwich with all the fixings'. The apostrophe marks the missing g; the spelling without one marks that nobody misses it.

text.what: The sides and trimmings that come with the meat: slaw, hushpuppies or cornbread, boiled potatoes in the east, hash and rice in South Carolina, pickles, sweet tea. 'Fixings' is American English of 1839 for the garnishing of a meal; fixins is how it is said and, on Carolina signs and menus, how it is spelled. Beth Tartan wrote of a Raleigh hostess telephoning Melton's — 'Ride me a party' — and Melton's putting barbecue and fixings on the bus to her.
text.story: Fix is a verb that does a great deal of work in the South, and its noun did the same: fixings, first the apparatus of a thing, in 1820, then by 1839 the food that goes round the main thing. The barbecue plate is the word's natural home because the meat is one thing and the rest is a list. The Skylight Inn tray is barbecue, slaw and cornbread; Melton's plate in 1929 was barbecue with boiled potatoes for 45 cents, and in 1988 came with coleslaw, hushpuppies and Brunswick stew; a pig pickin' is eaten with hushpuppies, coleslaw, baked beans or Brunswick stew, and in South Carolina with hash over rice or pilaf; the Dukes buffets run to collard greens, macaroni and cheese, black-eyed peas, hushpuppies, corn nuggets, potato salad, coleslaw and white bread. The spelling is the speech: a menu that prints fixin's is telling you how the owner talks. *Inference —* the word keeps the order of the plate — barbecue is the noun, and everything else is fixins.

names.name: hog
names.said: A Carolina pit cooks a hog, not a pig — 'we cook whole hog', 'a hundred-and-twenty-pound hog' — and gives its size in dressed weight, the carcass with the innards out.

etymology.root: Old English hogg, implied in the late-12th-century hogaster and written hogge by the mid-14th century; origin uncertain — a Celtic source (Welsh hwch, Cornish hogh 'swine') is proposed, and the OED, quoted by etymonline, calls it improbable. The original sense was age, not species: a castrated male, or a swine reared for slaughter at about a year old; stockmen also said it of yearling sheep and horses
etymology.first_attested: before 1100 (dictionary.com); hogaster late 12c., hogge mid-14c. (etymonline); 'go the whole hog' 1828, American English (etymonline)
etymology.note: Whole hog, 1828, is explained two ways in the Online Etymology Dictionary: the butcher's offer of the whole slaughtered animal at a discount rather than the choice bits, or — the entry leans this way — an allegory, in English from 1779 and in a poem by Cowper, of Muslim sophists who argued away the ban on pork one part at a time until the whole hog was exempt. Wiktionary's derivation from Old Norse hǫggva 'to cut', making the hog 'the cut one', is not in the Online Etymology Dictionary and is given here as folk.

text.what: In Carolina barbecue speech the animal is a hog. Whole hog is the eastern North Carolina and Pee Dee style; a hog killing is the winter work of the farm; a hog's size is its dressed weight. American dictionaries make a hog a domesticated swine of 120 pounds or more raised for market and a pig the younger, smaller animal; the pit's small hogs of 80 to 120 pounds dressed sit at the bottom of that range. The pig pickin' hog is a barrow, a castrated male, or a gilt, a young female — boars and sows are too big.
text.story: Hog is older than pig for the grown animal. Old English hogg meant a swine of a certain age — a castrated male, or one reared for slaughter at about a year; pig, until the fourteenth century, meant a young one. Dressed weight is the pit's unit: the weight after the organs, head and inedible parts are removed, about 72 per cent of live weight for a pig by Wikipedia's example. A pig pickin' hog is 80 to 120 pounds dressed; elsewhere hogs run to 300 pounds, but in the Carolinas small hogs cooked hot so the skin crisps and can be chopped in. Hog killing was the farm's winter work: NCpedia describes it beginning on the first frigid day of autumn or winter, neighbours gathering before dawn, as many as 100 hogs penned and fattened on gleaned peas, potatoes and corn, and the weeks after full of spare ribs, liver and sausage, the hams a month or two later. *Tradition holds —* the barbecue was what a hog killing or a church homecoming did with fresh meat before curing. 'Go the whole hog', American English of 1828, is the same animal as a figure of speech.

names.name: light bread
names.said: 'Light bread' is the store loaf or the soft bun, said against cornbread and biscuits; a sandwich is barbecue and slaw on light bread.

etymology.root: light (adj.), Old English leoht 'not heavy', from Proto-Germanic *lingkhtaz — of bread, risen with yeast, against the dense pone and quick breads of cornmeal — + bread. Midland and Southern American English for white bread, or any bread leavened with yeast (dictionary.com); 'Southern US: white bread' (Wiktionary)
etymology.first_attested: 1815–25 (dictionary.com)
etymology.note: The name is about leavening, not colour: the loaf is light because yeast lifts it. Cornbread was the South's daily bread because wheat withered and turned rancid in its heat and humidity (Wikipedia). *Inference —* wheat bread was the bought, occasional loaf, and the name marks it as the exception.

text.what: The Southern name for white yeast bread — a store loaf or a soft bun — as against cornbread, biscuits and pone, a dense cornmeal cake. On a Carolina barbecue tray it is what the sandwich is built on: chopped barbecue and slaw on a soft white bun. At the Skylight Inn the sandwich is on a white roll; Dukes buffets in South Carolina set out white bread beside the hash. Dictionary.com labels the term Midland and Southern U.S., and defines it as white bread or any bread leavened with yeast.
text.story: The word is old on the farm and young on the menu. Dictionary.com dates light bread to 1815–25; it is light in the baker's sense, risen with yeast, against the heavy cornmeal breads that fed the South because wheat would not keep in its heat. The barbecue sandwich is a twentieth-century form — Wikipedia says the tradition of whole hog as a sandwich filling began in the 1900s, and Melton's in Rocky Mount sold a barbecue sandwich for 15 cents in 1929 — and the bread it needed was the soft white bun that machine-sliced loaves made ordinary from the 1920s. The bun is never the point: Wikipedia's barbecue-sandwich article says the bread keeps the meat from drying and holds its heat, and in the east the slaw goes on the bun. *Tradition holds —* the tray, barbecue and slaw without bread, is the order for people who do not want the light bread at all; hushpuppies and cornsticks are the tray's bread and light bread the sandwich's. NCpedia's sides are baked corn sticks and fried hush puppies.

names.name: Pee Dee
names.said: 'The Pee Dee' is the river and the corner of South Carolina it drains — Florence, Marion, Kingstree, Hemingway; in barbecue it means whole hog with a thin, hot vinegar-and-pepper sauce.

etymology.root: from the Pee Dee (Pedee) people, an Indigenous nation of the South Carolina Piedmont and the river valley; the river took their name and the region took the river's. Their language was never recorded and the name's meaning is unknown
etymology.note: The anthropologist Frank Speck suggested Catawban words meaning 'something good' or 'smart, capable'; a story that a trader named Patrick Daley carved 'P.D.' on trees is folk etymology without scholarly support (Wikipedia). Spellings: Pedee, Peedee, Peadea, Pidee.

text.what: The river and the region. The Pee Dee rises in the North Carolina mountains as the Yadkin, takes the name Pee Dee below the mouth of the Uwharrie, crosses into South Carolina and reaches the sea at Winyah Bay. The region is the state's north-east corner — Chesterfield, Darlington, Dillon, Florence, Marlboro and Marion counties always, Horry, Georgetown and Williamsburg usually. Its barbecue is whole hog over hardwood coals, sometimes skinned first with the skin fried, and a sauce of vinegar, salt and pepper that Wikipedia calls virtually identical to eastern North Carolina's.
text.story: The people gave the river its name and the river gave it to the land. The Pedee were a Southeastern Woodlands people of the South Carolina Piedmont and the river valley, part of the South Appalachian Mississippian culture — the mound-building culture of the Southeast, about 1000 to 1500 — and numbered about 600 in 1600; their language was never written down, and the name's meaning is a guess. Four state-recognized tribes claim their descent. Its barbecue is the whole hog. The South Carolina Encyclopedia gives the Pee Dee sauce as 'watery thin and fiery hot pepper and vinegar concoctions'; the Wikipedia article on South Carolina barbecue calls the vinegar sauce heavily based on Native American basting sauces, a claim it makes without a document behind it. Scott's Variety Store and Bar-B-Q opened in Hemingway in 1972 and became known for whole-hog platters; Rodney Scott grew up at its pit and took the Pee Dee hog to Charleston in 2017. Kingstree holds a Pig Pickin' festival every fall for Williamsburg County's vinegar barbecue. *Inference —* the Pee Dee and Down East are one barbecue country cut by a state line.

names.name: Piedmont
names.said: In North Carolina barbecue talk 'Piedmont style' is Lexington style — shoulders and a red dip — and a Piedmont pit is west of Raleigh. South Carolina calls its Piedmont the Upstate, and once called it the Upcountry.

etymology.root: Italian Piemonte, from medieval Latin Pedemontium, ad pedem montium, 'at the foot of the mountains' — Latin pes, pedis 'foot' + mons, montis 'mountain' — the region below the Alps, in documents from the end of the twelfth century (Wikipedia); through French Piémont; applied to the American plateau at the foot of the Appalachians as piemont in 1755, with the d by 1855, and extended to the foot of other ranges by 1860 (etymonline)
etymology.first_attested: American sense 1755, as piemont (etymonline); Pedemontium, late twelfth century (Wikipedia)
etymology.note: The Piedmont Triad — Greensboro, Winston-Salem, High Point — is the region whose 'Official Food Festival' the legislature made the Lexington Barbecue Festival in 2007, a way of not naming a state barbecue.

text.what: The plateau between the coastal plain and the Blue Ridge, from New York to Alabama and nearly 300 miles wide in North Carolina; its eastern edge is the fall line, where rivers drop off hard rock onto the soft plain and towns grew at the head of navigation. In North Carolina barbecue, Piedmont style is Lexington style — pork shoulder, a red vinegar-and-ketchup dip, red slaw — and 'Western' means the same. In South Carolina the Piedmont is the Upstate, Greenville, Spartanburg and Anderson, where the sauce is a thin ketchup and vinegar and the hash is pork and beef.
text.story: Piemonte is the foot of the Alps, named in Latin documents by 1200; English took it through French and in 1755 applied piemont to the country at the foot of the Appalachians, adding the d by 1855. The fall line is where the name earns itself: the Piedmont's rivers leave the hard rock in a line of rapids, and the Congaree forms at Columbia on it. Wikipedia calls Lexington style 'Piedmont- or Western-style', most common in the Piedmont and west, pork shoulder only, with a red dip and red slaw; the South Carolina Encyclopedia has shoulders, hams and Boston butts in the Piedmont against the whole hog of the coastal plain. Lexington, 20 miles south of Winston-Salem in the Piedmont Triad, calls itself the Barbecue Capital of the World, and in 2007 the legislature made its festival the Official Food Festival of the Piedmont Triad Region. South Carolina's Upstate takes a light tomato sauce that Wikipedia attributes to North Carolina's influence, and its hash is beef and pork with onions. *Inference —* the Piedmont cooks the shoulder because a shoulder is what a town butcher sells; the whole hog stayed with the farm.

names.name: pit
names.said: 'The pit' is the brick or block box the coals go in, the room it sits in, and often the whole business: 'out back at the pit', 'the pit opens at ten'.

etymology.root: Old English pytt 'a hole in the ground, water hole, well, grave', a Germanic borrowing of Latin puteus 'well, pit, shaft'; the barbecue sense keeps the hole's name after the hole has become a box of brick or cinder block above ground, and then a gas cooker inside a building
etymology.first_attested: Old English (etymonline); the barbecue-pit sense is undated in the dictionaries consulted — Wiktionary lists two dozen senses of pit and none for barbecue
etymology.note: Wikipedia's article on pit barbecue says the word is applied across the 'barbecue belt' to an enclosed, above-ground pit; NCpedia says few commercial barbecue pits today are dug in the ground.

text.what: The place the cooking happens. First a trench in the ground filled with hardwood coals, the split hog on a rack above; then a wide, shallow container of cinder block, brick or steel above ground, still a pit; then, at many places, a gas cooker, still the pit. The word also names the room, the building — a pit house — and the restaurant, as in Backyard BBQ Pit or Dickey's Barbecue Pit. A smokehouse is a different building: a windowless outbuilding where hams and bacon are cured in cold smoke for weeks, not a place a meal is cooked.
text.story: Pit is a Germanic borrowing of Latin puteus, a well; in Old English a hole, a well, a grave and hell. The barbecue pit was that hole: Wikipedia's article on pit barbecue describes meat cooked buried below ground, an earth-oven practice of Indigenous peoples. The whole-hog article has the pit dug into the earth or built above it as a wide, shallow container, usually of cinder blocks, filled with charcoal burned down from wood in a fireplace or a burn barrel; the South Carolina Encyclopedia gives the traditional pit as an open pit fuelled by hardwood coals in a rectangular cement-block structure, the meat suspended above. NCpedia says few commercial pits today are dug in the ground; the whole-hog article says new restaurants mostly use gas-fired pits and many older ones have switched. At the Skylight Inn the pit crew makes its charcoal from oak and hickory logs in fireplaces beside the pits. names.name: pitmaster
names.said: Press and menus say pitmaster. Older Carolina speech says the cook, or the pit man, or the man's name — a cook forty years at the pit is called by his first name before either.

etymology.root: pit (Old English pytt, the cooking pit) + master (Old English, from Latin magister 'chief, teacher'; 'a workman qualified to carry on a trade on his own account' from c. 1300), on the pattern of quartermaster and the other -master compounds for the person in charge of a thing
etymology.first_attested: 'pit master', of a barbecue cook: 22 September 1939, Daily Times-News, Burlington, North Carolina — 'Jeter Crutchfield, pit master, will supervise the beginning of roasting pork for the barbecue tonight at midnight' — as quoted by Texas Monthly (2018) and Destination BBQ (2021); the one-word form 1980–85 (dictionary.com)
etymology.note: The compound had other lives first: an English coal-mining word in the nineteenth century, a sportswriter's word for boxing referees in the 1920s, and in the 1970s a label for snake wranglers and a cockfight ringleader (Texas Monthly). Wiktionary carries no citation; the OED was not consulted. Destination BBQ notes that Crutchfield was white and that the verb is supervise: the cooking that night was done by Black men.

text.what: The person who runs the pit — the fire, the coals, the turning of the hog, the call that it is done. A recent word for an old job. Wiktionary defines it as one who operates a barbecue pit and adds that it is used as a term of respect; dictionary.com dates it 1980–85; Wikipedia titles its articles 'Ed Mitchell (pitmaster)' and 'Rodney Scott (pitmaster)', and BBQ Pitmasters has been on cable since 2009. In the Carolinas the older words are the cook and the pit man, and a place is known by a family's name before any title.
text.story: Pit is the hole and master is Latin magister, the chief; the compound follows quartermaster. Texas Monthly traced 'pit master' through unrelated trades and found the earliest barbecue use it could in a 1939 North Carolina newspaper item: 'Jeter Crutchfield, pit master, will supervise the beginning of roasting pork for the barbecue tonight at midnight.' Destination BBQ gives the paper as the Burlington Daily Times-News of 22 September 1939 and points at the verb: Crutchfield supervised, and the men at the pit that night were Black. Adrian Miller's Black Smoke traces the history of those cooks — Black barbecuers, pitmasters and restaurateurs — and their place in the tradition. Dictionary.com dates the one-word pitmaster to 1980–85; the television series BBQ Pitmasters premiered on TLC on 3 December 2009. Rodney Scott of Hemingway, named Best Chef Southeast by the James Beard Foundation in 2018, was only the second pitmaster to win a Beard chef award. *Inference —* the word arrived with the audience: once barbecue was written about, the cook needed a title a writer could print. *Tradition holds —* in the Carolinas he still answers to his name.

names.name: pulled pork
names.said: In the Carolinas the meat is barbecue and the counter asks 'chopped or sliced?'; 'pulled pork' is what the same meat is called on a menu written for people from somewhere else, and on the Carolina menus that are.

etymology.root: pull (v.), Old English pullian 'to pluck off (wool), to draw out', of uncertain origin + pork (n.), c. 1300, Old French porc 'pig', Latin porcus; the participle names how the cooked meat leaves the bone — pulled apart, not cut
etymology.note: No dictionary consulted dates the compound: Wiktionary defines it without a citation, and the etymologies here are of the two words. The cut it assumes, the Boston butt, is the upper shoulder, named for the barrels, called butts, that New England butchers packed pork in; the name is in print by 1915 (Wikipedia).

text.what: Pork cooked slowly over coals or in a cooker until it comes off the bone in strands, then taken apart by hand or with forks rather than cut. Outside the Carolinas it is the name of the dish, and the dish is a shoulder — the Boston butt, the upper shoulder, is the cut it almost always means. Inside the Carolinas the meat is called barbecue, and 'pulled' is one answer, with 'chopped' and 'sliced', to how you want it: Memphis pulls by hand; the North Carolina east chops fine; Lexington serves it pulled or lightly chopped, leaving strands.
text.story: Pull is Old English pullian, to pluck off or draw out, and pork came in from Old French porc after 1300. Together they name a texture: meat cooked until its connective tissue gives way, which the Wikipedia article puts at an internal temperature of 195 to 205 °F, and taken apart along the grain. The cut the phrase assumes is the shoulder, and the shoulder's upper half is the Boston butt, named for the New England barrels, called butts, that pork was packed in; the name is in print by 1915. The Carolinas had the thing before the phrase. The east chopped its whole hog with cleavers; Lexington chopped or sliced its shoulders; Memphis built its sandwich on shoulder pulled by hand, not chopped with a blade. Ed Mitchell of Wilson builds a pulled pork sandwich from a whole hog, shoulder, ham and belly together; the Dukes restaurants of Orangeburg list pulled pork on the buffet; the South Carolina mustard sandwich is described as pulled pork. *Inference —* a Carolina menu that says pulled pork is speaking to the road; one that says barbecue is speaking to the county. No source consulted dates the compound.

names.name: slaw
names.said: 'Slaw', never 'coleslaw', on a Carolina tray; a Lexington sandwich comes 'with slaw', and the slaw is red.

etymology.root: Dutch koolsla 'cabbage salad' — kool 'cabbage' (from Latin caulis) + sla, clipped from salade (from French) — → American English cole slaw, 1794, heard and written as 'cold slaw' → slaw, the back half alone, by the 1860s
etymology.first_attested: cole slaw 1794 — 'A piece of sliced cabbage, by Dutchmen ycleped cold slaw' (etymonline); slaw alone 1860–65 (dictionary.com), about 1861 (Wiktionary)
etymology.note: 'Cold slaw' is a folk etymology, Dutch kool heard as English cold; it held until the 1860s, when cole was revived (etymonline). Wiktionary's definition of coleslaw now splits it into white slaw, dressed with mayonnaise, and red slaw, dressed with vinaigrette — the Carolina split written into the dictionary.

text.what: Shredded raw cabbage, dressed and served cold, on every Carolina barbecue tray and most sandwiches. East of Raleigh the dressing is mayonnaise or whipped salad dressing and the slaw is white or yellow; in Lexington it is vinegar, ketchup and pepper — the dip — and the slaw is red, also called barbecue slaw. South Carolina buffets list coleslaw among the sides. The word is the back half of coleslaw, and the front half is not said; coleslaw came to the colonies with the Dutch settlers of New York.
text.story: Dutch koolsla, cabbage salad, was written down in American English in 1794 as 'cold slaw', the Dutch kool heard as the English cold; the folk spelling lasted until the 1860s, when cole came back, and by then the back half had come loose and slaw stood alone. Dutch colonists brought coleslaw to the Thirteen Colonies. Jerry Bledsoe, the Greensboro columnist of the 1980s barbecue war, wrote in 1996 that barbecue is always served with slaw in North Carolina and always has been. The split is by region. The Wikipedia article on coleslaw calls North Carolina slaw fine and vinegary and says that around Lexington red slaw is made with ketchup and vinegar rather than mayonnaise and is the prevailing kind, unlike the rest of the state; NCpedia has white or yellow coleslaw in the east and red coleslaw, 'barbecue slaw', coloured with ketchup or dip, in the Piedmont. The Lexington sandwich's distinguishing feature, the town's article says, is its red slaw, and in the late 1990s Wendy's put red slaw on a 'Carolina Classic' burger. *Inference —* red slaw is the dip's second job, and a pit that makes one makes the other from the same pot.

text.what: Between about 1930 and 1945 an American restaurant could order its own postcards by the thousand. A printer took a photograph, had an artist colour it by hand, and ran it on paper with a woven texture — the linen card, whose surface takes bright ink and softens a plain building into something worth mailing. Roadside businesses on the highways through both Carolinas bought them and set them by the register. The caption on the back names the route number, because that is how a customer found the place again.

sections.h: Why a barbecue stand printed postcards
sections.text:
A linen card was cheap advertising that the customer paid to deliver. It carried the name, the highway, the distance from town and a picture of a building that was otherwise unremarkable, and somebody mailed it to Ohio.

The captions are the useful part. Barbecue Lodge, published by the Carolina News Company of Fayetteville and printed in the 1930s or 1940s, is the Carolina example in the Boston Public Library's Tichnor collection: a low red-brick building with a flat roof and a squat brick chimney, and along the parapet in illuminated letters BARBECUE LODGE, with a red strip beneath it reading AIR CONDITIONED · Charcoal STEAKS · PRIVATE DINING ROOMS. The neighbouring cards in the same file — Warren's Motel & Restaurant on U.S. 301 at Pleasant Hill, the White House Restaurant on U.S. 1 at Henderson, Clark's Restaurant at Santee on U.S. 301, 15 and 15A at the junction with S.C. 6 — show the pattern: the route number is doing the work a street address does now. These are highway businesses and the card is a map.

sections.h: Tichnor Brothers, and the Boston connection
sections.text:
Most of these were printed a long way from the Carolinas. Tichnor Brothers of Boston turned out linen postcards for the whole country, and the Boston Public Library holds around 25,000 of them, arranged by state and digitised. The library put the scans on Flickr under a licence that allows reuse with credit, which is why a project like this one can print a 1940 North Carolina motor-court card without asking anyone.

*Inference —* the distance shows. A Boston artist colouring a Fayetteville barbecue lodge from a black-and-white photograph is guessing at the paint, and the skies in these cards are all the same blue. What is reliable in them is the architecture, the signage and the caption; the colour is decoration.

sections.h: What the Carolina cards do not show
sections.text:
Pits, mostly. The card is a picture of a front elevation with cars parked at it, because that is what the owner wanted photographed: a clean building on a numbered highway, not a cinder-block cookhouse out the back with smoke coming out of it.

A reader looking for barbecue in this file finds it in the lettering. Barbecue Lodge says so on its face. Elsewhere the word turns up on a panel over a door, or on a board by the road at the edge of the frame, in a card that is nominally about a motel. *Tradition holds —* barbecue and lodging shared premises all along U.S. 301 and U.S. 1 through the eastern Carolinas in these years, because both were selling to the same car.

names.name: the pig that serves itself
names.said: Nobody who paints one calls it anything. It is just the pig.

text.what: A barbecue sign on which the pig is not the meat but the staff: a pig in a chef's toque carrying a covered tray, a pig in an apron at a pit, a pig in sunglasses eating a pork sandwich, a pig holding the restaurant's own name over its head. The animal about to be served is drawn recommending the meal, and the joke is never explained on the sign because it does not need to be. The form runs from nineteenth-century trade cards to lit plastic on a bypass, and both Carolinas are full of it.

sections.text:
Three arrangements cover most of them, and a reader can sort a sign from a moving car.

The pig is the cook. A toque — the tall white pleated chef's hat — an apron, sometimes a fork. Red Pig Drive-In at Nahunta, Georgia, photographed by John Margolies in 1979, is the neon version: a white pig in a toque, upright on two trotters, carrying a domed serving tray at shoulder height, the words RED PIG running down a red pylon beside it and DRIVE IN in neon along the base.

The pig is the customer. Carol Highsmith's photograph of the Pig on Beale sign in Memphis catches a neon pig in wraparound sunglasses with both trotters round a pork sandwich, mid-bite, under the line PORK WITH AN ATTITUDE!

The pig is the employee. Three Little Pigs Bar-B-Q in Memphis has a pig in blue dungarees holding the whole signboard over its head, and three more along the roofline each carrying one letter of BAR-B-Q. The pig here is not eating and not cooking. It is working for the business that sells it.

For five years a Seattle blogger collected these. Suicide Food ran from 20 December 2006 to 27 December 2011 and posted 929 times, most posts carrying several images. Its author signs himself Ben; the surname Grossblatt comes from a profile Lindy West wrote in The Stranger in November 2007, and appears nowhere in the blog itself.

The blog's own definition, from its header, is a depiction of animals that "act as though they wish to be consumed". Every entry got a rating on a five-point scale headed Psych Evaluations and counted in nooses, from one noose, mildly troubling, to five. The pig tag holds 539 posts and the bbq tag 399, which is the largest strand in the file by a wide margin; chef hat runs to 114 and sunglasses to 107. An eleven-part series across four years gave the recycled stock-clipart pig its own name: Repetitious Porcine Emblemology.

The blog is vegan advocacy and says so; the last post calls the project a pause rather than an ending. It is still online. This project uses it as what it is — the only systematic catalogue of the genre anyone has made — without taking up its argument.

The pig was doing this before electricity. Richard Sheaff, writing for the Ephemera Society of America, notes that American chromolithograph trade-card makers had a particular fondness for pigs on two legs, and singles out cards from J. S. & M. Peckham of Utica, New York — a firm that made agricultural furnaces and pig scalders — as apparently cannibalistic. The cards are not dated on that page, and Peckham was a nineteenth-century firm, so the genre is older than 1900 by an unfixed margin.

*Inference —* what the form solves is a drawing problem. A barbecue restaurant has to put an animal on its sign, because that is what it sells, and a dead pig does not sell lunch. Standing the pig up, dressing it and handing it a tray moves it out of the category of carcass and into the category of host. The sign painter is not making a point about slaughter. He is avoiding one.

The Carolina examples that are free to show are the ones a government camera happened to catch. Margolies photographed Maurice Bessinger's sign at West Columbia, South Carolina, in 1988: a pig called Little Joe in a red shirt, hands behind its back, standing on the crown of a BAR-B-Q sign over the words Flying Pig, Coast to Coast. The pit offices burned in October 2024 and the sign survived.

*Tradition holds —* the form is everywhere in both states, on plastic pylons, on painted plywood at a firehouse fundraiser, on a smoker trailer's door, and most of those pigs are the same few pieces of clip art bought by a sign shop and reused across a county. What is scarce is not the pigs but free photographs of them: most Carolina signs standing today are photographed under copyright, so this record leans on Georgia, Tennessee and one South Carolina survivor to show a form the Carolinas are thick with.

names.name: The FSA photographs of Carolina eating
aliases: Marion Post Wolcott in the Carolinas

text.what: The Farm Security Administration — a New Deal agency for rural poverty — kept photographers on the road from 1935, and their negatives went to the Library of Congress as federal work, free of copyright. Marion Post Wolcott worked North and South Carolina in 1939. What survives of Carolina eating is the occasion rather than the pit: a corn shucking at Tally Ho, near Stem in Granville County, North Carolina, with the tables that followed it; ministers and deacons at an outdoor picnic near Yanceyville; and a Fourth of July on St. Helena Island, South Carolina, shot on Kodachrome, which was new.

sections.text:
A corn shucking was a work party: neighbours came, shucked a farmer's crop, and were fed. Wolcott photographed one at Uncle Henry Garrett's place near Stem. The men sit on kitchen chairs in a chest-high drift of shucks with the crib behind them, hats on, working through the pile.

The agency's own caption sheet says who ate when, and the project reproduces its wording because the arrangement is the fact: 'White women don't go to Negro shucking to help with the cooking but white men are fed by Negro women just the same as at other shucking week previous at Mr. Fred Wilkins' home.' A second frame is captioned 'The Negro tenants and neighbors eating dinner after the white men have finished.' It shows a long white-clothed table, ten or twelve men at it, glasses and plates and a big enamel basin at the near end. Two sittings, in that order, at a meal the second sitting had cooked.

The FSA shot most of its work in black and white and a small part on Kodachrome, a colour film then a few years old. Wolcott's St. Helena Island Fourth of July is in that colour set, which is why these frames look nothing like the rest of the period.

Under pines hung with Spanish moss, a crowd stands around a cloth-covered table and a scatter of washtubs, pots and crates; one frame takes in a Texaco filling station behind the flag. The catalogue calls it a Fourth of July celebration and a Fourth of July picnic. It does not call it a barbecue.

sections.h: What is not in the file
sections.text:
No photograph in the Carolina part of this collection that reached Wikimedia Commons is captioned as a barbecue, and none shows a hog on a pit. The agency's photographers caught Carolina barbecue only in its surroundings: the work party, the church meeting, the holiday crowd, the table afterwards. Two frames from near Yanceyville in Caswell County are captioned as an outdoor picnic held during the noon intermission of an all-day meeting of ministers and deacons — the church dinner, mid-century, in a field.

*Inference —* that is a fact about the photographers' brief rather than about the food. The FSA sent people to document rural poverty and federal relief, so a camera went where a committee met or a crop came in. An all-night pit in a shed behind a store was nobody's assignment. The pictures that do exist of a Carolina hog on a pit come later, from restaurants and from towns, and are mostly still in copyright.

A caution on the captions: the descriptions carried with these files are the agency's, written in 1939, and they use the racial vocabulary of that year. They are quoted rather than rewritten so that what the file says and what the file shows can be read against each other.

names.name: the pig mascot
names.said: A place with a pig on it does not need to say what it sells.

text.what: One pig, drawn once, used everywhere a barbecue business puts its name: the sign, the menu, the sauce label, the takeout box, the trailer door, the roofline, the weather vane. It is standing, smiling and usually dressed. It has no job in the picture — it is neither cooking nor eating — and that is what separates it from the pig that serves itself. A mascot is an identity: a customer who sees a pig on a bottle in a grocery aisle is meant to think of a particular pit in a particular town.

sections.h: Little Joe, and what a mascot is for
sections.text:
Maurice Bessinger's pig is the clearest Carolina case because it was photographed under a public-domain licence. John Margolies shot the West Columbia sign in 1988: at the top of a tall pylon, above illuminated block letters reading BAR-B-Q, a pink pig stands on two trotters in a red shirt with LITTLE JOE across the chest, a small cap on its head, hands tucked behind its back. The panel beneath reads Maurice Bessinger's Flying Pig, Coast to Coast, and under that a changeable letterboard was advertising for waitresses on the day of the photograph.

Coast to Coast is the point. The same pig went on the Carolina Gold sauce bottles that by 1999 made this the largest barbecue operation in the country, which is how a pig painted for one drive-in in West Columbia ended up on shelves in states with no barbecue of their own. When grocery chains pulled the sauce in 2000 over the Confederate flags Bessinger raised at his restaurants, what came off the shelf was the pig.

sections.h: On a roof, and on a rod
sections.text:
The mascot does not stay on the sign. Wilber's Barbecue in Goldsboro put a pig on a weather vane, cut flat from sheet metal, turning above the roof of a restaurant that opened in 1962 — a running pig in silhouette, nose into the wind, with the four cardinal letters under it.

*Inference —* a weather vane is a particular choice. A sign faces the road and can be read only from one direction; a vane is visible from every direction and points nowhere in particular, so it says a building is here rather than pointing at a door. Putting the pig up there treats it less as advertising than as the thing on top of a church.

The form recurs: a fibreglass pig on a porch, a pig on a trailer, a pig outline in neon over an entrance. The animal ends up in the place a weathercock, a cross or a name would otherwise go.

*Tradition holds —* most house pigs are not commissioned. A sign shop keeps a book of pig artwork, a new pit buys one, the letters change and the pig does not, so a county can carry the same six or eight pigs across twenty businesses that have never met. The blog Suicide Food gave that recycling its own name across an eleven-part series: Repetitious Porcine Emblemology, the stock pig turning up again and again under different names.

A few are drawn once and stay drawn. Those are the ones that end up on a bottle, a T-shirt and a tattoo, and the ones people can describe from memory years after the restaurant closed.

names.name: Pigs in the City
names.said: Everybody in Lexington can name their favourite one.

text.what: Life-sized pig sculptures, painted by artists and set out on the sidewalks of Lexington, Davidson County. Uptown Lexington, Inc. — the non-profit set up to bring business back to the town centre — ran the first exhibition in 2003 with twenty pigs, each sponsored by a business for $1,000, which paid for the whole thing. More than 40,000 people came that first year. The pigs are fibreglass blanks, identical until the artist gets them, and they come back painted as anything: a fire engine, a bulldozer, a jigsaw puzzle, a winged horse. Retired ones stay out around town.

sections.text:
The form is borrowed. *Tradition holds —* the painted-animal street exhibition spread from the cow parades of the late 1990s, and each town that took it up picked an animal of its own. Lexington's animal chose itself: the town calls itself the Barbecue Capital of the World and has held a barbecue festival on Main Street every October since 1984.

The exhibitions ran 2003 to 2005, and again in 2008 and 2009. In 2019 Uptown Lexington announced the pigs would return in 2020. A sponsor paid $1,000 in the first round and got a pig with the sponsor's commission on it; the money covered the programme. What the town got was a reason to walk from one block to the next, which is what a downtown revitalisation programme is usually trying to buy.

The pigs are named, and the names are the point. Caterpiggar is a Caterpillar bulldozer: yellow, with an exhaust stack, a radiator grille, a dozer blade across the front, a model number P8 on the flank, and CATERPIGGAR lettered in the machine-maker's own typeface with its red underline. Fire Hog is a fire engine, red, with ladders down the side, the city fire department's crest on the shoulder and a black helmet over the snout. Pork Knox is money — banknotes and coins painted all over it, gold trotters, a bar chart along the back. Pigsaw is covered in jigsaw pieces. Pigasus is deep blue with gold wings, planets and stars. Newbee is banded teal and gold with gold antennae and a gauzy wing laid over its back. Deck the Halls is three small pigs in Santa hats and striped scarves around a signboard.

*Inference —* the naming is doing the same work as a barbecue restaurant's sign: it takes an animal that is about to be eaten and makes it a character with a job. The difference is that a Pigs in the City pig has no meat to sell, so the pun can be about anything at all, and usually is. None of these pigs is eating.

They do not go away. Dennis Brown photographed a set in 2008 and captioned them as previous entries now on display in various places in Lexington — a pig outside the business that sponsored it, a pig on a corner, a pig by a door. A visitor walking uptown meets pigs from several different years at once and cannot tell which round each came from without asking.

*Tradition holds —* the Barbecue Festival is when most people see them, because that is the Saturday the street is closed and everyone is walking. The festival brings its own inflatable and costumed pigs on top of the permanent ones.

names.name: Going the whole hog — the 1830s barbecue lithographs

text.what: A small group of American political prints from the 1830s in which the barbecue is the joke and the pig is the politician. A lithograph — a print pulled from a drawing made on stone, the cheap illustrated medium of the period — could be sold loose from a shop window within days of the news. H. R. Robinson of New York issued The Political Barbecue in 1834, laying Andrew Jackson on a grid iron over a brick pit lettered PUBLIC OPINION, with one bystander remarking that in South Carolina it is called barbecue. Others draw out the campaign phrase going the whole hog. They are the oldest barbecue pictures this project can show.

sections.h: What going the whole hog meant
sections.text:
The phrase was already a political term of art before the prints. To go the whole hog was to back a man or a measure entirely, without the hedging and half-support a faction could otherwise offer, and in the Jackson years it attached itself to the Democrats — a Whig could use it as an accusation of blind loyalty and a Democrat could use it as a boast, which is what makes it usable in a picture.

Both sides did use it. One of these sheets is not a cartoon at all but a ballot: a Democratic ticket for Martin Van Buren for President and Richard M. Johnson for Vice President, with the Ohio electors listed under them, and at the head a woodcut of a man in a tall hat carrying a hog across his shoulders. Two banners come off the hog. One reads Going the whole Hog. The other reads Pork 10 cts. p lb.

The pun sits on a real thing. A whole hog was what a barbecue actually cooked: the animal split and laid over coals, fed to a crowd assembled to hear a candidate. A print that draws a whole hog in an election year is making a joke and reporting a fact at once, and the audience had to be told neither half.

sections.h: Robinson's Jackson on the grid iron
sections.text:
The Political Barbecue, a lithograph on wove paper about 25.5 by 36.6 centimetres, was published by H. R. Robinson at 52 Courtlandt Street, New York, in 1834, and is held by the Library of Congress. Andrew Jackson lies stripped on a grid iron over a brick pit with two arched fireboxes, and the word lettered along the brickwork between them is PUBLIC OPINION. Justice stands at the left with her scales and a knife. Five men in tall hats lean over the body; two more crouch at the fireboxes working the coals.

The speech balloons are a survey of what the country called the thing. One man says that in Massachusetts they call it roasting; another that in Kentucky it is their High Game to their Low Jack. A third says: 'In South Carolina it is called Barbecue only he wants a little more Basting.' The sheet is a national joke that stops to name South Carolina as the place where the word lives.

A second treatment of the subject, undated but placed around 1832 to 1833, survives in the Digital Commonwealth from an unknown artist, captioned The political barbecue, Going the whole hog. Robinson's other sheet drops the fire altogether: Going the Whole Hog shows an enormous sow lying in a yard, a band across her shoulders reading THE EMPIRE STATE, and a litter of small pigs at her, each labelled with an office or a favour. A signpost points To Kinderhook, Van Buren's home village. Van Buren leans over the fence and says the sow and her litter have made him the greatest man in the Union; a farmer opposite, drawn with a Dutch accent, says the pigs will suck the life's blood out of that old sow.

sections.h: Why they sit in a Carolina catalogue
sections.text:
None of these prints is Carolinian. They are New York and Boston commercial lithographs about national politics. They belong here because the thing they are joking about is the Carolina and Virginia political barbecue: the free feed a candidate laid on to gather a crowd, which Robert Moss finds established in the colonies by the 1700s and running through the early republic.

*Inference —* a cartoonist only reaches for an image his readers already hold. That a northern print shop could draw a candidate on a barbecue grid iron in 1834 and expect the country to get it says the southern political barbecue was national furniture by then. South Carolina's Galivants Ferry stump meeting, which began in 1880 and is still held, is the same institution two generations later, with the pig still on the fire.

text.what: The sign a barbecue place puts at the road: a steel pylon with a lit box on top, neon or bulbs picking out a name, a bottler's disc above it, and a changeable letterboard underneath for the day's news. Most spell the word Bar-B-Q, hyphenated, because three short units fit a tall narrow cabinet better than nine letters do. What survives in photographs that anyone may reuse comes almost entirely from one man's slides: John Margolies drove American highways from the late 1960s to 2008 photographing exactly this, and the Library of Congress bought the archive and the rights with it.

sections.text:
Often not the restaurant. Steve's Bar-B-Q in Spencer, North Carolina, photographed by Margolies in 1982, is a blue steel cabinet with STEVE'S and BAR-B-Q in white neon script on two lines — and above it, larger than either, a Pepsi-Cola bottle cap in red, white and blue neon, chipped and weathered. The soft-drink bottler supplied and maintained signs like this in return for the top panel and the exclusive pour.

*Inference —* that arrangement explains a good deal about how these signs look. The restaurant's name sits under a national brand's disc, in the bottler's palette rather than its own, and the proportions are the bottler's too. A place that later bought its own sign generally got a bigger pig and a smaller cola.

Where the pit paid for its own, the pig went above the letters. Margolies photographed Maurice Bessinger's West Columbia sign in 1988 from two angles: a pylon in white and pale-blue stripes, a red panel of BAR-B-Q in bulb-lit block capitals with a chase of yellow lamps round the border, the pig Little Joe standing on the crown, and below the box a white panel reading Maurice Bessinger's Flying Pig, Coast to Coast. Under all of it the letterboard, on the day, said NOW HIRING WAITRESSES.

The layout is the standard one: brand on top, product word in the largest type, the human business — hours, hiring, specials — on a board somebody changes with a suction cup on a pole. Bessinger's offices and pits burned in October 2024; the sign was still standing afterwards.

sections.h: The Margolies archive, and why this record leans on it
sections.text:
John Margolies photographed roadside commercial architecture for about forty years and left 11,710 colour slides. The Library of Congress digitised them and bought the intellectual property, so the whole archive carries no known restrictions on publication — which makes it the largest freely reusable picture file of American signs in existence, and the reason a page about Carolina barbecue signs can be illustrated at all.

He shot only a handful in the Carolinas that touch this subject: Bessinger's twice, Steve's at Spencer once. Elsewhere in the same file are the Red Pig at Nahunta, Georgia, and a plain BAR-B-Q at Brownsville, Tennessee, bulbs round a rectangle on a pole in 1979. *Inference —* he was driving routes, not surveying a cuisine, so what he caught in any state is a function of which highway he was on that week.

The practical consequence for this project: the Carolina signs standing today — Lexington's, Ayden's, Hemingway's — are photographed constantly, and very few of those photographs are free to reuse.

Not every barbecue sign is lit. At the Lone Star BBQ and Mercantile at Santee, South Carolina, the signs are wooden boards hung from the porch roofs of old frame buildings moved to the site and set on brick piers: Shuler's DINING HALL on one, Dantzler's SOCIAL HALL on the next, painted in a serif face with the family name above the room's function. This is the older Carolina form — the building carries the sign rather than a pole beside it — and it reads at walking pace rather than at fifty miles an hour.

The third kind is cast. A bronze tablet set into a stucco wall in Lexington commemorates the site of the first known business selling Lexington-style barbecue, prepared under tents on open pits, and records that the North Carolina House of Representatives designated the city the Hickory-Cooked Barbecue Capitol of Piedmont North Carolina. The Lexington City Council commissioned it on March 11, 1985. *Inference —* a town that has a plaque made has stopped advertising and started claiming.

names.name: Where all of this came from

text.what: Everything on this site is built from things anyone can open: public-domain cookbooks, openly licensed encyclopaedias and photographs, open map data, oral histories published by the people who recorded them, and the directories that businesses list themselves in. This page is the list, so a reader can check the work or go further than we did.

sections.h: Recipes you may cook from and republish
sections.text:
Cookbooks published in the United States before 1930 are in the public domain, and the Southern ones are digitised. Michigan State University's *Feeding America* project holds scanned and transcribed historic American cookbooks; the Internet Archive holds the rest. The books this site draws on include *Dixie Cookery* (Maria Massey Barringer, Concord, North Carolina, 1867), *The Carolina Housewife* (Sarah Rutledge, Charleston, 1847), *Housekeeping in Old Virginia* (1879), *Mrs. Hill's New Cook Book* (1867), *What Mrs. Fisher Knows About Old Southern Cooking* (Abby Fisher, 1881) and *The Carolina Rice Cook Book* (1901).

Wikibooks' Cookbook is CC BY-SA: its recipes may be copied anywhere, with the page named and the licence carried along.

A recipe still in copyright is different. The list of ingredients is a fact and may be repeated; the instructions are the author's writing. Where this site gives a modern recipe it gives the ingredients and links to the rest.

Wikimedia Commons is the vein: every file states its licence, and this site accepts only CC0, public domain, CC BY, CC BY-SA and the Free Art License. The Library of Congress holds three collections worth the trip — Carol M. Highsmith's photographs, the John Margolies roadside archive of 11,710 slides of American signs, and the Farm Security Administration negatives from the 1930s and 1940s — all with no known restrictions, and much of it mirrored on Commons, which is how this site reached them.

The State Archives of North Carolina keeps 117,159 photographs on Flickr Commons, and it is the one place with postcards and pit photographs of named Carolina barbecue houses — Wilbur's, Parker's, Clyde Cooper's on East Davie Street in Raleigh in 1963. They are marked no known copyright restrictions, which is a weaker statement than public domain: it means nobody has found a rights-holder, not that there is none. The marking also runs photograph by photograph rather than collection by collection, and some images sit in that archive twice, once reserved and once released. Nothing from it is used here yet.

The New York Public Library's digitised *Green Book* collection is the record of where Black travellers could eat in these two states between 1936 and 1966. Twenty-two of its twenty-three volumes are public domain; the 1966-67 International Edition is not, and carries an orphan-works statement instead — the copyright may exist and no holder has been found. The scans carry no searchable text, so a Carolina listing has to be found by eye.

OpenStreetMap supplies every place point here, under the Open Database Licence, which is share-alike: the derived table at api/places.json carries the same licence. Natural Earth supplies the state outlines and is public domain. Nominatim, OpenStreetMap's own geocoder, filled in the towns and counties.

sections.h: Directories that make a tag possible
sections.text:
A tag on a place here means somebody published something, and this is where we look.

Black-owned: EatOkra's directory, Black Restaurant Week's listings, and the Southern Foodways Alliance's oral histories, in which owners speak for themselves.

Woman-owned: WBENC's certified directory and the federal Women-Owned Small Business search, plus press profiles that name the owner.

LGBTQ+ welcoming: the Charlotte LGBT Chamber of Commerce, Blue Ridge Pride in Asheville, the Alliance For Full Acceptance in the Lowcountry, SC Pride, and OpenStreetMap's own lgbtq=* tag, which businesses and mappers set deliberately.

Cooks over wood: True 'Cue's certified list, the North Carolina Barbecue Society's Historic Barbecue Trail, and the South Carolina Barbeque Association.

None of these is inferred. If a page does not say it, this site does not tag it — and a place without a tag has only not been read yet.

The Southern Foodways Alliance has recorded pitmasters in both states and publishes the transcripts and the audio. Where a place or a person here has an interview, the page links to it. It is the best single source on this subject that costs nothing to read.

names.name: How to order
aliases: what to say at the counter
names.said: The counter moves fast and the person behind it has heard every joke.

text.what: At a Carolina barbecue counter the words are short and they mean particular things. Barbecue is the meat, not the event. A tray has no bread; a plate does. Chopped, coarse chopped and sliced are three different textures off the same shoulder. Outside brown is the crust and you have to ask for it. This is the vocabulary, west and east, with what it gets you.

sections.text:
"Barbecue" on its own means chopped pork here, and ordering "pulled pork" marks you as from somewhere else — which is fine, and will be understood, and may be remarked upon.

In the Piedmont the shoulder comes three ways. **Chopped** is worked small on the block with cleavers. **Coarse chopped** is left in bigger pieces, which holds the smoke better and is what half the regulars order. **Sliced** is what it sounds like, and is the oldest form; Lexington Barbecue will do all three.

In the east it is chopped, and the crisp skin is chopped through it. That is the texture; there is no other option and no one wants one.

The outside of a shoulder that has been over coals for ten hours goes dark and firm and tastes more of smoke and dip than anything else on the tray. In Lexington you ask for **outside brown**, or **brownies**, or just **brown**, and you get it chopped through the rest or on its own. Some pits charge the same; some charge more; a few will tell you they ran out at eleven.

The eastern equivalent is not a cut but a texture: ask for **more skin** and the block will oblige.

A **tray** is barbecue and slaw in a paper boat, no bread. A **plate** adds hushpuppies or cornbread and usually a second side. A **sandwich** is chopped pork on a soft white bun with slaw on the meat, not beside it — if you do not want slaw, say so when you order, because it goes on by default.

By the **pound** is how a family eats. A pound feeds three people who are not very hungry. Sauce comes in a jar if you ask.

**Hash.** It is a thick meat gravy cooked from the hog, ladled over white rice, and in the Midlands it is not a side but half the reason to be there. Order **hash and rice** and you will be taken seriously. Many South Carolina pits run a **buffet** on Friday and Saturday only, which is the other thing to know before driving out.

Do not ask for brisket in a whole-hog house; they will point at the pig on the sign. Do not ask which sauce is correct — you will get an answer, at length, and it will be the house's. Do not arrive at two in the afternoon on a Saturday expecting a whole-hog pit to still be open: several of them close when the hogs are gone, which is the point of cooking only as many as they cook.

And whatever you order, they have heard it. The counter is not a test.

names.name: The Great Divide
names.said: Nobody in either camp thinks this is a matter of taste.

text.what: North Carolina cooks barbecue two ways and has never agreed to disagree about it. East of Raleigh the whole hog goes on the pit and the sauce is vinegar, salt and pepper with no tomato in it. In the Piedmont only the shoulder goes on, the sauce gets ketchup and a little sugar, and the slaw turns red because it is dressed with that sauce. The argument between them has run in newspapers, been put to a vote in the General Assembly, and is conducted daily at lunch counters in both places.

sections.h: Two columnists and a state legislature
sections.text:
The modern quarrel has named combatants. Jerry Bledsoe of the Greensboro Daily News, who styled himself the world's leading, foremost barbecue authority, wrote for Lexington. Dennis Rogers of the Raleigh News & Observer, the oracle of the holy grub, wrote for the east. Bledsoe's verdict on his opponent went into print: Rogers, he wrote, 'has ruined any chances of this state being distinguished in its barbecue.'

It got as far as the statute book. Bills in 2006 would have made the Lexington Barbecue Festival the official barbecue festival of North Carolina, and were defeated — naming one style's festival meant choosing a side. The 2007 compromise, House Bill 433, made it the Official Food Festival of the Piedmont Triad Region instead: a regional title, carefully bounded, so that no barbecue could be called the state's.

Four things, and a Carolinian can check all four from the doorway.

The animal. East: the whole hog, everything but the squeal, chopped together so that ham, shoulder, belly and crisp skin end up in the same forkful. Piedmont: the shoulder only, which is fattier and darker, cooked longer, and comes off the block in bigger strands.

The sauce. East: vinegar, salt, black pepper, crushed red pepper. Piedmont: the same, plus ketchup or tomato, water and sugar — thin enough to pour, reddish rather than red, and called dip.

The slaw. East: white, mayonnaise. Piedmont: red, because it is dressed with the dip. This is the fastest tell on a plate.

The bread. East: cornbread, or corn sticks. Piedmont: hushpuppies.

The two styles are closer to each other than either is to anywhere else in the country: both are pork, both are vinegar at the root, both are served with slaw and a soft white roll, and neither sweetens the way Kansas City or the South Carolina Upstate does. The tomato in a Lexington dip is a tablespoon of ketchup, not a sauce.

*Inference —* the loudness of the argument is a function of how small the difference is. Nobody in Ayden argues with Texas.

The other thing both sides skip: for most of two centuries the people at the pit through the night were Black cooks, enslaved and then paid, in the east and the Piedmont alike, and their names came off the signs as the restaurants incorporated. Adrian Miller's *Black Smoke* is the book that follows that labour and its disappearance, and it is the one history neither camp can claim against the other.

sections.h: South Carolina, which has four of these arguments
sections.text:
Across the line the map is busier. South Carolina's tourism office prints four sauce regions: mustard through the Midlands where German families settled, vinegar and pepper in the Pee Dee and along the coast, a light tomato sauce through the middle, and heavy tomato in the Upstate. The Pee Dee cooks the whole hog with vinegar and pepper, which makes it eastern North Carolina's first cousin and a long way from Columbia in every sense.

South Carolinians will tell you the four-way map is the more interesting problem. North Carolinians will tell you that a state which puts mustard on a pig has forfeited the right to an opinion.

kin_out.name: Lexington Barbecue Festival

kin_out.name: Jerry Bledsoe

kin_out.name: Dennis Rogers

kin_out.name: red slaw

kin_out.name: vinegar-and-pepper sauce

kin_out.name: Lexington dip
kin_out.as: the tablespoon of ketchup that started a war.
